en: The Dhvanyāloka composed by the venerable teacher Ānandavardhana.
— First Uddyota.
The *Dhvanyāloka* composed by the venerable teacher Ānandavardhana,

illuminated by the commentary named *Bālapriyā* written by Śrī Sahṛdayatilaka Rāmaśāraka, and accompanied by the *Viṣamasthaladarśinī* composed by Gosvāmī Śrī Dāmodara Śāstrin and the divine glossary (*ṭippaṇī*) named *Divyāñjana* written by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The first Uddyota, accompanied by the commentary named *Locana*.

The *Locana* composed by the illustrious Ācārya Abhinavagupta. Salutations to the Goddess of Speech (*Śrī Bhāratī*). That which reveals a reality never before seen, without the aid of causal factors; which, through the abundance of its own aesthetic essence (*rasa*), brings forth that which resembles the existence of the world.
And that reality of Sarasvatī, which is made beautiful by the successive unfolding of manifestation and description, illuminates it; thus, that which is called the "poet-sahr̥daya" is victorious.

The *Kāvyāloka* and the *Locana* are the grasped and the grasper for the wise; we praise those two teachers, the authors of those works, who are the foremost among connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasika*).
Previously, a commentary on the *Locana*, which is merely a first illumination, was composed here;
having seen that and other treatises, it is now obtained.
Relying upon the recensions renowned in Pāṭha and Kerala, we compose this *Bālapriyā*, a commentary for the eyes of the learned, according to our own judgment.

Now, the venerable and illustrious Ācārya Abhinavaguptapāda, desiring to compose a commentary on the *Kāvyāloka*, composes at the beginning of the work— through the text itself— the auspicious invocation consisting of a salutation to his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) performed for the sake of completing it without obstacle, as an instruction for his disciples, beginning with the words "apūrvam" and so forth.

I, named Abhinavagupta, whose ears have been perfumed by the teachings received at the lotus feet of Bhaṭṭendurāja— who beheld the essence of Sarasvatī in the form of poetry such as "The lotus, though not in water," and who has perceived the creative power of the Cause—
now clarify the *Kāvyāloka*, echoing whatever [truth] I have grasped, so that people may apply their own eyes to it.

Without even a fraction— a mere trace— of any well-known cause such as material or instrumental causes for those respective effects, [the Lord] manifests— that is, creates and expands— an unprecedented object, one of a different class from things renowned in the world and thus marvelous, which is yet distinct from non-existent things like a rabbit's horn, such as a lotus existing with water as its locus. This is what is called "Bālapriyā."

Furthermore, that which is like a pressing-stone— meaning all things in the world which by nature are as tasteless as stone— is made to yield its essence, or rather, is rendered substantial through the abundance (bharāt) of the poet's own aesthetic flavor (rasa), such as the erotic and so forth; that is to say, it is made manifest as rasa by means of the employment of the determinants (vibhāvas) and other poetic elements.
By these two statements, the poetic figure of *vyatireka* (distinction) is manifested, which consists in the excellence of the Creator Prajāpati—the essence of Sarasvatī who is the soul of poetry.
To further solidify that very point, he says "in succession" (*kramāt*), etc.; and the phrase "that which is the world" (*yaj jagat*) is to be supplied [from the preceding verse].
The "Prakhyā" is the genius (*pratibhā*) of the poet;

the "Upākhyā" is the expression (*vacana*). First there is the Prakhyā, and subsequently the Upākhyā; by that sequential unfolding of these two, [the work] is "subhaga"—meaning it is heart-pleasing and excellent.

The meaning is that it illuminates everything, making even that which is not naturally beautiful worthy of being relished (*rasanīya*) by endowing it with the capacity to manifest aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
The conjunction *ca* (and) is connected here;

it should be understood that its function is to indicate the causal relationship between the expansion of narrative (*prakhyā*) and anecdote (*upākhyā*) on the one hand, and the creation of new subject matter (*apūrva-vastu-nirmāṇa*) and the imparting of aesthetic flavor (*sarasatva-karaṇa*) on the other.

Regarding this, some commentators explain that by the first sentence the creation of a new subject matter is stated, by the second the imparting of aesthetic flavor to an existing subject matter, and by the third the manifestation of both as being delightful (*hṛdya*).
That [work] is distinguished by qualities such as being the first to manifest such an unprecedented subject matter; for the sake of attaining those qualities, he says "kavi" (poet).
That which has the designation "the poet and the connoisseur" is [the *kavisahṛdaya*].

In this context, the terms *kavi* (poet) and *sahṛdaya* (connoisseur) refer to poetry as the object of the connoisseur’s activity— which consists of reflection upon the poet’s creative operation and his imaginative representation— or else they denote that which is "called" (*ākhyāta*) by poets and connoisseurs;
or alternatively, it means that which has the "repeated manifestation" (*abhīkṣṇya-khyāna*) or flashing forth (*sphuraṇa*) of the poet and the connoisseur, namely, that whose essence is poetry.
The "reality" (tattva) is that which is to be understood as superimposed; it is the ultimate form of Sarasvatī, the deity who presides over the manifold expansion of words.
"Victorious" means he exists above all;
by this, the author's salutation to him is understood;
and furthermore, the reality of Sarasvatī is *dhvani-kāvya* (suggestive poetry).
It triumphs; the meaning of "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and so forth is to be understood as before, and thus the subject matter to be established has also been indicated in brief.

Now, avoiding arrogance while demonstrating his own skill in exposition, and providing a mention of his name for the sake of perpetuating his fame, he makes his formal declaration with the words beginning "Bhaṭṭa... and so on. [He says:
"By the dwelling in the proximity of the lotus-feet—meaning the feet resembling lotuses—of the teacher named Bhaṭṭendurāja; that is to say, by the service rendered to those lotus-feet."
"Hṛdyāni" means situated within one's own heart;
furthermore, it refers to one by whom the sacred scriptures (śāstra), which are pleasing to the hearts of those who hear them, have been heard.
Through this, a simile is suggested: just as a lotus possesses a heart-pleasing quality in the act of making an object fragrant, so it is here.
"Whatever it may be, even if it is very slight"—
here *api* has the sense of *eva*;
or alternatively, the construction is "even while reverberating."

The word *api* (also/even) indicates an apparent contradiction between the act of clarification and the mention of [the salutation] as being "very slight. The *Locana* states: "Although [the author] has already achieved his purpose through the uninterrupted completion of his own salutation to the Supreme Lord, he [nevertheless] utters a resonance (*anuraṇana*)—standing in the place of the ringing of a bell and so forth—for the sake of ensuring that the commentators and listeners attain the desired fruit, which is characterized by listening to the commentary without obstacles. Thus, it provides a resonance corresponding to the original statement of the author, which stands in the place of the ringing of a bell.
By the phrase "his own words in the form of an exposition," it is revealed that [it is] *sva* (his own).

That by which one sees or perceives is *locana*; thus, *svasya locanam* is his own mind (*manas*). By its thorough application—that is, by the focused concentration of the mind—he says: "I shall clarify, that is, make manifest to people, the *Kāvyāloka*."

Alternatively, by means of the application of my own "eye"—that is, knowledge—through the mediation of its resonance in the form of an exposition, I shall "make clear," meaning I shall reveal it; here too, the suggestion of a simile (upamādhvani) should be understood, as indicated by the phrase "just as by the application of eyes.
He shows the intended meaning of the verse beginning with "svacchā" (composed by the author of the commentary) through this introductory passage, starting with "svayam" and so forth.
"By himself" (*svayam*) is a reference to the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*).

"Uninterrupted" (*avyucchinna*) means devoid of interruption in the midst [of the work]. [It refers to] the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who assumes various *līlā*-forms for His respective pastimes.

"Salutation" (*namaskāra*) is the attainment (*sampatti*) of that [Lord], which is its excellence (*prakarpa*); by that, he has performed or obtained the goal (*artha*), which is the immediate purpose consisting of the removal of obstacles and so forth. He is one for whom that is the case.
The word "api" (even) indicates an apparent contradiction in the performance of an auspicious invocation for one who has already become such [an accomplished being].
The connection is with the phrase "for the attainment of the fruit" and so forth, referring to the commentators and listeners;
"without obstacle" means by the destruction of obstacles; and "desired" [refers to the fruit].
The exposition for the commentators and the hearing for the listeners are both desired; this commentary, named *Divyāñjana*, is offered. Śrī Śrīgaurakṛṣṇa is my refuge!
Having bowed to Gaurakṛṣṇa and my Guru, I compose the *Locana* upon the *Dhvanyāloka*, by means of this divine collyrium, so that its difficult-to-perceive meaning may be clearly seen.

Now, this commentary named *Divyāñjana* is intended by me, who desire primarily to clarify the difficult passages in the *Locana*— the commentary on the *Dhvanyāloka-nibandhana* composed by the venerable Ānandavardhana, the teacher who established the tradition of Suggestion (dhvani)— by the venerable Abhinavagupta, the preeminent author of the *Bhāṣya* on the *Sūtras* of the Bharata-darśana.

However, since this [rule] is incidental (*prāsaṅgikī*) and applies elsewhere as well, no contradiction with the *Pratiśrut* should be raised. As for the rule in the grammatical treatise stating "anaṅ is prescribed in place of the word *danta*, which denotes a connection with either *vidyā* or *yoni*, characterized by being immediately preceded by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*)— namely, 'anaṅṛto dvandve' (Pāṇini 6.3.25)— " here too, by means of the connection to a single sacrifice through the medium of *vidyā*, there is a connection with those who express the relationship to *vidyā*, such as the *hotṛ* and *potṛ*.

Someone objects that even though there is a *dvandva* compound of the words *vyākhyātṛ* (expounder) and *śrotṛ* (listener)—which denote two related parties connected by the relation of "possessing an activity conducive to the knowledge whose single subject matter is conveyed through the medium of *vidyā*"—the form *vyākhyātāśrotṝṇām* would be more appropriate; however, this objection is weak. This is because, since the word *ṛt* continues from the previous sūtra "ṛto vidyāyonisambandhebhyaḥ" (*ṛt* [substitutes for *ṛ*] occur after words denoting *vidyā*, *yoni*, or *sambandha*), the rule could have been satisfied by the continuation of the word *ṛt* alone; therefore, the explicit mention of *ṛt* again in the present sūtra indicates that the rule is intended to apply specifically to the prescription of *ānaṅ*.

Demonstrating the requirement that all the words being compounded, which fall within the scope of the delimiting factor of the object of designation (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), must end in the suffix *ṛt*, [the author] intends to include the state of denoting either "knowledge" (*vidyā*) or "womb" (*yoni*) within that very delimiting factor. Even if the word *vyākhyātṛ* (commentator) somehow denotes one of those two, since no such restrictive rule regarding its denotation is observed for the word *śrotṛ* (listener), it does not fall under the status of being the delimiting factor of the object of designation by virtue of the principle of the absence of the qualified (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) resulting from the absence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇābhāva*); therefore, the suffix *ānaṅ* [does not apply].
"Thus, the engagement of both the expounders and the listeners is indeed proper.

Homage to the illustrious Nṛhari! May the claws of the Enemy of Madhu—those lions of His own will, which have eclipsed the moon with their own pure radiance, and which sever the suffering of those who have sought refuge—protect you."
The author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) brings about the presence of the Supreme Lord by means of manifesting appropriate blessings through the verse beginning with "His own will" (*svecchā*):
"May the nails of the Enemy of Mura protect you"— that is, you who are the commentators and the listeners—
since they alone are worthy of being addressed.
For the meaning of the second person pronoun (*yuṣmad*) is essentially that of addressing;
and protection consists in providing assistance toward the attainment of what is desired,
which occurs by means of removing obstacles and the like that stand in opposition to it.
This much is intended here as the protection [of the work]:

since the Lord, who is ever-exerting, is perceived through His application of resolve free from delusion and so forth, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is desired; and for the attainment—that is, the accomplishment—of that [sentiment], the fruit consisting of the composition of this treatise, which has both of those as its cause, is achieved by the author. This is the underlying meaning. *Bālapriyā* is the commentary. For the attainment—that is, the completion—of that [heroic sentiment], the fruit consisting of the composition of this treatise, which has both of those [the sentiment and the hero] as its cause, is achieved by the author. This is the sense.
At the commencement of the formidable treatise, it is appropriate to manifest a benediction; by means of that speech,
he brings about— that is, accomplishes— the presence of the Supreme Lord, which consists in His being turned toward the commentator and the listeners in the form of a desire to protect them.
The meaning is that since protection depends upon the favor of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), he effects that favor— which is an auxiliary to protection— by means of a benediction;

or rather, by manifesting an appropriate benediction and composing it within the text, he thereby brings about or produces in the Supreme Lord a state of favor, which consists of the attentive engagement (*anusandhāna*) of both the commentator and the listeners.
By the phrase "the author of the commentary" (*vṛttikāra*), it is shown that [the words] "according to his own wish" (*svecchā*) and so forth are not verses in the form of *kārikās* or *sūtras*.
Regarding the explanation of "va" as "the commentators and the listeners," he states the reason for this with the word "of them" (*teṣām*).
To the question, "Why is there an occasion here for an address? he replies with "address" (*sambodhana*).
The essence [of the pronoun] is the vocative; it is that part which causes the status of being the referent of *yuṣmad*.
For one who is not being addressed is not designated by the word *yuṣmad*.
He explains what is intended here by the phrase "may they protect" (*trāyantām*) with the words: "And protection... (*trāṇañceci*).
The term "abhīṣṭā" means consisting of hearing the explanation;
"sāhāyaka" is the action of an assistant, and its opposite means that which obstructs the attainment of the desired object.
"Departure" means turning back;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the awakening of the intellect regarding the true nature of the object and so forth.
"This much" means that which has been described in the aforementioned form.
Now, regarding the statement that "the author of the commentary [regards] *dhvani* as the soul of poetry":
this means he is the author of the *vṛtti*, which is an explanatory commentary on the very root *kārikās* composed by himself.

For this very reason, there is no violation of established custom, even though an auspicious invocation was not performed at the beginning of the root text, since it was specifically the commentary (*vṛtti*) that he intended to undertake.

However, some maintain that even at the very beginning—in the first verse where the word "kāvya" (poetry) appears as the first member of the compound *kāvya-syātma*—even though that term refers to something else [namely, the Self], the mention of "poetry" by mere hearing constitutes an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) in the form of a statement of the subject matter (*vastunirdeśa*), because it reveals the Blessed Lord. This is just like seeing a water-jar brought for another's sake [which nonetheless brings good fortune]. They support this with such scriptural authority as: "Whatever poetic discourses there may be, and whatever songs, melodies, or hymns, these are all portions of the Great-Souled Viṣṇu, who bears the form of sound. Thus, they say the auspicious invocation has indeed been accomplished.
The non-difference between the author of the *kārikās* and the author of the commentary will be demonstrated later.

Regarding the phrase "for [it is] the essence of awakening": by being the locus of the awakening produced by itself, it is indicated (*dhvanyate*) as that which is delimited by being the object of the speaker’s intention.

In the act of protection, which must be performed by taking the nails as weapons and grasping them, the nails' status as instruments—being non-different from the agent—is indicated by their being the agent (*kartṛ*), thereby suggesting an excellence of power; and it is implied that the Supreme Lord has no need for any external instrument.
By the term "of Madhuripu" (the enemy of Mura), it is stated that he is always engaged in the effort of driving away the terror of the world.
Of what kind of Madhuripu? Of the lion [Kesarin] by his own will,
but not through dependence on karma.

Thinking that since this first verse composed by the author— who intends to provide instruction for the delight of the ignorant— is of the nature of poetry (*kāvya*), a suggestion (*dhvani*) must be applied to it as well, he first employs *rasadhvani*, which is the most prominent among the three types of *dhvani* distinguished by rasa and so forth,
beginning with the words "nitya" and so on.
The word "ca" (and) implies conjunction; the connection is that "the rasa is also suggested.
The meaning is not merely that the expressed meaning is stated by this [word], but rather that the rasa is also suggested—namely, [the rasa of] those who are eternally diligent.
What is called "exertion" (*udyoga*) has been shown to consist of the activity of effort characterized by external armor;

as stated by Bharata: "The heroic (*vīra*) sentiment consists of energy (*utsāha*) belonging to the highest character. By the phrase "through non-delusion"—meaning through the absence of delusion—"determination" refers to the ascertainment of the true nature of reality, namely the conviction that "this can indeed be accomplished"; the mention of this [non-delusion] is for the purpose of explaining the cause of energy.
Some maintain that it is through the possession of non-delusion (*asaṃmoha*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*);
[this is so] because of the perception of enthusiasm (*utsāha*).

The meaning is that for connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), enthusiasm directed toward the destruction of Hiraṇyakaśipu and others is perceived through suggestion (*vyañjanā*) by means of the words "of the lion at his own will," "of the enemy of Madhu," and "the one who dispels the distress of those who seek his grace."

This is an illustration of the cognition that deviates from [the literal] understanding; it demonstrates *vastudhvani* (suggestive power of the thing itself) through the verse beginning with "of the claws" (*nakhānām*), and so forth.
The phrase "by way of being weapons" (*praharaṇatvena*) provides the reason for their status as instruments, meaning they serve as the armaments of lions and other such creatures.
In the reading *praharaṇatve*, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitte*).

Now, one might ask: even if the nails function as weapons (*praharaṇa*), how can they be the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of protection? To demonstrate the possibility of this, he says: "by means of a weapon" (*praharaṇena*).
The point is that a weapon is indeed employed in order to effect the protection of oneself or another.

"Because it functions as an instrument by virtue of being non-distinct"—that is to say, "non-distinctness" means being inseparable or internal; thus, the meaning is "because it functions as an instrument characterized by that [internal nature].
Instruments are of two kinds: external and internal.
The external [instruments] are the sword and so forth;
the internal [instruments] are the hands and so forth.
The grammatical connection is that they function as the agent because of their status as instruments.
The meaning is that by stating "agency" (kartṛtva) instead of stating "instrumentality" (karaṇatva);
that is to say, by saying "May the nails of Madhuripu protect [us]" instead of what ought to have been said, namely, "May the nails of Madhuripu protect.
The intention is that this is a superior commentary (ṭippanī), because the person being addressed has been established elsewhere as the referent of the word *yuṣmad* (you).
Regarding the phrase "because of the perception of enthusiasm":

since the *vibhāvas* and the other [elements] are invariably concomitant with one another, it is said: "If the *vibhāva* and so forth exist, whether two or even one of them be present, there is no fault provided that the others are immediately implied."

The meaning is as follows: according to the direction stated above, in the present context, through the support (*ālambana*) of enemies such as Madhu and others, there arises—by virtue of propriety—the cognition of their fearlessness and so forth, which serves as the excitant (*udīpana*); this, together with the consequent disregard for those objects and the transitory emotion (*saṃcārī*) of pride, results from their conjunction in the manner of a blended drink (*pānakarasa*). Thus, there is the perception of two types of energy (*utsāha*). Nor [does it arise] through the desire of another; *Locana*.
Rather, the meaning is that he has assumed the form of a lion precisely because of his fitness for embracing such a desire as is appropriate for one accustomed to destroying the hosts of demons.
Of what nature are his claws?
They are those which sever the suffering of those who have sought refuge.

For while it is appropriate that nails should cut, the idea that pain itself should be cut—though seemingly impossible with respect to the nails—is indeed conceivable because of the propriety of [the Lord] fashioning them according to His own will; this is the sense.
Alternatively, Hiraṇyakaśipu was a thorn to the three worlds, causing distress to the universe; therefore, he alone is in reality [the enemy] of those who have sought refuge.

Because they cause the suffering of those people who have the Blessed One as their sole refuge, suffering itself becomes personified; by destroying that [personified] suffering, their actual suffering is severed.
Thus, the supreme compassion of the Supreme Lord even in that state has been described. Furthermore, those nails are pure through the quality of clarity, which is their stainlessness.

The state (*tattā*) of those things which possess the capacity (*śakti*), meaning the power (*sāmarthya*) to hold [objects] that are clear, soft, or sharp—which is what children delight in—is the meaning;
there is also a reading *śaktatā*.
He states another suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) as well: "and from the resonance" (*dhvanitaśca*).
The phrase "by means of that which has been stated as the manifestor" is the ellipsis;
[the term] "distinct instrument" means by means of an external sword or similar object.
"Jagattrāsa" means the effort made to remove whatever fear the world has from various wicked people;
"is stated" means it is manifested.
It should be understood that having kept this point in mind, [the Lord] previously stated "those who are ever-striving" (*nityodyogin*);
however, the connection with the phrase "not by dependence on karma" and so forth is not with the word "accepted" (*svīkṛtā*).
It should be understood that the first [meaning] is conveyed by the word "desire" (*icchā*), while the second is conveyed by the word "self" (*sva*).
"Viśiṣṭā" means distinguished (*viśiṣṭa*), being possessed of excellence in comparison to other killings of Dānavas;

or, it refers to the killing of that specific Dānava, namely Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was distinguished by the quality of being incapable of being slain by gods, humans, animals, and so forth. That which is appropriate for such [a deed]—namely, the [devotion] directed toward assuming the forms of Nara and Hari.
The acceptance of desire, or rather, the qualification of desire as "proper"—that is, the propriety belonging to oneself therein; for that reason, the meaning is:
"of one who has assumed the form of a lion."
The fact that the form of a lion is mixed with human flesh is well known; therefore, it is not mentioned [separately] in the phrase "those who cut.
The word "therein" (*tatra*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.

"Chedakatvam" means the state of being the agent of the act of cutting; its connection with the phrase "chedyatvam" is that the possibility of its being the object of the act of cutting is thereby implied.
"It is inconceivable" means that [the body] cannot be subject to affliction because it is formless;
"belonging to him" refers to those connected with Anarahari; "by her own will" [is the sense].

"By his own will" means by the will of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*); "by that creation" refers to the creation of fingernails, because of which there is the capacity to cut even a material object despite its being [ordinarily] uncuttable.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "by his own will," that is, by his sovereignty (*svātantrya*), through the act of creation consisting of cutting and so forth of the immaterial, [this occurs] due to the appropriateness (*aucitya*) of the nails.
It is indeed possible and indeed certain; however, in accordance with worldly perspective, he says "or else" (*atha vā*).

In this alternative view, it should be understood that the word *ārti* indicates the cause of suffering (*ārti-kāraṇa*), and by its non-deviation [from that state], it suggests its capacity to cause all forms of suffering.
"By those which destroy"— the word "naśaiḥ" (by those which perish) is to be supplied; thus, affliction itself becomes utterly severed.

The meaning is that the Lord’s intention was that the destruction of such a Hiraṇyakaśipu would result only from the pain of being killed, and not by the death of any other living being; this was "stated" (uktam)— meaning it was indicated— even in that state, namely, even in the state of his being killed.
The sense is that [the sword] cuts only distress and not any living being; this is the intended meaning.

Here, the qualifying epithets such as "one who has sought refuge" (*prapanna*) contain within them the reason for the blessing of protection; for a deity, when praised, becomes gracious and bestows what is desired.
In this regard, he explains the phrase "with a clear reflection" (*svacchasvacchāya*) by saying "by the clear," etc., in order to ward off the misconception that it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

The phrase "by the quality of clarity" (*svacchatāguṇena*) is an elaboration of the term "purity" (*nairmalyena*); the term "mental states" (*bhāvavṛttayaḥ*) refers to words denoting qualities such as lack of clarity and so forth; and "by the shadow" (*chāyayā*) is explained by the words "in the curved [form]" (*vakretyādi*).
Regarding this, he states "the suggestion of a fact (vastudhvani) by means of the sense" (*arthāt*).
For the eyes are primarily occupied with the internal state (*bhāvavṛtti*);
and by their own reflection, which takes the form of the beloved's face, the moon is "assailed"—that is, distressed—by them.

Here, by means of suggestion (dhvani) rooted in the power of the literal meaning (arthaśaktimūla), the state of being a "new moon" is suggested; through the act of causing distress, the fading of the moon's luster and its perception as unpleasant in his presence are suggested; and the quality of causing distress is well-known in the case of fingernails.

And that [nature] of the man-lion’s claws has been manifested through their supermundane form; moreover, having observed their transparency and curvature, the young moon experiences regret within itself:

"Even though we share an identical combination of transparent and curved forms, these [claws] are skilled at dispelling the suffering of those who have sought refuge, whereas I am not"—thus, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast) is also suggested (*dhvanita*).
Furthermore, whereas previously I alone was the recipient of the desire of all people due to my association with a common clarity and charming form,
today— because the young moon alone is capable of causing fatigue through its crooked yet charming appearance— the meaning is that this capacity for such an effect is rooted in that [very quality],
and thus his state as the "young moon" (bālacandra) is suggested (dhvanyate).
The meaning is that the youthfulness of the moon, which is the referent of the word *indu*, is suggested (*dhvanita*);
the term *āyāsita* signifies "distressed" through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*); he states the result of that [distress] with the words beginning "by the distress," and so forth.
"In his presence" means in the presence of the nails; "loss of luster" means the state of being devoid of beauty— this is what is suggested.
The meaning is that it is produced through the operation of sound (dhvani);
this is well-known.
The underlying intention is that it possesses the nature of an instrument (praharaṇa).
And that state of being free from exertion is established as being "supramundane," meaning by way of the previously described nature consisting of clarity and so forth.
And thus, the sense is that through the tearing [of enemies] and so forth, the distinction of the nails of Nara and Hari from worldly nails—which merely scratch—is manifested.

By means of the adjunct of the epithet "the destroyer of the distress of those who have sought refuge," he demonstrates the suggestion (*dhvani*) of another form of contrast (*vyatireka*) and another poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), starting with the words "But moreover" (*kiñca*). [The word *tadīyām*] means belonging to those [nails].
In the phrase "kuṭilimānam" (crookedness), the word "tadīyam" (his) is to be supplied by modification [of the case ending],
meaning "in himself";
that is to say, unknown to others.
He states the manner of experience with the words "Even though equal," etc.
Regarding the phrase "but not as 'I'," it should be understood that the word *iti* connects both with "experiences" (*anubhavati*) and with "the figure of speech of contrast" (*vyatirekālaṅkāra*).
The meaning is that through the perception of the implied sense (*dhvanita*), there is a manifestation of *vyatireka* (distinction) for sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*).
Thus, the reading "the figure of speech *vyatireka* is also suggested" (*dhvanita*) is used;
by the word "also" (*api*), the previously mentioned *vyatireka* is conjoined.
"Of such a kind" means endowed with a clear and pleasing form,
and skilled in cutting through the distress of suffering.
The meaning is that these [nails] possess skill only in cutting one's own torment, and not in alleviating all forms of suffering;
"with great esteem for the young moons" means with the high regard that these nails are not merely nails, but rather young moons. Thus, they have attained their state through effort.
The meaning is that one experiences suffering caused by ill-repute;
furthermore, there is a reading that omits the word "iva" (as if).

Regarding the phrase "the suggestion of hyperbole-cum-disguise" (*utprekṣāpahnutidhvani*): *utprekṣārthāpahnutiḥ* means "disguise whose purpose is hyperbole"; its "suggestion" (*dhvani*) refers to the suggestion of a commixture (*saṅkara*), because hyperbole and disguise exist in a relationship of mutual subserviency (*aṅgāṅgitayā*).
This is the meaning of the marginal note (*ṭippanī*) here: "by the power of the sense" (*arthasakti*).

It refers to the denoted object (*śakya*)—which is the referent of the word "himself" (*sva*)—namely, the nail of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu), which has become the delimitor of the delimitation of the mode (*prakāratāvacchedakatāvacchedakatāpanna*).

By means of the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), which is self-evident and rooted in a capacity characterized by the ability to withstand the substitution of words; [the phrase] "the state of being the moon for a child" (*bālacandratvam*)—meaning the status of being the object of the effort performed by the nails of the enemy of Madhu (Kṛṣṇa), an effort which brings about a loveliness based on a charming curvature—results, by virtue of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*), in nothing other than that very moon. This is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "by means of exertion" (*āyāsanena*):

here too, through the suggestion (*vyañjana*) prompted by the power of the ten [nails] whose meaning consists of exertion, the reality of being shadowless and so forth, which resides in the crescent moon, is manifested.

Furthermore, the *Locana* states: "Such nails as these—ten in number, shaped like the crescent moon, and skilled at cutting away the pain of distress—are regarded by the world with great reverence as the young moon itself."

However, there is also a suggestion (*dhvani*) of both poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) and concealment (*apahnuti*), in the form: "He seems to experience incessant exhaustion, thinking, 'But he does not regard me [with such high esteem as he does the young moon]'.

Thus, our teacher has explained that in this verse *dhvani* is threefold, according to the distinctions of object (*vastu*), ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and sentiment (*rasa*). Regarding the poetic fancy "the young moon seems to experience incessant exhaustion," the cause for this fancy is the aforementioned perception: "He regards only those people with great respect, but not me."
And in that case, there is *spaṣṭāpahnuti* (explicit concealment), because there is a public perception that "these are not nails, but rather young moons.

Thus, the *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) here is based on a cognition residing in the young moon—which is the object of public perception—consisting of the superimposition of the nature of a young moon preceded by the negation of the nature of nails with respect to the nails. Therefore, by the force of *apahnuti*, it [the *utprekṣā*] establishes itself.
The relationship of part and whole (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) should be understood from the words "obtains" and so forth; thus he concludes with "in this way," etc.
Here, the suggestion of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa-dhvani*) is the primary element (*aṅgin*).

It should be understood that this is because enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is perceived as predominant. Now, one might object: since it must be stated here that the love (*rati*) directed toward the Blessed One residing in the author is what is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), it is the suggestion of a transitory emotion (*bhāvadhvani*) alone that should be considered the primary element (*aṅgin*), while the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is merely its subordinate (*aṅga*). To this they reply: for the author—who has attained a state of identification (*tanmayībhāva*) with the Blessed One—it is by virtue of being the agent of the benediction (*āśīḥ-kartṛtva*)...

This [work] is not primarily concerned with *bhāva* (emotional states); for while the suggested *rasa* consists of the lover’s devotion directed toward the deity as the object of worship, the author’s state of being absorbed in the Lord (*tanmayībhāva*) is established both by his own status as the author of the Sūtras and by his role as the unprecedented founder of this system.
Furthermore, the *Ṭippanī* notes that there is also the suggestion (*dhvani*) of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) and concealment (*apahnuti*).

The meaning is that the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the experience of fatigue caused by Bālacandra takes as its basis the very denial of the state of being nails followed by the affirmation of the state of being the young moon—a characteristic that effects a concealment of the object; therefore, there is a "blending" (*saṃkara*) of these two in the form of a relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

As for the claim made by some that this [fancy] consists in the "single-vehicle entry" (*ekavyañjakānupraveśa*) of these two—since they both enter through the single expressive word *āyāsita*—that is not the case here.

That is weak; for *saṅkara* (commixture), which consists in the mutual entry of a single manifestor (*vyañjaka*), possesses compatibility only when things are established as separate by virtue of being mutually independent.
However, in the present case, it has been stated that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and *apahnuti* (concealment) are indeed mutually dependent in this way;
and one should not suspect that this leads to the consequence of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (coalescence), since coalescence occurs only in the absence of such dependence.

The intention is that since independence from the distinctions of word, form, and object is intended in the definition of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *saṃsṛṣṭi* even when there is a single manifestor (*ekavyañjaka*), because although the substantive (*viśeṣya*) exists, the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) are absent.
Thus [it is said]: "In this way, [there is conjunction] of matter (*vastu*), ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and rasa..."
Although every entity is indeed such, here the term "entity" (*vastu*) is intended to denote that which is distinct from rasa and the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*).

And the nature of being a poetic figure (*alaṅkāratva*) consists in being the delimitor of the delimitor of the capacity to produce aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*), as delimited by the relation of objectivity (*viṣayitā*) residing in either the word or the meaning, which is qualified by a difference having as its counter-positive the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*), and which itself has as its counter-positive rasa and the like.
Furthermore, rasa is a stable emotion (*sthāyin*) characterized by consciousness whose veil has been removed.
"Sound is threefold here":

the sense is that although there is a manifoldness of sounds (*dhvani*) through other classifications, it is not contradictory for sound to be threefold by virtue of the threefold nature of those properties which are the intended objects of the Teacher’s purport— properties that generate the division of sounds based on the distinctions among the objects being sounded.

That which has been traditionally proclaimed by the wise as the soul of poetry—*dhvani*—others have declared to be non-existent, while still others say it is merely figurative (*bhākta*). Some have stated that its true nature resides in a realm beyond the reach of words. Therefore, for the pleasure of the hearts of those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*), we shall describe its essential nature. (Dhvanyāloka 1.1)

That which has been traditionally proclaimed by the wise as the soul of poetry—*dhvani*—others have declared to be non-existent; still others have said it is merely figurative (*bhākta*). Some have stated that its true nature resides in a realm beyond the reach of words. Therefore, for the pleasure of the minds of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), we shall describe its essential nature.

Now, the *Locana*, primarily stating the nature of the subject matter (*abhidheya-svarūpa*) while implicitly revealing the purpose (*prayojana*) and the purpose of that purpose (*prayojana-prayojana*) along with their connection through the force of the context, states the opening sentence: "The soul of poetry" (*kāvyasyātmā*).

With the intention that the word "wise" (*budha*) here refers to those whose motive is the understanding of the soul of poetry—due to its proximity to the words "soul of poetry"—it explains [the term] as "by those who know the truth of poetry" (*kāvyatattvavidbhiḥ*).
*Bālapriyā*: The word "now" (*atha*) signifies the commencement [of the work].
"The nature of the subject matter" means the nature of the sound (*dhvani*).
"The purpose" [refers to the following].

The purpose of the "purpose"—namely, the knowledge of the expressed object in the form of suggestion (*dhvani*)—is the nature of joy; the word "expressing" (*abhidadhat*) is to be supplied here [to the phrase "the purpose of the purpose"].
Alternatively, the meaning of the sentence is that we state the nature of the expressed object itself.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the joy that is the purpose of the purpose," since it constitutes the meaning of the words, there is a distinction between the primacy and non-primacy of those two expressions.
"Connected with that" means connected with that purpose of the purpose.
The purpose consists in the knowledge of the subject matter; "by implication" means by the force of the meaning, that is to say, through suggestion. "Manifesting" means making it understood.
For the purpose of stating the nature of *dhvani* is for connoisseurs (*sahṛdayas*) to gain knowledge of that very nature;
and the purpose of that [knowledge] is the delight of the mind.

Thus, since delight—which consists of both purpose and ultimate purpose—is stated through the relationship of cause and effect between those two, it follows that the manifestation of the knowledge of the nature of *dhvani*, which is the cause of that [delight], is established. This is the intended meaning.

Now, since the word *budha* generally denotes "one who knows," why is it explained in the commentary as "by those who know the essence of poetry" (*kāvyatattvavidbhiḥ*)? To address this, he introduces [the term] with "kāvyeti.
That which has the knowledge of the soul of poetry (*kāvyātma-bodha*) as its cause—that is, its cause for application (*prayoga-nimitta*).
Alternatively, "cause" (*nimitta*) refers to the ground for its usage (*pravṛtti-nimitta*).
And that is the property which appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition produced by that word.
Now, [the commentary] says "predominantly" (*prādhānyena*);
this means "as the primary [object]," because it is what one intends to communicate.
Regarding the term "the subject matter" (*abhidheya*):
since it was previously promised with the words "therefore we say," it refers to the object consisting of *dhvani*.
Regarding the term "the purpose of the purpose" (*prayojanaprayojana*):

The purpose of explaining the nature of *dhvani* is the knowledge of the nature of *dhvani*, and the pleasure of the minds of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) is the purpose of that [knowledge]; thus, such pleasure is the purpose of its explanation. Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "mind" (*manaḥ*) within the scope of the defining characteristic of the purpose-of-the-purpose is intended to highlight that, in the section concerning the system of *dhvani*, the tradition of Bharata’s school largely follows the grammatical (*vyākaraṇa*) perspective.
For in this very system, it is accepted that specific qualities such as pleasure reside solely in the mind (*manas*) and not in the self (*ātman*).
The word "here" (*atra*) refers to this context.

When words denoting a general category are intended to denote a particular instance, one must resort to *lakṣaṇā* (indication); otherwise, their status as objects of verbal cognition would be untenable.
By the wise who know the essence of poetry,
the soul of poetry has been designated as *dhvani*;
it is that which was previously handed down through tradition, properly and completely memorized (*samāmnāta*), and fully revealed.

Although it illuminates the minds of those with refined sensibilities (*sahṛdaya*), [the author] considers it to be non-existent; yet, by explaining the meaning of the word *ātman* through the word *tattva*, he demonstrates its essentiality and its capacity to produce a distinction from other verbal expressions.
The word *iti* indicates that the word *dhvani* refers to its own form (*svarūpa*).
Because its referent, being the subject of dispute, lacks certainty and thus cannot logically possess the status of a referent (*arthatva*).
He explains this with the words "designated" (*saṃjñita*);
however, in reality, it is not stated by that designation alone.
However, there indeed exists that which is denoted by the term *dhvani*, and moreover, it is the very essence of all [poetry].
With the intention that otherwise the wise would not be able to recognize its tenth [category], he explains this with the words beginning "tasya sahṛdaye... [and so forth].
As for the question of why he did not simply say "by those who know the soul of poetry," he replies: "Because it is the soul... [etc.].
By the word *tattva*, which denotes an uncontradicted essential nature; "by others" means by other words— that is,
by worldly and Vedic words— its distinctiveness from them, such as being praiseworthy to those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*), and so forth, constitutes its causal function.
It shows and manifests;
"of that meaning" is the ellipsis.
Here, the word "self" (ātman) is used figuratively, as in the expression "the self-like self."

And for the purpose of making it known that the meaning in the form of *dhvani* is indicated (*lakṣyate*) by way of its identity with the self, which consists in having an unimpeded essential nature (*svarūpa*), the term "reality" (*tattva*) is used to explain that meaning;
the sense is that through this, its quality of being the essence (*sāratva*) and so forth is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
This is the meaning of the word "iti."

In the phrase "dhvaniriti," the word *iti* means "the word *iti*. It explains— that is, it causes one to understand— that all words have as their primary referent their own phonetic form (*śabdasvarūpa*), while their secondary referent consists of the respective objects conventionally designated by them.

In this context, the employment of the word *iti* indicates that the focus is on the form of the word itself; since the word *iti* follows the term *dhvani* in the present case, the meaning is that this word *dhvani* is a designator (*saṃjñā-rūpa*) of the word *dhvani*.

The manifestation of the named object (*saṃjñin*) according to the mode of its name occurs through implication (*ākṣepa*) and so forth, just as the manifestation of the individual (*vyakti*) occurs under the view that the word's power (*śakti*) resides in the universal (*jāti*).
Alternatively, the intention is that by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the word *dhvani* signifies "that which is designated as *dhvani*.
He states the reason for this stated meaning in the passage beginning with "tadarthasya" and so forth:
[it refers to] "tadarthasya," that is, of the object denoted by the word *dhvani*, which is characterized by being something that is being suggested (*dhvanyamānatva*).
"By being the subject of dispute" means by being the object of conflicting views as to whether sound exists or does not exist.
"By the absence of certainty":
in the reading *niścayābhāve*, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitte saptamī*).
The meaning is that there is no certainty regarding those subjects situated in the middle by way of their being suggested (*dhvanyamānatva*).
Alternatively, the phrase "of that object" (*tadarthasya*) is connected with "by the absence of certainty.
"Because of the impossibility of being an object" means because it is impossible for it to possess the nature of an object characterized by being suggested.
The word "dhvani" is to be supplied [to the previous phrase]. "This" means that the word "dhvani" refers to its own essential form (svarūpa).

Now, if it is thus stated that the meaning of the word "dhvani" is "that which is designated by the name dhvani," would this not contradict the immediately following text: "even though it is manifest to the minds of sensitive readers"?

To dispel the doubt that the phrase "shining forth in the minds of sensitive readers" (*sahṛdayamanaḥprakāśamānasya*) merely states that the object characterized by being suggested (*dhvanyamānatva-viśiṣṭārtha*) is the object of the perception of sensitive readers, he states the intended meaning of that passage,
beginning with "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*).
The word "that" (*tat*) [refers to the aforementioned point].
The meaning is "the word *dhvani*"; or alternatively, the meaning is "the entity whose nature is *dhvani*.
[The phrase] "by way of a mere designation" means:
The suffix -mātra excludes the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) consisting in the state of being merely suggested (*dhvanyamānatva*).
That which is denoted by the word *dhvani* is that which is qualified by the state of being suggested.
He states the reason for [the claim] "it certainly exists" with the words "for not otherwise," and so forth.
The phrase "he explains" means that he is expounding upon the word "of that" found in the verse;
"by [the words] beginning with 'sahṛdaya'" means by the expression "of that which is manifesting in the minds of sensitive readers."

The *Locana* explains it more appropriately as follows: the word "iti" (thus) is displaced in its position and refers back to the meaning of the entire sentence—namely, that "the meaning characterized as *dhvani* is the soul of poetry," as has been traditionally taught.
For if the term "word-meaning" (*śabdapadārtha*) were intended, what connection would there be between the name "*dhvani*" and the "meaning"?
In this way, it would indeed be said that "sound" (dhvani) is the soul of poetry,
just as in the expression "he says 'go'";
nor is that which is the subject of dispute non-existent.

On the contrary, it is only when the substratum (dharmin) exists that there can be a disagreement regarding the mere property (dharma); therefore, enough of this excessive digression which only causes distress to those of refined sensibility.
Such a statement might be made through negligence by a single wise person, but it is not fitting for many.
Therefore, the plural form "by the wise" (budhaiḥ) is used. He explains this very point with the words "by tradition" (paramparayā).
The intention is that this was stated by them through an uninterrupted stream [of transmission], even without its being committed to writing in specific manuscripts.

Nor is it the case that the wise are so numerous as to disregard this; for the reason why this entity characterized as *dhvani*—which is a particular kind of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*)—has been stated to be the soul of poetry is solely out of deference to the intellects of those people whose minds are impaired by a lack of faith.

This is because the meaning qualified by being "resonant" (*dhvanyamāna*) is established through the perception of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), and thus the subsequent text follows that [connoisseurly] understanding.

Alternatively, one might ask: "If the word *dhvani* here means 'that which is designated by the term *dhvani*, how can there be the objection raised by those who maintain its non-existence and so forth?"
Since there is no dispute regarding the designation "sound" (dhvani) itself, as the dispute concerns only its status as being "that which is sounded," he says "in reality, however," and so forth.
"Expounds" means "speaks by way of analysis."

Regarding the phrase "by [the words] *sahṛdaya* etc.": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such statements as "others have declared that even that which shines forth in the minds of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) is non-existent. With the intention that the commentary by the author of the *Vṛtti*—which employs the construction "it is *dhvani*"—is merely an illustration, he says: "But in this way," and so forth.
"Thus" refers to the audience or the explanation that is about to be stated; "the remainder" [of the sentence] is understood as "or the explanation.
By the suffix *-tarap* in the word *yuktataram*, it is indicated that while the previous explanation possesses a degree of correctness, this one is even more correct.
The term "displaced order" (*bhinnakrama*) means that because something is heard immediately following [a certain word], it should be construed elsewhere;
the sense is that the phrase "the soul of poetry" (*kāvyasyātma*) is to be construed with what was previously mentioned.
Regarding the phrase "reflecting upon the meaning of the sentence":

the sense is that it makes known the status of being a communicator of the sentence-meaning within the recited text—that is, what the nature of the Vyākhyā (exegesis) is—rather than implying an identity with that sentence; this is the intended meaning.
A "sentence" (*vākya*) here is a collection of words. He demonstrates the application [of the term] with the words beginning "sound" (*dhvani*), etc.
The explanation of the word "sound" is "the object characterized as sound."
The meaning is "qualified by the state of being suggested" (*dhvanyamānatva-viśiṣṭa*). And thus, the word *tasya* ("of that") refers back to this very same meaning.
Regarding the interpretation where [the compound] is joined as *dhvanir iti*, he states the fault if the word *dhvani* were intended merely as a name, beginning with the words "śabda... and so forth.

If the word *dhvani* were to mean "the object denoted by the word," that is, if it were used merely in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñāmātra*), what would be the connection? The meaning is that [the statement] would be incoherent.
He states the reason for this with the words "For thus," and so forth.
He dispels the suspicion that the term *dhvani* might be inconsistent with its intended meaning according to the previously stated method by saying "And not," and so forth.
The locus of disagreement (*vipratipatti-sthāna*) is the substratum (*dharmin*), which is the object of the disagreement.
"Caused by properties alone," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: just as there is a disagreement regarding properties such as permanence or impermanence when the substratum (dharmin), such as sound, exists; so too, in the present case, there is a disagreement regarding properties such as being included within *guṇas* or *alaṅkāras*, or being metaphorical (*bhākta*), when the substratum designated as "sound" (*dhvani*) exists.
He explains the meaning of the plural "by the wise" (*budhaiḥ*) with the words "of the wise," and so forth.
"Designation in that manner" refers to designation as the soul of poetry;
that is a designation made through negligence.
"By that" means for the purpose of indicating that the statement of that [fact] is to be accepted because it is authoritative (*prāmāṇika*).
"That very same" [means...]
The meaning is that the plural number itself serves the purpose already stated.
"By way of succession" is explained by the phrase "without interruption," and so forth.
"This" refers to [the aforementioned].
The meaning is that *dhvani* constitutes the soul of poetry.
Regarding the term "distinct" (*viśiṣṭa*):
it refers to being deposited—that is, established by means of writing—in distinguished manuscripts.
Therefore, the connection is "even without it being stated";
the sense is that this matter is established by direct instruction. They said:
Furthermore, those who maintain the non-existence of that [object] and so forth would have taught the eye with such emphasis if it were a mere thing;
however, this has been taught with emphasis.
Thus he says: "previously correctly handed down."
By the inclusion of the word "previous" (*pūrva*), he states that here a state of being "for the first time" is not possible;
and he explains this by means of the phrase "thoroughly and completely studied and revealed.
Regarding the word "of that" (*tasya*):
Since one must, on the contrary, strive for its realization, what possibility could there be for its non-existence?
Therefore, what can we do?
The sense is that the ignorance of those who propound non-existence (abhāvavādins) is boundless.
Furthermore, we have not heard the actual conceptual constructions (vikalpas) of these non-existence proponents; rather, having merely imagined them, we shall refute them.
Therefore, it is imperceptible;
nor is it proper to refute a future entity,
precisely because it has not yet arisen.

If it is argued that even that [future state] is subject to refutation because it is superimposed by the intellect (*buddhyāropita*), then precisely because it is superimposed by the intellect, its status as "the future" would be lost.

Therefore, because it manifests as belonging to the past, because it is remote (*pārokṣya*), and because there is no manifestation of its being "present-day," the use of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) suffix was made— namely, *jagaduḥ* ("they said").
He will indeed manifest a refutation by anticipating that very explanation;
moreover, this anticipation is not appropriate for what is impossible, but rather only for what is possible.
The intention is that otherwise, there would be no end to the possible combinations, and thus [the list] is "dear to the ignorant.
By the statement "by way of tradition" (paramparayā), the meaning is the intention of the author of the Vṛtti.
To demonstrate the meaning of the prefix *sam-* in the phrase "previously handed down" (*samāmnāta-pūrva*), he says: "And not," and so forth.
He states the purpose of including the word "prior" (pūrva) with the words "pūrveti.
Here, in this narrative,
he indicates [the meaning] by saying "thus he said."
"And he explains" means that he explains the meaning already stated. The intention is that by the words "correctly" (*samyak*) and so forth, the meaning of the preceding word has also been explained.
By stating that [the work] was "handed down by Buddha," he provides an explanation of what has been obtained—that which is manifest even to the minds of sensitive readers.
By means of the words beginning with "of whom" (*yasya*), he shows the meaning that is to be understood.

He says "and not... (*na ca*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate the justification for the use of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) in the word "they said" (*jagaduḥ*), and to show how [the phrase] "in the commentary they would explain" (*vṛttau vyācakṣīran*) and so on functions as an elaboration of that same point.
By us, the proponents of sound (*dhvanivādin*), contradictory conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and their conceptualized objects have been [already] considered;
if they have not been heard, how then will they be refuted? To this, he says: "having considered" (*sambhāvya*).
It should be understood that by the words "some might say" (*ke cid ācakṣīran*) and so forth, a possibility is raised;

and in the commentary on the passage "where [it is said] 'the word or the meaning' (*artha-śabda-vā*)," it should be noted that after first restating [the opponent's position] with the words "as for what was also said" (*yad apy uktam*), a refutation is provided with the words "that too is incorrect" (*tad apy ayuktam*) and so forth.
Therefore... (*ata iti*).
The meaning is "because it has not been heard.
He says "and not" in order to establish its reality (bhūtatva).
[He says] "precisely because it has not arisen."
The particle *eva* is reiterative; the meaning is "precisely because it will come into existence," as stated previously. He raises an objection with the words "that too."
That future object is projected upon the intellect, superposed by the intellect, and made an object of the intellect;
thus it is said that "the intellect composes itself."
"Application" (āropaṇa) means the act of making [something appear].
He concludes with "therefore" (ataḥ).
The term "unfolding" (unmeṣāt) is stated with the intention of indicating the impossibility of actual reality.
The meaning is that the basis for the use of the *liṭ* (perfect) suffix is the state of being delimited by past time as it appears [in cognition].
Regarding the term "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*),
the meaning is "having the nature of a specific time."

Having thus established the usage of the *liṭ* [perfect tense], he shows that usages such as *ācakṣīran* (they should tell) are relevant to the present context with the words "for the sake of explaining that" (*tadvyākhyānāyaiva*).
The meaning is "for the sake of explaining the *liṭ* alone";

the force of the particle *eva* is to exclude independence [of these examples]. The word "for the sake of explaining" (*vyākhyānāya*) is connected with the word "having been considered possible" (*sambhāvya*).

One might object: "Since the world has already been explained by [the words] 'nanv acakṣīran' and so forth, what is the purpose of the intervening passage beginning with 'tad-abhāvavādinām jānīmaḥ'? To ward off this doubt, he introduces [the next section] with the words "sambhāvanāpi," which is employed here to justify the use of the *liṭ* (perfect) suffix; for that which is impossible—that is, not even slightly perceived—[cannot be established otherwise].
"It would be endless" means that there is no attainment of a point of finality; such is the sense.
Thus, conceptual constructions arise.
And it would be the eye for [detecting] refutations.
Therefore, in order to support the "possibility" (sambhāvanā) that is about to be stated, he first says "they are possible.
On the other hand, if one were to say "they are being considered possible" (sambhāvyante), it would merely be a repetition of the same meaning.
Nor is there even the possibility of a possibility; rather, it is the present state itself that is manifest, and thus the designation is made precisely in terms of the present.
Anticipating the objection that "what is imagined by a possibility whose basis is an impossible entity cannot be refuted," he says: "They are conceptual constructions" (vikalpāḥ).
But no such real entity exists from which this possibility could arise; rather, they are merely conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
And these might indeed manifest because they are bound by the lack of realization of reality (*tattva*).

For this very reason, the uses of the optative (*liṅ*) such as "they might say" (*ācakṣīran*) in this context, which refer to a possibility, ultimately terminate in a past ultimate reality. As it is said: "If indeed what is inside this body were to be outside, people would take up sticks and drive away dogs and crows."
"Desiring to please the ignorant" means that [the author] intends to state what is about to be said, as indicated by the phrase "they might say... and so forth.
"In order to establish" means to prove it through the logical pervasion (*vyāpti*) that whatever is possible is conceivable.
He says, "they arise," etc.;
the meaning is that he states the passage beginning with "of those who deny its existence" and ending with "they arise.

Now, one might object: instead of "they arise" (*sambhavanti*), should it not be said "they are possible" (*sambhāvyante*), so that the initial thesis would be established? To this, he replies: "it is said, 'they are possible' (*sambhāvyante*)."
"Redundant in meaning" means by way of the indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Now, one might ask: is even the possibility (*sambhava*), which is the foundation of the conceit (*sambhāvanā*), itself something to be conceived as possible?
He says "no," meaning "not so.
"By the present" means by the [suffix] *laṭ*.
He introduces the statement "it has been said that they are conceptual constructions" with the words "nanu ca" (but if...).

[The compound] means: by that [conceptual construction] which has as its basis (*āśraya*) a possible real entity (*sambhavadvastumūla*), [the object] is either conceived (*sambhāvita*), made an object (*viṣayīkṛta*), or produced (*utpādita*).

To explain how the objection is resolved by the statement "they are conceptual constructions" (vikalpāḥ), he elucidates that method with the words beginning "but not" (na tu). The possibility of such [a thing]—that is, a postulated entity existing as ultimate reality—is impossible.
The reason for this is indicated by the word "since" (yataḥ).
"This" means that it has become the cause.
If one asks, "Then what is the objective support (ālambana) of this conviction? he says, "But rather," and so forth.

"Alternative positions" (*vikalpāḥ*) are those views that are conceived as contradictory regarding the nature of *dhvani*, which constitutes the essence of poetry and serves as the substratum for both fallacious means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and fallacious reasoning (*yukti*).
Now, one might ask: "How can there be a conception of non-existence with respect to something that exists? To this, he says: "And those... and "The reality... [and so forth].
The meaning is: "in the absence of self-awareness of the nature of poetry as *dhvani*.
"They would manifest" means they certainly do manifest.
"For this very reason" [refers to the following].
The meaning is "precisely because these positions are imagined through delusion. Regarding the term *atīta*:
those for whom the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*), has passed away or become past (*atīta*).

The reading is *paramārthatva* (the state of being the ultimate reality). Regarding the phrase "they conclude" (*paryavasyanti*) in the root text, although the use of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) in the word *jagaduḥ* is present, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) there is also the use of the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of possibility, such as in *ācakṣīran*. This means that even when an action is based on its being superimposed by a cognition in the form of a possibility, it results in [the meaning] "they conclude."
He provides an illustration for the point already stated with the words "Just as" (yathā).
The phrase "Even if it were so" (yadi nāma) is a statement intended to produce dispassion by means of revealing the true nature of reality.
"Of the body" means of the physical frame;
"that which" refers to the flesh and so forth.
The phrase "dogs and crows" implies that they have set out for the purpose of eating; this is established by the sense of the context.
As for the expression "in this case," the connection is with the phrase "only the state of being a living being."
"Thus" means:
by way of having flesh and so forth existing externally and internally. Regarding the term "the eye":
If the body were thus visible, then it would be observed in this way; therefore, it is simply the state of being a real living being (*bhūtaprāṇata*).
If it were not so, what would happen? To this also, the point is simply this: "What has occurred [is that] there is no possibility of existence as before. Enough of this extraneous elaboration.

In this regard, there are only these three primary modes of misconception: first, that because a word conveys meaning only by depending on convention (*samaya*), there is no suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) distinct from the expressed sense (*vācya*);

or second, that even if it exists, it is merely figurative (*bhākta*) because it is drawn forth by the force of the meaning understood from the word, being implied by the function of denotation (*abhidhā-vṛtti*);

or third, that even if not so implied, it cannot be spoken of [as distinct], just as one who does not know the pleasure of a husband cannot speak of it regarding virgins. These are the three principal types of disagreement.

In that regard, there are three types of the conceptualization of non-existence (*abhāva-vikalpa*): because words, meanings, qualities, and ornaments alone cause the beauty of words and meanings, [it refers to] the body (*kāya*)—that is, the physical form—which consists of beautiful words and meanings that transcend those of worldly life and secular treatises.
"In this way" (*evam*) means as follows.
The meaning is that the world is being driven away by its state as dogs and crows;
thus, the essential meaning of the verse has been shown through two statements:
"it is merely the vital breath of beings."
The meaning is that it is precisely the ultimate reality of the past.
That is to say, what is perceived is simply the fact that the action—such as being outside of that [object] which is the object of imagination—is delimited by past time.
To show that this is exactly the same in the case of negation as it is in the case of affirmation, he says "yadi" (if), etc.
This sentence consisting of a single quarter-verse, "yadi na syāt," serves as a supplement to the verse beginning with "yadi nāma. Its meaning is: "if [the body] were not [to exist].
The sense is that if it were not so, there would be no internal or external [distinction] for the body;
rather, this body would simply be established as having its internal and external parts exactly as they are.
"What would happen from that?

means "even then, what fruit would there be? The sense is that even then, this body is utterly contemptible and indeed fruitless, because its utility is limited solely to the enjoyment of very inferior objects.
This is how the phrase "even here" is connected with the statement "this is precisely the meaning."
He explains the statement he himself has uttered with the words "What has occurred," and so forth.
The construction is: "If there is no possibility of arising, what has occurred? Then, the explanation of the phrase "What would happen" is given as "What has occurred."
Even then, what result has arisen? The meaning is: none at all.
The explanation of the phrase "if it were not" is "if there were no possibility of arising.
The phrase "as before" is stated as an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "yadi nāma" and so forth, the sense is that just as there is a possibility (*sambhāvanā*) of coming into being, this very same meaning applies even in the case of a negation; thus, the intention is that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is indeed possibility. Then, for the sake of ease of understanding at the outset, he demonstrates the intended purport (*tātparya*) with the words beginning "tatra."

In that regard, concerning the object of sound (*dhvani*): because it depends upon convention— that is, because it functions through the cooperation of linguistic agreement— for this reason, [it is not a direct perception].

That is to say, because a word conveys a conventional meaning; "distinct from the expressed" means distinct from the conventional meaning. That which is intended as the suggested sense (vyaṅgya) [is what is meant].

"It does not exist in poetry" means that what is intended to be the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) does not become something expressed by poetry, because it is not conventionally designated by the word "poetry.
[The phrase] "even though it exists" [is used].
The connection is that even though the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is distinct from that which is expressed (*vācya*), it is still figurative (*bhākta*).
The reason for this is "it is implied by the function of denotation" (*abhidhāvṛttyākṣiptam*).
This means it is implied by the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which is the tail-end of the function of denotation (*abhidhā*).
"Projected" means made known.
The reason for this is "by sound.
"Power" is the auxiliary cause.
"Not implied by that" means not implied by the function of denotation (*abhidhā-vṛtti*).
The words "that" (*tat*) and "existent" (*sat*) are to be supplied [to the previous phrase]; thus, the construction is "even though it exists" (*sad api*).
"To speak" means to demonstrate by way of a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*);
"it is not possible" implies that there is no such capacity among the wise.
Here, the illustration is "as in the case of young girls."

The locative case is used with the intention of expressing the substratum of the power of speech (*vacanaśakti*). "Among those who do not know that" means among those who do not know the happiness of the master.
"Principal contradiction" (*pradhānavipratipatti*) refers to this.
Because these have been mentioned in the *kārikā*, they are primary. He states those very categories beginning with "sound" (*śabda*), etc.
The qualities and ornaments that belong to word and meaning pertain to those very two;
for they are established by both parties as the causes of beauty.
Regarding the word "śabda" (sound): the meaning is "because it produces the beauty of poetry.
This reason is to be understood everywhere in what follows—namely, wherever there is the production of poetic beauty, [therein lies the quality].

In this regard, there are two possible interpretations: one is that the Locana [asserts] that the state of being any one among the word-meaning-qualities (*śabdārthaguṇa*) and so forth is the cause of the beauty of poetry, and that there is no other such cause which has not been enumerated by us; the other is that whatever has not been enumerated by us is indeed some other cause of beauty.
Or, secondly, that which is not included [in our categories] cannot possibly produce beauty;
for if it does produce beauty, then it is necessarily included within either a *guṇa* (excellence) or an *alaṅkāra* (ornament) as we have described them.
To give it a different name—how much learning is this?

Furthermore, even if there is no inclusion within the aforementioned *guṇas* or *alaṅkāras*, nevertheless, a different name is assigned by relying on some slight trace of distinction, because the varieties of the charm (*vicchitti*) of simile (*upamā*) are innumerable.
Even so, there is simply no absence of being included within the *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*.
And what is achieved by that alone?
For it is possible to conceive of other varieties as well;
indeed, ancient authorities such as the sage Bharata and others accepted only *yama* (paronomasia) and *upamā* (simile) as verbal and semantic ornaments (*śabdārthālaṅkāra*).
The indication of the direction of its elaboration has, however, been performed by other authors of alaṅkāra works;
for example, having heard the illustration of "potter" (kumbhakāra) and so forth under the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*, one might oneself infer words such as "city-builder" (nagarakāra) and so on—
what self-importance is there in that?
The phrase "even in such a case" (*evaṃprakṛte ’pi*) indicates that pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been shown by this.
Regarding the word "world" (*loka*):
the terms *loka* and *śāstra* refer respectively to worldly and Vedic words.
The connection is that there is nothing else distinct from the qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras).
The thesis is that there exists no cause for the beauty of poetry other than the qualities and so forth.
The reason "due to the absence of valid means of cognition" (pramāṇābhāvāt) is to be understood here.
Now, [an objection is raised]: this proposition is not tenable;

for if a cause of beauty distinct from qualities and so forth were established, its negation would be impossible, and if it were not established, its negation could not be effected. To this, he says: "That which by us... and so forth.
And by implication, it is established that this is your own accepted position;

thus, the sense is that according to the opponent's view, there is a negation of that [non-existence] based on the establishment of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Now, one might object: "According to the principle stated in the passage beginning 'In some cases, when a form has been apprehended,' the [negation] depends upon the establishment of the substratum's (*dharmin*) own nature, and therefore it must have as its object a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*)."

Since a negation must be something that can be affirmed, a negation of the very existence of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is not possible; therefore, he states the second alternative with the words "or that which," and so forth.
"Not counted" means, by implication, as being distinct from both poetic qualities (guṇa) and ornaments (alaṅkāra).
The word "sa" (that) means that which has not been counted as equal by us, and is intended by you to be the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Now, one might ask: how can the capacity of the suggested meaning to produce beauty—which is witnessed by one's own experience—be denied? To this, he states another alternative: "atha" and so forth.
The word "sa" is to be supplied [from the previous context].
Now, if it is argued that [the *rasa*] is included [within the *dhvani*],
the meaning is that it must be either a *guṇa* or an *alaṅkāra*, since it is intended to be manifested [by the *dhvani*] and because it serves to beautify poetry.

[Objection: But surely, the establishment of its distinctness [from the rest] follows from designations such as "dhvani" (suggestion) and so forth; to this, he replies with the words "nāmāntara" (under another name). [Objection: But surely it is not merely a matter of assigning a different name, for there is a specific basis for that [designation]; therefore, it is not included within the [other categories] such as "guṇa" (poetic quality) and so on. Anticipating this doubt, he accepts it with the words "athāpi" (even though), etc.
"There is no inclusion" means that the intention is that [it is distinct] due to specific qualities such as being the life-force of poetry (*kāvyajīvita*).
He refutes this with the words "Even so," and so forth.

"Assigning a different name" means that you are assigning alternative names such as "dhvani" (suggestion) and so forth to the *guṇas* and other elements we have described, based on their specific characteristics such as being the "life-force" (*jīvita*) of poetry.
He states the reason for this with the word "comparison" (*upamā*).
"Vicchitti" means variety.
"Upamā" (simile) is the general characteristic of other figures of speech as well as of poetic qualities (*guṇas*).
He states the conclusion: "Even so," and so forth.
Nevertheless, it is so;
to the question "What follows from that?", he says: "To that extent" (tāvat).
This means by merely giving it another name, relying on some slight trace of a distinction, even though it is only that much.
"What has been done?
means that not even the slightest bit of scholarship has been accomplished.
The reason for this is stated as "of another."
He establishes that very point with the words beginning "by the ancients" (*cirantanaiḥ*) and so forth.
He concludes the stated meaning with a derisive illustration using the words beginning "that" (*tat*) and so forth; "that" means "therefore."
Alternatively, there is the reading "tatra" (in that case); the meaning is "that being so.
In this regard, some might say: "Poetry, first of all, has as its body the word and its meaning."
And therein, the causes of beauty residing in words, such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and so forth, constitute the third type.
