Thus, there is one threefold classification and two others; this is the intended meaning, namely that there are five classifications in total.
He states those very [points] in sequence, beginning with "First, the body of word and meaning," and so forth.
By the use of the word "first" (*tāvat*), he shows that there is no disagreement on this point by anyone.
In that regard, word and meaning are certainly not sound (*dhvani*).

For what benefit is there in a mere name? Now, if it is the beauty of both word and meaning that constitutes *dhvani*, even so, beauty is of two kinds: that which resides in the essential form alone, and that which depends upon the structural arrangement (*saṃghaṭanā*).

In this regard, the beauty of words arising from their mere intrinsic form belongs to the figures of sound (*śabdālaṅkāra*), whereas that which depends on their structural arrangement belongs to the qualities of sound (*śabdaguṇa*).
Likewise, the beauty of meanings residing solely in their own nature belongs to similes (*upamā*) and the like.

Since it is concluded that [excellence] resides in the composition rather than in the qualities of meaning, there is no such thing as *dhvani* distinct from qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
The phrase "properties of composition" implies "of word and meaning."

That which is distinct from qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) does not produce beauty, just as defects such as the permanent (*nitya*) and occasional (*anitya*) faults, or those such as being unrefined (*asādhu*) and harsh to hear (*duḥśrava*).
And *dhvani* is the cause of beauty.
Therefore, that [beauty] does not exist apart from them; thus, this is a negative (vyatireka) reason.
Now, it may be objected: surely the *vṛttis* and *rītis*, like the *guṇas* and *alaṃkāras*, are well known to be distinct from those [qualities and ornaments] and yet to be causes of charm.

Metaphors and the like are contained within the meaning (*artha*), and qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and others, which are properties of phonemes and their arrangement (*varṇasaṃghaṭanā*), are also perceived. Since the *vṛttis* (metres) function without exceeding those [phonemes and meanings], and likewise *dhvani* would also exist without being distinct from them while still being a cause of beauty, the logical reason (*hetu*)—namely, "being distinct"—is unestablished (*asiddha*). With this intention, he says: "functioning without exceeding those... (*tadanatiriktavṛttayaḥ*).

Thus, it is not established that *vṛtti* (styles) are distinct from *rīti* (diction). For indeed, in order to distinguish the nature of the harsh (*paruṣa*), the smooth (*lalita*), and the intermediate (*madhyama*)—which serve the purpose of describing objects that are brilliant, soft, or middling—the three groups of consonant classes were established for the sake of arranging alliteration (*anuprāsa*) itself. Thus, there are three...

The varieties of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) have been called "styles" (*vṛtti*), because the different types of alliteration function within them. As it has been said: "The arrangement of similar consonants occurs in these three styles."

Some say that "bālapriyā" means "alone. Having explained the essential meaning of the commentary (vṛtti) from the words "śabdārthaśarīram" up to "pratīyante," he introduces the subsequent portion of the text by showing its relevance to the subject at hand, beginning with "nanu" and so forth, [concluding] with "asiddho vyatirekaḥ."

The meaning is as follows: since there is a negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)—namely, that whatever is distinct from *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras* does not produce beauty—the [proposed definition] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because it deviates (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of *vṛtti* and *rīti*, which are admitted to be causes of beauty despite being distinct from *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*.
This is stated with this intention.
The meaning is that this is said with the intention of providing an answer to such a doubt.
He clarifies that intention with the words "not at all," and so forth.
"Distinctness from those" means distinctness from both the qualities (guṇas) and the ornaments (alaṅkāras).

In order to demonstrate that the *vṛttis* (styles) are indeed included within the figure of speech known as *anuprāsa* (alliteration), he says: "For it is thus, of the *anuprāsas* alone," and so forth.
The phrase "of the *anuprāsas* alone" is connected with the expression "for the purpose of accomplishing the three groups.
To the question "And for what purpose is that? he replies: "On account of harshness," and so forth.

The meaning is that this is for the purpose of specifically demonstrating the essential natures of harshness and so forth. He states its result as well: "blazing" (*dīpta*), which refers to the *raudra* (fierce) and other rasas.

Smooth and sweet [intonation] is used for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others; moderate [intonation] is used for the comic sentiment (*hāsya*) and others; likewise, such is the case regarding the objects of description, such as the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.

The meaning is: "for the sake of establishing the worthiness of accepting specific types of alliteration," by virtue of their utility, that is, their utility for the specific [subject] being described. "Types of alliteration" (anuprāsajātayaḥ) means the types that serve as the substrata for alliterations.
This will be explained further below. "Vṛttis" means they have been described as "vṛttis"; regarding that, he states their etymology: "they proceed" (*vartante*).
"Varieties of alliteration" (*anuprāsa-bhedāḥ*) refers to specific types of alliteration.
Regarding "in these": the intention is that in the word *vṛtti*, the suffix *ktin* is applied to the root *vṛt* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
As for what he says:
The remainder [of the name] is Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa.
Regarding the term "sarūpa" (having similar form):
poets always desire that among these [anuprāsas], the *locana* (the eye) [be placed] separately and separately.
Thus:
"separately, separately"—
this is the *paruṣānuprāsa* (harsh alliteration) of the *nāgarikā* (urbanite).
The *upanāgarikā* style is smooth and possesses alliteration;
it is called "graceful" (*lalitā*) because it is compared to a refined (*vidagdha*) urbanite (*nāgarikā*).
The term "intermediate" (*madhyama*) means that it is neither soft nor harsh.
For this very reason, because it resembles the rustic women who are by nature devoid of wit, delicate, and soft-spoken, this *vṛtti* is called "rustic" (*grāmyā*).
Among these, the third is the "soft alliteration" (*komalānuprāsa*); thus, the *vṛttis* are indeed varieties of alliteration.
Furthermore, the *vṛtti* intended here is not the one defined in the Vaiśeṣika system.

They desire— that is, they accept— an *anuprāsa*, which is the placement (*nyāsa*) or composition (*upanibandha*) of similar consonants (*sarūpa*) belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*), occurring individually within the three types of harsh (*paruṣa*) and other styles (*vṛtti*) that are dear to the ignorant.
The nature of the *paruṣā* and other styles (*vṛtti*) has been stated by means of the three verses beginning with "śaṣābhyām"; this should be seen in that [original] work.
He explains the portion beginning with "pṛthag vṛttā" as follows: "paruṣetyādi. That style in which there is *anuprāsa* (alliteration) consisting of harsh phonemes is called *paruṣā*.
The term *nāgarikā* (urban) applies specifically to the harsh [style].
Regarding *masṛṇā* (smooth):
it is that in which there is smooth alliteration (*anuprāsa*) because it is composed of sweet-sounding syllables.
He states its two names: *upanāgarikā* (the semi-urban) and *lalitā* (the graceful).
He explains that the name *upanāgarikā* is etymologically significant, meaning "one compared to a city-dweller (*nāgarikā*)," as indicated by the phrase "by a city-dweller.

As for the reading "harsh alliteration" (*paruṣānuprāsa*) and "smooth alliteration" (*masṛṇānuprāsa*), it should be understood as intending the identity of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the poetic function (*vṛtti*).

In order to demonstrate that alliteration possesses a middle status within the rustic style (*grāmyavṛtti*) about to be described, he states the meaning of the word "middle": "The middle is neither soft nor harsh.
This means it is distinct from sweet phonemes and distinct from harsh phonemes;
thus, the alliteration composed of such [phonemes] is called "middle alliteration" (*madhyamānuprāsa*).
Having first introduced the designation "vulgar" for a style that lacks alliteration, he says "for this very reason," and so forth.
"For this very reason" means precisely because it is devoid of sweetness and harshness.
"Vaidagdhya," and so forth.
The meaning is: because of her resemblance to a village woman who is naturally devoid of cleverness, coarse by nature, lacking sweetness, yet neither harsh nor of an overtly striking character.
Among these, the third is called *komalānuprāsa* (soft alliteration).

This means that among the types of alliteration already mentioned, the middle type of alliteration is designated by the name *komalānuprāsa*. By this, the designation *komala*, which is established for the *grāmyā* (vulgar) style of composition, as stated by Bhaṭṭa Udbhaṭa, is demonstrated.
He concludes with the words "the styles" (*vṛttayaḥ*) and so forth:
those styles, such as the *upanāgarikā* and others, which have been expounded by certain [authorities],
have also come within the range of hearing.

In the *Locana*, it is stated that for the possessor of birth (*jātimat*), there would be no presentness (*vartamānatva*) in the birth itself, for presentness therein consists precisely in its being assisted by that [possessor].
As someone has said: "For rulers of the earth abide in a profundity that transcends the world."

Thus, the *vṛttis* (styles) do not possess functions distinct from alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like, nor do they have operations exceeding them. For this very reason, since there is no difference in their operation, they do not have a nature that must be inferred separately; such is the intended meaning of the word *vṛtti* when it denotes "operation."
Precisely because they are not distinct [from the alliteration itself], Bhāmaha and others did not employ the technical term "vṛtti" (metre/rhythm).
With the intention that even when used by Udbhaṭa and others, no additional meaning has entered the path of the heart, he says: "they have come within the range of hearing.
The *vṛttis* such as *paruṣā*, which consist of the arrangement of various letters beginning with *śa* and so on, actually reside within the alliterations (*anuprāsa*).
Just as depth (gāmbhīrya) resides in a king and is manifested by qualities such as harshness through alliteration and the like—

just as the universals (jāti) such as "cowness" are manifested by individuals such as cows— the meaning is that the styles (vṛtti) are metaphorically designated as "universals" because they share the common property of being manifested by their own substrates.

Now, it might be argued that it is incorrect to say that alliteration—which possesses that genus—subsists in a genus consisting of recurrence, because that would contradict the Vaiśeṣika doctrine; therefore, he says "And not," etc.
Here, in our own view.
"Like the Vaiśeṣika" means as in the Vaiśeṣika doctrine;
"subsistence is not intended to be expressed" means that the mode of being as an inherent property (ādheya-tva-rūpa) is not intended to be expressed.
To the question, "In that case, what is meant by 'subsisting' there?", he says: "It is indeed its favor.

The meaning is: it is the very favor bestowed by the genus (jāti) acting as the agent through the form of subsistence (vṛtti). And that [favor] consists either in the imparting of distinguishing attributes by that [genus] as agent, or in the conferring of the capacity for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
To illustrate this stated point, he provides an example: "transcendental" (lokottara).
"They abide in profundity" means that they are sustained by profundity. And the sustenance provided by profundity consists in such forms as bestowing the capacity to accomplish all tasks.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), while showing the referent of the word "tat" (that) in the phrase "not having a function distinct from that" (*tadanatiriktavṛttayaḥ*), he concludes with the words "therefore, [distinct] from alliteration and so forth," etc.
He explains this by stating "not additional," meaning those whose function or operation (*vṛtti*) is not distinct—that is, whose operation does not exceed that.
The operation of alliterations which has as its object the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), [is not distinct].

The intended meaning is that this very [nature] applies to the mental modes (*vṛtti*) as well. By stating it in this way rather than saying "they are not distinct from that," he demonstrates the result: "For this very reason," and so forth.
The construction is: "For this very reason" means precisely because there is no difference in their activity as previously stated.
Thus, they do not have a nature that is to be inferred separately.
The meaning is that [the figures] do not have the nature of being inferable (anumeya) apart from the perception of the alliteration (anuprāsa);
rather, they are to be understood through the mark (liṅga) of the alliteration, which consists of specific phonemes that manifest the function (vṛtti).
There is also a reading: "they do not have the nature of being separately denotable" (na pṛthagabhideyasvarūpāḥ).

However, if there were an additional function for *anuprāsa*, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the *vṛttis* would have to be stated separately; such is the [author's] intention. To provide the consensus of the elders regarding this point, he says: "not surpassed" (*anatī*).
Regarding the claim that *anuprāsa* was indeed employed by Udbhaṭa and others, he says: "by Udbhaṭa and others."
When that conventional usage has been applied and established,
it does not have [any external] referent.
*Artha* refers to the meaning of words as they function [in a sentence]. *Adhika* means "additional," specifically that which exceeds the meaning consisting of alliteration (*anuprāsa*).
And the *rītis* are those beginning with Vaidarbha and so forth.
"What then is this thing called *dhvani* that is distinct from those? [The answer is: "The *rītis* (styles) and so forth.
The connection is: "even though they do not exist as something separate from those [other elements], they have come within the range of hearing."

By the word "tat" (that) here, the qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and so forth are meant; and regarding their presentation through appropriate modes of operation, there occurs— due to their mutual compatibility— a state of unified integration, like the flavors of jaggery, black pepper, and other ingredients in a *pānaka* drink, which pertains to objects described as brilliant, graceful, or middling, and which manifests in abundance according to the regional styles of the Gauḍīya, Vaidarbha, and Pāñcāla schools.
That very [quality] is said to be the threefold *rīti*; this is stated with the intention that *jāti* is not distinct from that which possesses *jāti*,
and that the aggregate (*samudāya*) is what is meant by "dear to the ignorant" (*bālapriyā*).
The meaning is that the passage beginning with "gatā" refers to the matter already stated.
Regarding the phrase "and the styles" (*rītayaśca*), he completes the sentence by supplying the appropriate word and says "tad-" and so forth.
He states "by the word 'tat'" because the word *tat* here refers back to the *guṇas*.
The words "they were reflected upon" are to be supplied as the ellipsis;
such is the reading.
He explains how it is that the *guṇas* are not distinct from the *rītis*, beginning with the words "And of these," and so forth.
"Of those qualities":

"appropriate" means that the style (*vṛtti*), which is a specific arrangement of phonemes, possesses the propriety (*aucitya*) of the subject matter to be described, such as its intensity and so forth.

The meaning is: "in that [process] which consists of the imparting of qualities. Some maintain that it refers to the occasion of imparting that *vṛtti*—the function or operation—which is appropriate (*samucitā*), meaning suitable for the manifestation of this or that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

"Mutually" (anyonya) means by way of the cause consisting in their mutual fitness for conjunction. The phrase beginning with "blazing" (dīpta) and so forth establishes the threefold nature [of the fire].
The *bahuvrīhi* compound [is formed] with the word "object" (*viṣaya*) as the final member of a *karmadhāraya* that contains a *dvandva*. "Aggregation" (*saṅghāta*) means, in short,
the attainment of a different form through the state of being a collection.
The illustration for its being charming by virtue of being a composite form is "like a beverage" (*pānaka*).

Thus, the meaning is that sweetness and other such qualities do not individually possess the status of being denoted by the word *rīti* in their own specific forms; rather, they possess it by virtue of possessing the attributes of a particular composite whole.
To the doubt, "By whom was this stated?", he provides the answer—beginning with the words *gauḍīyā* and so forth—while demonstrating the grounds for the application of terms such as *Vaidarbhī*.
The term *gauḍīyā* and the others refer to the regions associated with Gauḍa, Vidarbha, and Pāñcāla; that is to say, they refer to the poets residing in those places.
Regarding the subject of specific description, there exists a particular consensus (*hevāka*), which is either their inherent nature (*svabhāva*) or their freedom of expression (*svācchandyam*).
"By him" means by one who perceives that [object] in its abundance;
the sense is "by the dwarf. Alternatively, the meaning is "by the cause which is the vision consisting of an abundance of graceful gestures (hevāka)."
The sense is that these specific designations [such as Gauḍīya and Vaidarbhī] arise because they are observed in Vidarbha and other such regions.
By the term "threefold," it is indicated that there is also a threefold division pertaining to *rīti* (diction), namely Gauḍīyā, Vaidarbhī, and Pāñcālī.
As stated by Vāmana: "Rīti is the soul of poetry."
*Rīti* is a distinguished arrangement of words;
its excellence consists in the *guṇas*.
It is threefold: Vaidarbhī, Gauḍīyā, and Pāñcālī.
"Because it is observed in the Vaidarbha and other regions, it is designated by those names: the Vaidarbha possesses all the *guṇas*;
the Gauḍīya possesses *ojas* and *kānti*; and the Pāñcālī is endowed with *mādhurya* and *saukumārya*."

But, one might object: according to the method already stated, since there is a relationship of genus and individual between *vṛtti* and *anuprāsa*, and a relationship of whole and parts between *rīti* and *guṇa*, how can there be identity? To this he says: "The genus," and so forth.
"Whole" (*samudāya*) means the composite;
"parts" (*samudāyin*) refers to the constituents.

Others might say: "There is no such thing as *dhvani* at all; for a type of poetry that deviates from the well-known established systems would forfeit its status as poetry. [To this we reply: Since the constituent parts (*samudāyin*) are nothing other than [the elements themselves], it is established that the *vṛtti*s (modes of expression) and *rīti*s (styles) are not distinct from the *guṇa*s (qualities) and *alaṃkāra*s (ornaments). Thus, this [reason] remains indeed a valid reason of exclusion (*vyatirekī hetuḥ*).
To this he says: "What is this 'dhvani' that is distinct from those [two]?
This is not a locus of beauty, because it lacks the nature of either word or meaning;
nor is it a cause of beauty.
"Because it is distinct from both qualities (guṇa) and ornaments (alaṅkāra).

By this he means that even though poetry is to be relished through an undivided cognition (*akhaṇḍabuddhi*), if it is analyzed through a process of analytical abstraction (*apoddhārabuddhi*), nevertheless, no separate entity denoted by the word "suggestion" (*dhvani*) is found therein; thus he states this by means of the word "name" (*nāma*).
Now, one might object: "Let it be that this is not the inherent nature of word and meaning, and let it not be the cause of their beauty;

therefore, it must be something distinct from both poetic qualities (guṇa) and ornaments (alaṃkāra). Anticipating this doubt, he states the second type of the theory of non-existence with the words "anya" ("something else").
Let it be so;
nevertheless, there is no such thing as "sound" (dhvani) that you wish to define.
For this must be described as something belonging to poetry.
The sense is that [the Lord] is neither "dear to the ignorant" nor "other," because their identity is precisely what is accepted. He concludes the subject at hand with the word "iti."
"Remaining indeed" means "having been born indeed.

With the intention that the passage beginning with "distinct from that" (*tadvyatirikta*) serves as the conclusion (*nigamana*) for the aforementioned inference, he introduces it with "That [he] says," etc.; "that" refers to what was said.
Thus he says: "Therefore, he says."
In the phrase "distinct from that" (*tadvyatirikta*), the word "that" (*tat*)—which contains the reason—refers to words, meanings, their qualities (*guṇas*), and ornaments (*alaṃkāras*).

Regarding the question "What is this?", the word "what" (*kiṃ*) intends to negate the alternatives as to whether this [dhvani] is the locus of beauty or the cause of beauty; with this intention, he explains it by saying "This is not," and so forth.

It should be understood that by this, the negation of the existence of a qualified *dhvani* is established by implication—that there is no such thing as *dhvani* characterized as the cause of the beauty of poetry, distinct from words, meanings, their qualities, and ornaments.
‘This’ means that which is intended as sound (dhvani). After the word ‘iti’, the remainder of the sentence should be understood as ‘what [did he] say? (kiṃśabdanāha).
Since the intended meaning is already obtained by the word *kiṃ* alone, one might ask: "What is the purpose of the word *nāman*? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.
"By the cognition of abstraction" means by the cognition of differentiation.
By the phrase "nāmaśabdenāha" (he says by the word "nāma"),
the intention is that the word *nāma* indicates absolute non-existence.

By this much, it is established that there is simply no such thing as *dhvani*, which is distinct from word, meaning, and their poetic figures (*alaṃkāra*), and which is characterized as the cause of the beauty of poetry.

However, since the sound (*dhvani*) does not [disappear] by way of its own nature, he introduces another position in order to establish that; with this intention, he introduces [the argument] with "But surely" (*nanu*), etc.
"That" refers to the sound (*dhvani*).
"By that" has the same meaning as "even so" (*tathāpi*).
Alternatively, the meaning is "due to the absence of being a cause of beauty.

For it is precisely because they are causes of beauty that qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are subsumed [under suggestion]; however, if that is not admitted, then the existence of *dhvani* as something distinct from them becomes entirely worthy of consideration—this is the intended sense.
"Qualities and ornaments" is an elliptical expression for both word and meaning. "Having raised this [objection]" means having taken into account the doubt of the proponent of *dhvani*.
"If it be so," [meaning] in the case of such an admission;
[the opponent replies] "then we have won"—to this he says, "Even so," and so forth.
To the objection, "But its existence has already been stated," he says, "Of whatever kind," and so forth.

The word "tādṛśa" (such) is connected with what precedes; it refers to that which is intended to be characterized as being associated with poetry, and which one desires to make endowed with the [proper] definition.
Demonstrating this meaning, he says: "For of poetry," and so forth.
The definition of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*) is simply that which consists of both word and meaning, such that when combined, it delights the hearts of those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*).

This [definition] is not possible for a path that exceeds the aforementioned systems. Nor is there any element within that tradition—such as dance, song, or instrumental music—that serves as a counterpart to poetry. And this [element], namely the *locana* (the eye), is like something belonging to the category of dance, song, or instrumental music, rather than being a part of poetry itself.
Poetry (*kāvyam*) is that which is to be composed (*kavanīyam*); its state of being such is "poetic nature" (*kāvyatvam*).
And dance, song, and the like are not said to be "that which is to be composed."

Regarding the term *prasiddha*: "established" refers to the established path (*prasthāna*), which consists of words and their meanings, as well as their qualities and ornaments; it is called a "path" because by means of it people proceed and engage in discourse through tradition.
Regarding the phrase "of the type of poetry":
that path is intended by you as a type of poetry,
because it has been stated that "it is the soul of poetry."
Now, one might ask: "Why is that not considered poetry? To this he replies: "In whose heart...
and so on. By the phrase "of the path," the meaning is:
of the effort consisting of meter, song, winking of the eyes, and so forth.
The word "tat" (that) refers to the definition of poetry beginning with "sahṛdaya" (sensitive reader) and so forth.
Now, one might object: what of those who recognize such an unprecedented thing as being the nature of poetry?
They alone are the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). For this [poetry] must be described as being connected to poetry by virtue of its being a composite whole;
and since it is distinct from the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, its connection to poetry cannot otherwise be established.
Like dance, song, and so forth.
Thus, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: the sound under dispute is not poetry.
Because it is distinct from both word and meaning;
nor is it related to poetry,
because it is distinct from the qualities (guṇa) and ornaments (alaṃkāra) thereof.
"Like dance, song, and so forth.
Nor is the example deficient in the property to be proven (sādhyavikala);
for it is well known that because those [things] cannot be composed, they lack the status of being poetry (kāvyatva) and lack the connection with it—this is the meaning.
Having kept in mind the specific quality of being a source of beauty in the context of drama, such as dance and song, [the author] mentions them by way of illustration.
He explains the passage beginning with "well-known" (*prasiddha*) as referring to his own stated meaning: "well-known," etc.;
and he provides the explanation of the term "they stand firm" (*pratiṣṭhante*) as "by tradition," etc.
"By tradition" means by an uninterrupted stream;
"they employ" means they carry out the literary practice;
"by which path" means by that which is equivalent to a path.

Anticipating the objection that the statement that *dhvani* is a variety of poetry (*kāvyaprakāra*) contradicts those who deny the existence of *dhvani*, he says "poetry," etc., to show that such a statement is made by relying on what is commonly accepted by others.
The meaning is: "as a variety of poetry" means as a subdivision of poetry; the sense is that it is intended as being of that nature.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the previously stated reason is shown by the words "because [it] is not well-known" (*aprasiddha*) and so forth; and by the words "due to the loss of the nature of poetry" (*kāvyatvahāneḥ*), the probandum (*sādhya*) is indicated—this is how it should be understood.
Thus he says.
The meaning is that he speaks thus in response to this doubt.
He explains what is intended by the word "path" (mārga) with the words "dancing" (nṛtta) and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), other possible modifications occurring in the eyes are included, such as the contraction of the eyelids.
The word *prāya* has the sense of "mostly" or "for the most part.
Regarding the phrase "sahṛdaya," and so forth:
it means that [the work] consists of words and meanings that delight the hearts of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*).
By the phrase "delighting the hearts of the connoisseurs" (*sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādī*), the beauty of its qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) is expressed.
The commentary passage beginning with "And not at that time" (*na ca tatsamaye*) consists of a single unit in the form of an objection and its reply.
He explains the portion containing the objection with the words "Now, [is it not so]? (*nanu*) and so forth.
"Such as that" means:
that very nature of sound (dhvani) which was mockingly described by you there as consisting primarily of dance, song, and so forth; "unprecedented" (apūrva) means not previously manifested.

By the phrase "those who know," he imagines certain "sensitive readers" (*sahṛdaya*) who fall within that same time-period; and although the designation "poetry" (*kāvyavyapadeśa*) has been applied to *dhvani* based on their consensus, [the author] anticipates the objection that "being accepted by them" would merely result in a definition of poetry that deviates from the established tradition, and thus says: "And not...
For it is like saying, "I shall compose a definition of a sword," and then describing a garment consisting of warp and woof that covers the entire body.
Those who claim that a sword is "excellent" because it is delicate, fashioned from variegated threads, capable of enduring being rolled up and unrolled, and is both uncuttable and easily cuttable—

when they are questioned by others on the impropriety of their position, since a cloth is indeed of such a nature but a sword is not— they might say this; however, [the author] refutes such swords with the word *sakala* (whole/entire).
The meaning of the commentary (*vṛtti*) has been explained. Its "convention" (*tatsamaya*) is the linguistic agreement regarding words and sounds (*dhvani*).
He explains the portion beginning with "for its establishment" (*tatprasiddhyai*) as follows: "tadabhi... [and so on].

By using the word "name" (nāma), he indicates that the status of being a definition of poetry belongs to that which is intended by it; having raised this doubt, he says [the following]. The meaning is: having restated the objection of the proponent of *dhvani* through one part [of the argument], he states the refutation.
Clarifying the intent of the refutation-text beginning with "In all... (*sakale*) along with an illustration, he says: "Just as... (*yathā hi*), and so forth.
"The characteristics of the sword" refers to the essential nature of the sword.
"I shall do" (*karomi*):
here, the verb *kṛ* denotes the act of speaking.
Regarding the phrase "saying 'for this very reason,'" it will be explained later.
As for "extension" (ātāna): extension means lengthening or expansion.
*Vitāna* is a horizontal expanse; that which has this as its *ātman* (self-nature) is so described. *Pravriyamāṇa* means being made into a covering.
And there is also the reading *prāvaraṇasvarūpa*.
Regarding *saṃvartanā*: *saṃvartana* means contraction.
"Vivartana" means unfolding;
"te sahiṣṇuḥ" means capable of that; thus he spoke.
The meaning is that he speaks as if saying, "An object distinguished by its *ātāna* and so forth is a superior sword. Being questioned—that is, being challenged—he says, "It is like this," and so on.
Regarding the question "How would he say? he replies with the words beginning with "it is like this."
The meaning is: "An object of this very kind is intended by me as being the sword. Regarding the word *etad* (this):
the meaning is that the definition of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*) has been stated through the imaginative conception of another sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*).
[Objection: "What has been achieved by this sarcastic remark?
Nothing of ours has been cut away. To this, he says: "It is well-known. A subject (*lakṣya*) must be defined by its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); it is not something merely imagined.
"It becomes the object" is understood as being supplied [to the previous statement].
Thus he says: "from the state already mentioned";
the meaning is that he speaks the words with the intention already expressed.
The sense is that because activity is possible only toward an object appropriate to the minds of the learned, the intended meaning [of the verse] is indicated by the word "learned" (*vidvat*).
He states the result of saying "all" with the words "even the learned.
Those who know its conventions are those who know the conventions of *dhvani*.
Now, let it be granted that [this view] does not capture the minds of all scholars;
yet others might describe its non-existence otherwise, saying: "There is no such thing as *dhvani* at all, something entirely new.
For whatever does not transcend loveliness is already included within the causes of beauty already mentioned."
The meaning is that even if [the Locana] were composed in this manner, nothing at all would have been accomplished; rather, only madness would have been revealed.
As for the one who explains the intended meaning here: "Suggestive poetry (dhvani), which is the very lifeblood [of poetry], is indeed what you accept;
yet it is well known in the world that 'life'—being something beyond the established systems and not mentioned by the authors of the treatises on poetic ornaments—is not poetry."
All of this is self-contradictory for him.

For if that [poetic figure] was accepted by the proponent of the prima facie view as the vitalizing element of poetry, yet was not mentioned by the ancients, it would, on the contrary, be precisely what ought to be defined.
Therefore, the intended meaning here is indeed the former one.
One might object: "Granted that this [charm] is the cause of beauty and is included within the qualities and ornaments of word and meaning;

nevertheless, no one has ever stated that its life-force is 'dhvani'—that is, by means of this terminology. Anticipating this concern, he introduces the third argument regarding non-existence with the words "Furthermore, another... [punarapara iti].
The term *kāmanīyakam* is the abstract noun derived from *kamanīya*.
The meaning is that it is the cause of the cognition of beauty.
To the question "What is the fault [in this definition]?", he says: "For in this way," and so forth.
This refers to when the definition—consisting in being that which causes delight to the hearts of sensitive readers (sahṛdayas) as newly conceived—is established.
A certain characteristic would not be established;
rather, only madness would be revealed, and not wisdom—this is the meaning.
He restates another interpretation, beginning with "But he who," and so forth.

The "intention" refers to the intention of the proponent who maintains that a second [sound] does not exist. Regarding the word "life," the connection is that sound is intended to be the very essence of life.
The phrase "and that" means both the essence of resonance (*dhvani*) and the life [of poetry]. It does not mean "poetry."
The formal argument is that sound, being the very life of poetry, is not poetry because it is not [itself] an ornament. He refutes this with the words "of that," etc.
He demonstrates the contradiction with his own statement with the words "if indeed," etc.
Therefore, then:
"it is unspoken"; because of the reason that it has not been spoken.
"Only worthy of being characterized" means that it is only to be defined; the sense is that it is not worthy of being negated.
"Prāktanaḥ" means previously stated.
"Abhiprāyaḥ" refers to the intention of the proponent of non-existence (abhāvavādin). He introduces the third [point] with the words beginning with "nanu" and so forth.
If this is so, one might ask: "What is the point of your effort? To this he replies: "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

Even though it has not been stated by anyone—meaning that no author of a definition (*lakṣaṇakāra*) has said that this sound (*dhvani*) is the soul of poetry (*kāvyātman*) by means of such a designation;
therefore, the sense is that our effort is for the purpose of declaring that [fact] preceded by a formal definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
The phrase "this intention" refers to the intention of the proponent of *dhvani*.
After the word "suspecting," the words "set forth" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Furthermore, if the suffix *vuñ* were to signify a state (*bhāva*), the statement that it is included within the cause of beauty would be untenable; therefore, he explains it as "the action of that which is desirable."
He states the result [of the discussion] with the words "In its beauty," etc.; by implication, this refers to poetry.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "its" (*tasya*) means "of *dhvani*."
The phrase "in the causes of beauty" means "in the qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras).

If one were to apply a new designation to only one of these, it would be a mere arbitrary statement. Furthermore, since verbal constructs are infinite, even if some [definition] were possible, it would not be shown by those who are renowned for formulating the definition of poetry.
Regarding this [claim] that "dhvani is but a mere fraction of a type"— this which is danced by those whose eyes are closed by the cultivation of a false state of being a connoisseur—

[we reply]: Locana, surely because the varieties of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) are innumerable, we have seen in some instances such a charm as does not fall within [the categories of] *anuprāsa* and so forth.

Nor can it be included within the previously stated definitions of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and so forth; anticipating this objection, he offers a rebuttal by way of admission: "Of the verbal constructions" (*vāgvikalpānām*).
That which speaks is *vāk*, meaning sound (*śabda*);
that which is spoken is *vāc*, meaning the object (*artha*).
It is said that "by means of this" refers to the activity of verbal expression.
In that regard, the modes of variety in both word and meaning are infinite;
even the modes of variety in verbal expression are innumerable.
Regarding the phrase "a mere trace of variety":
for that is either a quality (*guṇa*) or an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) which serves as a cause of beauty;
and it is indeed already included by the general definition.
As they have said: "The qualities (guṇas) are those properties that produce the beauty of poetry; the ornaments (alaṅkāras) are the causes of its excellence.
Likewise: "The expression of words with a crooked (vakra) meaning is held to be the ornament of speech."

The repetition "dhvaniḥ dhvaniḥ" indicates agitation and shows respect; thus he says, "it dances. [The author] introduces the passage beginning with "Furthermore, of the verbal conceptualizations... which is about to be explained, by reflecting upon it, saying: "Now, by the Locana... [This refers to: By those who have composed the definitions of that [dhvani], by those who compose poetry endowed with it, and by those whose aesthetic wonder (camatkāra) is aroused by hearing it—[the word "dhvaniḥ" is repeated]. Bālapriyā introduces [the following] by considering the text yet to be explained, starting with "Furthermore, of the verbal conceptualizations...":
"Now, by the Locana..."
Regarding the term *vicchittīnām*: "various things are cut" (*vividhaṃ chidyante*) are *vicchittayaḥ*, meaning diversities; [the word] "of these" refers to them.
In the phrase "alliteration and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes similes and other such figures.
"Having the previously stated definition" is an adjective qualifying both [the subject and the predicate]; the meaning is "having the definition as you have stated.
"Preceded by an admission" means:
By the phrase "kitr ca," the acceptance [of this view] is indicated.

Regarding the expression "of speech-conceptualizations" (*vāgvikalpānām*), he explains that the word *vāk* (speech) has the sense of "various" and the word *vikalpa* (conceptualization) has the sense of "diversity," as in the passage beginning with "he speaks," etc., namely:
"the diversity of denotations."
This, however, has been stated according to the view of Kuntaka and others.
He explains the underlying meaning [of the verse] with the words "sa hi" and so forth.
"Saḥ" (he) refers to that slight indication of the manner.
And that is also the cause of beauty.
He states its definition as expressed by Vāmana: "Of the beauty of poetry," and so forth;
[and] "its excellence," etc.

The meaning is "the excellence of poetic beauty. And he states what was said by Bhāmaha: "Likewise, expression (*abhidhā*) is the utterance of both the expressed and the expressive—the signified and the signifier—which is crooked, variegated, and producing aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*)."

And thus, the sense is that whatever further variety of poetic figures is delineated, since each of those is subsumed under the general definitions of the aforementioned *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*, it is impossible for them not to have been perceived by their author. The term "by repetition" (*vīpsayā*) means by the use of the double [word-form]. The term "with agitation" (*sambhramam*)— The meaning is as follows: if one were to say, "This is a *guṇa*," then another would say, "No, this is an *alaṅkāra*"; and if one were to say, "This is an *alaṅkāra*," then another would say, "No, this is a *guṇa*. In this way, because there is a mutual exclusion between the two, they cannot both be established simultaneously; therefore, the statement "this is a *guṇa*" or "this is an *alaṅkāra*" is not tenable. Consequently, the sense is that even if such a variety is depicted, it is included within the general characteristics of the aforementioned *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*, and thus it is inconceivable that its creator did not perceive it. The word "by repetition" (*vīpsayā*) means by means of the double occurrence [of the term]. "With agitation" (*sambhramam*). This refers to the state of being agitated due to the mutual exclusion of the two. "Agitation" (*sambhrama*) is defined as the state of being agitated (*sambhrāntatā*). It is called "agitation" because it causes one to become agitated (*sambhrāmayati*). For example, when someone says, "This is a *guṇa*," another person might say, "No, this is an *alaṅkāra*. Or, when someone says, "This is an *alaṅkāra*," another might say, "No, this is a *guṇa*. In this manner, because there is a mutual exclusion between the two, they cannot be established simultaneously; therefore, the statement "this is a *guṇa*" or "this is an *alaṅkāra*" is not tenable. Consequently, the sense is that even if such a variety is depicted, it is included within the general characteristics of the aforementioned *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*, and thus it is inconceivable that its creator did not perceive it. The word "by repetition" (*vīpsayā*) means by means of the double occurrence [of the term]. "With agitation" (*sambhramam*). This refers to the state of being agitated due to the mutual exclusion of the two. "Agitation" (*sambhrama*) is defined as the state of being agitated (*sambhrāntatā*). It is called "agitation" because it causes one to become agitated (*sambhrāmayati*). For example, when someone says, "This is a *guṇa*," another person might say, "No, this is an *alaṅkāra*. Or, when someone says, "This is an *alaṅkāra*," another might say, "No, this is a *guṇa*. In this manner, because there is a mutual exclusion between the two, they cannot be established simultaneously; therefore, the statement "this is a *guṇa*" or "this is an *alaṅkāra*" is not tenable. Consequently, the sense is that even if such a variety is depicted, it is included within the general characteristics of the aforementioned *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*, and thus it is inconceivable that its creator did not perceive it. This refers to the state of being agitated due to the mutual exclusion of the two. "Agitation" (*sambhrama*) is defined as the state of being agitated (*sambhrāntatā*). It is called "agitation" because it causes one to become agitated (*sambhrāmayati*). For example, when someone says, "This is a *guṇa*," another person might say, "No, this is an *alaṅkāra*. Or, when someone says, "This is

The meaning is that [the author] expresses haste in establishing the system of *dhvani* (suggested meaning). The sense is that the doubling of the word "indicating" (*sūcayan*) is used here to signify agitation (*sambhrama*).
Regarding the word "respect" (ādara): the meaning is that those who maintain the doctrine of *dhvani* (dhvanivādinaḥ) have respect for *dhvani*.
In the phrase "is dancing," he supplies the subject (*kartṛpada*) as "that [poem]," etc., according to the requirements of propriety.
That term [dhvani] signifies "suggested meaning" (dhvanyartha). Some are authors of the definition of *dhvani*, while others are composers of poetry characterized by it.

Some experience a sense of wonder arising from hearing that poem, yet we do not know the cause for it; for thousands of other great souls have revealed and continue to reveal various types of poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*),
and such a state [of aesthetic rapture] is not reported to occur upon hearing them.
Therefore, sound is merely conventional discourse;
indeed, not even the slightest essence capable of withstanding scrutiny can be revealed of it.

And thus, another verse has been composed on this point: "In which there is no real object whatsoever that delights the mind, [even] when accompanied by poetic ornaments"—the phrase "by the perceivers" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The sense is: "What great regard can there be for the word *dhvani*?
This [verse] shows it;

the meaning is that there is both self-conceit and being praised by others. Or, "verbal constructs" (*vāgvikalpāḥ*) refers to the various modes of the operation of creative intuition (*pratibhā*), which is the cause for the activity of speech.
Therefore, [it is] "mere conventional expression.
This is the common conclusion for all proponents of non-existence (*abhāvavādin*);
because, in its capacity as a cause of beauty, it is not distinct from qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāra*).

The meaning is: because it is not a cause of beauty when distinct [from the object], and because even if it were a cause of beauty, it would not be a fit object of regard; therefore [he says this]. Nor is this possibility of non-existence baseless and thus refuted; he states this with the words "and likewise by another," referring to those who understand [the text] as contemporaries of the author. *Bālapriyā* [is the name of the commentary].
The meaning is "by those three.
However, some [commentators] say: "he shows disregard," and "in poetry not joined with that."
And they also read "atacchravaṇa" (not hearing that).
In that interpretation, the phrase "disregard for it" means disregard for sound on the part of those who deny its existence.

As for the passage beginning with "atadyukta," since it is impossible for the authors of that definition to say [it refers to something else], it results in having as its object merely the word "sound."
The sense is that this results in nothing but a cause for derision. "By others" means by those who compose poetry endowed with *dhvani*.

Following the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokananyāya*), he explains the term *vāgvikalpa* (verbal conceptualization) differently in the passage beginning with "due to the infinity of verbal conceptualizations" (*vāgvikalpānāmānantyāt*)—namely, "speech," and so forth.
With the intention that since the doctrine of non-existence (*abhāvavāda*) is presented through mutual connection, its conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) must also correspond to that, he says "of all," etc.
He clarifies their commonality with the words "since," and so forth.

The phrase "not a locus for respect" means that since [the suggested meaning] is included within the ornaments of word and sense (*śabdālaṅkāra* and *arthālaṅkāra*) respectively, its novelty consists solely in the word itself; this is the intended sense.
With the intention of showing the basis for the impossibility of the previously mentioned doctrine of non-existence (*abhāvavāda*), he introduces that passage with the words "And not," and so forth.
This previously demonstrated impossibility regarding non-existence is not refuted because it is rootless,
but rather because it is indeed rooted; such is the meaning.
Although the refutation of the argument against non-existence (*abhāvavāda*) was yet to be performed, the past tense is used because it was effectively completed by being present in the mind;
thus,
"he said" means that he spoke with such an intention.

Nor should it be asked how the previous statement— "nor have we heard the alternatives of the proponents of non-existence"— is consistent with the fact that this verse beginning with "in which" (*yasmin*) is actually heard in scripture, since its indirectness (*pārokṣya*), understood through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the word "the world" (*jagat*), requires such support.

For although this verse is heard with its literal meaning, the aforementioned statement refers specifically to those many varieties of the doctrine of non-existence (*abhāvavāda*) that were previously presented, as none of them were individually heard in scripture.

When asked by a wise man about the true nature of *dhvani*, the dull-witted one—praising with delight that poetry which is composed by the learned using words not devoid of *vakrokti* (poetic deviation) as the very cause for the author’s statement, and claiming "that poetry is endowed with *dhvani*"—does not know how to answer; we do not understand what he says.
It was composed by the poet named Manoratha;
since it lacks ornamentation, it does not gladden the mind.
By this, the absence of *arthālaṅkāras* (figures of sense) is stated;
and by the phrase "not at all composed with words [requiring] learned [skill]," the absence of *śabdālaṅkāras* (figures of sound) is indicated. *Vakrokti* is an excellent composition (*saṃghaṭanā*).

Regarding the phrase "that [verse] is devoid [of ornament]," some maintain that by the expression "devoid of *vakrokti*," the absence of all ornaments is stated due to the absence of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of words and their meanings.
However, they have not at all avoided the charge of tautology; so, enough of this.
"By Prīti" means by way of affection that follows those who have already gone [on the path]. "By Sumati" means... [as above].

The sense is that when questioned by an insentient being, one might as well give an answer merely through the knitting of eyebrows, side-long glances, and so forth; thus, one would indeed be describing its true nature.
In this way, these conceptual constructions of non-existence have arrived in a sequential chain, rather than being entirely unrelated to one another.
For indeed, at the commencement of the investigation into the third mode of non-existence, this is precisely the intended meaning of the word "again" (punaḥ),
and it is consistent with the unity of the conclusion.
Furthermore, the non-existence theory is described as being "established" (bhūtatva) because it possesses the status of a plausible possibility.
The figurative discourse (bhāktavāda), however, is uninterrupted; this indicates that "in which" refers to the poem.
"In which" means in the poem.
"Possessing ornaments" (sālaṅkṛti), and for that very reason, "delighting the mind" (manaḥprahlādi).
When some object (*vastu*) is being described, there is no such thing as "something" (*kiñcana*).
Regarding the term "by those who are proficient" (*vyutpannaiḥ*):
if the reading is *naiva*, then the word *yat* (from the preceding *yad-asti*) is to be supplied.
The reading is "yanneti" (and that which is not).
"Yat" refers to poetry.
"Vacanaiḥ" means by words, produced as variegated through the employment of alliteration and other such figures, by those who are proficient.
Furthermore, when that which is "not even composed" and likewise "devoid of *vakrokti*"— that is,

such a work devoid of poetic figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) and so forth— is praised with affection as "poetry endowed with *dhvani*," what can a dull-witted person say when questioned by one of superior intelligence regarding the true nature of *dhvani*?
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "We do not know.
He explains the meaning of the state of being (*bhāvārtha*) with the words beginning "since" (*yataḥ*). By this [he means]:...
The meaning is "by the first sentence. Regarding the word "stated" (ukta), the word "poetry" (kāvyam) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

It should be understood that the phrase "it is said to be non-existence" (abhāva ukta) also applies to both of these: "of verbal ornaments" (śabdālaṅkārāṇām) and "of the qualities of word and meaning" (śabdārthaguṇānām).
Regarding the term "structure" (saṅghaṭanā), the words "of word and meaning" (śabdārthayoḥ) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He restates another interpretation, beginning with "vakrokti" and so forth.
*Vakrokti* is exceptionally beautiful expression, and beauty is indeed variety (*vaicitrya*).
Since that is the general definition of poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), the meaning is that the absence of all ornaments has been stated.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "by those" (*tair iti*).
"Gatānugatikatā" means the following after what has already been gone; that is, the tendency to follow along with what others have already accepted.
The suffix *ka* is used in the sense of contempt;
thus, [the term] means "through attachment to that.

Alternatively, *gatānugatika* refers to those who possess *gatānugata*—that is, following after what has already gone, namely, following along with others' movements (*anyagamana*). Thus they are called *gatānukatikas*.

That is to say, they merely follow the words of others without engaging in independent inquiry. [The author] explains the purpose of the term "Sumati" by means of the passage beginning with "by the dull-witted," etc., referring to their possible attachment to those [words].

In response to the doubt as to why these conceptual constructions (*vikalpas*) have been explained as being mutually connected, he says "Thus," etc., [stating] that it is because they accord with the text of the commentary (*vṛtti*). They have come down in a chain-like sequence and are thus mutually connected.
To the question "Why?", he says "For instance" (*tathāhi*).
The intention of the word "punaḥ" (again) is precisely this:
regarding the expression "punaraparam" (furthermore), some say that the word "punaḥ" is used figuratively;
others, however, say that this [element] called *dhvani* is the soul of poetry (*kāvyātman*) through the function of secondary metaphor (*guṇavṛtti*).

The statement "in the books" is said figuratively with the intention that [the word] is used in reference to those [books] which are not currently active, in consideration of their constant engagement; thus it is a designation.

"Bhakti" is a property consisting of proximity and so forth between the denoted object and its meaning, because it is resorted to (bhajyate), served, or imagined through its well-known association; that which comes from this is the "bhākta," i.e., the secondary or metaphorical (lākṣaṇika) meaning.
As they say: "Metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is considered to be fivefold: by proximity to the primary meaning, by similarity of form, by inherence, by contrariety, and by connection with action."
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that it possesses exactly the intention already stated.
If, however, the word *punaḥ* were to have the sense of "distinction," then one should have said, "others, moreover" (*apare punaḥ*).
Having set that aside, the word "punaḥ" (again) is placed at the beginning;
the sense is that it indicates the immediate succession of what follows with respect to the manner previously mentioned, thereby making the connection understood.
And this connection has already been shown by the introductory remark (*avatārikā*).
He states another indicator with the word "upeti" (and so on).
The sense is that if there were no mutual connection [between the parts], there would necessarily have to be a distinction in the concluding summaries (*upasaṃhāra*).
He expresses the meaning of the usage of the phrases "they said" (*jagaduḥ*) and "they said" (*āhuḥ*) with the verse beginning with "abhāva... and so forth.
"It has been said" means "by this [verse] they have declared," such is the ellipsis; "in books" refers to the treatises on poetics (*alaṅkāra*).

In this context, the meaning of the term *nityeti* (in the phrase *nityeti īśvaro 'sti*) is that the present tense (*laṭ*) is used for that which is constantly active, as in the rule of Bhoja: "The present tense is used for what is constantly active. To explain the meaning of the word *bhākta*, he states the derivation of the word *bhakti* through the sense of the object (*karma-vyutpatti*), beginning with "it is partaken of" (*bhajyate*).
He states the meaning in order to exclude [the literal sense]: "it is served" (*sevyate*).

To the question "by what?", he says: "by the word-meaning" (*padārthena*). This means by the meaning such as the bank, which is indicated (*lakṣya*) by words like "Ganges. Now, one might ask: what is this so-called "serving" whose agent is the word-meaning? To this he says: "it is imagined" (*utprekṣyate*).
The meaning is that it is perceived by means of the object-entity;
that is to say, it is resorted to as the cause of its own cognition.
The reason for this is stated as "by way of being well-known."
The meaning is that [proximity] is well-known as the cause [of the metaphorical usage].
Alternatively, it is stated figuratively that "it is served by the object.

And by this, he states that what is intended here is the imaginative conception (*utprekṣaṇa*)—in the form of a deliberation upon proximity and so forth—which occurs when the speaker or the listener conveys the bank and such by means of a word like "Ganges" as the cause [for the metaphorical application]. Thus he says: "It is imagined due to its being well-known."
Thus [it is said];
the ellipsis is "by the speaker or by the listener.
The connection is that proximity and so forth are properties belonging to the denoted object.

Then, [the word] "come" (āgata) is understood based on such causes as proximity; as to what that [referent] is, he says: "it is the one characterized by definition" (lākṣaṇika); the meaning is "that which is to be defined" (lakṣya).
Regarding this, he cites a corroborating statement: "Because of its proximity to the denoted object," and so forth.
The meaning of this will be explained by himself later.
*Locana* [comments]: For a word that functions through a collection of qualities (*guṇa*), a portion of the meaning such as sharpness and so on is *bhakti*.
Therefore, the meaning derived from a quality (*gauṇa*) is figurative (*bhākta*).
"Figurative application" (*bhakti*) is an excess of faith directed toward what is to be conveyed—such as proximity, sharpness, and so on.

With that [faith] as the intended purpose, [the author] says "guṇa... with the intention that although the figurative meaning is obtained by the aforementioned method, its attainment should also be stated by another way.
The meaning is: for that [word] whose occurrence is in a collection of qualities (guṇasamudāya), it expresses that collection of qualities;
[this refers to] "of the word" (śabdasya).
The meaning is "of words such as 'lion'.

The point is that although words like 'lion' denote either the universal (jāti) of lionhood or the individual (vyakti) qualified by it, they also convey qualities such as bravery—which are invariably concomitant with their own referent—by way of implication (ākṣepa).
"A portion of the meaning" refers to a single part of the referent, which consists of a collection of qualities.
Sharpness and so forth, as well as bravery and so forth;
the point is that in expressions such as "The boy is a lion," there is only the cognition of a single portion of qualities, namely bravery and the like.

However, some say that the phrase "functioning through a collection of qualities" means that which functions—by way of its qualities—in a collection, that is, in the possessor of qualities (guṇin) such as the boy.
The word "tataḥ" means "from sharpness and so forth"; that is to say,
it means "due to similarity as the cause."

Now, he states the meaning of the word *bhakti* even through its derivation as an abstract noun (*bhāvavyutpatti*), beginning with "devotion" (*bhakti*) and so forth. "In the object to be established" means in that which is to be made known.
"In proximity, sharpness, and so forth" [is the meaning].
Now, in cases such as "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā," what is to be conveyed regarding the indicated object— the bank and so forth— is precisely the sanctity and other qualities belonging to the Gaṅgā,
and not [merely] proximity and the like.
Similarly, in cases such as "The boy is a lion," what is to be conveyed regarding the boy and so forth is either the identity with a lion or the excellence of valor and the like.
This is clear from the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and other such works; furthermore, this will be stated later in the *Locana*.
If it is asked, "In that case, how can the statement regarding 'proximity,' 'sharpness,' and so forth be consistent? [the answer follows].

Regarding this, some maintain that this reading has arisen from a scribe’s error and that it should instead be read as "pāvanatvādi" (purifying nature, etc.). Others, however, argue that because proximity and so forth serve as means to the goal through a causal chain, the term "proximity" (*sāmīpya*) indicates "purifying nature" and so on by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), while the term "sharpness" (*taikṣṇya*) indicates "lion-likeness" and so on; therefore, this is an excellence of the meaning (*arthātiśaya*).
Faith (śraddhā) consists of the worshiper’s mental contemplation of the speaker;
the meaning is "the excellence of that [faith]. Regarding the word "tām" (that):
The meaning is that it consists of qualities such as purity which have become its object;
or alternatively, it is the excellence of conviction (*addhātiśaya*), a specific mode of cognition on the part of the perceiver.
"That" refers to this [conviction].
The meaning is: by means of devotion consisting of an excellence of faith;
it has come forth, it is applied, and it is technical (lākṣaṇika).
The word "sound" (*śabda*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].

Although there is no difference in their etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), he states that they have different meanings due to the difference in their roots (*prakṛti*) with the words "and of the primary [meaning].
"Bending" (*bhaṅga*) means "figurative usage" (*bhakti*).
The state [of being] is formed by adding the suffix *ktin* to the root *bhañj* with the suffix *dāc*.
Following the word "iti," the phrase "derived from that" (*tata āgataḥ*) is to be supplied as "bhākta" (metaphorical).
"Āgataḥ" means understood or recognized.
He states the result of the manner of explanation just described, beginning with "Thus" (*evam*) and so forth.
"Locana" (the eye) has come to mean "secondary" (*bhākta*), that is, figurative (*gauṇa*) and indicative (*lākṣaṇika*).
"Bhakti" is the bending away from the primary meaning; thus, it is the sublation of the primary meaning.
It is thus stated that the presence of these three— the sign (nimitta), the purpose (prayojana), and [the object]— constitutes the basis for metaphorical designation (upacāra).
Furthermore, the nature of poetry (kāvyātman) consists in the function of qualities (guṇavṛtti).

The meaning of this grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is as follows: although there is metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) in certain varieties of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is not intended— such as in "like a mirror blinded by breath"—
nevertheless, *dhvani* is not identical to that [metaphor],
because it exists even in the absence of that [metaphor].

We shall explain that even in the case of the "unintended literal meaning" (*avivakṣitavācya*), the varieties such as "the unintended as other than what is intended to be said" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*) are merely metaphorical (*upacāra*), and not *dhvani*.
And so he will say:
Out of deference [to convention], this term *dhvani* does not maintain a single identity due to the diversity of its forms;
for it is neither over-extensive nor under-extensive, nor is it perceived in such a way.
Thus:
"But that [exclusion] may be a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa) of some particular sound-differentiation," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: the result of explaining the sense of "bending" (bhaṅga) is the establishment of the seed, namely the sublation of the primary meaning; the result of explaining the sense of "service" (sevana) is the establishment of the cause; and the result of explaining the sense of "excessive faith" (śraddhātiśaya) is the establishment of the purpose.

By the word "three," he shows that they constitute the state of being a seed only when combined, as in the phrase "the metaphorical seed. Metaphor (*upacāra*) refers to both indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and secondary usage (*gauṇī*);
linguistic usage proceeds by means of both indication and secondary usage.
Or, it is the cognition of the indicated (lakṣya) or the secondary (gauṇa) meaning.
Some maintain that "metaphorical application" (upacāra) is the transfer of a term from one object to another.

Now, since it ought to be stated that what is called "suggestion" (dhvani) is not distinct from metaphorical function (guṇavṛtti), what is the intention behind its designation through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya)? To this, he says: "Of grammatical coordination... [and so forth].

The meaning is that there is a reference by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the phrase "that is figurative" in the root text and the words "designated as *dhvani*" and so forth in the commentary (*vṛtti*).

It should be understood that in this view, there is no citation of the pratīka (the initial word of a verse) such as "the soul of poetry" (*kāvyātmānam*). Coreferentiality between two words means their capacity to denote a single substratum (*ekadharmibodhakatva*).

"This is the [intended] meaning. The proponents of *dhvani* (the theory of suggestion) must reject only the identity (*tādātmya*) between the sound (*dhvani*) and its qualities or functions; they do not, however, reject that *dhvani* is entirely untouched by figurative usage (*upacāra*). To illuminate this point, this reference made through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is intended to introduce the position of identity, which contradicts their own established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
The meaning is "existence. He explains that very existence with the words beginning "even though," etc. [He uses] the term "metaphorical designation" (upacāra).
The meaning is "the functioning of qualities. "That which has that as its essence" means having the nature of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
"Even apart from that" means even without metaphorical designation.
Because of the existence [of the term], that is, because sound exists;
as to where [this applies], he says: "in the case of the divisions of the expressed meaning, such as 'intended but subordinate' (vivakṣitānyaparavācya)," and so forth.
[The phrase] "where the expressed meaning is not intended" (avivakṣitavācya) [is used].
The meaning is "in the case of suggestion where the literal sense is not intended to be expressed" (avivakṣitavācyadhvani).
"We shall explain" refers to such instances as "I am Rāma," and so forth; this is the intention.

"He will say"—the words "the author of the root-text" (mūlakāra) are to be supplied. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "functioning through qualities" (*guṇavṛtti*) is an explanation of the word "figurative" (*bhākta*); he elucidates the meanings intended in the present context by that term with the words beginning "qualities" (*guṇā*).
By "means" (*upāyaiḥ*) is meant "causes" (*nimittaiḥ*).

And although those who formulate the definition of poetry have not, by the mention of the term *dhvani*, revealed any other mode such as secondary metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*) or the like, nevertheless, because they employ the term "poetry" for [works] through non-primary function, [we explain it thus]: the qualities (*guṇas*) are properties such as proximity and so forth, as well as sharpness and so forth;
that which has its function toward another meaning by means of these instruments [is *guṇavṛtti*].

That word or meaning in which there is a function (*vṛtti*) by means of those [secondary] methods is a "word or meaning with secondary function" (*guṇavṛtti*). Alternatively, "functioning by way of qualities" (*guṇadvāreṇa vartanam*) is the secondary operation of denotation (*amukhya abhidhā-vyāpāraḥ*).
This is what is meant: it either "resounds" (*dhvanati*), or...

Whether it be that which is "sounded" (*dhvanyate*) or the act of "sounding" (*dhvanana*), even if it is called *dhvani*, it is nonetheless nothing other than the operation of words and meanings in a metaphorical sense.

Since denotation (*abhidhā*) operates only in the primary sense, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), suggestion (*dhvani*) must reside in the non-primary sense alone, as there is no third category.
Anticipating the objection—"But who has said that suggestion is a function of secondary indication (*guṇavṛtti*)?"—he says: "Even though... (*yadyapi ca*).
"Or another" means:
in a different sense, such as a riverbank or a young brahmin;
"of which" refers to words such as "Ganges" or "lion."
"In which" means:
in the sense of a bank or similar object.
"By way of a quality" means: by way of proximity, sharpness, and so forth.

"Vartana" is an explanation of the meaning of the word "vṛtti. He states the conclusion with the words "non-primary" (amukhya). By the term "non-primary," both metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) and secondary usage (gauṇī) are included.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "This," and so forth.

Regarding the term "metaphorical" (upacarita): the meaning is that it is distinct from the operations of word and meaning that are conveyed by words functioning through their secondary qualities (guṇavṛtti).
"This [object] is something called *dhvani*, it is something specific.

Now, if it is argued that because *dhvani* does not exist, its non-difference from a secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*) is being established, then let its non-difference from primary denotation (*abhidhā*) also be established; to this he replies with the words "mukhyārthe" (in the primary sense).
By means of the word "only" (eva), he shows that even the possibility of suggestion (dhvanana) does not exist here.
He states the conclusion with the words "thus" (iti).
[He explains] by the phrase "by way of elimination" (pāriśeṣyāt).
When something remains, that conviction is "remainder" (pariśeṣa);
that itself is "the state of being a remainder" (pāriśeṣya); the meaning is "therefore."
It is indeed non-primary; it is merely a figurative function (*guṇavṣtti*).
The reason for this is "the third.
The first category consists of the denoter (*vācaka*), the denoted (*vācya*), and the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*).

The meaning is that [your position is untenable] because of the absence of that which you intend: namely, the second [type of relation] consisting of the indicator (*lakṣaka*), the indicated (*lakṣya*), and the indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and the third [type] consisting of the suggester (*vyañjaka*), the suggested (*vyaṅgya*), and the suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
And thus it follows that what is called *dhvani* is indeed a function of poetic quality (*guṇavṛtti*), because it is non-literal (*amukhyatvāt*).
[The author] says "Now, however" (*nanu*) and so forth.
The word "iti" (thus) is connected to both [parts].
Having raised the doubt, "By whom was this said?", he says [the following].
The meaning is that, having formulated the doubt with the words beginning with "yadyapi" (even though), he states the resolution with the words beginning with "tathāpi" (nevertheless).

In the commentary, regarding the phrase "or another," there might be the misconception that "another" refers to the primary (mukhya) as opposed to the secondary (guṇavṛtti); therefore, he explains it with the word "guṇa.
The word "vā" (or) is used for the sake of providing an illustration:
just as those who maintain the theory of non-existence (abhāvavādins) have not stated that sound is a type of figurative ornament (guṇālaṅkāra).

The meaning is that even by those who maintain the theory of secondary metaphorical usage (*bhākta*), it has not been explicitly stated in so many words that "suggestion" (*dhvani*) is a function of poetic quality (*guṇavṛtti*).

Although they have slightly touched upon the path of suggestion while demonstrating [their own views], they did not perceive it; thus, having made such an assumption, it was said: "Others call it metaphorical.
The word *locanam* means "in short, it is a variety of poetic quality and ornament."

"Show [the distinction]," [said] Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa, Vāmana, and others. Bhāmaha stated: "Words are for the purpose of denoting [objects]. In order to explain the distinction between words and denotation (*abhidhāna*), Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa declared: "The denotation of words is the primary function of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*)."

And [it is said], "the function of qualities" (guṇavṛtti). Vāmana also states, "Indirect expression (vakrokti) is indication (lakṣaṇā) based on similarity. [The term] "slightly touched" (manākspṛṣṭa) [is used].
By them, the direction of the sound was first disclosed; however, by those who recite it incorrectly, the cause for even a slight touch is shown to be as if it were dear to children.
Here, the singular number is intended in a general sense.

With the intention that only those who prescribe the characteristics of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇavidhāyin*) are intended here, he completes [the thought] with "Bhaṭṭa," etc. He shows their respective statements in order with "By Bhāmaha," etc.: "Stories based on history, worldly logic, and the arts—these should be considered the causes of poetry. This refers to the remaining three quarters of the verse.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is "it has been said thus.
To the question "What follows from that? he says: "of the designation" (*abhidhānasya*).
The word "here" (*atra*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Vāmana also said so"— this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*). "Because of similarity" refers to *vakrokti*, a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) by that name.

The implied meaning is that Bhāmaha demonstrated the use of figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*) in poetry through the statement "tathā cābhidhānam," Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa through the statement "guṇavṛttiḥ," and Vāmana through the statement "lakṣaṇā.

He explains the portion "the path of *dhvani*, though slightly touched, was not defined" in accordance with the introduction of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), beginning with "By them, for their part," and so on.
The word "first" (*samprati*) refers to the process of comprehension (*sampratipatti*).
The phrase "the path of suggestion slightly touched" is explained as "the direction of suggestion revealed.

This is because the function of figurative indication (*guṇavṛtti*) is invariably connected with a specific purpose (*prayojana*), and that purpose, according to the method to be explained, falls exclusively within the domain of the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanavyāpāra*).

The meaning is that by Bhāmaha, Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa, and others—who themselves demonstrated the conventional usage [of the term] through the function of *guṇavṛtti* (the function of quality)—the indicator (*gamaka*) of *dhvani* was shown.
Although they touched upon the path of *dhvani*, because they did not define its specific nature separately by providing a formal definition, *dhvani* is nothing other than *guṇavṛtti*;

it is not something distinct from it. Relying on this fact, which is established by their own statements, this school of the "figurative theory" (*bhāktavāda*) proceeded; thus he says, "Just as written," and so forth.
The word *tu* (but) has the sense of "nevertheless. The explanation of the phrase "it was not characterized" (*na lakṣitaḥ*) is: "its essential nature (*svarūpa*) was not analyzed.

However, some whose intellects were confident in their ability to formulate definitions have declared that the true essence (*tattva*) of *dhvani* is beyond the reach of words and is to be experienced only by the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).

Since such conflicting opinions (*vimati*) thus exist, [Abhinavagupta] states that the analysis of its essential nature was not performed by those who, though unable to produce the *Locana* for the delight of the minds of connoisseurs, failed to provide that analysis of its essential nature.
He is being criticized for merely memorizing those texts exactly as they were heard, like an unbroken coconut;
therefore he says: "This was stated after having thus reflected."
If it were not applied in this way, then the statement of the prima facie position— that the path of sound is touched— would be contradicted.
"Those of modest intellect" means those whose minds are lacking in confidence.
And these three possess progressively superior intellectual capacities;
the reason for this is that they are unable to effect a discrimination of the true nature [of things].
The word "by them" (taih) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis.
The phrase "for the sake of [the purpose]" and so forth provides the reason for the incapacity.
The meaning is: by those who have recited the poetic works (*dhvanikāvya*) which constitute the *lakṣya* (the object of definition), without deviating from the written text.
Alternatively, the word "as" (*yathā*) is used in the sense of a comparison; thus, the meaning is "just as by those who read what has been written."
This means by those who do not know the distinction.
It is not merely that they fail to distinguish the true nature of sound; rather, they even deny its nature which ought to be distinguished. Thus he says, "On the contrary," and so forth.
"It is censured" means it is rejected;
"by them" is the ellipsis [to be supplied];
"sound" is the remainder [of the sentence].
This censure is inferable from Bhāmaha and others,
but it is directly evident from the commentators on the works of Bhaṭṭa Udbhaṭa and others;
it is like an unbroken coconut.
The suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the sixth case.
Its connection is with the term "udgrahaṇa" (seizing). He shows the reason for the censure by saying "yathāśruta" (as it was heard).
The meaning is: "merely by the grasping and retaining of those texts which are the objects of study—namely, works on grammar and poetry—without any investigation according to what has been heard.
There is also a reading: *abhagnanārikelakalpayathāśrute*.
"For this very reason" [is the phrase].
