Otherwise, when the expressed meaning itself becomes subordinate— due to the absence of [further] subordination— it is designated as "suggestion of ornament" (*alaṅkāradhvani*) by virtue of the power of prior recognition, according to the maxim of the "Brahmin-ascetic.
However, when it is characterized by the absence of that very nature [of suggestion], it is called a mere matter-of-fact statement (*vastumātra*).
For by the use of the term "measure" (*mātra*), other forms [of aesthetic experience] are excluded.

That which, even in a dream, is not denotable by its own name nor fallen within the sphere of worldly transaction, but rather—presented by words—is characterized by a form to be relished through the operation of tasting the bliss of one's own self-consciousness, which is tender with the passion of the latent impressions of love and so forth established previously, and which is beautiful through its harmony with the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and the concord of the heart; [that is the essence of rasa].
That "subordination" (*guṇībhāva*), which is the exclusive domain of poetic function (*kāvyavyāpāra*), is absent here.
Now, one might ask: if its nature is not that of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), how can it be designated as "ornament-suggestion" (*alaṅkāradhvani*)? To this he says: "By the previous...
The connection is with the phrase "it is designated by way of logic" (*nyāyena vyapadiśyate*).
A *śramaṇa* is one who has entered the system of the Arhats;
[the term is used] because of the absence of that nature and the absence of the nature of ornamentation,
by means of the inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*).
The meaning is: "by the word *mātra* (only) found in the commentary [on the verse] ‘vastumātram’ (the mere thing-in-itself).
"Another form" means the nature of being an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
"Even in a dream" refers to... [the following].
For in a dream, even that which is impossible in reality occurs;
it does not fall within the scope of worldly convention.
The meaning is that it is not of a nature equal to the joy of a son's birth or similar events.
Regarding the word "śabda" (words): by "words" is meant those words of poetry beautiful with qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).

"Being presented" (*samarpyamāṇāḥ*) means being properly offered in a manner suitable for manifesting aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and thus being reflected within the mirror-like interior of the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
By this, it is shown that the actual existence (*vāstavasattva*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth is not a necessary condition [for their function].
This is clearly stated in the *Daśarūpaka* and other works.
For this very reason, the status of being an excitant and so forth is established for characters such as Mālatī, just as it is for Śakuntalā and others.

He states that it is not only the aesthetic factors (vibhāvas) and so forth as presented by the words of the poem that [constitute the cause], but also those brought about by the resonance within the hearts of connoisseurs— by saying "hṛdaya" (heart).
Those excitants (vibhāvas) and ensuants (anubhāvas) which are presented by words and are beautiful through resonance with the heart, their [correspondence] from previous births...

Beginning with the direction stated in the passage, "For no living being is devoid of mental fluctuations," there are subtle latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of pleasure and so forth that are specifically settled within the self; by means of their coloring through attachment, which acts as the gateway for their awakening.

That which has become delicate and fit for the chewing of aesthetic flavor (rasa) is the consciousness (*saṃvit*) of the sensitive connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*), the chewer himself; that by which this [consciousness] correctly knows is the mind (*manas*). Through the blissful activity consisting of the chewing of that [flavor], it possesses a form that is to be relished and tasted.
As it was said by the Sage: "They relish with the mind," and so forth.
Alternatively, *sukumāra* means eternally charming;
*svasaṃvit* is established through one's own experience.
The meaning is: "by that," namely, the operation of aesthetic relishing (*carvaṇā*).
After the words "rasadhvani," the word "is stated" (*ucyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
For thus, the first variety [of dhvani] is indeed far removed from the literal meaning (*vācya*) in its distinction.
For sometimes, when the expressed meaning is positive in form, it takes a negative form, as for example:
"O pious man, roam about with confidence; that dog has been killed today by a fierce lion dwelling in a thicket on the bank of the Godāvarī."
The *Locana* states that it is the suggestion of rasa (*rasadhvani*),
and that this is indeed *dhvani* itself,
and that this alone is the soul [of poetry] in its primary sense.
As for what Bhaṭṭanāyaka stated— that "being a part is not the same as being a form"—

if that criticism applies only to the suggestion of a thing (*vastu-dhvani*) and the suggestion of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra-dhvani*), then he has nonetheless accepted the suggestion of rasa (*rasa-dhvani*) as its very essence.

Since the third aspect, which consists of the relishing of rasa, is determined to transcend the two aspects of denotation (abhidhā) and suggestion (bhāvanā), we ourselves shall explain in various places that the dhvani of objects (vastu) and figures (alaṅkāra) culminates precisely in the dhvani of rasa; let this suffice for now. [The author] states the distinction of this [dhvani of rasa] from the dhvani of objects and so forth, beginning with "And that": *sa ca* etc. "Suggested by the power of the expressed" (*vācyasāmarthyākṣiptam*) is a term that pervades all three varieties [of dhvani]. *Bālapriyā* [comments]: He states the specific difference of this from the dhvani of objects and so forth. "And that" (*sa ca*). The meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is that [the word] has the suggested sense alone as its object; it is the suggested sense itself,
not the expressed sense.
The word *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*).
"That very" refers to *rasadhvani* alone;
by the restrictive particle *eva*, there is an exclusion of *vastudhvani* and the other types of suggestion.
The sense is that "self" is [applied] primarily;
the nature of being a self in words such as "entity" (*vastu*) and so forth is merely figurative,
not primary.
The word *iti* implies that what follows is stated immediately thereafter; this is the ellipsis.
The word *tat* means "that statement"; such is the sense.
The phrase "yadi nāma" (even if) expresses certainty when there is [otherwise] uncertainty;
it is a censure or a rejection, meaning, in effect, a negation of selfhood.
The word "should be" (bhavet) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

The meaning is that such a statement would constitute a negation of the very nature of *vastu-dhvani* and *alaṅkāra-dhvani* alone, but not of *rasa-dhvani*. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of *rasa*... (rasa-iti).

To the question "How is this understood?", he says: "By the relishing of rasa," and so forth, ending with "from the determination. He states "the object" (*vastu*) [etc. to show that the negation of the status of being the soul (*ātmatva*) for both the suggestion of an object (*vastudhvani*) and the suggestion of a poetic figure (*alaṃkāradhvani*) is precisely what we ourselves maintain; thus, that [objection] is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). [The phrase] "ending precisely with the suggestion of rasa" (*rasadhvaniparyantatvam eva*) [is used].

The meaning is that, just as between the two expressed elements—namely, the matter (*vastu*) and the figure (*alaṅkāra*)—so too between those two when they are suggested (*dhvanyamāna*), they ultimately result in being suggestive of some *rasa* by virtue of their nature as *vibhāvas* and so forth; thus, they find their final rest (*viśrānti*) solely in *rasadhvani*.
For it is the state of being the locus of repose that constitutes primary selfhood (*ātmatva*), and that belongs exclusively to *rasadhvani*.

However, in the case of suggestion (dhvani) consisting of a matter (vastu) or an ornament (alaṅkāra), there is a superiority over the expressed meaning (vācya) due to its being suggested; thus, its status as the "self" (ātman) is non-primary.
And with reference to that, the general statement "dhvani is the soul of poetry" is made—this is the intended sense.

A misconception might arise because of the use of the neuter singular ending in the phrase "suggested by the power of the expressed" (*vācyasāmarthyakṣiptam*), leading one to think it is an adjective qualifying "mere matter" (*vastumātra*) alone; therefore, to dispel that, he explains: "suggested by the power of the expressed."
Regarding the phrase "bhedatraye" (in the three divisions):
by changing the gender and number of the term "vācyasāmarthyākṣiptam" (suggested by the power of the expressed), the general definition [of suggestion] is [stated as] *analaṅkāra* (non-ornament).
For although the function of *dhvanana* (suggesting) belongs exclusively to the word (*śabda*), [it is here attributed to the meaning].

Nevertheless, because the capacity of the meaning (*artha-sāmarthya*) as a cooperative factor is never absent anywhere, [the suggested sense] is implied by the capacity of the expressed (*vācya-sāmarthya*).

Even in the case of what is manifested through the resonance (*anuraṇana*) rooted in the power of the word (*śabda-śakti*), the comprehension of the suggested sense occurs solely through the capacity of the meaning;
we shall explain that the power of the word is merely an intermediate cooperative factor.
"One who possesses distinction is far [from contradiction]"—no one has any doubt that affirmation and negation are contradictory.
For this reason, he first cites those very two as examples: "O righteous man, wander with confidence; that dog has been killed today by him."
By the haughty lion dwelling in the thicket of creepers on the bank of the Godāvarī river.
The intention is that the application of the phrase "rasa and so forth are dear to the ignorant" is intended for both [of these cases].
If one reads "vācyasāmarthyakṣipta" (suggested by the power of the expressed meaning), then it serves as an adjective for the word "artha" (meaning). This is the general definition.

The meaning is that being suggested by the power of the expressed (*vācyasāmarthyākṣiptatva*) is the characteristic common to the three varieties of suggestion, such as the suggestion of a fact (*vastudhvani*).

One might object: "Since the operation of *dhvanana* (suggestion), like the operations of denotation (*abhidhā*) and so forth, has sound as its locus, the aforementioned definition is impossible for the suggestion of a fact and the other types"; thus he raises this doubt with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). He provides the resolution with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), and so forth.

Now, one might object: "In *dhvani* rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*), it is the power of words alone that acts as the auxiliary cause, and not the others. To this he says: "The power of words," and so forth.
Then, [anticipating the objection] "In that case, let there be no power of words," he says: "The power of words" [is present].
It is an intermediate auxiliary cause, which assists the capacity of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*).
"We shall explain" means that the remainder [of the sentence] is "in the determination of the subdivisions based on the power of words. In the commentary (vṛtti), it says "the first subdivision."
The meaning is that difference consists merely in the nature of things such as injunctions and prohibitions. "Possessing a vast distinction" means being exceedingly different.
He establishes an absolute distinction in the *Locana*, beginning with "vidhi" and so forth:
"Affirmation and negation" refers to the affirmation and negation of a single action;
they are "contradictory."
Contradiction (*virodha*) means either the impossibility of coexistence in one place at the same time, or difference (*bhinnatva*).
The particle *iti* indicates a manner or mode.
The meaning here is "in this regard.
"Vimati" means a contrary opinion; "avimatyartham" means for the sake of [eliminating] such contrary opinions.
That is to say, because there is an absence of disagreement regarding the reason;
or rather, for this purpose, namely to demonstrate absolute difference—
those very two, which have become the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*), are indeed affirmation and negation.
The explanation of the word "yathā" (as) is "udāharati" (he cites).
This means that having extracted [passages] from elsewhere, he brings forward those sentences that establish that point, thereby leading them into this treatise.
He recites the "chāyā" (shadow-text): "bhrama," and so forth.
The reading is also "vastabdham.
The gloss is "godānadīkacchanikuñjavāsine" (dwelling in the bower of the marshes of the Godā river). In that context, the word "godā" refers to the Godāvarī.

The gloss on the words *kaccha* and so forth is "riverbank, creeper-thicket, and forest" (*locanam*). This statement is made in order to protect a certain secret meeting place—which is regarded as the very essence of life—both from the fault of obstructing the movement of righteous people and from being deprived of its luster by having its sprouts and flowers plucked away.

In this context, although wandering is established by its own nature, it is set aside out of fear; thus, [the prohibition] consists in the absence of a prohibition, taking the form of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
But here the injunction (*vidhi*) is not of the nature of a command (*praiṣa*) and so forth; for this *loṭ* suffix denotes both permission (*atisarga*) and the proper time (*prāptakāla*).
Since there is a contradiction between existence and non-existence, it is impossible for both to be denoted simultaneously.

Anticipating the objection that the manifestation of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) would not arise if the specific identity of the speaker were not mentioned, the author provides the introductory remark beginning with "of a certain woman" (*kasyāścit*).
The reason for her protection is stated as "regarded as her very life and all-in-all";
the intended sense is that she is exceedingly dear to him.
Because of the obstacle caused by wandering—which is the hindrance consisting of a brief interruption of theft and sexual intercourse—there is that defect.
He states another defect as well: "tadava" and so forth;
by that righteous person, the shoots, flowers, and so on, are being plundered or seized.
Therefore, from that which effects the casting of a shadow and the production of complete darkness;
"therein" means "that being so."
"From itself," and so forth.

Here, the connection is as follows: in this sentence-meaning, which consists of an error (*bhrama*), there is a non-injunction (*avidhi*)—that is, an absence of prohibition (*niṣedhābhāva*)—but not an injunction (*niyoga*) consisting of a command (*praiṣa*) or the like.
To the question, "Why should it not be the primary [meaning] itself? he says: "consisting of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*)."
He states the reason for this with the words "by itself" and so forth:
[it is] "repelled," meaning prohibited, by an agent who fears a dog.
The word *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*).
As it has been stated: "When a prohibition has been established, there is indeed the application of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).

Regarding the injunction (*vidhi*) which consists in the absence of a prohibition, he states the meaning of the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) as the reason for this: "in the sense of permission" (*atisarga*), and so forth.
This is the meaning: the fear of dogs had previously negated the naturally established wandering.
Now, the absence of a negator for that wandering which has been negated is being stated;
therefore, this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
For that [prohibition] consists in the removal of a negation;
therefore, since there is currently no obstacle to wandering, the absence of a prohibition here constitutes a positive injunction,
but it is not a mandatory command (niyoga).
Indeed, she is not acting like a wanton woman by following the rule of wandering like a king, nor is she prohibiting wandering out of fear of dogs;
rather, she is stating the absence of anyone who would prohibit her from wandering.
Consequently, the optative suffix (*loṭ*) enters into the category of that which is being enjoined;
therefore, this *loṭ* is used in the sense of permission (*atisarga*), which consists of authorization for acting according to one's desire, and it also has the meaning of "the time having arrived."
Now, intending to establish that the prohibition of wandering is implied (*vyaṅgya*), he refutes its being directly expressed (*vācya*) and so forth, beginning with the words "In that case," etc.
"In that" refers to such a statement;
"of the two" refers to wandering.
The eye [perceives] the two meanings in the form of injunction and prohibition simultaneously, at one time,
and not successively.
Because the function [of denotation] ceases due to the absence of further operation;
for it has been stated [in the passage beginning] "the denotative power (*abhidhā*) cannot proceed to the qualificand" that the function of denotation cannot possibly operate after having ceased.

Now, one might object: the power of intention (*tātparya-śakti*), being inexhaustible, [proceeds] by the force of the sublation of the primary meaning—which consists in the non-connection of the referents of words such as "haughty religious student" (*dṛpta-dhārmika*) and so forth—with the intended [meaning].

In the view of Abhihitānvaya, because the cognition of the negation—which constitutes the sentence-meaning—is produced through the function of contradiction and the function of contrary indication (*viparītalakṣaṇā*), that meaning is rooted solely in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*).
For such is the conventional usage: "This was stated by him."
Therefore, it is neither "dear to the ignorant" (bālapriyā), nor "expressible" (vācyatā), nor "denotable" (abhidheyatā).
The reason for this is given as "being" (bhāva);
the meaning is that there is a contradiction between the two, just as there is between a pot and its absence.
This is because those two contradictory [qualities] cannot simultaneously enter the path of cognition;
that is to say, not successively.
The term "denotability" (vācyatā) is understood by ellipsis [from the preceding].
Here he states the reason: "because there is no operation after having ceased.
This means that once denotation (abhidhā) has ceased, it is impossible for it to occur again.
Since a single word, having made known one object through denotation (*abhidhā*), does not again make known another object through that same [denotation], for that reason—this is the meaning.
He states the proof for this: "the qualified object," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the phrase "having unexhausted power as its qualifier" (*akṣīṇaśaktiviśeṣaṇa*) is included.
"Denotation" (*abhidhā*) refers to the denotation of words such as "cow" (*go*). The "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the object, such as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*).
"Exhausted" means ceased;
"power" refers to the capacity for producing cognition—she who possesses that [capacity] is thus described.
The qualificand is the form of the individual, such as a cow and so forth.
The meaning of that is: "one should not go" and "one should not cause [another] to understand.
Therefore, the intention is that the denotatum of both the injunction and the prohibition is one and the same.
If this is so, then one might raise the objection: "In that case, let there be the cognition of the prohibition alone here," and so forth.
For that in which there is *tātparya* (intentional focus) is indeed the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). And here, the object of the *tātparya* is the prohibition of wandering;
therefore, that alone is the meaning of the sentence.
Because it is intended by him through that desire to speak (*vivakṣā*),

the *tātparya-śakti*— the power residing in the word, consisting of the capacity to produce the cognition of the intended meaning— is "unending" (*aparyavasitā*) in its operation of conveying [the sense], failing to reach a final conclusion.

It brings about the cognition of the negation which has become the meaning of the sentence. To the question "By what operation?", he says: "by indication" (lakṣaṇā). He states the cause for this indication: "due to contradiction" (virodha).
The meaning is: "on account of the relationship being of the nature of contradiction.

By stating, "because the literal meaning has no possible connection with the sentence-meaning," he demonstrates the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*) through the passage beginning with *dṛpta*.

Since the word *bhrama* would otherwise have its primary meaning [if taken literally], the mention of qualities such as "arrogance" (*dṛptatva*) would result in redundancy; therefore, there is a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) between the primary meaning—which consists of an injunction to wander—and the sentence-meaning constituted by the referents of the words *dṛpta* and so forth.
"Of that nature" means that which is the primary sublation of the object; "by its force" means by its assistance.
"In the view of the expressed connection" (abhihitānvaya) means by way of the theory of the connection of what has been expressed.
This means "in accordance with the view of the proponents of the theory of expressed connection" (abhihitānvayavādins). He states the conclusion: "Thus," and so forth.
Verbal power is denotation (abhidhā), and [the relation] is rooted in that.
The meaning is that the powers of *tātparya* (implication) and *lakṣaṇā* (indication) abide by relying upon *abhidhā* (denotation).
And it will be stated later: "Indication is the tail of denotation.
That is the meaning.
The meaning is that there is a prohibition against such wandering.
Regarding this, the *Locana* states: "The meaning is something other than the expressed.

This is not so; for here three operations are perceived: the operation of denotation (*abhidhā*) with respect to word-meanings whose nature is universal; [the operation of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)]; and [the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanā*)].
For denotation (*abhidhā*) is the capacity to comprehend a meaning based on convention (*samaya*); and that convention pertains only to that much [the general],
not to the specific portion.

Because [the general] is infinite and because it would deviate from two [of the particulars], the power of *tātparya* (intentional focus) resides in the sentence-meaning as a specific form, wherein [the words] are mutually related;
for according to the maxim: "Generalities, being otherwise established, lead to the understanding of the particular."
Bālapriyā says: "Thus," and so forth.
The meaning is that the conventional usage is "it has been stated" (*uktam*), and not the conventional usage "it has been manifested" (*vyañjitam*).
He provides the summary: "That is not so. [The term] "beyond the expressed" (vācyātirikta) means "beyond the denotable" (abhidheyātirikta).
Here, the cognition of a negation cannot occur through the function of contrary indication (viparītalakṣaṇā).
With the intention that there is no room for such a [fault], he refutes this view with the words "This is not," and so forth.
The meaning is that this view is not tenable.
To the question "Why?", he says "The three," and so forth.
In this worldly convention,
there are three operations— namely, denotation (*abhidhā*), intention (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—
belonging to the word.
The remainder [of the verse] is as follows:
"they are experienced" means they are known.
He states the object of the first operation: "in regard to word-meanings."

"In universal natures" means in the forms of universals such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth; the phrase "the function of denotation" refers to words such as "cow" and so forth— this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
He states its essential nature with the words "depending on convention" (samayāpekṣayā) and so forth.
This means by way of depending on convention, that is, through the cooperation of grasping a linguistic sign (*saṅketa*).
There is also a reading: *samayāpekṣe*.
The phrase "for that purpose" means that it depends upon the grasping of a convention (*saṅketa*).
"Capacity for understanding the meaning" is the power to convey the meaning.
"In that much alone" refers to the very category (*sāmānya*) of the word-meaning itself.
He states what is excluded by the particle *eva* with the words "not," and so forth.
Regarding the specific aspect, which consists of the individual (*vyakti*), he asks "Why? and answers with the word "because of infinity" (*ānantyāt*).
The meaning is that because particular instances (*viśeṣa*) are infinite;
thus, it is impossible to establish a convention (*samaya*) regarding every particular instance,
and the implication is that [the convention] would have to be infinite.
He states another reason as well: "And because of the deviation of one [part]" (*vyabhicārāccaikasya*).

This means that because each individual specific feature (*viśeṣāṃśa*) deviates from the others. For instance, by the word "cow" (*go*), the cognition of a particular cow-individual (*govyaktiviśeṣa*) arises.
In that case, one should understand the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) by the principle that there is no convention (*samaya*) pertaining to other individual cows.
Alternatively, in the phrase "and convention" (*samayaśca*), the word *samaya* means the grasping of a linguistic convention (*saṅketagraha*).

He states the fault in the grasping of a convention being a constituent of linguistic usage (*vyavahārāṅga*) with respect to every particular (*viśeṣa*) as follows: "Because of infinity" (*ānantyāt*).

The meaning is that because particulars (*viśeṣa*) are infinite, it is impossible to grasp the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) for every single particular. To the objection that the grasping of that convention might then serve as the basis for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) with respect to just one particular, he replies: "And because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding a single [particular]. The meaning is that since the cognition of a specific individual such as a cow arises through a word like "cow" even for someone who has not grasped the convention for that specific individual, the grasping of the convention is thus subject to deviation.
Now he shows the second operation along with its object, beginning with "tataḥ" (therefore): "tataḥ" means from the aforementioned reason;
"parasparānvite" means mutually connected through the relationship of subordinate and principal by virtue of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

Regarding the sentence-meaning as its object—which consists of a particular form composed of the particulars (individuals) implied by those various general-category entities—the power of intention (*tātparya-śakti*) resides therein. That sentence-meaning is the "supreme" one, insofar as it is to be presented as the primary [meaning]. Those [words] which have that [meaning] as their purpose are called *tatpara*; the state of being such is *tātparya*, and the power is of that nature.
The word "of words" (*padānām*) is to be supplied [as the object].
To make this implication understood, he says: "universals," and so forth.
Universals are the meanings in the form of universals expressed by words; otherwise, there would be no comprehension of particulars.
Because [the universal] is unestablished— meaning that its connection with action and so forth is unestablished—
they cause one to understand the particular, which consists of the individual instances that serve as its substratum;
they make it known through their invariable concomitance with it.

However, if the reading is *sāmānyānanyathā*, then in that context, at the second stage, nothing other than "error" (*bhrama*) is perceived, because only the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is apprehended.
For it is not the case here as it is in expressions such as "a hamlet on the Ganges" or "the boy is a lion," where the one desiring to establish mere positive concomitance is frustrated.
Because of the absence of fitness;
likewise, that dog which did not prevent your wandering was killed by the lion.
Therefore, since the cause for preventing your wandering is now complete, your wandering is no longer appropriate—thus, there is no deficiency whatsoever in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Therefore, since there is no possibility of sublation of the primary meaning here, there is no occasion for indirect indication (*viparīta-lakṣaṇā*). Or, let it be so;
nevertheless, this [indication] does not yet transfer to a second position.

For it is thus: the application of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) occurs when there is a sublation of the primary meaning, and sublation is precisely the cognition of contradiction. Yet, in this case, there is no contradiction among the word-meanings within their own nature.
If it is argued that there is a mutual contradiction—then this contradiction must be understood to lie in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
[The word] "words" (*padāni*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

The meaning is that because the generalities—the objects in the form of the generalities expressed by themselves—are established otherwise [than through the specific], they lack invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Having thus established the preliminary framework, he begins to refute the [theoretical] characteristics—starting with the words "In that regard" (*tatra ca*) and so forth.
"In that regard" (*tatra*) means in the sphere of the power of intention (*tātparya-śakti*).
"In the second stage" (*dvitīya-kakṣyāyām*) means in the second level, in relation to the object of the function of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*).
The meaning is that from the injunction "wander" and so forth, only the act of wandering is understood, and nothing else in the form of a prohibition;
this refers to the mere positive concomitance (*anvayamātra*).
The meaning is "of the sentence-meaning alone.
The particle *eva* (only/alone) is for the purpose of clarifying the sense of the word *mātra* (mere/only).
It should be understood that what is excluded by this is the aforementioned [category], namely, that which is distinct from an injunction (*vidhi*), and so forth.
"Because it has been undertaken" means "because it has been known.
He establishes what was stated with the words beginning "for not," and so forth.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "Thus, there is indeed no deficiency in the positive concomitance (anvaya). If "in the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyām*) and so forth were an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), then "positive concomitance" (*anvaya*) means the concomitance between the expressed property (*vācya*) and the subject (*dharmin*).
"Even while desiring to exist," that is, even as one has begun to come into being,
"one is struck down," meaning one is afflicted;
this is because of a lack of fitness.

The meaning is that there is an absence of a relationship such as the locus-and-located (ādhārādheya) relation between the substratum denoted by words like "Gaṅgā"—namely, a particular stream—and [the object] such as a hamlet (ghoṣa).
"Kṣati" means sublation (bādhā).
He states the resulting conclusion with the words "ata eva" and so forth.
Precisely for this reason— namely, because there is no failure of the positive concomitance (anvaya)—

the author, intending to demonstrate the function of suggestion (dhvani) regarding the purpose of indication (lakṣaṇā), says "Let it be so," etc., while provisionally accepting that indication belongs within the level of the power of intention (tātparyaśakti) as conceived by the opponent,
yet refuting its inclusion therein.
That is *lakṣaṇā* (indication). "Transferred to the second stage" means that it resides within the level of the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
The word "tāvat" is used either in the sense of agreement or as an embellishment of the sentence.
He establishes this very point with the words beginning with "tathāhi."
"The postulation of indication" (lakṣaṇāyāḥ praklṛptiḥ) means the conceptualization of the presentation of the indicated meaning (lakṣyārthopasthitikalpanā).
"And sublation" (bādhā ca) [is as follows].
The meaning is that "the object of sublation" (bādhāpadārtha) [is the definition].
There is a variant reading, "sā ca" (and that), in some places.
[This means] "only the cognition of contradiction."
The term "sublation of the primary meaning" (*mukhyārthabādhā*) means the very cognition of the contradiction of that primary meaning.
By the use of the particle *eva* ("only"), he shows that there is no dispute on this point.

Having kept in mind the dilemma—whether the contradiction of the stated [meanings] occurs within their own nature or between them—he refutes the first alternative with the words beginning "And not... (*na ca*).
This is the meaning of the verse.
Here, in the context of the definition, the connection is:
"But there is no contradiction among the meanings of words within their own selves."

"With itself" means together with its own self. He raises a second objection with the word "mutually" (*parasparam*); the phrase "of the categories" (*padārthānām*) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis.
He explains this with the words "Therefore, this... and so forth. There is no cognition of contradiction when the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has not been apprehended;

moreover, the apprehension of the concomitance does not occur through the power of denotation (*abhidhā-śakti*), because that power, having been exhausted by the apprehension of the word-meanings, ceases to function. Thus, the apprehension of the concomitance occurs solely through the power of intention (*tātparya-śakti*).

[Objection: "In that case, [the sentence] 'A hundred excellent elephants on the tip of a finger'—but since that connection is sublated by another means of knowledge, such as perception, even though it is understood, the sentence that causes that cognition is invalid, just like [the cognition of] silver in mother-of-pearl. [Reply: In the case of "The boy is a lion," after the emergence of the sublation of the connection provided by the power of intention (*tātparyaśakti*) residing in the second stage, there arises a distinct power of denotation (*abhidhā*) and power of intention which is different from those two. *Bālapriyā*: Then...
That [relation] is well known as being rooted in the definition [of the terms].
This contradiction has been accepted by you.
"In the mutual connection of word-meanings" means that which is to be understood or known when there is a mutual connection of the referents of words.
"And not," and so forth.
"In the case of what is not apprehended"—that is, what is unknown—"there is no cognition of non-contradiction"; this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).

The meaning is that when the locus (*dharmin*) is not cognized, it is impossible for a contradiction in the form of a property (*dharma*) to be cognized therein. To the objection, "In that case, let it be so [when the locus is cognized]," he replies with the words beginning "And the cognition...
[and] "Because of the lack of operation."
The meaning is that there is an absence of [literal] function (*vyāpāra*).

"Sublation of the primary meaning" (*mukhyārthabādha*) refers to that [condition] in the context of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), such as in the case of "The boy is a lion," where—by virtue of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and intentionality (*tātparya*)—there occurs an apprehension of a relation, such as identity (*tādātmya*), between the primary meaning of the word "lion" and the referent of the word "boy. It is in the presence of such a connection that [indication operates].

There is the cognition of contradiction (*viruddhatva*). And that contradiction consists in the fact that, within that anvaya, both the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogikatva*) with respect to lions and the coreferentiality (*anuyogikatva*) with respect to boys are absent; thus, it is sublated (*bādhitatva*) by virtue of having that nature.
For this very reason, some maintain that it is the absence of the speaker’s intended meaning (*vaktṛvivakṣitatvābhāva*).

The sense is that even when there is a certainty of sublation (*bādhaniścaya*), the cognition produced by the sentence still occurs. In this context, he raises an objection incidentally with the words "But if this were so," and so forth.
This means that one would have to admit the comprehension of a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) from a sentence even when that connection has been sublated.
Anticipating this objection, he responds with "What is it not? and so forth;
that is, it certainly does exist.
He provides an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) with "Ten," and so forth.
The meaning is: "as in the case of the collection of sentences cited in the Mahābhāṣya, such as ‘ten pomegranates, six cakes,’ and so forth.

In that instance, although there is a comprehension of the connection [of words] from each individual sentence—such as “ten pomegranates”—upon the ellipsis of the verb *bhavati* (there are), there nonetheless does not arise a cognition of a single qualified object consisting of the mutual relation (*saṃsarga*) among all the sentence-meanings, due to the absence of causes such as syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
The meaning is that, since that [positive concomitance] exists in the case at hand, the cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) indeed occurs.
He states the distinction with the words "but" (*kiṃ tu*):

the connection is that "even though that positive concomitance is apprehended, it is sublated by another means of valid cognition, such as perception, just like [the cognition of] silver in mother-of-pearl."
The word "iti" indicates the reason; the meaning is that the positive concomitance (anvaya) is sublated. [This refers to] that cognition.
[Objection: "In that case, would not expressions such as 'The boy is a lion' also lack validity? To this, he says: "The lion," and so forth.

When the connection has been offered—that is, made known—by means of *śakti* (power), there follows immediately thereafter the manifestation—that is, the cognition—of contradiction (*bādhaka*), which is opposition.
Regarding the phrase "devoid of its sublation" (*tadvādhakavidhurī*):

in the process of neutralizing that sublation—that is, the sublation of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—the third power itself, known as *lakṣaṇā* (indication), which is skilled in neutralizing that sublation, manifests.
[Objection: But if this were so, would not even the expression "The boy is a lion" (*siṃho vaṭuḥ*) possess the nature of poetry?
Because the self, characterized by resonance (*dhvanana*), exists here as well, since it will be explained immediately thereafter.
[Objection: But would not the conventional usage of "living being" (*jīva*) also apply to a jar?
For the self, being all-pervasive (*vibhu*), exists there too.

If it is argued that the designation "living being" (jīva) applies only to a body endowed with a specific substratum when a self exists—and not to just any body—then it is equally the case that the designation "poetry" applies to a body consisting of words and meanings made beautiful by the propriety of qualities and ornaments, provided that the essence called *dhvani* exists;
and there is no lack of substance in the self [in either case]. Thus, the two cases are identical.
Nor is it the case that *bhakti* alone is *dhvani*;
for *bhakti* is the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) residing in the third stage,
whereas the function of suggestion (*dhvanana*) resides in the fourth stage.
For indeed, you yourselves maintain that figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) operates only when three conditions are present.
Among these, the sublation of the primary meaning is rooted in other means of valid cognition such as direct perception;
and the ground for the indication—such as proximity and so forth—which is enjoined, is likewise to be understood solely through other means of valid cognition.
The term *bālapriyā* means "skilled" or "capable" in causing sublation (*bādhanā*).
It "shines forth" or "proceeds";
thus, the intended meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) therein is not subject to sublation—this is the sense.
Fearing the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in accepting [the existence of] defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), he raises an objection: "But if this were so...
The connection is that [the objection] is made because the self (*ātman*) exists here as well, that is, because it possesses being (*sattva*).
He answers by means of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*): "But [is it not the case] even in the case of a jar?"
He states the rebuttal to that [objection] with the words "of the body" (*śarīrasya*).
Regarding "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*):
it refers to that which is endowed with a specific substratum or configuration (*saṃsthāna*) characterized by limbs such as hands and feet.
He says, "Our reply is equal," with the words beginning "guṇa" (quality).

The body of that [poetry] consists of word and meaning alone, which are beautiful through the propriety (*aucitya*) of qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) directed toward aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
And so forth.

And the phrase "it is the same" means that just as there is no lack of essence in the Self (ātman) even when it is connected with insubstantial things like jars and so forth, likewise there is no lack of essence whatsoever in the Self known as resonance (dhvananātmaka), even though it exists in worldly sentences.
Anticipating the objection that "in this case, devotion itself would be *dhvani*," he refutes it with the words "But it is not so," and so forth.

The meaning is that even when there is the presence of suggestion (*dhvanana*) in a case of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is not [the case that] "there is no *dhvani*. This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
He states the reason for this: "Because devotion...
Since the two are situated in different categories, there is a difference in their objects;
that is the meaning of "therefore."
"In the presence of the triad" means when the three conditions, such as the sublation of the primary meaning, are present. "You yourselves say" refers to this.
The meaning is that you yourselves, who assert the non-difference between indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and suggestion (*dhvanana*), have said this;
and there is also the reading "your opinion" (*bhavatāṃ matam*).

Intending to establish later that among the three conditions—the sublation of the primary meaning and so forth—it is only the last one that is cognizable through the function of suggestion (*dhvani*), [the author] first states that the first two are established by others, beginning with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*).
The phrase "it is designated" (abhidhīyate) means that it is expressed by such statements as "due to proximity with the object to be designated" (abhidheyena sāmīpyāt).

Having thus stated that the two causes of sublation (*bādhā*) have different objects, he states that the purpose (*prayojana*) has no other object than its own nature by means of a descriptive explanation, beginning with "As for that which... (*yattu*).

As for this "locana" (the eye), which is the purpose— such as the extreme purity, coolness, and desirability of Ghoṣa’s voice, or the boy's possession of extraordinary prowess— which cannot be expressed by other words and is not apprehended through other means of knowledge, the word has no operation therein.
For instance: the inference that [the boy] possesses those qualities because of his proximity to them is inconclusive;
furthermore, being denotable by the word "lion" is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the boy.
Now, if the inference is that wherever there is the application of such a word, there is the possession of those qualities—
For that [perception] as well, another fundamental means of valid cognition must be stated at the time of grasping the pervasion, yet none exists;
nor is this a case of memory, because memory is impossible regarding what has not been previously experienced.
Regarding the phrase "but [the fact] that it possesses extreme purity and so forth, or an excellence of prowess," the connection is as follows.
As for the expression "of the cowherd settlement" (ghoṣasya):

this was stated with the intention that, although extreme purity and the like are conveyed primarily through the riverbank, they are also conveyed in relation to the cowherd settlement by way of the latter being situated on the bank; for that [settlement] alone is the object of the ultimate purport.
Alternatively, its meaning is "that which has the primary sense (ghoṣa) as its basis. "Not expressible by another word" means not cognizable by a word other than a figurative (lākṣaṇika) one.
Regarding the phrase "by another means of valid cognition" (pramāṇāntara):
The meaning is "a means of valid cognition other than verbal testimony. As for the phrase "or of the student," the triad beginning with "the purpose" is to be supplied [to each].
[Objection: "In that case, then, there is no cognition of that [object] even by means of a word; so enough with searching for another operation. To this, he says:
"In that regard," and so forth. He confirms what was stated previously—that there is indeed an operation of the word regarding the aforementioned purpose—by saying: "For thus," and so forth.
"Because of its proximity to that": the riverbank possesses qualities such as being extremely pure because of its proximity to the Ganges.
The meaning is that this is an inference such as "like a sage or similar person.
It is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it deviates (*vyabhicāri*) in the case of skulls found on the banks of the Gaṅgā and so forth.
[Regarding the word] "lion" (*siṃha*):...
"The boy possesses the nature of a lion because he is denotable by the word 'lion,' like an acknowledged lion"—
in this [argument], the reason consisting in being denotable by the word 'lion' is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).
Anticipating another inference, he refutes it with the words "Now," and so forth.
"Thus" means by way of indication (*lakṣaṇayā*). "This is inference" [means:]...

Therefore, the bank possesses the properties residing in that which is denoted by the word "Ganges," because it is the object of the application of the word "Ganges" through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā);
likewise, the boy possesses the properties residing in that which is denoted by the word "lion," because he is the object of the application of the word "lion" through secondary signification.

The formal argument (prayoga) to be understood here is as follows: "That which is the object of the application of a term by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) possesses a property that resides in what is denoted by that term," and so forth;
or alternatively, this is the inference.
Thus, the meaning is that the reason (hetu) is qualified by pervasion (vyāpti). Regarding the phrase "of that too" and so forth:
it refers to the time when the apprehension of that pervasion occurs.

"Fundamental" (maulikam) means that which exists as a means of proof (*sādhana*) in the "root," namely in the form of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is a constituent part of inference. "Other means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntaram*) refers to perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.
And it is not the case that there exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is to be supplied [to the sentence].

In a case where an inference depends upon a pervasion (*vyāpti*) established through a general principle (*sāmānyamukha*), it must be stated that the apprehension of the pervasion between the subject property (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*) under consideration—or between their respective homologues—is achieved through perception (*pratyakṣa*) or other such means.
The meaning is that, because there is a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases involving secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), such [a cognition] ought not to arise.
As for the phrase "and not":

this refers to the cognition of a purpose such as sanctity; for otherwise, since no restrictive rule would be understood, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the listener could have no determination that "this is what the speaker intended. Therefore, in this case, there must indeed be an operation of the word itself.
And the function is not of the nature of denotation, because of the absence of convention; nor is it of the nature of intentionality.
Because it is perceived through its own continuity,
it does not consist of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), for the reason already stated— that there is no faltering in its application— is absent here.

For even in that case, if there were a faltering of the literal sense, there would be an infinite regress, as the cause or purpose for that faltering would require yet another primary meaning to be sublated.

Therefore, the name "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) given by some is merely a whim. Consequently, this [fourth type] is not distinct from direct denotation (*abhidhā*), intention (*tātparya*), or indication (*lakṣaṇā*); it is simply non-remembrance (*asmṛti*). This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).
And the meaning is that this is not established by memory.
He states the reason for this: "because it is impossible [to have memory] regarding what has not been experienced.
Now, one might object: "How could that memory be produced? To this, he states another reason: "due to the restriction," and so forth.
The meaning is that because no such regulator is perceived, there would follow the consequence of uncertainty regarding the intended purpose here.

However, the point is that if one accepts the operation of manifestation (*vyañjana*), the restriction will be established through specific auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-viśeṣa*). He concludes with "Thus," and so forth.
The word *iti* here indicates the reason; the meaning is:
"since the purpose is not to be understood from anything else in this way, therefore [it is stated].
Regarding the word *atra*:
The meaning is that [the purpose] lies in sanctification (*pāvanatva*) and so forth.
Now, in order to demonstrate the establishment of the function of suggestion (*vyañjanavyāpāra*) by means of the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), he says: "And the function," etc.
The word "here" (*atra*) is to be supplied as a syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
"Due to the absence of convention" means because there is no conventional agreement regarding the purifying power and so forth of words such as "Ganges.
"In the cognition of the connection" means in the initial comprehension of the connection between the expressed meanings.
"From what has been stated," and so forth.
The previously mentioned reason is the sublation of the primary meaning and so on;

from that [reason] arises "the state of having a faltering course"—that is, the quality of a word whose cognitive operation (avabodhana-vyāpāra) is faltering, meaning its course is stumbling or being obstructed. That state is the essence [of the word].
The meaning is that there is an absence of "falling away from its own primary meaning.

For instance, when words such as *gaṅgā* (the Ganges) must convey a bank or similar object due to the sublation of their primary meaning and other factors, they indeed fall away from their own primary meaning, which is the specific stream of water and so forth.
Likewise, when a purpose such as purification is to be understood, there is no deviation from its own meaning, such as "the bank" (tīra); this is the sense of the word "therefore" (yataḥ).
Alternatively, it means "for the very reason already stated."
The meaning is: "because of the previously mentioned reason, such as 'due to the non-occurrence of [the cognition of] day'";
and he states another reason: "because of the absence of faltering gait.
The meaning of this is to be understood as before.
Even while conceding this fault, he states: "In that case also," and so forth.

The meaning is that even if one accepts that there is a faltering of the word's movement from the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) due to a motive (*prayojana*), there would still result an infinite regress of indication (*lakṣaṇānavasthā*) through the repeated conceptualization of further bases for indication. Furthermore, the passage ending with "and the function is not of the nature of denotation" (*nābhidhā*) is an explanatory expansion (*vivaraṇa*) of the preceding text. It is not denotation;... [text continues] ...is not denotation.
One should consult the *Kāvyaprakāśa* for the passage beginning with "due to the absence of convention" (*samayābhāvāt*).
Some maintain that when a word such as "Ganges" indicates the riverbank through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it further indicates a purpose such as its sanctity;
for this very reason, they call this type of indication "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).
He refutes that view with the words "for this very reason," and so forth.
"For this very reason" means precisely because of faults such as infinite regress; thus, [the name] has been assigned.
The phrase "of the operation [directed toward] the object of the purpose" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Mere obsession" means merely the persistence in refuting *dhvani*; that is to say, it is caused by that [refutation].
And it will be stated later: "Therefore, this is not the domain of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on what is indicated."
"Therefore," and so forth.
Regarding "suggestion" (*dhvanana*):

one must accept that the function (*vyāpāra*)—which consists of suggestion and the like—is designated by synonymous terms such as *dhvanana*, *dyotana*, *vyañjana*, *pratyāyana*, and *avagamana*. This is what is to be admitted.

As he will say: "When, having set aside the primary function, there is a perception of the meaning through a secondary function (guṇavṛtti), the word's operation does not falter with respect to the result aimed at therein."
Thus it is.
Accordingly, the power to convey the meaning by depending on context is the power of denotation (*abhidhā-śakti*).

The power to bring about the comprehension of the meaning through the assistance of the impossibility of the meaning being otherwise is the power of intention (*tātparya-śakti*). The power to manifest the meaning by depending on auxiliary factors such as the sublation of the primary meaning is the power of indication (*lakṣaṇā-śakti*).

The function of *dhvani* (resonance) is the power to illuminate an object, aided by the cognition of the perceiver which is purified by the appearance of that object and rooted in the comprehension of the meaning produced by those three powers.
This is determined—meaning ascertained—by those designations or words which are synonyms for it.
Thus, the designation "dhvani" and so forth is well-established.

The meaning is that since a designation does not exist without that which is designated, this [definition] must be determined through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the hearing of that [designation]; "it must be accepted" implies "even by those who do not wish it.
Regarding the point that there is no definition in the case of the purpose (*prayojana*), he states the consensus of the root text: "just as... and so forth.

Having thus established the function of suggestion (*dhvanana*) as having the [implied] purpose for its object, he demonstrates the nature of the various functions in order to clarify that very function as distinct from the other three functions—beginning with the words "by that" (*tena*), etc. "Dependent on convention" (*samayāpekṣā*):

the meaning is that the power residing in a word called "denotation" (*abhidhā*) is the capacity to convey a specific meaning, operating in conjunction with the grasping of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) for that meaning.
It should be understood that what is called "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) is a distinct category of reality (*padārthāntara*), a synonym for "power" (*śakti*).
"Otherwise than that" means otherwise than that denotation (*abhidhā*).

Otherwise, it is that [inference] which has as its companion the impossibility (*anupapatti*)—the non-occurrence—of a specific form of meaning (*anvitārtha*) without the self (*ātman*), due to the absence of purpose (*prayojana*) and so forth.
However, some explain it as: "that which has as its companion the impossibility of that specific form of the connected meaning occurring otherwise, namely, in the absence of *tātparya*."
"Artha" means "having a combined meaning. "Mukhya" means...
"It depends on that" means it depends on the triad beginning with the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādhā*) which acts as its auxiliary.
"By its power" means by those three powers previously mentioned, such as denotation (*abhidhā*) and the rest.

That which has been produced is the comprehension or understanding of meanings— namely, the meanings of words (*padārtha*), the meanings of sentences (*vākyārtha*), and the indicated meanings (*lakṣyārtha*)— and it arises from that very root;

for, by means of its manifestation, it is purified through the continuous perception of the denotable meanings and so forth, and thus possesses an excellence characterized by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

And he [the author], suppressing the three prior functions and making *locana* the primary essence of poetry (*kāvyātman*), has stated— with the intention that negation is foremost— that even though the subject matter is a purpose (*prayojana*), it is treated as a subject matter of negation.
Furthermore, this was stated merely as a formal admission (*abhyupagamamātreṇa*).
But there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) here,
because of the absence of either complete rejection or transference to another meaning; for its operation does not occur in that which is rooted in the power of the literal sense.
Furthermore, a difference in capacity due to a difference in auxiliary factors is quite evident;

for example, when that very same word is assisted by the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, its operation is that of an inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*) in the apprehension of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*); whereas, when it is assisted by the sense organs (*akṣa*) and so forth, its operation is that of a conceptualizer (*vikalpaka*).

The capacity to illuminate the meaning—namely, the power to manifest the meaning characterized by the purpose (*prayojana*) and so forth—is accompanied by the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) of the recipient who has been prepared for the sake of the "delight of the simple" (*bālapriyā*). This is what is meant; the word "it is said" (*ity uktam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
Let it be that such is this [poetry]; but how is it the very soul of poetry? To this he says: "And that" (sa ca).
The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis.
"And that [suggestion] is the soul of poetry"—this is the connection.
The reason for this is "because it is the predominant element.
The reason for that is "having occurred previously," and so forth.
The meaning is that although [suggestion] proceeds spontaneously with respect to the triad beginning with denotation (*abhidhā*), it nevertheless subordinates them.
Since the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) constitutes the very soul of poetry (*kāvyātman*), it should be understood that suggestiveness (*vyañjanā*) likewise possesses that same status.
Now, one might object: "In such cases as 'O pious man, wander about' (*abhrama dhārmika*), the prohibition of wandering is the object of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."

It follows, therefore, that the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) has as its object another purpose [beyond the literal]. Now, one might ask: how is it that the author of the *Vṛtti*, by stating "it takes the form of a negation," has declared that the function of suggestion has negation as its object? To this he replies with the words "with this intention" (*ityāśayena*), and so forth.

The connection is as follows: "With this intention"—meaning with the aforementioned purport—it was stated that "although it has a purpose as its object, it is said to have negation as its object because it is primarily characterized by negation."
That which has a purpose and an object is [the subject].
Here, the purpose consists of such things as the protection of a secret meeting place and the independent roaming of a wanton woman.
This is by way of producing the cognition of a prohibition, primarily through the nature of a prohibition.
Regarding the phrase "it has been said":
the meaning is that it has been demonstrated by the statement that sometimes, even when the nature [of the object] is inexpressible, there is a form of negation.
In this context, the prohibition of wandering is indeed the very thing to be indicated (*lakṣya*).
The meaning is that because the stated purpose is an object of cognition preceded by the cognition of a negation, it is expressed as having the nature of a negation.

However, in reality, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) does not operate here; thus, in accordance with the text of the Vṛtti, he says "by mere admission," etc., meaning by mere admission, that is, by mere bold assertion (prauḍhivāda).

This is the communication of a negation through the function of contrary indication (*viparītalakṣaṇā*). He states the reason why indication does not apply here with the words "absolutely" (*atyanta*).
For where there is either the absolute negation of the expressed meaning or its transference to another sense, there indeed lies indication (lakṣaṇā).
But here, neither of these two applies to the expressed meaning in the form of an injunction to wander; this is the sense.
[Objection: "In that case, let this be simply suggestion (dhvani) based on the power of the meaning (arthaśaktimūla)."
To the question, "Why is it not a definition even in that case? he says: "For it is not... [and] "rooted in the power of the object," which contains the reason within itself.
The word "in the case of *dhvani*" (*dhvanau*) is to be supplied [as the locus].
Its function is the operation of *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

Furthermore, for the function of *dhvanana* (suggestion) rooted in the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*), factors such as the specific characteristics of the speaker and the person to be addressed (*vaktṛ-boddhavya-vaiśiṣṭya*) serve as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

He states that there is a distinction between these two because of the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*) and so forth in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), by saying "the auxiliary" (*sahakārī*).

He clarifies the stated point through an illustration with the words "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth; [it refers to] "of that very [word]," meaning of that which was employed precisely for the purpose of conveying a meaning.
"Of the word" refers to words such as "bring the cow.
By the phrase "recollection and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes the cognition of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*).
"The function of being an inferential indicator" means the capacity to serve as an inferential indicator.
The logical application (*prayoga*) to be understood here is as follows: "This speaker intends to say this very thing, because he employs this specific word," and so forth.
And this has been stated in the third *udyota* [of the *Locana*] regarding the term *akṣādi*:
*akṣa* refers to the sense organs such as the eye (*cakṣus*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), its contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth are included.
Thus much must be conceded by those who maintain the theory of "expression of the related" (*abhihitānvaya-vāda*).

Furthermore, even the proponent of "expression of the already-related" (*anvitābhidhāna-vāda*), having grasped in his heart the principle that "the meaning of a word is that toward which it is directed," desires the function of expression (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) to extend very far indeed, like an arrow.
If its operation is long-lasting, how can it be one?
Because its objects are distinct.
Or is it manifold?
Due to the difference in its object and auxiliary causes, it is logical that [the result] be of a different class.

Furthermore, regarding an effect that is of the same class, scholars who know the nature of things have refuted the notion of an operation occurring after a cessation [of activity] in the case of sound, action, cognition, and so forth.
And in the case of an effect that is of a different class, our own position alone holds true.
The function of conceptualization (*vikalpakatvavyāpāra*) is the capacity to produce determinate cognition (*savikalpakajñāna*).
For a word, through the cooperation of the auditory organ and other factors, produces its own direct perception;

furthermore, according to a specific view, a name-word (*saṃjñāśabda*) being known at the time of the contact of the eye with the named object (*saṃjñin*) produces a direct perception of that named object qualified by itself (the name). This is the distinction between the views.

"Iyad" means "only this much": namely, that there exists the operation of sound (*dhvani*) which transcends the triad beginning with denotation (*abhidhā*). It is "not to be denied" (*anapahnavanīyam*), meaning it is not to be rejected.
The sense is that, on the contrary, it must be accepted.
Regarding the phrase "even he who," etc.,
the word *api* has the meaning of the word *tu*.

The connection is with the phrase "to whomever [it] desires. First, there is the apprehension of the relationship (*saṅgati*) between a specific sentence, such as "Bring the cow," and its respective sentence-meaning; subsequently, through the methods of inclusion (*āvāpa*) and exclusion (*udvāpa*), there is the apprehension of the relationship of words such as "cow" with their own meanings as connected to others. This process, belonging to the school of those who maintain that the meaning is the related (*anvitābhidhānavāda*), should be understood from other sources.

Regarding the phrase *yatparaḥ*: that meaning which is "supreme"—meaning that which is primarily expressed and constitutes the object of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*)—is the word-meaning, that which is denoted by the word.
The term *śara* [in the compound *śaravat*] is equivalent to the operation of an arrow (*śaravyāpāra*).

"It desires" means as it has been said: "This is a single, long-lasting operation, like that of an arrow. Just as an arrow discharged by an archer performs various actions—such as piercing another's armor and breaking their limbs—by means of a single operation called "velocity," so too does this [cognition].

The meaning is that a word employed by a skilled poet produces the cognitions of both the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning—as well as those intended to be indicated (lakṣya) or suggested (vyaṅgya)—by means of a single operation known as denotation (abhidhā).

Having thus presented his view, [the author] refutes the first alternative of the question—"Is that long operation of denotation one, or is it manifold for each respective object?"—in order to make him accept the process of suggestion (dhvanana), stating "of that," etc.;
the word "intended" (abhimata) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
The connection is: "If its activity is intended to be long-lasting. Then, for that reason, how is it that this [activity] is one?
The meaning is that it cannot be one.
The reason for this is given as "diverse" (bhinnā):
because its objects—the denotable meanings such as the expressed sense and so forth—are diverse.
The sense is that when there is a difference in the object (*viṣaya*), a difference in the operation (*vyāpāra*) related to it is also necessary.
Having restated the second [view], he refutes it with the words "Now" (*atha*), etc.;
here, "now" (*atha*) has the meaning of "if" (*yadi*).
In that case,
[the word] "objects" (viṣaya): objects are those meanings intended as being denotable (vācya), indicative (lakṣya), or suggested (vyaṅgya).

Now, if what is intended by the term "extremely long" is that the very meaning which resides in the fourth stage is expressed directly by the sentence all at once, then, since no convention has been established for that [meaning], how can there be direct comprehension?
If it is argued that the convention applies to the signs (nimitteṣu), while the signified object (naimittika) itself is independent of convention— behold the eloquence of this Vedic scholar!
For that very object which possesses the fortune of reaching the ultimate stage first enters the path of cognition.

The subsequent cognitions of the objects [of that word] are its auxiliaries (*sahakārin*), such as the occasion (*samaya*), the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*), and the specific qualities of the speaker (*vaktṛvaiśiṣṭya*).
Due to the difference among these,
[the cognition] is of a different kind— that is, of a distinct class (*bhinnajātīya*).
By demonstrating the fault in the case of homogeneity (*sajātīyatva*), he establishes exactly what was stated: "In the case of being homogeneous," and so forth.
The word "this" (*asau*) from the phrase "this [agent] is manifold" (*aneko 'sau*) is to be supplied by way of transposition (*vipariṇāmena*).
The meaning is: when this manifold activity is accepted as being homogeneous.
The ellipsis is that "it does not proceed further.
He states the reason for this with the words beginning "kārye":
"with respect to the effect," that is, toward an effect.
By the "knowers of categories," such as the Naiyāyikas and others.
To the objection, "Let it be non-homogeneous," he replies with the words "non-homogeneous" and so forth;
the meaning is: "and when multiple [entities] are admitted within this non-homogeneous [category]."
"It is precisely our own view.
The meaning is that by establishing a distinction between functions (*vyāpāra*), the function of *dhvani* (suggestive power) is established.

Alternatively, the meaning of the passage beginning with "of the same class" (*sajātīya*) is as follows: Furthermore, keeping in mind the dilemma—whether the effect of the function, which is the cognition of multiple meanings, is of the same class [as the cause] or something else—the author says "of the same class," and so forth.
With respect to an effect of the same class,
its operation— such as denotation and so forth—
is precluded.
Therefore, the intention is that if another operation were admitted, it would simply be our own position. The term "asajātīya" (of a different class) is to be construed with "in the effect."
The meaning is this: [the process] must indeed belong to us.

Since the effect is of a different genus (*vijātīya*), there must necessarily be a difference in the genus of the operation that constitutes its cause; thus, the operation of *dhvani* (suggestive resonance) is established.
Now, what is called the "length" of an operation is neither its oneness nor its belonging to a single genus.
However, there is indeed a distinction in the immediacy with which the intended meaning is communicated.
Therefore, one might raise the objection that the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is certainly within the scope of denotation (*abhidhā*), beginning with the words "Now, if...
(*atha yadi*).
The connection is with the phrase "the intended meaning.
"Fourth" means "last."
He himself also provides the response, beginning with "In that case" (tarhi) and so forth;
therein, it refers to the object situated in the final stage.
"Directly" means by way of denotation.
How so?
The word "is" is to be supplied;
the meaning is "it does not exist.
Now, since the relationship of cause and effect is accepted between the meaning of words and the meaning of a sentence, when the meanings of the words serve as the causes—

Having raised the objection that "by the mere grasping of the convention, the cognition of that sentence-meaning occurs through the function of denotation (abhidhā) without depending on a separate convention regarding the final sentence-meaning," he refutes it with the words "in the causes," and so forth.
"In the causes" means in the word-meanings.
This meaning refers to the meaning of the final sentence.
"Behold," and so forth, is a statement made in jest;
it is to be connected with the phrase "skill in speech."
"One who partakes" (*bhāgī*) means one whose nature is to partake (*bhajanaśīla*).
"Subsequent" (*paścāttanāḥ*) means those that arise at a time subsequent to the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
By saying "they go to the state of being a cause" (*nimittabhāvaṃ gacchanti*), it is clearly intended that causality (*naimittikatvam*) is attributed to the grandson of the Mīmāṃsaka.

Now, it might be argued: "In that case, because one who has previously been conditioned by the apprehension of convention thereupon attains such a cognition, the word-meanings possess the status of being causes (*nimitta*) by virtue of this factual state of affairs; therefore, nothing at all useful for following that [process] has been stated.
Furthermore, the apprehension of convention did not actually take place regarding the individual word-meanings (*prakpadārtha*).

Since words are always employed only as already connected [with meanings], if it is argued that their nature is such due to insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*), then—given the admission that the convention (*saṅketa*) applies only to the mere word-meaning—the cognition of the specific [meaning] would necessarily be subsequent.
Now, if it is said: "The comprehension of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is indeed seen to occur instantaneously; what can we do about this?"
We, too, do not fail to accept this very point,

as we shall state: "In the same way, that object appears instantaneously in the intellect of those with clear minds— whose nature is turned away from the [conventional] meaning of sentences— as it shines forth in its true reality."
Thus it is.

However, due to the practice of intensive and repeated cultivation, although a sequence is possible therein, it is not perceived— just like the sequence in the recollection of the time of pervasion regarding a familiar object— because there is no arising of a succession of similar conceptualizations of that [sequence].
"Understanding of word-meanings" (*padārthāvagama*) refers to the cognitions of word-meanings (*padārthapratīti*).
"Regarding the great-grandson," and so forth.
The meaning is that, with respect to the great-grandson as the cause (*nimitta*), one's own status as the effect (*naimittikatva*) would be intended.

Now, even though the cognition of the word-meaning occurs subsequent [to the cognition of the word], since the apprehension of the convention (*saṅketa*) regarding that object has already occurred previously, the designation of the word-meanings as causes by way of that [apprehension] is not contradictory.

Having raised the objection that for a cognizer who has grasped the convention, an immediate and instantaneous realization of the ultimate meaning—such as coolness and purity—indeed occurs upon hearing a sentence like "There is a bath in the Gaṅgā," he refutes it with the words beginning "Now, if it is said... and so forth.
[The phrase] "following that" means...
The sense is that, in following the comprehension of the final meaning, whatever is useful for the conclusion according to one's own view—

or rather, how could there be an understanding of the final meaning, which is not conventionally established, through the pursuit of those word-meanings? Furthermore, he states "nor even" (*na cāpi*) to show that even the prior apprehension of the convention regarding word-meanings is not possible.
That is to say: only those [words] which are already connected, which convey a connected meaning,
and which have attained the status of a sentence.
He raises the objection: "The convention," and so forth. "Existing separately" means the occurrence of the grasping of conventions with respect to individual objects.
He refutes this with the words: "The convention," and so forth.
"The cognition of the specific [meaning] occurs only subsequently" means that the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises only later,
not at an earlier time.
The meaning is that, in such a case, your own established doctrine would be contradicted.
Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth:
"comprehension of the intended meaning" (*tātparyapratipatti*) refers to the cognition of the ultimate sense.
"What can we do about this?"—the sense is:
whether or not there is a causal basis for the apprehension of conventions regarding objects, let it be so.
If that is the case, then our desired conclusion is established; thus he says "that," and so forth.
He states the distinction with the words "But... and so forth.
"Therein" means:
in the cognition of the suggested meaning, which consists of the ultimate sense.
"Even if it were possible"— that is, even if it were known through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—
"the sequence," meaning the priority and posteriority of the apprehension of word-meanings,
"is not perceived"; this is the syntactic connection.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "sajātīya" and so forth.

Those which are "of the same class" (*sajātīya*)—namely, those conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) regarding word-meanings that serve as factors for the cognition of the sentence-meaning—it must necessarily be admitted that there exists between them and the *locana* (the direct perception) a relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*).

Otherwise, there would be a distinction between the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary or figurative (*gauṇa-lākṣaṇika*), which would result in the collapse of the entire system of the six means of proof— beginning with "the relative weakness of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth"— since that system is established precisely through the diversity of causal conditions (*nimittatā*). And if such a diversity of causal conditions is accepted, what further ground is there for our detractors to harbor malice?

Even those who assert that the sentence is an indivisible *sphoṭa* and its meaning is likewise indivisible must follow this very same analytical procedure, for they too have fallen into the realm of ignorance (*avidyā*).

However, let us leave it at this: our own teacher, while composing the *Tattvāloka*, was certainly not unaware that, upon transcending that [realm of ignorance], everything is the non-dual Brahman which is the Supreme Lord.
The meaning is that there is no mention [of sequence] because the succession of the "beloved of the ignorant" does not arise.
For sequence is a property of two things existing in a cause-and-effect relationship;
the point is that for the cognition of that [sequence], the cognition of those two [things] is required.
He states the reason for its non-arising: "sātiśaya" (possessing excellence).
The meaning is: from the repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) of that cultivation (*anuśīlana*), which is a superior reflection (*paryālocana*).
