And since the subject matter possesses a security and well-being distinct from the joy of a son's birth, and since the act of suggestion (*dhvanana*)— which is distinct from inference— is to be performed in a manner different from the nocturnal meal inferred from fatness qualified by the absence of eating during the day, its *sāmarthya* (capacity) or power consists in the totality of expressive words appropriate to that specific [context];
this is the meaning of the term *bālapriyā*, as explained in the passage beginning with "upon which [the meaning] rests."
He states the [author's] intention with the words "na hi" (not indeed).
The syntactical connection is: "for that which is produced by those [factors] is not [so].
But [one might object]: if there is an absence of the presentation of the transitory emotions (*vibhāva*) and so forth, how can there be the nature of poetry (*kāvyatva*)?

Dispelling the doubt that this would result in an instruction as if [the definition] were already established, he says "In your view," etc., with the intention of demonstrating that the very thing desired by the opponent would necessarily follow as being poetry.

The meaning is: according to this view—that the cognition of rasa and so forth is produced by the words themselves and not by the excitants (vibhāvas) and so forth—even that which is not intended to be poetry would become poetry.
He provides an example of exactly such a case: "Śṛṅgāra... and so on.
Quelling the suspicion that the commentary passage beginning with "yataśca" might be redundant by stating that it serves as a conclusion, he says "evam" and so forth.
In the commentary, it was concluded that [the meaning] is implied by the power of the denoted sense (*abhidheya-sāmarthya-ākṣiptatva*);
however, he explains that this consists in being apprehended through the function of suggestion (*dhvanana-vyāpāra*) pertaining to both word and meaning, by saying "abhidheyam eva" and so forth.
The explanation of the term *sāmarthya* (capacity) begins with "together" (*saha*) and so forth.
Capacity (*śakti*) is precisely the cooperative factor (*sahakārin*), for it is that by which one is able (*śaknoti*); its nature is such.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "the excitants and so forth" (*vibhāvādikam*).
The term *dhvanana* (suggesting) is an explanation of the word *ākṣepa* (implication).

Having applied it to the word (*śabda*) by resorting to a *karmadhāraya* compound, he now applies it to the meaning (*artha*) by resorting to a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound—beginning with "of the denoted" (*abhidheyasya*) and so forth.
The connection of the word "of the denoted" (*abhidheyasya*) is with the word "suggesting" (*dhvanana*).
Because their acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are distinct and their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct—
just as the birth of a son indeed produces joy,

whereas an object such as a dramatic representation (*vibhāva*) does not produce rasa in the same way— the suggestiveness residing in the object (*artha-gata-dhvani*) possesses a character different from that [of rasa].
He refutes the position of inference as well with the words "in the world" (*divā*).
He provides an explanation of the term "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) by stating "power" (*śakti*).
He further elucidates this very power with the words "specific" (*viśiṣṭa*).

Thus it is established that the third variety [of suggestion], by means of a denotative word distinguished by qualities (*guṇa*), ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), and so forth, which is appropriate and in harmony with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), is indeed distinct from the expressed meaning.
However, its cognition occurs simultaneously with that of the expressed meaning, as will be shown later.
That very meaning is the soul of poetry; and thus, in ancient times, of the first poet...
That very meaning is the soul of poetry; likewise, in the beginning, for the First Poet [Vālmīki], the function of both word and meaning is suggestion (*dhvanana*).
Thus, having introduced two positions, the first has been refuted.
The second [view], however, is somehow refuted and somehow accepted:
it is refuted with regard to the operation of inference as production (*janana*),
but accepted with regard to the operation of suggestion (*dhvanana*).
He who considers even here that *dhvanana* (suggestive power) is merely the power of intention (*tātparyaśakti*) does not know the true nature of reality.
For in a sentence that expresses the excitants (*vibhāva*) and ensuants (*anubhāva*), the power of intention must terminate either in a distinction (*bheda*) or in a relation (*saṃsarga*).
But not in *rasa*, whose essence consists in being relished; enough with this prolixity.
The word "iti" has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). The connection [of the sentence] is: "For this reason also, even the third variety is indeed distinct from the denoted (*vācya*)."
Regarding the phrase "saheva" (together, as it were):
by the word "as it were" (iva), he shows that although a sequence exists, it is not perceived—namely, [the sequence] "at the beginning.
This is from the second Uddyota. // 4 //

Thus, by the statement "that which is being apprehended is indeed something else," the nature of *dhvani* has been explained. Now, he demonstrates its status as the soul of poetry by means of a historical illustration, stating: "the soul of poetry.
Since the discussion was already underway regarding the apprehended [meaning] in general, it should be understood that this refers specifically to the third type of *dhvani*, namely *rasadhvani*.
This is by virtue of historical precedent and by virtue of the meaning of the text concerning the subject matter under discussion.
"Bālapriyā" means completeness or fullness.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason.
"In the first" means the position [stated as]: "by virtue of being communicated by its own word. "In the second" means...
The meaning is that this refers to the position [stated as] "by way of establishing the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.

Someone says: "For the author of the *Vṛtti*, who maintains that rasa and the rest are merely implied by the force of the denotable meaning (*abhidheya-sāmarthya-ākṣiptatva*), the function of suggestion (*dhvanana-vyāpāra*) is intended to be none other than the power of implication (*tātparya-śakti*).

It is not something distinct from that which resides in a fourth level [of meaning], because the power of implication is precisely the capacity to convey a meaning aided by the fact that the denotable meaning would otherwise be inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*)."
Having restated that opinion, he refutes it with the words "But he who," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "either in difference or in connection":
in cases such as "Bring the cow," the sentence-meaning is either the difference [of the cow] from other objects of action or from other actions.

Some maintain that *saṃsarga* (relation) is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), while others hold that *bheda* (distinction) is the sentence-meaning; [the former argue that] the relation in the form of a connection between a specific action and a specific object or the like is the sentence-meaning, whereas the latter maintain that distinction is the sentence-meaning.

Now, one might ask: "Since the nature of *dhvani* has been established as distinct from the expressed meaning (*vācya*), what is the connection of this verse—which sets forth its very essence—before its definition has been stated? To address this, he presents it following a recapitulation of what has preceded, beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*).
[The phrase] "has been explained" (*vyākhyātam*) refers to this.
The meaning is that, between the two subjects under discussion— the nature of *dhvani* and its status as the soul (*ātman*) of poetry— the first has been established.
Regarding the phrase "by means of a historical narrative" (*itihāsavyājena*),
the word "pretext" (*vyāja*) indicates that the primary intent lies precisely in establishing *dhvani* as the soul [of poetry].
It has been shown that this is the introduction of a narrative (itihāsa).
He explains it in accordance with the context, beginning with "sa eva" and so forth.
Immediately after [the word] "sa eveti":
The grief arising from the separation of a pair of curlews has attained the form of a verse.
The grief arising from the separation of a pair of curlews has been transformed into a verse.
The *Locana* [states]: "Therefore, in reality, Rasa alone is the soul (*ātman*).

As for the suggestion of matter (*vastu-dhvani*) and the suggestion of poetic figure (*alaṅkāra-dhvani*), they both ultimately resolve into Rasa; thus, with the intention that these two are superior to the literal meaning (*vācya*), it was stated in general terms that 'Dhvani is the soul of poetry.
[Regarding the word] "sorrow" (*śoka*).

The *sthāyibhāva* (permanent emotion) of grief—which arises from the Krauñca bird’s separation from its mate due to the killing of his companion, and which is distinct from the *ratisthāyibhāva* (the emotion of love) appropriate to *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (erotic love-in-separation) because it is a state of indifference—is that very same [emotion] which, through the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of such *vibhāvas* (determinants) and the resulting *anubhāvas* (consequents) like wailing, reaches a state of being tasted through a process of sympathetic resonance (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*) and identification (*tanmayībhavana*).
By the word "that" (*tat*), [it is meant]; and after the phrase "rasadhvani," the word "is referred to" (*parāmṛṣṭaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
"It should be reflected upon" means it should be ascertained through reasoning. He states this [reasoning] with the words "Itihāsa," and so forth.
"By the force of the historical narrative" (itihāsabalāt) means by the force of the remainder of the verse (kārikāśeṣabalāt).
"Having been introduced" (prakrāntā) [is the meaning].
The phrase "the third, however," etc., means that which was previously mentioned.
This also serves as an indicator for the immediately preceding passage of the commentary beginning with "and of that which is being perceived.
By that [means].
The meaning is: "because that very thing is to be considered as nothing other than rasa-dhvani.
The connection is with the phrase, "it was stated in general with this intention.
He states the intention indicated by the word *iti*—namely, "rasa itself," and so forth.
"In every way" (*sarvathā*) means "both as the principal factor (*aṅgin*) and as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*).
"Thus" (*iti*) indicates the reason (*hetau*).
In order to exclude any other possible interpretation, he explains what he intends to say with the words beginning "of the krauñca.

He states the cause of the separation from its mate with the words beginning "its companion," and provides the explanation for the phrase "by the separation from its mate" with the words "by the destruction of their companionship."
"Utthitaḥ" means arisen;
the word "krauñca" is to be supplied as the subject.

By the phrase beginning with "nirapekṣa," he negates the status of being a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which would otherwise have been implied by its arising from the destruction of companionship (*sāhacarya-dhvaṃsa*).
Because it has emerged from the expectation of union with equanimity (*upekṣā*), its nature is one of indifference.
Having explained the verse beginning with "krauñca," he elucidates how grief attains the state of being a *śloka* (verse) with the words "sa eva" and so forth.

By intending to express the identity established through the cognition of non-difference between the grief of the Krauñca bird and the grief of the Primordial Poet (*Ādikavi*) which exists in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*), he says "that very same [grief]."
The connection is: "that very [state] has attained the form of a verse.
The reason for this is: "it has assumed the nature of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of compassion," and therein, "it has attained the state of being relished."

The meaning is that mental states such as passion (*rati*) and so forth, when being relished, indeed fall within the scope of the designations "erotic" (*śṛṅgāra*) and the like. The cause for attaining this state of being relished is indicated by the words beginning with "of the heart" (*hṛdaya*): first, there is a resonance with the heart of the sensitive spectator (*sahṛdaya*).
From that arises the attainment of identification with that [object], and following that, there is aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*); such is the sequence.
Here too, the reason is given by the words "of such a nature" (*tathābhūta*) and so forth.
An excitant (*vibhāva*) of such a nature is one whose association [with its object] has been destroyed, such as the form of Krauñca.

Having entered the *locana* (the eye), he has attained the nature of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of compassion— a state distinct from worldly grief, whose essence is to be relished through the internal vibration of one's own mind. Just as a jar filled to the brim overflows, and just as the outpouring of mental activity manifests as the play of speech regardless of conventional rules, so too— by the principle that it reveals the movement of the mind even without dependence on formal conventions— he assumes, through the force of his immersion, the form of verses constrained by appropriate words, meters, and prosodic structures, all while remaining uncreated (*akṛtaka*).
He attained [this state]: "O Niṣāda, may you not find stability for eternal years, because you killed one of the pair of krauñca birds while it was deluded by passion."
Thus it is.
But it should not be thought that the Sage experiences grief;
for if that were the case, then because he too would be pained by that suffering, the principle that "taste is the Self" would be rendered untenable.
Nor is this condition one of one who is tormented by suffering.

Thus, because its nature consists in the arousal of the *karuṇa* (compassionate) rasa, which has grief as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) suitable for aesthetic relish (*carvaṇa*), [the text] mentions "wailing" and so forth; by the word "and so forth," actions such as rolling upon the ground are to be understood.
He states the result of attaining the form of the *karuṇa* rasa: "worldly," etc.
The intended meaning is that there is a difference between the ordinary [state] and the aesthetic state due to the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of their essential natures.

In order to demonstrate that the extraordinary aesthetic flavor (*alaukika-rasa*) is established by the means of valid cognition known as self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pramāṇa*), he says "sva" and so forth.

That [flavor] has as its essence the *sāra*—the vital core—which is to be tasted and experienced by the mind through the *dguti* (exaltation) of one's own mind, the relisher; this exaltation is produced by becoming one with that [flavor] and is indicated by such signs as horripilation.
To the objection—"How can there be a transformation of a flavor that has become one's very self into an external verse?"—he provides an answer by way of an illustration, saying "rasa" and so forth.
The meaning is as follows: just as when a water-pot placed on the top of one's head, which is full of water, is moved, the water contained within it flows out, so it is here.

Anticipating an objection regarding a disparity based on the pot being material (mūrta) and consciousness being immaterial (amūrta), he provides another illustration, beginning with the words "the fluctuations of the mind" (cittavṛtti).
The meaning is: "just as" lamentations and the like, which consist of transformations of mental states such as suffering, are verbal in nature—
the word "and the like" (ādipadena) including praise and so forth— so too [is the case here].
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of an alternative.
Now, one might object: "If rasa is the soul of poetry, its being the object [of poetry] must be stated precisely as its being the subject matter;

however, it is not possible for sound, whose operation depends upon convention (*samaya*), to have that as its subject matter. Anticipating this doubt, he demonstrates that it is its object by virtue of being suggested (*vyaṅgyatvena*), stating: "in the absence of dependence on convention..."

"By the method beginning with 'through affection,' etc. means: for in the world, modes of speech such as lamentation and praise manifest mental states consisting of grief and high esteem; this is the sense according to the stated manner.
"By way of being uncreated" means that it is without any prior intention such as "I shall reveal this meaning by this [means].
To the question "In that case, how [is it revealed]?", he says: "By the force of possession (āveśa)."
"Āveśa" means pervasion of the self.
"Appropriate" (samucita) means that only appropriate words and so forth manifest the aesthetic flavors (rasa) and so forth; this is the intended sense.

Having explained that [the verse] "attained the status of a *śloka* for the Ādikavi," he dispels the misconception of the word order (*anvaya*) as "the sorrow (*śoka*) of the Ādikavi" by saying "but not... and so forth.
By using the word "muni" (sage), he dispels the possibility of [the sage's] suffering.
He states the fault in such a word-order with "in this way... and so forth.
"By that suffering known"— meaning by the suffering of the Krauñca bird—
"he too," meaning even the Primordial Poet;
"thus having [considered]" means for this reason.
The word "iti" means "the statement.
He states another fault as well: "And not... and so forth.
"This is the tenfold [vision]" means that it is the vision consisting in the act of pronouncing a curse or the composition of verses. He concludes with the words "In this way," and so forth.

In the manner thus described, that very essence which consists of the *karuṇa* (compassionate) rasa—whose dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is sorrow suitable for relish—is the essential core of that poetry which is beautiful through its manifold elaboration of expressed meanings, expressive words, and compositional structures. Indeed, the *Locana* states: "The soul of poetry is this very essence, whose nature constitutes its core and which differentiates it from other verbal compositions. This same point is stated in the *Hṛdayadarpaṇa*: "As long as one is not filled with this [rasa], so long does one not truly vomit it forth [in poetry]."
Thus,
by the augment *āṭ* according to the rules of the Vedic language (*chāndasa*),
he says "that very one" (*sa eva*) with the vowel *ā*; that is to say, there is no other self.

Therefore, as Bhaṭṭanāyaka has said: "Relying on the primacy of the word, they know that [type of composition] there as *śāstra* (treatise); but when it is joined with the reality of the meaning, they call those two *ākhyāna* (narrative)."
When both [the word and its meaning] possess the status of a quality and the emphasis is on the function, there arises the cognition of poetry (*kāvyadhī*).
Thus, that [objection] is refuted.
For if the function (*vyāpāra*) consists of *dhvanana* (resonance) or has the nature of *rasana* (tasting), then nothing new has been said.
On the other hand, if the function is indeed *abhidhā* (denotation), even so, it has already been explained previously that its primacy is not established.

He explains the verse with the words "vividha" and so on: because of the state of that [verse]—"Mā niṣāda" and so forth—whose nature (svarūpa) is a diverse outward movement (samuccalana), that is, an expansion outward, having made it manifold (vicitra) in accordance with the various rasas to be manifested therein.
That state is its "tattva"; from that [tattva].
That very thing—namely, the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of compassion—is the soul of poetry.

This is because a poetic work such as "Amā niṣāde" and so forth has the nature of being an outpouring of the flavor of compassion; therefore, the intended meaning is that rasa alone is the soul of poetry.
The explanation of the term "self" (ātman) is "the essential nature.
To establish that, [the author] says "others," and so forth.
He corroborates Bhaṭṭanāyaka’s statement regarding the fact that the nature of poetry is the arousal of aesthetic flavor (rasa) with the words "as far as," and so on.
The word "poet" (kavi) is to be supplied as the subject. By this aesthetic flavor (rasa),
until they are filled through the process of becoming one with the determinants (vibhāva) and so forth, [the audience remains incomplete].
For that long,
he does not vomit forth this aesthetic flavor (rasa) by bringing it into external manifestation, nor does he make it available for others to savor;
the poet remains entirely filled with rasa.
The sense is that since poetry emits aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in the form of a literary composition, the very nature of poetry—which consists in the emission of *rasa*—is indeed *rasa* itself.

Regarding the potential objection that the augment *aṭ* (in the form "agama" in the verse beginning with "amā niṣāda... which he himself composed) would be prohibited by the rule "na māṅ-yoge," he states the justification for its occurrence in the passage beginning with "agama.
As for the word "tena": [it refers to that aforementioned reason].

The meaning is: "by means of establishing that rasa is the very self [of poetry]. This connects with the phrase "that has been refuted. Regarding the word "śabda" (sound/word): [it refers to the following].
"Having relied upon" means that the word "proceeded" is to be supplied;
[the object] is the scripture, such as the Vedas and so forth.

"By way of the true nature of the matter" means by way of the predominance of the meaning; "history and so forth" is appropriate. Furthermore, there is a reading "yukte" (in the case of what is joined).
Regarding these two [types of] verbal artistry (*śabdārthau*),
"poetic cognition" (*kāvyadhīḥ*) refers to the poetic convention (*kāvyavyavahāraḥ*); the ellipsis is to be supplied as "in a composition possessing those [qualities]."
"Operation" (*vyāpāra*) means the referent of the term "operation" in the phrase "the predominance of operation.
The word "now" (*atha*) indicates a doubt.

Intending the analysis that [the word] *cāru* (charming) means "beautiful through elaboration (*prapañca*) in the various compositions of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*"), he explains it with the words beginning "tattad" and so forth: "in accordance with that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) which is to be manifested by those respective signified objects and so on."
"Having made it variegated" means as follows:
for instance, from the primordial poet Vālmīki, grief itself—born from the cry of a *krauñca* bird distressed by the separation from its slain mate—was transformed into the form of a *śloka*.

"Locana" (the eye) refers to that which is beautiful through its elaboration in the expressed meaning (*vācya*), the expressive word (*vācaka*), and the composition (*racanā*), being endowed with the ornaments of sound and sense (*śabdārthālaṅkāra*) and the poetic qualities (*guṇa*).
Therefore, although the capacity to suggest (dhvanana) exists everywhere, such conventional usage does not occur [everywhere];

as was stated previously, the conventional usage of "living being" (jīva) occurs only in certain instances despite the existence of the self (ātman). Consequently, this [objection] is without foundation.
As it is said in the *Hṛdayadarpaṇa*: "In that case, the designation 'poetry' (*kāvyavyavahāra*) would apply everywhere.
Here, the "one whose companion has been slain" is stated as the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause), and the sound of "wailing" (*ākrandita*) is the *anubhāva* (the consequent effect).

The word "vācyādīn" (the expressed meaning and so forth) is to be understood as the ellipsis for "bālapriyāḥ. The word "kṛtvā" (having made) is connected with "prapañcena" (by means of elaboration), and the triad beginning with "vācya" (the expressed meaning) is connected with "cāru" (beautiful).
"By means of elaboration (*prapañca*) and expansion (*prapañcana*";
"charming" means beautiful.
By this, he states what is intended to be expressed, beginning with the words "sound," and so forth."
"By that" means by virtue of being poetry, as stated in the passage beginning with "various," and so forth; "everywhere" refers even to cases such as "Devadatta is a lion."
"Thus, the linguistic usage [is] the poetic usage;
the connection is: 'what was stated thus is without scope.
Regarding "the determinants" (vibhāva):
The Krauñca bird, whose companionship has been destroyed, is the objective determinant (*ālambana-vibhāva*); the slaying is the excitant determinant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).

Now, one might think that according to the literal wording of the text beginning with "he was slain" (*nihatet*), the meaning appears to be that the sage’s grief was produced by the bird's lamentation.

How then is it that sorrow (*śoka*) is indeed the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of compassion (*karuṇa*), and how is it said that "the eye [of aesthetic experience] is produced" even when other distinctions are perceived in what is being apprehended?
The ellipsis to be supplied is "by virtue of being the object of relish (*carvaṇā*)."

One might object: "If a verse (*śloka*) has arisen from the relishing of grief (*śoka*), then on what grounds can it be said that the suggested reality (*pratīyamāna-vastu*) is the soul of poetry? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For grief... Grief is the stable emotional state (*sthāyibhāva*) of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa-rasa*), which consists in the domain of its relishing. For when grief is the stable emotional state, those excitants (*vibhāva*) and ensuants (*anubhāva*) and the corresponding mental disposition (*cittavṛtti*) being relished constitute the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Thus, by virtue of this propriety (*aucitya*), it is said that the stable emotional state attains the status of aesthetic flavor.

The *Bālapriyā* explains [the verse] beginning with "carvaṇā" because the collection of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttijāta*) was previously known through self-awareness and later inferred in another; therefore, there is first a negation of that.
The meaning is: "produced by his wailing" means "brought within the range of relishing (*carvaṇā*).
The intended sense is that the meaning of the word "sorrow" (*śoka*) is "the sage's sorrow existing in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*)."

Now, one might object that the restatement here—beginning with the passage "For grief... (*śoko hi*) and so forth—that grief is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇarasa*) is pointless; therefore, he introduces that passage with the words "Now" (*nanu*) and so on.
The word *tat* means "in that case" (*tarhi*).
"The suggested entity" means *rasa* (aesthetic flavor). It is stated in this way for the purpose of not forgetting the subject matter at hand.
He explains [the verse] as being conducive to the accomplishment of meditative concentration (*samādhāna*), beginning with "of the compassionate one" (*karuṇasya*) and so forth.
"The savoring of that" (*taccarvaṇā*) means the savoring of sorrow (*śokacarvaṇā*).

The meaning is as follows: by the very statement that "sorrow has attained the state of being a *śloka* (verse)"—that is, by saying that the *śloka* arises from the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of sorrow—the self-nature of *rasa* is indeed revealed; for the essence of the *karuṇa-rasa* (the pathetic sentiment) consists precisely in its being the object of the relishing of sorrow.
Now, one might ask: how can one thing [the relishing] have another thing [sorrow] as its object? To this, he provides the justification beginning with "In sorrow," etc.
"In sorrow" refers to the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), such as the sorrow occurring in the described state of the Krauñca bird and others.
The locative case is used in the sense of "on account of" (nimitte); that is,
"those which are the transitory and the involuntary states."
The meaning is: those *vibhāvas* which are the causes of grief and so forth, and those *anubhāvas* which are their effects;

"appropriate to them" means appropriate to those *vibhāvas* and *anubhāvas* as they are being relished—that is to say, belonging to the same genus as the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) residing in the particular [character] being described.

The mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) exists in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) within the one who relishes; it is the mental modification consisting of sorrow and so forth. That which is being relished is the essence (*rasa*), the referent of the term "rasa. It is the nature of that which is being tasted.
"By way of propriety" means by way of a metaphorical designation based on utility; the sense is that it is not by way of primary [denotation].
The attainment of the state of rasa (rasatāpatti) means the acquisition of the nature of rasa (rasatvaprāpti).
It is stated [in the text] by the passage beginning with "the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) is rasa," and so forth.
He demonstrates its utility with the words beginning with "previously" (prāk), and so forth.
The word "by one who possesses a sensitive heart" (sahṛdayena) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Svasaṃviditam" means experienced within oneself;
"paratra" refers to another, such as the Krauñca bird.
"Inferred from weeping and so forth" means by implication.
"Mental state" (cittavṛtti) means the stable emotion (sthāyin).
"Saṃskāra" and so forth:

the meaning is that, having deposited the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of one's own direct experience and the impressions of one's own inference, and thereby establishing a correspondence with the heart through those two; "because it is employed, therefore [it is] propriety (*aucitya*)"—this is the connection.

The indication is made primarily by way of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the transitory emotion (*bhāva*), because it is through the sequence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) that [the work] brings about a resonance in the heart, which is what serves the purpose of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*).
Now, it may be objected: "In that context, the nature of the suggested meaning (*pratīyamānarūpa*) was explained as having three varieties, and not as being solely of the nature of *rasa*."
Anticipating the objection that this historical account implies that rasa alone is the soul [of poetry], he provides the answer by way of admission, stating: "And of that which is being perceived.
Another distinction consists of the nature of *vastu* (fact) and *alaṅkāra* (ornament).

By the mention of *bhāva* (transitory emotion), it is stated that even a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*), when being relished—even if it does not rest in itself alone—attains the status of the vital breath (*prāṇatva*) because it culminates in the relishing of the stable emotion (*sthāyin*), even though it has not yet attained a firm foundation in rasa.
For example: "Scratching her nail against the tip of her other nail, turning her swaying bracelet, she gently traces the ground with a foot whose anklet emits a soft tinkling sound."
In this context, shame [is included];
and by the terms "rasa" (flavor) and "bhāva" (emotion), its semblance (*tadābhāsa*) and its subsidence (*tatpraśama*) are also indeed subsumed,
because they possess that same essential nature despite their internal variety.
"By virtue of predominance" means "by virtue of culminating in rasa.

The sense is that even when there is no rest in that alone, it is stated with propriety that the suggestion of matter (vastu-dhvani) and the suggestion of ornament (alaṅkāra-dhvani) also constitute the life-breath [of poetry], because they effect a distinction from other forms of verbal expression. //5//
The *Bālapriyā* [commentary] states: "The suggested form (*pratīyamānarūpa*) is the self (*ātman*).

The intended meaning is that because it is stated [by Ānandavardhana] that "suggestion (*dhvani*) is the soul of poetry," the general category of the suggested (*pratīyamānasāmānya*) is designated as the self.
In the *Vṛtti*, the passage beginning with "in rasa" (*rase*) and so forth [is relevant].
The meaning is: "by means of rasa alone" and "by means of bhāva alone.
Regarding the term "indication" (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is to be connected with the word "of the suggested" (*pratīyamānasya*).

When, among things related to one another through some connection, the primary element indicates something else, that is *upalakṣaṇa* (indication by implication); for example, in the expression "the king is going," the king indicates his retinue.
Here, he states the purpose of including the term *bhāva* (abstract state/being) with the words beginning "bhāva" and so forth.
The connection is: "it has been stated by means of the mention of existence.
The word "tāvat" means "in that much alone," that is, in the mere intrinsic nature (svarūpa) alone.

"Non-resting" (aviśrānti) means the absence of rest; the word "even" (api) indicates that this [rest] is not primary. If it is asked, "In that case, there must be a foundation for rasa," he says: "the stable emotion" (sthāyin), and so forth.

The culmination of the relish (*carvaṇā*) of the latent impression (*sthāyin*) is characterized by the act of bringing it to fullness; this very state is what constitutes the establishment of the appropriate rasa. The meaning is: even without reaching that [establishment], it becomes the "vitality" (*prāṇatva*), which is to say, the life-force of poetry (*kāvyajīvitatva*).
Thus it is said.
The meaning is that aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) arises precisely through the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of that [beauty].
Regarding the word "nail" (*nakha*):
here, by the mention of the turning of the bangle, the emaciation produced by the sight of the beloved is suggested (*vyañjita*).

Regarding this, he states "here, of the shame" (*atra lajjāyāḥ*), with the phrase "the state of being the life-force" (*prāṇatvam*) to be supplied. He explains that the life-force of shame— which is manifested by the excitants (*vibhāva*) such as hearing news of the beloved, and by the ensuants (*anubhāva*) such as the scratching of nails mentioned here— does not reach a state of rest within the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), but instead becomes the object of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*).
The phrase beginning with "rasa" means that by the word *rasa*, the semblance of sentiment (*rasābhāsa*) is included;
and by the word *bhāva*, both the semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) and its subsidence (*tatpraśama*) are included.
In the commentary, the phrase "due to its predominance" (prādhānyāt) means "due to the predominance of this rasa.
He states the reason for this: "because it culminates in rasa" (rasaparyavasānāt).
The word "of others" (anyeṣām) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
He states [this] as a corollary: "tāvat" and so forth.
"Tāvanmātrāviśrāntau" means in the absence of resting upon the mere nature of the object (vastu) or the ornament (alaṅkāra). Furthermore, the particle "api" has the sense of "even" (api).

The connection is: "by way of its propriety, which causes it to differ from other verbal [expressions]. "The sweet flow of the substance of that meaning, issuing forth from the great poets, Sarasvatī, reveals a particular flash of intuition (pratibhā) that is extraordinary in the world. (Dhvanyāloka 1.6)
The Sarasvatī, flowing forth as the sweet essence of the subject matter of great poets,
reveals a throbbing excellence of intuition that is extraordinary to the world.

The speech of great poets, flowing forth from that reality of things, is an eye unlike anything else in the world; having thus demonstrated through the medium of history that this [reality] constitutes the very soul of poetry as it is perceived, [the author] shows that "this is established by one's own experience" with the words "Sarasvatī.
The meaning is: the Blessed Lady whose form is Speech.
He explains the word *artha* by the word *vastu*, and the word *vastu* by the word *tattva*, [using the term] "flowing forth" (*niḥṣyandamāna*).
The meaning is: "spontaneously milking the divine essence of bliss.
As Bhaṭṭanāyaka said: "For the cow of speech has milked this very essence for the thirst of the child."

Now, this must be considered by the connoisseurs: by Śrī Vālmīki, in the verse beginning with "mā niṣāda" and in other verses, the killing of a male *krauñca* bird together with its mate was indicated;

however, here, according to the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the author of the *Vṛtti*, it is based on the text as heard, "nihate" (when [he] was killed), and according to the explanation by the author of the *Locana*, "arising from the killing of the female companion" and "the killed female companion is stated as the *vibhāva*."

Regarding the statement "the young *krauñca* bird whose companion was slain by a hunter" and other such words, as well as the fact that the author of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* has presented the killing of the companion, what is the reason for these authors to propound a meaning that contradicts the statements in the *Rāmāyaṇa*?

On this point, some say: "In the commentary passage beginning with 'was slain,' [it refers to] the *krauñca* who was already slain, being distressed by separation from his companion and naturally unable to endure separation from her."
The meaning is: "the lament directed toward that [object] which produces that [state].
In the *Locana*, at the point where it says "sahacarī-ārohaṇe," the reading should have been "sahacare.

Regarding the statement "the excitant (*vibhāva*) is stated as 'nihatasahacarī'," the meaning is that the excitant is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "nihatasahacarī"; thus, there is no contradiction with the statement from the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
"Thus," and so forth.
"Established by self-awareness" means established by the experience of those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*).
"This" refers to [the aforementioned].
The meaning is that the suggested sense (*pratīyamāna*) constitutes the soul of poetry.
Regarding the word "shows":
it was stated in the preceding verse that the *itihāsa* (epic narrative) serves as the authoritative proof for the suggested sense being the soul of poetry.
However, in order to stabilize that [realization], the means of valid cognition characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is stated by this [verse].
For there is no disagreement regarding self-awareness among anyone; such is the meaning.
"Sarasvatī" [is used]...
The meaning is: "by means of the verse beginning with 'Sarasvatī'.
He explains the word *sarasvatī* as "the Blessed Lady whose form is speech.
The word "that" (*tat*) means "what was previously stated."
He states that "the reality of the subject matter" (*vastutatvam*) is an explanation of "the subject matter as an object" (*arthavastu*), saying "by the word *vastu*, etc.

Among objects—namely, subjects (*vastu*), poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), and sentiments (*rasa*)—the "subject matter" (*vastu*) is the essential core; this is the "subject matter as an object" (*arthavastu*).

He explains the meaning resulting from the phrase "the reality which is its object" (*tadarthavastu*) as found in the verse beginning with "flowing forth" (*niḥṣyandamāne*): "divine" means supramundane;
"by itself" indicates constant presence;
"milking forth" means pouring out.
By this, the similarity of Sarasvatī to a cow is indicated. He states the authority for the aforementioned explanation, saying: "She said," and "Speech."
Speech, in the form of poetry, is that very cow;
[she yields] this divine essence.
Yet, through the thirst of childhood, one does not perceive it with the eye—that essence which is indeed milked by the yogis.
For it is by means of his penetration, even without physical treading, that he is milked by yogis.

Precisely for this reason: "Having imagined him as the calf, while Meru stood as the skilled milker, all the Śālvas milked the earth—taught by Pṛthu—to yield radiant jewels and great medicinal herbs."
By this, it is stated that the Himavat is a vessel for the most excellent and essential substance.
Regarding the phrase "it manifests that which is quivering," that *pratibhā* (intuitive flash) is not something merely inferred by those who understand it.
Rather, the meaning is that it appears through being permeated by that [inspiration].
As our teacher Bhaṭṭatōṭaka has said: "From that, there arises an identical experience for the hero, the poet, and the listener.
"Pratibhā" (inspiration) is the wisdom capable of creating unprecedented objects.

Its "distinction" (*aviśeṣa*) consists in the clarity and beauty of the immersion in aesthetic flavor (*rasāveśa*), which is the capacity for the composition of poetry. Because of the cause of affection for her, like a cow toward her calf or a connoisseur toward his child, she indeed yields milk.
For that reason, he would not possess the essence of this sap flowing from his childish craving— that essence which is the flavor of bliss.
The meaning is that [the world] is indeed milked by yogins.
To clarify its incomparability, he states the meaning of the fourth quarter beginning with "by absorption in that" (*tadāveśena*):
"by absorption in that" means by absorption in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
The word *api* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed).
"By means of *ākrānti*" means by force; that is to say, by the perfection of the excellence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consisting in becoming one with the Lord whose nature is bliss.
As for the "cow of speech" (*vāgdhenū*), the sense is that she is the milker of that [bliss] due to the power of being possessed by it, like the thirst of a child.
He states the proof for the excellence of that which flows forth spontaneously from the milk produced by the pressure [of the calf]: "For this very reason," and so on.

"For this very reason" means: because Himavat, who is like a calf, possesses the agency itself regarding the flowing forth of the cow—who is then filled with rasa and overcome by its possession. The connection is: "By the phrase 'for this very reason,' it is stated that Himavat is a vessel for the essence."

It explains [the verse], removing the misconception regarding its meaning by stating that it "manifests" (*abhivyanakti*)—that is, it causes one to infer—the specific power of Sarasvatī’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*).
In the phrase "it manifests," the word "toward the cognizers" (*pratipattṝn prati*) is to be supplied; thus, the meaning is "for the cognizers."

That *pratibhā* (creative intuition) belongs to the great poet; it is not something that is being inferred. The meaning is that it is not an object of inference whose probans (*liṅga*) is such a Sarasvatī (poetic power).
The word "tat" (that) means by means of the immersion in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) which has become the object of intuition (*pratibhā*).
The word "bhāsamānā" (appearing) [is used].

The meaning is that it becomes an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Such Sarasvatī manifests a corresponding excellence of *pratibhā* (creative intuition) characterized by its flash of inspiration—by means of a manifestation consisting in the removal of the veil in the form of being unprepared for the immersion in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Thus, she makes it an object of direct perception for the perceivers; this is the sense of the verse. This is the intended meaning.
To the question of how rasa, which resides in the poet, comes to reside in the audience, he says: "As it has been stated," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of the hero":
the sense is that [rasa belongs] to the hero through the poet's superimposition, whereas for the listener, it arises through the savoring of rasa.
He explains this "distinction of intuition" (*pratibhāviśeṣa*) with the words beginning "intuition" (*pratibhā*), etc.
"Wisdom" (*prajñā*) means intelligence (*buddhi*).
"Taste" (*rasa*), etc. [is as follows].
It manifests a particular excellence of genius that flashes forth,

by virtue of which, in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) flowing with an exceedingly diverse succession of poets, only two or three, or perhaps five or six, such as Kālidāsa and others, are counted among the great poets (mahākavi).
And this is another proof establishing the actual existence of the suggested meaning (pratīyamāna-artha):
It is not perceived merely through knowledge of grammar, semantics, and logic;
rather, it is perceived only by those who truly know the essence of the meaning of poetry.
It is not known merely through knowledge of the science of words and their meanings;
rather, it is known only by those who truly understand the essence of the meaning of poetry. (7)
That meaning is such that it is understood solely by those who know the true essence of poetry;
and if the expressed form (*vācyarūpa*) is as the Sage said— "the internal state of the poet"—
then by what [is it known]?
That is to say, the reckoning of one as a great poet is based on the sign of a distinct, manifest, and throbbing flash of genius (*pratibhā*).

"And this" means: not only are the distinctions of essential nature (*svarūpa*) and object (*viṣaya*) indicated by this verse—namely, that "what is being cognized is something else entirely"—but rather, even the fact of being cognizable by a distinct causal complex (*bhinnasāmagrīvedyatva*) is a proof for its being something over and above the denotable meaning (*vācya*). This is the sense.
It is understood that "clarity" (*vaiśadya*) is the cause of the immersion in aesthetic flavor (*rasāveśa*), which consists in the absence of any lack of orientation toward such immersion;

the "beauty" (*saundarya*) resulting from this is characterized by being devoted to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth. Alternatively, "clarity" through the immersion in aesthetic flavor refers to the absence of defects indicated by the sūtra beginning with "by intentness upon what one wishes to express" (*vivakṣātatparatvena*);
the "beauty" resulting from this is the presence of the qualities (*guṇas*) indicated by those [sūtras], meaning the capacity for the composition of poetry in that form.
He provides a corroborative statement regarding the fact that Sarasvatī manifests a particular excellence of creative intuition (*pratibhā*) for those who understand, saying "As he says.
He explains the passage from the commentary beginning with "By which" as follows: "By that which is manifested," and so forth;
that is, by that which is manifested, and therefore vibrating, and which has become an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for those who understand.
The phrase "by means of the cause" (*nimittena*) is an explanation of the word "by which" (*yena*).

The expression "the reckoning as a great poet" implies the following sequence for the recipients [of the poetry]: first there is the experience of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), then the emergence of creative intuition (*pratibhā*), and finally the reckoning as a great poet. // 6 // // //
The section beginning with "not merely" (*na kevalam*) and ending with "even the state of being cognizable" (*vedyatvam api*) is an elaboration of the phrase "and this other [point]" (*idañcāparam*).

He explains that the meaning of the passage starting with "of its existence" (*sadbhāvasya*) is that existence is something distinct from the denotable object (*vācya*), by stating "the denotable," and so forth.

In this way, the very meaning would be contained within the verse itself; for the realization of that [existence] would occur precisely through the thorough knowledge of the relationship between the denotable and the denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*).

Moreover, this meaning is entirely beyond the reach of those who labor merely over the definitions of the signified and the signifier, and who are averse to the cultivation of the true essence of poetry— just as the science of music (*gāndharva-lakṣaṇa*) is inaccessible to those who know its technical definitions of notes and scales (*svara-śruti*) but do not sing.
Thus says the *Locana*.
The point is that it is not the case that it is not experienced, such that it would not exist; rather,

it refers to those who are averse to the cultivation (*bhāvanā*)— that is, the continuous relishing— of that meaning which constitutes the very essence of poetry, which transcends the literal expression (*vācya*).

The notes (*svaras*) are seven, beginning with *ṣaḍja*. That which is called *śruti* is a specific variation of sound that produces a distinct quality; it is of twenty-two kinds, categorized according to the intervals between the notes (*svara*) and their sub-intervals (*antara*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is no intention to demonstrate differences in qualification (*adhikāribheda*), such as *jāti*, *aṃśaka*, *grāma*, *rāga*, *bhāṣā*, *vibhāṣā*, *antarabhāṣā*, and *deśī*. *Bālapriyā*: [This commentary] is not intended to show distinctions among those qualified for practice.
However, the intention is that this [verse] is intended to demonstrate the difference in the causal complexes (sāmagrī):
for the cognition of the expressed meaning (vācyārtha), the causal complex consists of the knowledge of the words and their meanings as instructed;

whereas for the cognition of the suggested meaning (nyaṅgyārtha), the causal complex consists of being a connoisseur (sahṛdayatva) and so forth—this is what is shown by the first and second halves [of the verse] respectively.
Since sensation (*vedanā*) is already established, there is scope for an inquiry into its causal complex; with this intention, it was stated again that "it is felt.
He explains this with the words "But not... and so forth.
By which non-feeling...
This is the implied meaning.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the first half-verse beginning with "tasmāt" is connected to the latter half-verse beginning with "so 'rthaḥ";
the explanation of that [latter half] begins with "yadi hi," and so forth.
‘This object’ refers to the suggested meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*). ‘The cognition of that’ refers to the cognition of the suggested meaning.
He avoids the objection of an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) with the words beginning with ‘But if,’ and so forth.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "And yet, this meaning is beyond the reach of those who are averse to the cultivation of the true essence of poetry and have exerted themselves only in the mere definitions of the signified and the signifier.
In this regard, there is an illustration: "just like the characteristics of *svara* (pitch), *śruti* (interval), and so forth, for those who know the definition of *gandharva* but do not sing.
"Beyond the reach" (*agocara*) means ungraspable.

"For those who know the characteristics of music through the study of treatises on the characteristics of *gāndharva*, there is the reading 'sa hi' or 'sa tu' in the verse (*kārikā*). He explains the passage beginning with 'of poetry' (*kāvya*) as follows: 'of poetry,' and so forth."
“Of sound” means of sound in the form of song and so forth.
“Producing mere difference” means producing merely a mutual distinction.
The meaning is that it does not bring about any quality.
"Another form" (*rūpāntara*) refers to a specific form (*rūpaviśeṣa*).

The sense is this: when there is the hearing of sounds such as singing, that which arises by taking as its cause another form of that sound—namely, a temporal fraction (*lavādi-kālāṃśa*)—is what is meant.
The word "tat" means that which has that measure of time as its duration; that is to say, "lasting for just that long. The word "svare" [is used].

The meaning is that the "division" (bheda) is imagined based on the interval between those notes—that is, the space between two notes, which implies both sides—and what is called a *śruti* is simply a portion of a note.
Regarding the term "jāti," and so forth: [it refers to the musical scales].
The essential nature of the *jhāṭī* and other such meters should be understood from other sources.
Regarding the term "not sung" (*apragītānām*), [the commentator] explains the word *pragīta*, which forms part of the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), as follows: "excellent," and so forth.
He states another view: it becomes twenty-two-fold by virtue of the division of *kaṇāḍīs*.
These very divisions are designated as *śrutis*.

The word *śruti* is derived from the verbal root *śru*, meaning "to hear," with the suffix *ktin*, based on the etymological derivation "that which is heard. Regarding this subject of the classification of *śruti*, which is synonymous with *nāda* (sound), many varieties exist; some maintain that there are twenty-two *śrutis*.

Others, however, declare that there are sixty-six distinct types of *śruti*, while still others speak of their infinity. For this very reason, Kohala said: "Those who are skilled in investigating the knowledge of *śruti* cite twenty-two *śrutis*."
Indeed, some who differ by sixty-six [points] demonstrate their very infinity.
Thus it is.
In this context, the position of twenty-two strings alone is the one intended by the author of the text.

The mutual distinction among these notes is as follows: having imagined twenty-two strings on the body of a lute (*vīṇā-daṇḍa*) in a sequential order, when those strings beginning with the second are played after being tightened slightly more than the first, [the resulting notes constitute the scale].
It can be understood through direct perception.
From these scriptural authorities, there are seven notes known as ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama, dhaivata, and niṣāda.
It is called a *svara* because it, by its own nature and independent of auxiliary causes, delights the mind of the listener and makes it impassioned.
Such is the derivation of that term.

Since these seven notes, when existing individually, do not serve as a means for attaining either visible or invisible results, the necessity of the *grāma* arises for the sake of achieving those ends.
A *grāma*, by name, is a collection of notes.
If only this much were stated, since a collection of notes (svarasamūha) is also possible in worldly and Vedic sentences, there would be an over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition to them;

therefore, to exclude those, the definition must be stated as follows: "The state of being a *grāma* is the quality of being a collection of notes while serving as the substratum for *mūrcchanās*, scales (*krama*), fixed-note ornaments (*tāvarṇālaṅkāra*), musical modes (*jāti*), and so forth."
The definitions, classifications, and other details concerning *mūrchanās* and so forth are to be understood from the *Svarādhyāya* chapter of the *Saṅgītaratnākara*.
Furthermore, this *grāma* is of two kinds: the *ṣaḍja-grāma* and the *madhyama-grāma*.
In that regard, having arranged twenty-two strings on a single neck of a lute, the note *ṣaḍja* is on the first string,
*ṛṣabha* on the seventh,
and *gāndhāra* on the ninth.
On the thirteenth day, Madhyama;
on the seventeenth, Pañcama;
and on the twentieth, Dhaivata.
When the notes are arranged such that Niṣāda is placed on the twenty-second [string], the Ṣaḍja-grāma arises;
this very basis is conventionally designated as the "pure" (śuddha) Ṣaḍja-grāma.
Likewise, on the other neck of the lute, Madhyama is located on the fourth string from the beginning.
On the seventh day, Pañcama; on the eleventh, Dhaivata;
and on the thirteenth, Niṣāda.
When the notes are arranged such that Ṣaḍja is on the seventeenth, Ṛṣabha on the twentieth, and Gāndhāra on the twenty-second, the Madhyama-grāma is formed.
This very same modified basis (vikṛtāśraya) is designated as the Madhyama-grāma.
And thus, in the Ṣaḍja-grāma— the notes Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Pañcama are produced from four *śrutis*,
while Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata are produced from three.
Gāndhāra and niṣāda are produced from two [notes];
in the madhyama-grāma, madhyama, dhaivata, and ṣaḍja are produced from four [notes],
while pañcama and ṛṣabha are produced from three [notes].

Niṣāda and Gandhāra are produced from two [notes] each; thus, these twenty-two *śrutis* belonging to the two *grāmas* (Ṣaḍja and Madhyama) are established as being differentiated by both the primary notes (*svara*) and the intervals between them (*antara*).
In that regard, combining the *Ṣaḍja-grāma* and the *Madhyama-grāma*, there are eighteen *jātis*: Ṣāḍjī, Ārṣabhī, and so forth.
Gāndhārī,
Madhyamā,
Pañcamī.
Dhaivatī, Naiṣādī, and Pañcamakaiśikī.
"Six [types of] northern [styles], or six [types of] gaits.

Having thus established the existence of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) as distinct from the expressed meaning (vācya), he demonstrates that it alone possesses primacy: "The paths are grasped. (Locana) [This refers to] the paths.

Those for whom singing (*gīta*)—that is, chanting (*gāna*)—is excellent are called *pragītāḥ*; or [the term] is derived from the root *gai* with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the action having begun (*ādikarmaṇi*).
And here, by the mention of the beginning, the state of reaching the final result is indicated. // 7 //

"Thus" means by way of a difference in their own nature and by way of being objects of knowledge through distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*). Regarding the term "to be recognized" (*pratyabhijñeya*), [the suffix -ya] is used in the sense of the initial action (*ādikarman*). *Bālapriyā* [comments]: "in the sense of the initial action."
The meaning is that "commencement" (prārambha) refers to the sense of form (rūpa).
Regarding "fruit" (phala): here, the fruit is the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of the vowels and so forth. // 7 //
Lest there be the misconception that the word "evam" (thus) refers merely to what is proximate, he explains:
"By way of a distinction in essential nature," and so forth; that object is endowed with the capacity for its own manifestation, and so too is any given word.
Those two—the word and its meaning—of the great poet must be recognized with effort.
That meaning and that particular word, which possesses the capacity to express it—these two, the word and the meaning, must be diligently recognized as belonging to the great poet. (8)
The suggested meaning and the particular word endowed with the capacity to manifest it—
not the mere word—
are those very same word and meaning that must be recognized as belonging to the great poet.
The suffix -tavya (kṛtya) is used here in the sense of "worthy of" (*arha*) with respect to both the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) and the suggester (*vyañjaka*), when they are well-employed;
for everyone strives in that manner—by this much, the fact that [this] predominance is established in common worldly usage is stated as the proof.
And by the suffix -tavya in the sense of "mandate" (*niyoga*), the sequence of instruction is stated.

By the word "to be recognized" (pratyabhijñeya), he says this: although this [work] flashes forth within himself according to the principle that "poetry may indeed arise in someone endowed with creative intuition (pratibhā)," nevertheless, when it is specifically determined as "this is thus," it branches out into a thousand directions.
(The reading "svarūpaviṣayabhedena" is also found.)
To explain how preeminence is demonstrated, he says "in the sense of 'deserving' (arha)" and so forth.
"Kṛtya" refers to a kṛtya suffix.
"Sarvaḥ" means every single person who possesses a cultivated heart (sahṛdaya).
The connection is "for thus" (*tathā hi*).
The meaning is "because of being an Arhat. He exerts himself; that is, he proceeds with the desire to know such sounds and meanings.
He states the conclusion with the words "iti" and so forth.

By this much—that is, by the statement that [the suggested meaning] is to be recognized by those of sensitive taste (sahṛdaya)—[he establishes] the primacy of the suggested meaning; that is, regarding the subject of its primacy.
Regarding the word *loke*:
it means "among those with sensitive hearts" (*sahṛdaya*).
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "That meaning and such a word of the great poet—those two, word and meaning—must be recognized with effort by those with sensitive hearts."
The word "tāu" (those two) indicates the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

The meaning is that these two—the word and the meaning—belong to the great poet and are worthy of being recognized by the connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*) in the form: "These are those very same [word and meaning] of such a kind. Furthermore, one should understand another sense: that these two, the word and the meaning, are to be recognized by the great poet. Thus he says, beginning with "niyoga," etc.
In this interpretation, the word "atāvi" means "as previously stated. Furthermore, the first half of the verse may be a separate sentence.
"Śijñākramaḥ" refers to the method of poetic instruction.
He states the fruit of the recognition of word and meaning with the words beginning "pratyabhijñeya" (to be recognized), etc.
The term "kāvyamataci" [is used];
the particle "tu" (but) indicates its distinction from the sciences (śāstra) and so forth.
"Jātu" means at some time or occasion; it is not for everyone, but for someone.
To the question "Who is this?", he says: "one who possesses creative intuition (pratibhā)."
By himself, indeed by himself;
this poem of this poet.
"This" refers to the manner of determining that "this must be done in this way. "That which is being determined" refers to the object of such determination.
The meaning is "being performed after having been examined. The word "that" (tat) is supplied from the context.
[The word] is "suddenly" (sahasā).
The meaning is that it becomes a thousandfold;
the intention is that the modes of differentiation are infinite.
He supports the necessity of defining its specific varieties by means of an example of the negative instance (vyatireka), stating "as it has been said."
The phrase "at the end of the Pratyabhijñā treatise" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The attainment of the status of a great poet belongs to those who are truly great poets, and not merely through the composition of words and their meanings.

Regarding this, it has been stated by our supreme guru, the venerable Utpaladeva, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā*: "Just as a lover, though standing nearby, is no different from any other person to a slender woman because he has not been recognized despite her various entreaties, so too the Lord of the Universe, whose own nature is not perceived for its qualities by the world, is not at all capable of manifesting His own glory. Therefore, this *Pratyabhijñā* (Recognition) has been proclaimed."
Thus it is.

Therefore, even for that which is already known, what is here termed "recognition" (pratyabhijñāna) consists specifically in a detailed investigation characterized by synthetic reflection (anusandhāna),
and not merely the thought "this is that very same thing.
[The phrase] "of the great poet" [is used].
He prays, "May I become a great poet.

Thus, by one who asserts the primacy of both the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) and the suggestive word (*vyañjakaśabda*), this verse is intended to demonstrate the point that—even though the Lord is understood in a general sense—without a specific realization of Him, one does not attain the ultimate fruit [of liberation]. This is expressed by the phrase "by those various [means]" (*taiḥ taiḥ*). *Bālapriyā* [comments]: Even if the Lord is known in a general way, the attainment of the final result is not possible without a particularized comprehension. This is the purpose of the present verse.
"By those various entreaties"—meaning by requests preceded by formal courtesies such as the dispatching of female messengers and the reporting of one's own circumstances;
the construction is "even though he was won over.
It is not merely that he was won over, [but he was also entreated].

Although standing in the presence of the slender maiden, he remained thus unrecognized; for although I had heard that he was distinguished by qualities such as supramundane beauty and so forth, and had therefore sought him with an excess of passion, I did not specifically recognize him as "this is my beloved.
Consequently, he became like anyone else in the world, having attained the status of being common to all people.
A "beloved" (kānta) is a man who is the object of a slender woman's desire;
[the phrase] "is not able" is to be supplied [to complete the sense], as in: he is not able to sport with, that is, to delight, the slender woman so as to bring her joy.
Having thus demonstrated the illustration, he states the subject at hand, beginning with "of the world" (*lokasya*). The connection is "the self of the world.
[The term] "unexamined" (*anavekṣita*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.]
The meaning is that [the connection] is not specifically known by the world.
Since it is possible for there to be ignorance regarding a specific detail even when something is known in a general sense,
the point is that it is entirely appropriate for a great poet to effect a recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of word and meaning, even though they are self-evident.

In that case, what is the referent of the term "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*) here? To this, he states its nature by way of its result, beginning with "by that" (*tena*). Fearing that an injunction might be inappropriate because one who has already attained great poetic skill (*mahākavitva*) does not require further instruction, he explains [the verse] starting with "he who is great" (*yo maha*). The meaning is that the sense of the term "great poet" (*mahākavi*) is "one who is the object of the cognition having the mode of being a great poet. This is the intended point.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the construction should be understood as: "those two, word and meaning, of the great poet (*mahākavi*) are to be recognized by connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*)," and "those very same word and meaning of the great poet are to be recognized. Alternatively, the construction should be understood as: "[word and meaning] are to be recognized by the great poet," and "those very same word and meaning [are such that] recognition occurs for the great poet.
The phrase beginning with "the suggested" (*vyaṅgye*) and so forth serves as the justification for the statement that they are "to be recognized by the great poet."
"By those well-employed" means employed after having been specifically examined.
The meaning of the phrase "of the great poets" has already been stated.
Since the commentary (vṛtti) has shown that the suggestor (*vyañjaka*) is also primary, he says "in this way," and so forth.
"It is appropriate.

Regarding the term "sound" (*dhvani*): even though at present the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) hold primacy, it is nonetheless fitting that poets first employ only the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*). Thus he says:
"Just as a person seeking light exerts effort toward the flame of a lamp..."
Because it serves as a means to that [ultimate goal], one should likewise pay heed to the expressed meaning. (Dhvanyāloka 1.9)

Just as a person seeking light exerts effort toward the flame of a lamp because it is the means to that end, so too one who desires the expressed meaning applies attention to the words because they are the means to it. (9)
For just as a person who desires light exerts effort toward the flame of a lamp because it is the means to that end—
since light cannot possibly exist without the lamp's flame— in the same way, a person who intends to convey a suggested meaning exerts effort toward the expressed meaning.

It is stated that the threefold—namely, *locana* (the vision), *dhvani* (that which resounds as the primary meaning), and *dhvananam* (the act of resonating)—is all logically established; thus it is said that "the predominance has been declared. // 8 // // 8 //

Anticipating the objection that "since it is grasped first, the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācaka-tadbhāva*) alone must be primary," he demonstrates that this reason is contradictory when proving primacy, by means of the passage beginning with "now" (*idānīm*), with the intention of showing that it is the means (*upāya*) themselves that are grasped first.
Illumination (*āloka*) is the act of looking (*ālokana*).
The meaning is the beholding [of the truth] from the lotus-like face of a woman;
and in that regard, the means is the flame of a lamp. // 9 //
The meaning is that what is about to be stated is appropriate for those who delight in the simple. // 8 //

The statement in the *Vṛtti* that the denoted (*vācya*) and the denoter (*vācaka*) are appropriately mentioned first by way of restating their predominance as the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is improper,
because such a restatement of predominance serves no purpose; therefore, he connects [the following] as a response to this objection, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth,
and "The denoted" (*vācya*) and so forth.
The compound is treated as a singular collective (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*).
To the question, "What is the fault in [the reason] being presented first?", he says—"of the means alone," etc.—showing that very point. [It is] contradictory (*viruddha*).
The meaning is that [the reason] is pervaded by another [property] which is absent where the probandum is absent; or rather, the meaning is that it is "unproving" (*aprayojaka*).
Since the word *āloka* is well-known in the sense of "light" (*prakāśa*), he states its meaning in the present context as "illumination" (*ālokana*).
The meaning is "visual cognition.
"Beholding" (*ālokana*) is the very explanation of this [term], as expressed by "the woman," and so forth. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says "of the communicator" (*pratipādakasya*).
The meaning is "of the speaker. // 9 //
By this, the operation of the poet, the communicator, with respect to the suggested meaning has been shown.
To demonstrate it for the recipient as well, he says: "Just as the meaning of a sentence is understood by way of the meanings of the words..."
In the same way, the cognition of that [suggested] entity is preceded by the expressed meaning.
Just as the meaning of a sentence is understood by means of the meanings of its individual words,
so too is the comprehension of a real entity preceded by its expressed meaning.

For just as the meaning of a sentence is understood by means of the meanings of its individual words, so too is the comprehension of the suggested meaning preceded by the cognition of the expressed meaning.
[In the commentary] *pratipad* is used with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāve*).
"Of that entity" means of the essence consisting of the suggested form.

By this verse it is shown that for one who is not an extremely sensitive connoisseur (*atyanta-sahṛdaya*), this sequence is indeed clearly perceptible—just as the sequence of word-meanings and sentence-meanings is clear to one who is not an extreme expert in verbal composition. However, for one whose state of being a connoisseur has reached its ultimate limit, even though this sequence exists just as it does for one skilled in verbal composition, it is imperceptible; it is like the recollection of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) through practiced inference, which, despite existing, is not consciously perceived. // 10 // // .//
In the *Bālapriyā* commentary, the phrase "of that which is to be established" (*pratipādyasya*) means "of the expressed meaning" (*vācyārthasya*). The word "that" (*tam*) [refers to this].
The meaning is "the operation with respect to the suggested sense. And that [operation] consists in the production of its own cognition.
Regarding the word *pratipatteḥ* in the verse, he says *pratipad* and so forth in order to exclude any other kind of apprehension.

The meaning is that "practice" (pratipatti) refers to the purpose of that [knowledge]. In the verse, the terms "padārthe" and "vācyārthe" mean "that respective object as it is being known," or alternatively, "the cognition of that respective object."
Regarding the term ‘sampratīyate’: the meaning is that it is cognized by perceivers.

He states "by this," etc., because there is another result in explaining the similarity between the cognition of the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya) meanings to the cognition of word-meanings (padārtha) and sentence-meanings (vākyārtha).
The connection is: "it is shown by this verse.
Whosoever is the cognizer;
for such a cognizer as that.
This [type of suggestion] is based on both the expressed and the suggested meanings.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration beginning with "just as" (yathā) and so forth.
[The phrase] "occurring through the function of words" (śabdavṛtti) [is used].
The meaning is "occurring through the function of the sentence.
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the word," and so forth,
the term "clearly cognizable" is to be supplied as a continuation.
"Having reached the ultimate limit" means having attained the highest excellence.
"Of one skilled in the application of speech" [is the meaning].
The meaning is: "of one who knows the *vākya-sphoṭa* and so forth.

As for the example regarding the non-perception of sequence even when it exists—[it is given by] the words beginning with "abhyasta" (practiced). In the case of a practiced object, "inference" (*anumāna*) is the inferential cognition (*anumiti*), which is the recollection of the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*), that is, the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*); [the compound refers to] those two.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the remembrance of the pledge (samaya-smṛti) and the understanding of its meaning are included;
the sense is that it is like that [the former], namely, possessing the sequence culminating in that [the latter]. // 10 //

Now, he demonstrates how the primacy of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is not undermined, even though the cognition of that [suggested meaning] is preceded by the cognition of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*):

"Just as, while conveying the sentence-meaning solely through its own inherent power, the word-meaning is no longer perceived once the function [of conveying that meaning] has been accomplished. (Dhvanyāloka 1.11)

Just as the meaning of a word is not separately perceived when its function is accomplished by the very power of its own capacity while conveying the meaning of the sentence, [so too is the meaning of the sentence]. (11)

"The eye was not torn away" means that, precisely because of its predominance, [the sequence] does not come to rest in the middle, being hurried by the restless longing to follow it all the way to the end; thus, even though the sequence exists, its imperceptibility is the cause for its predominance.
Its own capacity consists of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhi*).
Regarding the term "vibhāvyate": by the prefix *vi*, "distinctness" (*vibhaktatā*) is expressed.

In the commentary, he introduces the two verses beginning with "svasāmarthya" by saying "now" (*idānīm*), and so forth. This is because distinctness implies that [the cause] acts through its own capacity. Thus, he provides the transition to the two verses starting with "svasāmarthya."
‘From the cognition of that’ means from the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). ‘It is not obscured’ means it does not disappear; on the contrary, it is established.
Now, it may be objected that although a sequence exists, its non-perception was shown in the verse.
To the question, "How does that establish its status as the primary element? he says: "Precisely because of its primacy," and so forth.
This means: "precisely because of the primacy of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya).
"That" refers to...
"Up to that point" means up to the implied meaning which serves as the purpose; "the pursuit" refers to the mental following or tracking of that [meaning].
In the reading "that *tātparya*," the meaning is: the pursuit directed toward the implied sense, which constitutes the *tātparya*.
In that context, "being hurried by *raṇaraṇaka*" means being impelled by eagerness (*autsukya*).

The word "sahṛdayāḥ" (connoisseurs) is to be supplied [as the subject]. "In the midst" means during the relishing of the expressed element; "they do not come to rest" means they do not find satisfaction therein.
And thus, what need is there to mention the consideration of the sequence? This is the intended meaning. "The reason" (hetu) means the indicator (jñāpaka).

With the intention that the phrase "its own capacity" (*svasāmarthye*) means the capacity of its own word-meaning, which is the cooperative factor (*sahakārī*), he explains it with the words beginning "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*).

In the verse, the phrase "upon the accomplishment of the function" (*vyāpāraniṣpattau*) means that when there is the accomplishment of its own function—namely, the form of communicating the sentence-meaning—it results in the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthabuddhi*).
He dispels the misconception that the term "distinctness" (*vibhaktatayā*) in the commentary is a mere embellishment (*upaskāra*) of the verse by stating "by the word *vi*."
It is cultivated— that is, it is known— by practitioners by means of this [word].

Even though the word-meaning reveals the sentence-meaning solely through its own inherent capacity by means of the negation of mere cultivation (*vibhāvanā*), it is not cultivated as a distinct entity once its function has been accomplished.

In the same way, that object appears instantaneously in the intellect of those possessed of consciousness whose minds are turned away from the literal meaning, provided that intellect perceives the true reality.

In the same way, that meaning appears instantaneously in the intellect of those possessed of consciousness who have turned away from the literal meaning, provided that intellect perceives the true reality.
The meaning is that the sequence is not perceived;
by this, it is stated that the sequence exists but is simply not cognized.
Therefore, those who explain—on the basis of the doctrine of *sphoṭa*—that "the sequence is merely imminent," are in fact contradicting [the author's] very point.

By the phrase "those whose self—that is, their heart—is turned away from the expressed meaning and finds no satisfaction as a basis for repose," the very meaning of the term *sacetasām* (of those possessed of feeling) is made manifest.
Anticipating the objection that "then let this greatness belong only to the sensitive readers (*sahṛdayas*), but there is no particular excellence in the poem itself," he says: "it appears."
Therefore, it does not appear here as something distinct, but it is not that the expressed meaning (*vācya*) fails to manifest altogether.

For this very reason, there is no contradiction between this passage and what the author will state in the third chapter (*udyota*), where— by means of the analogy of a jar and a lamp— he will explain that even at the time of the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), the cognition of the expressed meaning does not cease.
The meaning is: "because of the admission of the existence of the entity.
The meaning of "by that" is: "by the demonstration of the characteristic of the existing sequence."
