The word "only contradictory" is connected with this [preceding statement]. "With the intention of the *sphoṭa*" means with the intention that both the sentence and its meaning are of the nature of an undivided *sphoṭa*.
In the *kārikā*, "that object" refers to the denotable meaning (*vācyārtha*) in the form of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). "In the true sense" means—
The meaning is "the suggested sense.
Regarding the phrase "with a nature turned away from the expressed sense" (*vācyārthavimukhātmanā*), he explains it by taking the word *vimukha* as its contextual meaning— namely,
"that which has as its basis or cause nothing but repose in the expressed sense," and so forth.
The sense is that it is not entirely turned away from the expressible meaning.
He states the purpose of this qualification with the words "by this," meaning "manifested" or "demonstrated."
Regarding the phrase "only for those who possess aesthetic sensitivity" (*sahṛdayānām eva*) and so forth:

if its immediate manifestation is conditioned by the intellect of a sensitive person (*sahṛdaya*) possessing the aforementioned characteristics, then—by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—since that intellect alone is the cause of it, this excellence is something superior belonging only to sensitive persons, and not to the poem itself; such is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "it appears as such":

the sense is that because one determines that this manifestation— which arises immediately upon the occasion of hearing the poetry and whose production is perceived with perfect clarity— is solely dependent upon the operation of the poetry, this excellence belongs to the poetry itself.
"By that," and so forth;
by that aforementioned method of explaining the two verses,
regarding this subject matter to be expressed.
"Distinctness" (vibhaktatā) means separateness with respect to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).
"Does not appear" means that there is simply no manifestation of distinctness; that is the sense.
"In every way" (*sarvathaiva*) [is used].
The phrase "even by its own nature" (svarūpeṇāpi) means up to that point.
However, some read it as "vibhaktatayā," in which case "here" (atra) means "in the intellect" (buddhau);
thus, "by way of being differentiated" (vibhaktatayā).
"From the expressed"—this means from the literal meaning (*vācya*).
"It does not appear"—the remainder of the sentence is "the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya-artha*).
They explain that by this [non-appearance], sequence would be indicated.
"From this very [fact]" means "from the explanation already stated.
This signifies that while the nature of the denoted object is admitted to appear, the mere division [of its parts] is not admitted to appear.
Having thus established the existence of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) as distinct from the expressed meaning (vācya), he applies this to the subject at hand, saying:
"That particular kind of poetry in which either the meaning or the word suggests that [suggested] meaning while subordinating their own literal senses, is called 'dhvani' by the wise. (DhvK 1.13)
Where either the meaning or the word manifests that [intended] meaning while subordinating their own literal senses, that particular kind of poetry is called *dhvani* by the wise. (13)
"Locana" means "true existence" (*sadbhāva*); that is to say, it means existence (*sattā*), excellence (*sādhubhāva*), and preeminence (*prādhānya*).
For two things are intended to be explained.
"In the context" means in the definition;
"employing" means causing it to reach its application; and "that object" refers to this very application.
The word *sva* denotes the self (*ātman*).
Both the self and the object are "self-and-object" (*svārthau*); those by which these two are made subordinate [are called *svārthika*].
According to their respective order, by that [word], the object has its nature made subordinate, and the word has its denotation made subordinate;
[the phrase] "that object" refers to this.
"Sarasvatī [speaks] that sweet substance which is the meaning"—there is no contradiction here.
This is an illustration; it should be understood that there is also no disparity between the example and the case at hand. // 12 //
The explanation of the term ‘sādhubhāvam’ is ‘preeminence’;
this is the meaning.
As it has been said: “The word ‘sat’ is employed in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness.”
"The two [meanings] are the two meanings already explained.
Regarding "the definition":
the meaning is "the definition of the *dhvani* under discussion."
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of utility":
since it is asked in what respect there is utility for the existence of that which is indicated by the two meanings, he says: "that."
The sense is that since the existence of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is established, it is indeed already proven; therefore, its reference by means of the word "that" (*tat*) is appropriate.

He explains the absence of a separate meaning for the word *artha* with the words beginning "and its own" (*svaś ca*). The gloss of the phrase "made subordinate" (*upasarjanīkṛtau*) is "rendered secondary" (*guṇīkṛtau*).
He states the conclusion with the words "by that," and so forth.
This means a corresponding object and a corresponding word.
Where there is a specific object—that is, a specific denoted meaning—or a specific word—that is, a specific denoter—they both manifest that object.
That specific excellence of poetry is *dhvani*.

By this, it is stated that [the poem] is "the eye" (*locana*) with respect to the causes of beauty in the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*), such as metaphors (*upamā*) and alliteration (*anuprāsa*).
It "manifests" (*vyaṅktaḥ*), meaning it illuminates.

By using the dual verb form "vyaṅktaḥ" (they two manifest), he says this: although in cases where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*), the word alone is the suggester (*vyañjaka*), nevertheless, the status of the meaning as a cooperative factor (*sahakāritā*) is not lost;
otherwise, even a word whose meaning is unknown would be a suggester of that [meaning].
And in cases where the expressed meaning is intended but subordinate (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*), the word indeed possesses the status of a cooperative factor as well.
Since that meaning cannot be manifested without being denoted by a specific word, the function of suggestion (*dhvanana*) belongs to both word and meaning in all cases.
Therefore, the criticism leveled by Bhaṭṭanāyaka against the dual designation [of suggestion as belonging to both] is merely a "blindman's gaze" (*gajanimīlikā*).
As for the alternative statement that it is either the meaning or the word [that suggests], this is stated with the intention of referring to their predominance.

It is both poetry (*kāvyam*) and its specific variety (*tad-viśeṣaḥ*), or else it is a specific variety of poetry (*kāvyasya viśeṣaḥ*). By the inclusion of the term "poetry," it is stated that the "soul" characterized as *dhvani* follows upon the words and meanings embellished by the imposition of excellences (*guṇas*) and figures (*alaṅkāras*). [The author] says "by the dual number," etc., because [an objector might argue]: "But since only one of the two—word or meaning—is the suggester in each individual case, the use of the dual form 'suggests' (*vyaṅktaḥ*) is inappropriate. To this he replies: "By the dual number... and so forth.
The function of both [the word and the meaning] is suggestion (*dhvanana*); the connection is expressed by the phrase "this is stated by means of the dual number.
Regarding the term "qualified word" (*viśiṣṭaśabda*), the intended sense is that it is due to the differentiation of phonemes (*varṇa*) according to the specific aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
"By that" means by the justification of the dual number through reasoning.
"With the closing of the eyes like an elephant" means—

Just as the closing of an elephant's eyes is not preceded by conscious intent but occurs solely by its very nature, such lack of deliberation is indicated by the term "elephant-like closing" (*gajanimīlikā*).
Now, if it were a conjunction (*samuccaya*), then one would have to say "the word *artha*," and so he says "the word *artha*" and so forth.
[He explains this] by the word "primarily" (*prādhānyena*).
The meaning is that the emphasis is on the phoneme (*vyañjana*).

This is the intended sense: here, the particle *vā* does not indicate an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the two—the word and its meaning—as being the agents of the act of manifestation (*vyañjanakriyā*), such that a singular number would occur as in the example, "A dog or a crow or the son of Dru[pad] shall touch the head."
Rather, when word and meaning are connected as the agents in the act of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), they bring about a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the predominance of suggestion;
thus, the sentence-meaning is that "word and meaning, having the predominance of suggested [meaning] through conceptual construction, suggest [the final sense].
With the intention that the word *viśeṣa* (particular) signifies a qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*), he explains it with the words "poetry" (*kāvyam*) and so forth.
He states another alternative: "or of poetry" (*kāvyasya vā*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "of poetry":
the connection is as follows: "That which is the self characterized by *dhvani* is dependent upon such word and meaning; this is stated by the inclusion of the term 'poetry' (*kāvya*)."

"In that case, [the suggestion] would be a secondary meaning (aṅgya) because it follows upon the word and its literal sense. To this, the *Locana* replies: "Therefore, this objection is without foundation; for even in the case of 'presumption based on what is heard' (*śrutārthāpatti*), the designation of 'suggestion' (*dhvani*) would apply.
As for what was said—"In that case, the perception of beauty would be the soul of poetry"—we certainly accept that.
"This dispute is merely over a name.

As for what was said—"If the apprehension of *cāru* (the beautiful) is the soul of poetry, then that [apprehension] occurring even through means of valid cognition such as perception would likewise be the soul of poetry"—in that context, since we are discussing the designation of the soul of poetry as consisting of word and meaning, what possible occasion is there for this objection? It is nothing at all.
The word "it" refers to either the object, the word, or the operation.
As for the object, it is either that which is denoted or that which resounds.
The word (*śabda*) is also like this.
[The term *dhvani* refers to] that which is manifested, or the act of being sounded; or else, as the *Bālapriyā* explains, "by that" means:
because the designation *dhvani* applies to the word and meaning when they are embellished by *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*. This is the sense.
The sense is that [it] "might be so," because in such cases as "Devadatta does not eat during the day," the eating at night and so forth is understood.
As for the passage beginning with "In that case, there would be the cognition of beauty," etc.: [this refers to the following].
If the soul of poetry were something other than the qualities (*guṇas*) and so forth, which are well-known as the causes of beauty, then let the very perception of beauty itself be that soul;
for since that [perception] is directly observed, it is cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate another unseen entity. Thus, the objection is that there is no *dhvani* distinct from that.
To the question, "Why is this accepted? he says: "In name only" (*nāmni*).
The particle *khalu* is used for emphasis.

Regarding the phrase "the cognition of beauty" (*cārutvapratīti*), the point at issue is that there must be something other than the [poetic] qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth that serves either as the object or the cause of this cognition of beauty; it is precisely on this matter that the dispute concerns the name "suggestion" (*dhvani*). Thus, [it means] "the cognition of that which is beautiful."
The meaning is the cognition of a beautiful object;
that is to say, the cognition of beauty having the object as its qualificandum. "That" refers to this [cognition].
The meaning is that there is the cognition of a beautiful object;
likewise, it is the object of the conventional usage of the term "dhvani.
This proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) is ignorant of the context.
Therefore, he refutes [the objection] by saying "it should be disregarded," beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*) and so forth.
The connection is: "In that case—namely, regarding the objects of perception and the other means of knowledge—what such a consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be?"
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that poetry is defined as consisting of word and meaning? To this, he says: "Or the meaning," and so forth.
To the question, "Of what [is it the meaning] and why is it designated by the term *dhvani*? he says: "The meaning also," and so forth.
Everywhere, the word "iti" is connected with the phrase "it has been established that it is *dhvani*."

"Thus" means "in the manner of sounding. The meaning is that all four— namely, the denotable object (*vācya*), the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), and the two types of suggestion (*vyañjanā*)— are denoted by the word *dhvani* through their conjunction.
"By way of predominance" is the reason for its being primary; for a whole is predominant in relation to its constituent parts.

It has been demonstrated that the domain of *dhvani* is indeed distinct [from other poetic figures]. Furthermore, as for what was stated— that "because it deviates from established modes of composition, a path that lacks *dhvani* forfeits its status as poetry"—
that too is incorrect.
For that [dhvani] is not merely established by those who compose definitions;
rather, when the object of definition is examined, it is precisely that which brings delight to the hearts of the sensitive (sahṛdaya), the very essence of poetry.
Locana: [It is] the manifestation (dhvanana) of both word and meaning.
However, by means of the *kārikā*, it is established that primarily the collection itself, in the form of poetry, is essentially *dhvani*.
It is said to be "divided" because qualities (*guṇas*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāras*) have as their life-breath the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*).
The meaning of the word "object" (*viṣaya*) is as follows.
Thus, it has been refuted [by the opponent] what this "sound" (*dhvani*) is that is distinct from that [object].
[The phrase] "only for those who provide definitions" (*lakṣaṇakṛtām eva*) [is explained as follows]:
The reason is contradictory because it is unestablished for the author of the definition;
for it is precisely for that reason that [the object] must be defined with effort. However, if it is unestablished in the subject (*lakṣya*), the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
The phrase "primarily for the delight of the ignorant" implies that for others, however, it is not primary. This refers to the term "suggestion" (dhvani) and so forth.
The meaning is that it is stated as the conventional referent (*padārtha*) of the word *dhvani*.

Thus, that specific kind of poetry (*kāvyaviśeṣa*), which consists of the aggregate of the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) along with their respective suggestors (*vyañjaka*), is called *dhvani*.
The meaning of the verse (*kārikā*) is that it is stated as the conventional denotation (*vācyatva*) of the word *dhvani*.

The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is "the state of being a specific type of poetry," while the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is "being denotable by the term *dhvani* through conventional usage.
It should be understood that although the definition is formulated as consisting of a "specific type of poetry," it is stated here precisely because it is useful for the present context.
In the commentary, "by this" means by the presentation of the definition in this manner;
"from *upamā* and so forth," and so on.
The meaning is "from those objects [of comparison].
"Vibhaktaḥ" means "distinct. To the question, "In what way is the domain of sound distinct from similes and the like? he says: "guṇa... and so forth.
Because it depends upon the denoted and the denoter, it subsists by virtue of their existence.

In order to establish the meaning already stated, he explains the meaning of the word *viṣaya* with reference to its etymology—"it specifically binds (*sinoti*) or fastens (*badhnāti*) the object related to itself"—saying: "existence nowhere else" (*ananyatra-bhāva*), which means the absence of existence elsewhere.
The meaning of the word "object" (*viṣaya*) is that which is conveyed by the word "object" as a qualifier.
The intended sense is that the meaning of the phrase "the object of *dhvani*" refers to that wherein the conventional usage of the term "*dhvani*" exists and does not exist elsewhere.

With the intention that the position of the first proponent of non-existence has already been refuted by the very presentation of the definition [of *dhvani*], the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) states "And as for what was said... and so forth, in order to demonstrate the formulation of the refutation of the second proponent of non-existence;
he says "In this way," and so on.
"In this way" means by virtue of the existence of *dhvani* having been established through the statement of its faultless definition.

"Thus" (*iti*) means that this is the summary statement. The opponent's view is that *ghaṭana* (or *ghaṭanā*), as a type of poetry, is not denotable by the word "poetry" (*kāvyam*), because it transcends the established tradition (*prasiddha-prasthāna*).

Intending the dilemma as to whether, by the phrase "because it transcends the well-known systems," the author wishes to express that the definition itself is unestablished or that the object to be defined is unestablished, he explains the refutation beginning with "yataḥ" (from which).
He establishes the contradiction [of the reason] with the words "tata eva" (for that very reason).
The meaning is that because it is unestablished by the authors of the treatises (*lakṣaṇakāra*),

and because it exists even among those things denoted by the word "poetry" (*kāvyasabdavācya*)— namely, specific types of poetry that follow the definition of *dhvani*— the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*).
We shall demonstrate later that what is other than that is indeed merely the "marvelous" (*citram*).

As for what was also stated— that "for that which does not transcend the quality of loveliness (*kāmanīyaka*), there is an inclusion within the aforementioned varieties of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) and so forth"—
that too is incorrect;

for how could *dhvani*, which is established upon the basis of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and the suggester (*vyañjaka*), be included within a system that relies solely upon the relationship between the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*)?

For the causes of beauty in the expressed (vācya) and the expressive (vācaka) are merely its subordinate members (aṅga), since it will be demonstrated that it [dhvani] is essentially of the nature of the "limb-possessor" (aṅgin). And here is the introductory verse (parikaraśloka): "Because dhvani is based upon the relationship between the manifested (vyaṅgya) and the manifestor (vyañjaka)..."
How could it possibly be included within the categories of the expressed meaning, the expressive word, or the cause of beauty?
And that which consists of prose, song,
and so forth, is not considered "poetry" at all;
it is merely "literary art" (*citram*).

The meaning is that it is so called because its subject matter and such cause wonder, but not because it consists of the flow of rasa, which is the essence of the aesthetic charm desired by connoisseurs;
or else, it is called *citram* (the "picture") because it imitates poetry.
Or because it is merely a drawing, or merely a small portion;
thus it is called "the foremost."

Thus, poetry is established as being of two kinds according to whether the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) functions as the primary or subordinate element; that which is other than these is called "figurative" (citra).
Thus he will state in the third Uddyota. A "parikara-śloka" is a verse intended to provide an additional supplement to the meaning of a *kārikā* for the purpose of the *parikara*.
He also refutes the claim that [the *bhāva*] distinct from the *guṇas* and so forth consists primarily of dancing and the like, with the words beginning "And that which... (*yac ca*).
"Of poetry" means:
of that which is characterized by the definition of *dhvani*.
"Nothing at all" [is meant].

The meaning is that it brings about ridicule. In the *Vṛtti*, with the intention of including both *dhvani* (suggestion) and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) under the phrase "delighting the hearts of the sensitive" (*sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādakārī*), he explains the word "wonderful" (*citra*) in the passage "other than that, the wonderful" (*tato 'nyaccitram*) as "causing astonishment. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "alliteration, simile, and so forth" (*vṛttyādi*), alliteration, simile, and the like are included. He states what is intended to be excluded by saying "but not," and so on.
Or rather, he states that the designation "picture" (citra) for poetry is used in a secondary sense, beginning with the words "kāvyetyādi.
Regarding the word "kāvya":
it means *dhvani*-poetry.

The meaning is that the application of the word "citra" (picture) to poetry occurs because it possesses the qualities of imitating Viṣṇu and others, being merely a painted representation, and having the nature of artistic parts (*kalā*), as these are well-known in worldly paintings;
the particle "vā" is used for conjunction.
In the commentary, the term "prasthāna" (mode of proceeding) is used.
The meaning is "in the case of ornaments and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the expressed" and so on,
the meaning is "ornaments and the like."
"Of that" refers to the sound (*dhvani*). "That" refers to the sound. "Because it is about to be explained" means because it is about to be stated.
Since the term *parikara* (accessory) is dependent [on another], in response to the expectation "of what?", he says: "of the meaning of the *kārikā*.
The explanation of the phrase *parikārtham* is "to provide an addition" (*adhikāvāpam*).
Now, one might object: surely that case where the suggested meaning is not perceived with clarity should not be the domain of *dhvani*.

However, in cases where there is a direct apprehension—as in the case of the figures of speech such as *samāsokti*, *ākṣepa*, *anuktanimitta*, *viśeṣokti*, *paryāyokta*, *apahnuti*, *dīpaka*, and *saṃkara*—it might be argued that these will be included within *dhvani*.
To refute this, it was stated: "those which have made their own literal meanings subordinate."

That in which a meaning whose own nature has been subordinated, or a word whose own nature has been subordinated, or a word whose expressed meaning has been subordinated, manifests another meaning, is *dhvani*.
How is it included among those?
For *dhvani* occurs when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is predominant;
and this [type of compound] is not present in that case, because in the *Locana* it is said that [it is absent] "wherein the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is clear."
The meaning is "by way of its beauty and clarity.
The term "abhihita" (stated) uses the past passive participle because, at the outset, the word "vyañjaka" (manifesting) was already explained [as having that sense].
The phrase "guṇīkṛtātma" (having its own nature made subordinate) [is used].
By the word "self" (ātman), the meaning of the term "one's own" (sva) is explained.
And "not this" refers to the predominance of that which is to be manifested.

And although primacy does not manifest in the act of cognition— since, according to the principle that "in the intellect which illumines reality," there is a resting in the relish of the indivisible [whole]—

nevertheless, when the discerning seek out its life-force, if the suggested meaning remains further enlivening the expressed meaning itself, then its status as an ornament (alaṅkāra) is due solely to its being an instrument for that [expressed meaning].

Therefore, the attainment of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) arises from the expressed word itself as embellished by that [suggestion]. Although, in the final analysis, there exists the suggestion of rasa (*rasadhvani*), nevertheless, this suggested meaning situated in the intermediate stage is for the purpose of performing the "insertion"—that is, the addition—of that further required meaning which was not explicitly stated in the verse (*kārikā*). *Bālapriyā* explains: "the insertion" means the act of inserting or adding a further required meaning that was not mentioned in the verse.
Regarding the term "alaṅkāra" (ornament):
the meaning is "in [figures such as] simile, essential nature (svabhāvokti), and so forth.
He states the reason for using the word "abhihitam" (stated) instead of "āha" (said)—namely, by the passage beginning with "abhihitam."
He recalls what was stated previously with the words "ātma" and so forth.
Since the absence of the perception of predominance is equal in both cases— namely, in the case of *dhvani* and in the case of that where the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*)—
he raises the doubt that their predominance might be equal, and then refutes it by revealing his intended meaning with the words "prādhānyaṃ ca" and so forth.
"Primacy of the suggested" (*vyaṅgya*) means the primacy of that which is suggested.
Regarding "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*):
a "division" (*khaṇḍa*) is a distinction characterized by the predominance of the subordinate elements (*guṇa*) and so forth.

"Devoid of that" means free from [the distinction between word and meaning]; "unbroken" refers to the repose of the minds of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) during the relish (*carvaṇā*) of such suggested meanings as *rasa*, which have become the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
By "connoisseurs" (*vivecakaiḥ sahṛdayaiḥ*), it is meant that this occurs immediately after the unbroken relish.
The phrase "when the search for life is being conducted" applies to both [the expressed and the suggested].

Regarding the words "yadā" (when) and so forth: the meaning is that when that which previously transcended the level of the expressed (*vācya*)—because it is suggested by it (*vyaṅgya*)—though it had entered another stage, returns once more to the prior stage of the expressed and remains there, enlivening the expressed itself.
The connection is "that is the ornament";
the word "is determined" is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
[it is so called] because it serves as its instrument.
The meaning is that it [the expressed] serves as an instrument or a subordinate member (*aṅga*) for that [suggestion].
The implication is that its aesthetic charm (*cārutva*) cannot be established without the suggested (*vyaṅgya*). Thus ends the section.
The meaning is "not other. Regarding that which is to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*), one might ask: "Let it be so; what follows from this? To this, he says: "From that," and so forth.
Therefore, because it serves as an ornament for that [suggested meaning],
and because it is embellished by that [suggested meaning] which is itself adorned [by the ornament],
there is the attainment of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).

Furthermore, when the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya-artha), embellished by the expressed meaning (vācya), remains vitalizing the poetry, then the attainment of aesthetic charm (camatkāra) results from that [suggested meaning]; this is established by implication.

Anticipating the objection—"If it is itself a subordinate element (aṅga), why does it terminate in another subordinate element (aṅgāntara) within the whole (aṅgin)?"—he provides the resolution beginning with "yadyapi" and so forth.
The phrase "madhyakakṣā" means...
It exists in *samāsokti* (synecdoche) and other such figures.

First, regarding *samāsokti*: "The moon seized the face of night with its trembling pupils and rising passion in such a way that she did not even notice her entire garment of darkness slipping away before her due to that very passion."

In such cases, as stated in the *Locana*: "The expressed meaning alone, accompanied by the suggested meaning, is perceived primarily; it does not turn toward the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Rather, the expressed meaning itself rushes forward to embellish the sense [of the poem]; thus, it is called 'subordinated suggestion' (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).
This refers to the case of "condensed expression" (*samāsokti*).
When another meaning is understood from what is stated through qualifiers similar to it,
that is called *samasokti* (concise expression) by the wise because of its condensed sense.

In this verse, the definition and nature of *samāsokti* (speech of compendium), its cause (*hetu*), and its etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) are stated respectively by the four quarters [of the verse]:

"The evening glow (*upoḍha-rāga*) is the redness of twilight; where there is an accumulation of passion (*prema-caya*), the flickering stars (*vilola-tārakā*) are the lights, and the three parts of the eyes."
"So be it," she said;
and instantly, with an impetuous rush of love,
she seized him, embraced him, kissed him, and overwhelmed him.
The "face" is the beginning of the night, and it is also the "lotus-face.
The word "as if" (yathā) refers to both the sudden grasping and the impetuosity of love.

*Timira* refers to darkness; *aṃśukāḥ* are fine particles, and *timiśaṃśukam* is a mass of darkness variegated by rays of light. *Timiśaṃśukam* also means a blue veil (*nīlajālikā*), which is appropriate for a newly married, mature woman. Because it is red due to passion (*rāga*) following the creation of twilight, and because it takes the form of love (*prema*), the established position is that this verse belongs to the first category as *vācya-dhvani* (literal suggestion), the second as *vastu-vyaṅgya* (suggestion of a fact), and the third as *rasa-dhvani* (suggestion of aesthetic flavor). This is the state of affairs according to the *Bālapriyā*.
"Independently"—
this refers to what must be stated, namely "the definition" and so forth.
"The nature of the definition."
The meaning is "the definition of its own nature" (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*).
There is also a reading: "the definition is the own nature.

Here, intending that the account of the night and the moon is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) because it is relevant to the context (*prākaraṇika*), whereas the account of the hero is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) because it is not relevant to the context (*aprākaraṇika*), he explains the state of having common adjectives with the words beginning with "upoḍha."
The flickering of the lights is perceived through direct experience. "The third parts of the eyes" means gazes made with the third parts of the eyes.
He explains "grasped in such a manner" in accordance with the context as follows: "by means of devotion alone," and so forth.
Regarding "overpowered":
it is because kissing, in that very way, brings about aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
As it has been said: “For desire is the left.
In order to clarify the meaning of the word *yathā* (as) for the sake of establishing uniformity, he explains it with the words beginning with *bhaktaṭiti*.
Regarding the phrase *timirāṃśukam*, he dispels the misconception that it is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) by stating *timiraṃ ca* and so forth.

With the intention that the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of "small," he explains the word *aṃśuka* as "fine rays" (*sūkṣmāṃśavaḥ*). By implication, this refers to the moon. The compound *timira-aṃśukam* is a singular collective (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*) [meaning "darkness and fine rays"].
He states the result [of the argument] with the words "the rays," etc.
"Variegated" means multicolored. "A net of blue" means...
The name of one who wears a garment of blue color is well-known from the *Kāmaśāstra*. He states "navoḍhā" and so forth because its mention here is appropriate.
Since the slipping away of the garment of darkness is not the cause of passion in the present context, he fills out the sense with the word "anantaram" (immediately after).
The explanation of the word *pura* is "in the east," and so forth. *Locana* means "because. *Pura* refers both to the eastern direction and to what is in front.
It is fallen, calmed, and dropped;
it is entirely mixed by means of the night acting as the instrument,
or [the term "night"] is used as an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa).
"It was not marked" means it was not known that "this is the commencement of night";
for when one perceives rays of light mingled with darkness, it is characterized by the world as "the beginning of night," but not so when the light is clear.
In the case of the heroine (*nāyikā*), however, "by her" (*tayā*) is the agentive word (*kartṛpada*).
In the *lakṣya* (implied) interpretation, however, the word "api" (even/also) follows immediately after "lakṣitam" (indicated).
And here, the connection is that when the hero, having approached from behind, begins to kiss, there is the slipping or falling of the blue garment in front;
or else, the construction is: "the face was thus grasped by the hero in front, before him."
Therefore, although the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is perceived here, it does not hold primacy.
For instance, the conduct of the hero, by embellishing the night and the moon—which serve as the excitants (vibhāva) of the erotic sentiment—attains the status of an ornament (alaṅkāra);
from that expressed meaning, which has thus become the excitant, there flows forth the aesthetic relish (rasa).

As for the one who explains: "The word 'tadatiśaya' (that excellence) is the agentive term; and since agency is not possible for that which is insentient, the conduct of the hero is here inferred by the word itself and must be denoted, not suggested; therefore, this is *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation)."
He did not abandon the very meaning of the text under discussion, as it was followed by the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).

In this way, there would be a *rūpaka* (metaphor) that is "partially manifest" (*ekadeśavivartin*), just like the example: "The lake-kings were fanned by royal swans, as if by the autumn season itself."
But this is not *samāsokti* (synecdoche), because of the absence of common adjectives (*tulyaviśeṣaṇa*).

Since night can be considered the "hand" in relation to the mixing of darkness with subtle rays, he says "by that which has become the instrument" (*karaṇabhūtayā*), explaining that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

Since it is possible for the night to function as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) by way of being a signifier (*jñāpaka*) with respect to that mixture, he says "or by way of being a secondary indicator" (*upalakṣaṇatvena vā*) to explain that the third case ending is used because of that secondary indication.
The connection is: "mixed by means of that [night] as a secondary indicator.
There is also a reading: "or by means of a secondary indicator" (*upalakṣaṇena vā*).
Demonstrating this form by stating "it was not observed," he explains [the verse] beginning with "at night" and so forth.
"It was not known"— the word "by people" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In the word *labhitam*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
The phrase ending with *galitam* constitutes a separate sentence.
For this very reason, he says "in darkness," etc., in order to indicate the relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumad-bhāva*) between "not having obtained" and the subsequent state.
Regarding the phrase "on the night-side":
by this it is shown that the connection is simply "even elsewhere before [the night]. Regarding the word "immediately": [it refers to the following].
Thus, the word "api" (also/even) serves to conjoin the two characteristics of "flowing" and "descending"; this is the meaning.
To explain how there is a "flowing forward" from the blue-clad one (Nīlāmbara), he says "atra ca" and so forth.
He speaks according to the propriety of kissing, saying "yadi vā" and so forth.
The intention is that the word *puraḥ* is construed with the word *gṛhītam* even though they are separated [by other words].
By the phrase "by that," it is meant "by the two meanings already stated."
Regarding the phrase "in the suggested [meaning] (*vyaṅgye*)":
this means in the suggested meaning consisting of the hero's narrative.
The words beginning with "at night" (*niśā*) are qualifiers containing the reason why [the suggestion] possesses the status of an ornament (*alaṅkāratām*).
"Adorning" means embellishing by means of superimposition.
Having thus demonstrated that the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) has become subordinate, he says "tataḥ" and so forth in order to show that there is also the status of *dhvani* with respect to rasa.
"Tataḥ" means from that which has been refined (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding the phrase "from having become manifest" (*vibhāvībhūtāt*):
it means that after the impression (*saṃskāra*) has occurred, one attains the manifestation [of the object] without having previously experienced its manifestation.
Regarding the phrase "by means of sound" (*śabdena*): [it refers to the verbal expression].
The meaning is "by the word 'night-moon'";
it is inferred (*unnīta*), that is, deduced (*anumita*), or postulated (*kalpita*). It is precisely the denotative function (*abhidhā*) [that effects this].
The intended meaning is that there is no function [of the word] distinct from its primary denotation (*abhidhā*).

Furthermore, he states "precisely for this reason," etc., because the determination of [the word's] denotative status follows from the force of the technical name *samāsokti* (metaphorical identification).
He refutes [this objection] with "that," etc.
The connection is: "thus [is] the meaning of the text.
He states another refutation, beginning with "ekadeśa" (one part), etc. "In this way" means:
The meaning is that the conventional behavior of the heroine and hero constitutes the subject matter (*abhidheya*).
"Just as in this case" means:
just as here, because the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) consists solely of the night and the moon, upon which the conventional behaviors of heroine and hero have been superimposed.

Even in the case of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), although it implies a specific suggested meaning, it is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) itself that possesses beauty primarily; this is understood as the sentence-meaning through the very power of the statement of *ākṣepa*. For instance, in that context, a prohibition—which is mounted upon words—is understood through the desire to express a particular [point], and by this, the function of direct denotation (*abhidhā*) is excluded. Enough with these intermediate details. The conduct of the heroine toward the hero is superimposed upon the night.

In the explanation that the behavior of the hero toward the heroine is superimposed upon the moon, there is no contingency of applying the *naikaśeṣa* (the rule for retaining only one of two identical items).
As for "suggestion" (*ākṣepa*):
it is like a prohibition of something desired, intended for the purpose of expressing a specific distinction.
That *ākṣepa* (objection), whose subject matter consists of what is yet to be stated and what has already been stated, is considered to be of two kinds.
Among these, the first is as follows: "If I do not behold you even for a moment, I shall then be filled with longing;
let this much suffice, so what is the use of telling you anything else that is unpleasant?"
By the statement "dear to children" (*bālapriyā*), it follows by implication that the royal swans possess the nature of chowries and the autumn possesses the nature of a chowrie-bearer;

likewise, in the present case, by virtue of the words *timira-aṃśuka* ("darkness-garment"), the night and so forth possess the nature of a heroine (*nāyikā*) and so on. Thus, the meaning is that this would be a "partially manifest metaphor" (*ekadeśavivartirūpaka*). He states the reason why this is not "synecdoche" (*samāsokti*) with the word "tulya" ("equal").
He refutes the compatibility with the stated and implied words— beginning with "it is understood" (*gamyate*) and so forth.
"By this" means by the statement of the definition (*lakṣaṇavacanena*).
The term "utterance" (ukti) is appropriate precisely because it refers to the subject at hand, since the passage begins with "where there is an utterance," etc.; this is the sense.
Regarding "of the heroine" and so forth:
in the heroine's conduct, the activity consists of actions such as not looking at the falling of her blue garment, and so on.
"But [the state] of the hero, characterized by the beginning of kissing her face and so forth"—this refers to the "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*).
The meaning is: when there is an explanation of the intended sense in this manner.

Regarding the phrase "there is no contingency of a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*)," the meaning is that in the case of *nāyikānāyaka*, there is no contingency of applying the rule "pumāṃs striyā" (a masculine noun remains when combined with a feminine noun) as a single-remainder compound.

Thus, having demonstrated that in *samāsokti* (condensed expression) the expressed meaning (*vācya*) alone—when embellished by the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)—is primary, and therefore the definition of *dhvani* does not over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to it; he states that the same principle applies to *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis) as well, saying: "In *ākṣepa*... [as in the verse] *vṛtta*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "api" and so forth:
even in the case of a suggestion (ākṣepa), the connection is that "the beauty of the expressed meaning itself is primarily perceived."
The reason for this is stated as "the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*), and so forth.
The meaning is: by virtue of the power of that implied statement (*ākṣepokti*) which occurs with respect to the subject matter of the sentence-meaning.
To the question "How is there an implication (ākṣepa) therein?", it is said: "In the suggested" (vyaṅgye).
The meaning is: because they imply—that is, attract—the specific feature that is suggested.
"Mounted upon the word" (śabdopārūḍha).
The meaning is "that which is denoted by the word.
He shows the definition and examples of that as stated by Bhāmaha in the *Locana*—namely, "negation" (*pratiṣedha*).
"With the desire to indicate a specific [quality]" means with the desire to convey a specific [quality] that has become manifest (*vyaṅgya*).
The "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*)—
as in the upcoming verse beginning with "locanam"— which takes as its object death and consists of a prohibition, is a *ākṣepa* (paralipsis).

In this case, the very phrase "let this much be" implies "I shall die here," and being the basis for the beauty [of the passage], the implied (*ākṣepaka*) is adorned by that which is implied (*ākṣepya*), and thus the implied element is predominant.

The subject matter already mentioned is as follows, from my own work: "O traveler, why, why have you fallen here so unexpectedly? What other recourse is there for me, who am parched with thirst? That very man of wicked mind hides the water from me!

O friend, be angry at this thirst that has arisen out of place and is difficult to satisfy at the wrong time; for while the snow-mountain Himavat is world-renowned for its power, this path here is once again a desert!"
For the *bālapriyā* [commentary]: A semblance of negation (*pratiṣedhābhāsa*) is indeed [an instance of] what is intended;
that is *ākṣepa* (paralipsis).
He states its twofold nature with the words "that which is about to be said" (*vakṣyamāṇa*).
In this context, it should be understood that there is a prohibition against the very act of speaking regarding the subject matter about to be described;
however, regarding the subject matter already mentioned, the prohibition applies sometimes to the object itself and sometimes to the description of the object.
"I am [here].
This is the speech of a certain woman full of longing for her beloved who is about to depart.
"If I, being eager, were not to see you even for a moment," [I would perish].
Therefore, let there be only this much speech, extending to this point;
for this reason, the phrase "by another [means] than that which is unpleasant to you" contains a logical ground (*hetugarbha*),
namely, by means of the speech already spoken.
The meaning is: "Why should I not speak? Here, he applies the definition with the words beginning with "iti" and so forth: "having the nature of a negation."
"What is meant by 'by what is said'?"—the meaning is that it consists of a semblance of a prohibition against speaking.
Here too, he shows that the expressed meaning (*vācya*) alone is primary, with the words "In that [context]" and so forth.
"This very thing" refers precisely to the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).
It projects; it manifests;
by means of that which is projected—that is, by the manifestation consisting of the determination to die.
The phrase "ākṣepakam iyad evāstu" and so forth has already been stated.
Regarding the vocative "bho bho," there are two readings:
"khalasṛtis seyām" and "khalamatis so 'yam."
In this context, the expressed meaning (vācya) concerns a traveler on a desert path;
however, the contextual matter (prakṛta), the account of serving a wicked master, is the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya).
By the repetition "O, O," an excess of regard for the person being addressed is illuminated.
"At the wrong time" means at an improper occasion;
the sense is that by coming here and by practicing this [path], whatever desired fruit one seeks will not be accomplished.
By the word "pāntha" (O traveler), his lack of experience in service is indicated.
When someone who has been serving for a long time spoke thus, the traveler, somewhat provoked, said—starting with "kāni" and ending with "khale"—"O you rogue! [he says].

For one who is so intensely parched by thirst—where "thirst" means both the craving for water and the desire for wealth—there is no other recourse or support for me; this is the meaning. Because no other path has been found, I have come here; because no other refuge has been found, I have taken refuge in this Lord; such is the sense.
Having heard that, another said: "The path," and so forth; that [path] has been resorted to by you.
This is the path, this is the way, and this is the Lord.
Water is *vāri* and it is also *dhana*.
"He conceals [it] in the jar"; the sense is, "from where could there be a greater impossibility?
However, in the reading *'khalamatiḥ so 'yam'*, the statement "that very one" refers to Māra and the Lord on the path.
Some maintain that everything up to "gūhate" (he hides) is the speech of the traveler alone.
Another person, mocking the anger manifested by the word "khalu" (wretch), says "asthāna... and so forth.
When an object is easily accessible, craving does not arise at an improper time.
Furthermore, when it is difficult to obtain [the object], then it occurs; thus, there is "difficulty in obtaining at the wrong time.
The sense is: "Be angry with craving for the sake of craving, not with me.
To the question, "In what way is it 'arisen out of place'?", he says: "The three worlds," and so forth.
The greatness of its power consists in its extreme harmfulness and so forth, as well as its extreme greediness and so forth.
"Mārava" refers to a path associated with the desert (*maru*),
and yet it is also a bad master (*duṣprabhu*).

In this regard, a certain servant has arrived here; his heart is being pierced by the hope, "What is to be obtained from this that I have not yet received? He is then awakened by a certain objection (*ākṣepa*).

Therein, by means of the objection—which takes the form of a negation—the expressed meaning itself, consisting of service to a wicked man, its fruitlessness, and the resulting agitation, becomes a source of aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) by serving as the determinant (*vibhāva*) for the state of despondency (*nirveda*), which is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*).
However, Vāmana’s definition of *ākṣepa* is: "An objection is the denial of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*)."
The implication (*ākṣepa*) of the standard of comparison, such as the moon, is: "If this [face] exists, what is the use of you?
For example: "She possesses that face, gentle and beautiful—what need is there for the full moon? And if her eyes are the very seat of beauty, what indeed is the use of blue lotuses?"
Intending the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) that has been stated, [the author] says "here," etc.
The connection is: "A certain servant is being enlightened by someone.
The two words beginning with "prāpta" (attained) are qualifiers of the servant.
He has obtained the Lord who is to be served;
he has obtained that which is to be obtained, such as wealth and so forth,
from this Lord.
"What is it? means "for what reason?

"I do not obtain" refers to one whose heart is being torn asunder by a renewed hope arising immediately after the initial thought, a hope produced at every moment; this is the cause for awakening [to the truth].
By someone who has long served him, by some agent;

by this censure— performed with the desire to convey specific suggested meanings such as the service of wicked men and its fruitlessness— in the form of a prohibition, "Why [has he] fallen so unexpectedly?",
he is being awakened.
The meaning is that, although the Lord’s nature—such as his extreme greed and so forth—was already known, he is being awakened [to it] out of compassion.
Here too, he demonstrates that the suggested sense (vyaṅgya) serves as an embellishment for the expressed sense (vācya), beginning with the words "In that case" (tatra).
"In that case" refers to the example.
"By way of negation" (niṣedharūpeṇa): the meaning is "by way of negating what [is the cause]?"—that is, by way of negating the fruit of falling.
"By way of objection" (ākṣepeṇa): the meaning of the instrumental case is "distinction," which is connected with the expressed object.
The meaning is "that which is expressed together with it.
Regarding the phrase "of the expressed alone":
the meaning is "only with respect to the expressed object, such as a traveler on a desert path."
This is connected with the phrase "the quality of producing wonder.
To the question "of what? he says: "the wicked," and so forth.
An "unworthy person" (asatpuruṣa) is a bad ruler.
[This refers to] "of the suggested meaning" (vyaṅgyasya), by implication.
He states the cause for the production of aesthetic charm (camatkāra) in this suggested meaning [which is] the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*)—beginning with the words "peaceful" (*śānta*), etc.
The futility of serving wicked persons is the determinants (*vibhāva*).
The resulting agitation is the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion).

By means of the *ākṣepa* (paralipsis)—which takes the form of a denial of the result of the fall of something desired, namely, "Why has this fallen so unexpectedly?"—that which is being denied, such as the fruitlessness of serving a wicked person, serves as its ornament; thus, the sense is that the expressed meaning (*vācya*) alone is the primary element.

It should also be understood that, as in the verse beginning "By whom the vital breaths were surrendered," there is here also *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), so this *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) is mixed with that.
It is connected with the phrase "the definition of *vāmanatva*.
He demonstrates the meaning of the word *ākṣepa* with the words "in this," and so forth.
In this [context], regarding the face and so forth which are intended to be the objects of comparison (upameya),
there is a purpose or result (phala) produced by you, the moon and so forth, who serve as the standards of comparison (upamāna).
Regarding the word *tasyāḥ*:
the pronoun *tat* (in the compound *taddṛśau*) refers to that which was previously experienced, and it should be construed by modifying the word *dṛśau* accordingly.
It is gentle (*saumyam*), meaning sweet to behold, and for that very reason, it is also beautiful (*subhagam*).
"What fruit, what fruit?"—
"Two eyes," [he said];
"they exist" is the ellipsis.
The word "yadi" (if) indicates a restatement of what is already established; "by them" means by those things well-known;
"therein" means in that [context].
"Hī" means "alas, what a pity!
That very suggestion (ākṣepa) which takes the form of this exclamation, while itself suggesting a particular suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), constitutes the primary body of poetry.

For the intention to emphasize either the expressed (*vācya*) or the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) meaning is based on the excellence of their respective beauty. As, for example: "The twilight is full of passion; the day is its precursor. Is it the eye, or rather the sprouts of tender luster? Alas! While that lower lip already exists, the Creator’s persistence in beginning the composition of redundant things is truly unprecedented. In this verse, the emphasis is placed on the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which is the lover's face, because of its superior beauty compared to the expressed objects.
In this case, even though the meaning of the simile (*upamā*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), it serves only to embellish the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
As for the question "What is the use of that?", the *ākṣepa* (objection) consisting of a dismissal is itself the cause of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) within the expressed meaning alone.
Alternatively, *ākṣepa* may mean the implication of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) through its own force (*sāmarthya*).
For example: "The autumn season, bearing the rainbow—resembling a fresh nail-mark—upon her pale cloud-breast, while pleasing the spotted moon, increased the heat of the sun even further."

Thus, in this [verse] by Atri, although another hero defiled by jealousy is suggested as the object of comparison, it serves as an ornament for the expressed meaning itself; therefore, this is indeed *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
He states this with the words "excess of beauty" (*cārutvotkarṣa*).
To provide a well-known illustration of this very point, he says: "full of passion" (*anurāgavatī*).
Therefore, it should be understood that the demonstration of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) remains incomplete.
In this regard, the phrase "again" (*punar*) is given as an illustration:

it refers to those undertakings or activities (*ārambha-vyāpārāḥ*) directed toward the creation or composition of things that are redundant, unworthy of acceptance, and fruitless, such as the full moon and so forth.
*Apūrvaḥ* means not seen elsewhere;
*grahaḥ* refers to a particular intention (*abhisandhi-viśeṣaḥ*).
Here too, he demonstrates the subordinate status of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) by saying "here," and so forth.
The meaning of "comparison" (upamārtha) is the sense consisting of similarity with the moon and so forth. It "embellishes only the expressed," meaning it decorates only the literal meaning.
He states the reason for this with the words beginning "why," and so on.
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "In this way, it must be said that the *ākṣepa* (objection/parody) itself is the cause of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
It takes the form of dismissal or refutation.
He explains the sūtra "Upamānākṣepa" (Parody of the Simile) differently, beginning with "If, however," and so forth.
By implication means by the power of the meaning;
"manifestation" (vyañjana) is the drawing forth [of the sense],
as in the word "Aindra."
*Payodhara* means cloud, water, and breast.
Regarding the phrase "making [them] gracious," and so forth:
for during the autumn season, there is an extraordinary clarity of the moon and an intensity of the sun's heat.
Here he applies the definition, beginning with "atra" and so forth.
"Irṣyeti" means that the object of comparison is another lover who has been defiled by *irṣyā*, that is, by intolerance (*ākṣānti*). This is the meaning.
"Suggested" (ākṣipta) means "manifested" (vyañjita).
This is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the manifestation of the heroine.

In the case of the heroine (*nāyikā*), although the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is heard [in the text] as residing in the nail-marks, it must be applied to Indra’s bow; thus the meaning is: "bearing nail-marks resembling a rainbow.
Regarding the phrase "this one" (*eṣā*) and so forth:
according to the opinion of Vāmana, this is stated as an example of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), whereas according to the opinion of Bhāmaha, it is simply an example of *samāsokti* (condensed expression).
"He says this" means that he states the reason for the point already mentioned— that the expressed meaning alone possesses primacy, not the suggested meaning.
"Right here" [refers to this very point].

The meaning is that primacy is established by the excellence of beauty; this is precisely the point. The particle *eva* (only/precisely) is used to dispel any doubt that this might be an example of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
[The word] "anurāgavatī" (possessing passion).

*Anurāgau* refers to both redness and a particular kind of love. *Tatpurassaraḥ* means that which flows before her—that is, flowing previously and directly in front of her. Through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of these two meanings as one, their identity should be understood; for this very reason, the justification for expressions such as "aho" (oh! and so forth is established. In the case of the hero (*nāyaka*), however, the meaning is "present before her."
"Thus" means:
by way of stating an illustration—alas, such is the course of fate that even so, there is no meeting!

In this case, even though there is a cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), it is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) alone that possesses beauty and excellence; therefore, it is the expressed meaning itself whose predominance is intended to be conveyed.

Just as in instances such as *dīpaka* or *apahnuti*, although a simile (*upamā*) is perceived as being suggested, it is not designated by that [simile] because it is not intended to be predominant, so too should it be understood here. (The verse on *samāsokti* has been recited. *Locana*: The verse on *samāsokti* has been recited.
"Alas, the course of destiny!"—
this means that non-encounter is caused by dependence on a teacher and so forth.
"Of that very [person]" refers to this.

The meaning is "of the expressed alone. This objection is raised from the perspective of Vāmana; however, from the perspective of Bhāmaha, it is *samāsokti* (speech of compression). Keeping this intention in mind, the author of the treatise has provided this single example for both *samāsokti* and *ākṣepa* (objection) by means of a logical argument.
Whether this be considered *samāsokti* (synecdoche) or *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis), what does it matter to us?

Our thesis is that in all poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) becomes subordinate to the expressed meaning (*vācya*); this is the intention established here in our treatise by my teachers.

Having thus stated an example regarding the intention to express predominance, he provides an example well-known to both himself and others to show that designation (*vyapadeśa*) also occurs solely on account of predominance, beginning with "And as... The phrase "of the comparison" means "of the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)."

By the word "tayā" (by her), the simile is indicated; for the definition of *dīpaka* (the illuminator) is: "The *dīpaka* is held to be threefold, according to whether its scope lies in the beginning, the middle, or the end. [Examples follow:
"A gem polished on a whetstone; a victor in battle crushed by weapons; the moon with only a digit remaining; a young woman worn out by amorous play."

An elephant whose rut has faded, a river in autumn with its sandy banks dried up, and people whose wealth has vanished—these all shine with a beauty born of thinness when faced with those who seek them.
The meaning is: "because it lacks the status of being an illustration (*udāharaṇa*) for the *Bālapriyā-alaṅkāra*.
The construction is: "it remains indeed incomplete.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
The meaning is "the justification of the objection.
He shows the implied cause for the non-union of the two lovers with the words beginning with "guru" (heavy).
He states his intention in presenting the example beginning with "anurāga" (passion) with the words beginning with "vāmana" (Vāmana).
"By the intention of Vāmana" means by way of the position that establishes the simile;
"this" refers to the passage beginning with "anurāga," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "herein the text": the meaning is that the text extends from the words beginning with "cārutva" up to the end of the section ending with "prādhānyavivakṣā.
As for the phrase "for in the case of *dīpaka*": [it refers to the following].
The grammatical connection here is: "In this case, the beauty consists precisely in what is produced by the *dīpaka*.
Furthermore, in place of the reading "for in the *dīpaka*," there is also the reading "for instance" (*tathāhi*).
He shows another definition and example of that [figure] as stated by Bhāmaha, beginning with "ādī" and so forth.
In this context, words such as "ādi" (and so forth) refer to the subject matter of the sentence.
Among these, he provides an example of the final *dīpaka* (illuminator): "The jewel," etc.
In the phrase "the eye," the aesthetic charm arises solely from the function of illumination (*dīpana*).
"Apahnuti (concealment) consists of a desired [object] having some internal resemblance.
In that case, the beauty arises precisely through the concealment.
For example: "This is not a swarm of bees repeatedly making noise with intoxication; it is she who cries out."
This is the sound of the bow of Kandarpa being drawn.
Thus [it is said].
Having thus considered this objection, he states another object of knowledge in accordance with the order of enumeration, beginning with the words "anuktanimittāyām":
"When one part has vanished, the praise of another quality for the purpose of manifesting a particular excellence is known as *viśeṣokti* (the description of a particularity)."
For example: "That flower-armed god alone conquers the three worlds;
though his body was taken away by Śambhu, his power was not taken away."
And since this [suggestion] has an inconceivable cause (*acintyanimitta*), there is no existence of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) within it.

Even in the case of that which has a stated cause (*uktanimitta*), the matter culminates in being merely the intrinsic nature of the thing (*vastusvabhāvamātra*); thus, even there, there is no suspicion of the existence of the suggested.
For example: "Like camphor, he who remains potent in every person even when burnt..."
Homage be to that Flower-Bowed One, whose valor is irresistible!
The verse from the *Bālapriyā* has also been cited in the *Kuvalayānanda* as an example of what is called "illumination" (*dīpana*),
which consists precisely in the connection of a single attribute across multiple loci.
By the word "eva" (only/itself), the exclusion of suggested simile (*vyaṅgyopamā*) is intended.
He shows the definition and example of *apahnuti* according to Bhāmaha with the words beginning "apahnutiḥ" and so forth.
Here, it should be understood that the word *apahnuti* is to be repeated.
*Abhīṣṭasya* means of that which is intended to be described.
*Kiñcidantargatā* means that in which a suggested (*vyaṅgya*) simile is contained within something.
*Apahnutiḥ* is negation.
Apahnuti is the figure of speech (alaṃkāra) bearing that name. There are two readings: "apahnutya" and "apahnavena."
"Beauty" means loveliness;
"this is not [it]"—
this is the connection with the phrase "she cries out repeatedly."
The statement "drawn by intoxication" (*madena mukharā ākṛṣyamāṇasya*) is expressed through the relationship of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).

Showing the connection between the preceding text and the passage beginning with "when the cause is unstated" (*anuktanimittāyām*), he introduces [the next section] with the words "Thus," and so forth.
Regarding the term "enunciation" (*uddeśa*):
The meaning is that it refers to what was previously stated, such as "samāsokti," "ākṣepa," and so forth.
Beginning the explanation of the purpose of stating [the phrase] "of that whose cause is unmentioned" (anuktanimittāyām), he says "eka" and so on.
The definition beginning with "eka" belongs to Bhāmaha.
The "praise" (saṃstuti) is the description of one part— the cause, such as its subtlety— and another quality— the effect, such as its power.
"For the sake of manifesting a distinction" means for the purpose of proclaiming a certain excellence. "He" refers to that well-known one.
The word "api" (also/even) should also be applied here to the phrase "by means of union.
Since strength depends upon the body, it is logical that strength perishes when the body perishes;
however, in this case, it is stated that strength persists even when the body has perished.
And regarding that, whatever sign (*nimitta*) there may be, it is nevertheless inconceivable; thus he says:
"And this... [meaning] that it culminates in the mere intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing itself.
The meaning is that it is the manifestation of another meaning.
In the word "karpūra," the phrase beginning with "avārya" is the statement of the cause.
"By that" means:

because the existence of the suggested [meaning] occurs even in a *viśeṣokti* where the cause is not explicitly stated, as in the following example: "Though summoned by his companions, though having said 'yes' and shaken off sleep, the traveler, though intending to depart, does not loosen his hesitation at all."

Thus, and so forth: there is merely the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) by virtue of the power of the context; however, the *Locana* [states] that this is not the cause for the cognition of that [context]. Therefore, setting aside those two modes, he raises the third possibility: "even in the case of [suggestion] whose cause is unexpressed. Regarding the phrase "of the suggested": [it refers to the fact that the cause is not expressed].
Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa maintains that the cause here is indeed the distress caused by the cold;
with this intention, he says: "But there is no production of beauty whatsoever here.
As for the cause imagined even by connoisseurs: "In the company of one's beloved, sleep is a means even lighter than departing."
Thinking that he did not abandon his contraction because he perceived it as the onset of sleep— that too has not been posited as a cause of beauty by those who know the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*);

rather, it is precisely the portion of *viśeṣokti* (the "specification of the effect")— namely, that [the contraction] does not slacken— which, being thus manifested and embellished by its cause, serves as the cause of beauty.
Otherwise, this would not even be a case of *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation).
Thus, the author has set forth both these intended meanings through a common expression; it should not be thought that the text is established solely according to the intention of Udbhaṭa.
This also applies to *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
Paryāyokta (periphrasis) is that which is expressed by another manner,
being devoid of the functions of the denoted and the denoter, and consisting of comprehension.
Such is the definition.
For example: "By means of this bow, the teaching of the Dharma has been shown to Rāma, the sage who desires the firm destruction of his enemies and who has gone astray."
Thus it is said.
The term *bālapriyā* does not exist; therefore, this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "the cause" (*nimitta*) here:
The meaning is that the "sign" (nimitta) is that which is to be understood as the loosening of contraction. Regarding the term "lighter" (laghutara):
the sense is that the onset of sleep is obtained by not abandoning contraction.
"That too is a cause" means that it is considered by connoisseurs (*rasika*) to be a cause in the form of the cognition that sleep has arrived.
"But rather," and so forth.
The construction is as follows: "it does not slacken" refers precisely to that portion which constitutes the *viśeṣokti* (the statement of distinction).
"With its cause being manifested" means with its previously mentioned cause.
"But otherwise" means:
due to the absence of the specific form consisting of the embellishment of the manifested cause.
"Two intentions" refers to:

The meaning is that there are two intentions of the connoisseur Udbhaṭa. By the statement "through the commonality" (*sādhāraṇīkṛtya*) and by the statement "of the suggested meaning" (*vyaṅgyasya*), he states the definition as taught by Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa: "it is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis)."
The word "that" (tat) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
He shows the meaning of the synonymous term by saying "by another";
he clarifies that very point by saying "the denoted," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the destruction of enemies": the existence of enemies is not appropriate for a Sage;
therefore, the desire to destroy them is even more inappropriate.
The firmness of that [resolve] was utterly unprecedented;
for this very reason, he says "arose" (utpate).
It refers to Rāma Bhārgava.
By this Bhīṣma acting as the agent and the bow as the instrument,
a teaching of the Dharma— that is, an instruction on the Dharma— was imparted or performed.
Here too, he demonstrates that the expressed meaning alone is primary—beginning with the words "atrāpi" and so forth.
Since it is merely the production of a certain beauty, it does not possess primacy.
Even in the case of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), if the suggested meaning were indeed primary, let it be included within *dhvani*.
But there is no inclusion of *dhvani* therein,
because it will be demonstrated that its scope is vast and that it functions as the predominant element (*aṅgin*).
In this regard, although it is perceived that Bhīṣma’s power here surpasses the power of Bhārgava, [the Locana continues:]
Nevertheless, by the very statement that "the teaching of the Dharma was taught with its assistance," the meaning of the poem is embellished.

Therefore, that which is being expressed (abhidhīyamāna)—being characterized by the suggested (vyaṅgya) sense, which consists of comprehension through a synonym (paryāya), that is, by another mode—is called *paryāyokta*. Here, "that which is being expressed" (*abhidhīyamāna*) is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), while "paryāyokta" is the term to be defined (*lakṣya*).

If it is maintained that the general definition [of suggestion] is "the state of being a figure of sense" (*arthālaṅkāratva*), then everything is consistent; provided, however, that the phrase "is expressed" (*abhidhīyate*) is explained as "is expressed," "is understood," or "is presented as a gift," and the example is taken as "Wander,
O pious man" (*bhama dhammia*) and so forth.
In that case, its status as an ornament is set aside from afar because it culminates in being the very self [of the meaning];
and then, it should not be counted among the ornaments.
Furthermore, other varieties of this [figure] must be stated.

Thus he says: "If [it occurs] primarily," and "in the case of *dhvani*. The meaning is that because it is included within the self (*ātman*), it would be the self itself and not a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): "is perceived by the simple-minded" (*bālapriyā pratīyate*) means "is manifested" (*vyajyate*).
"By its assistance" means by that which is embellished through the implied meaning; or rather,
it means by the expressed meaning alone.
The meaning of the poem is the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa).
"For this very reason" means that everything is consistent; such is the connection.
The sense is that if the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) were predominant, all of this would be untenable; therefore, the predominance of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) alone must be accepted.
Bhāmaha’s definition is merely this much: "Paryāyokta is when something is expressed by another manner";
therein, the explanation of the phrase "by another manner" extends from "by way of synonym" (*paryāyeṇa*) up to "characterized by [the aforementioned]."
In order to indicate that the very meaning of the synonymous term has been stated here by means of another method, the word "paryāyeṇa" (by way of synonym) is used.
For this very reason, its explanation is given as "prakārāntareṇa" (by another method).
To the question "What is that method?", he says: "avagamātmanā" (by way of comprehension).
This is its explanation: "by the suggested" (*vyaṅgyena*).
He states the meaning of the instrumental case as "characterized" (*upalakṣitam*).
The connection is as follows: "that which is expressed, being thus expressed, is called 'expressed through implication' (*paryāyoktam*)."
The explanation of the term ‘abhidīyamānam’ (being denoted) is: “it is precisely that which has been stated [as existent]. This refers to the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇapada*);
the meaning is that this is a sentence expressing a definition (*lakṣaṇavākya*).

The sense is that by this very definition-statement, the predominance of the expressed meaning (vācya) as it follows upon the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is understood. Regarding the phrase "the word *lakṣya*":
the sense is that by this term, which is [used] according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha*), what was stated previously is also understood.
The general definition [of poetry] is that it consists of figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*).

The underlying point is that if the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) were predominant, it would attain the status of being the primary object of ornamentation (*alaṅkārya*), and consequently, its status as a mere figure (*alaṅkāra*) would be undermined.
The general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is the common property (*sāmānyadharma*).
He raises another alternative view with the words "if, however" (*yaditu*).
[He says] "by force" (*balāt*).
The meaning is "by means of the pressure of sound. It is understood as being primary.
The prefix *abhi-* signifies "towards" or "facing."
The sense is that this [distinction] is based on predominance (*prādhānya*).
He states "at that time," etc., to show that under this view, what is intended would not be established.
To the objection, "Let it then not be a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*)," he replies with "at that time."
Not only does this involve the abandonment of a well-established nature, but it would also entail the postulation of an unestablished internal distinction; thus he says "bhedetyādi.

Furthermore, in *paryāyokta*—such as that cited by Bhāmaha—the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) alone is predominant, whereas in the case of the primary and the manifested (*prādhāna-vyaṅgya*), this is not so.
Because in those cases, the expressed meaning is not intended as the primary focus due to its subordinate status.

Furthermore, in the figures of speech *apahnuti* (concealment) and *dīpaka* (illumination), the expressed meaning is intended as a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*); such [expressed meaning] is not included within *dhvani*, nor have we defined *dhvani* in that manner.
For suggestion (dhvani) has a vast scope, pervading all poetic figures (bhāva) and the like; moreover, it is the primary element (aṅgin) because it is the locus of the establishment of everything.
Furthermore, a poetic figure is not pervasive, as other figures are not;
nor is it the primary element, because it is dependent upon that which is to be embellished (alaṅkārya).

The sense is this: if its pervasiveness and status as the primary element (aṅgin) are admitted while its status as an *alaṅkāra* is abandoned, then this very position of ours is being adopted under the name "Paryāyokta" (Indirect Expression) solely due to the grip of envy.

And he shows that this has not been seen even by previous [writers], but has been revealed by us alone, with the words "not again" (*na punar*). Bhāmaha’s own intended form of *vakrokti* is demonstrated through an example. Even there, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) does not possess primacy, because it is not the cause of beauty (*cārutva*).
Therefore, the logical connection is that even when another similar example is conceived in accordance with that [definition], the suggested meaning still lacks primacy.

If, however, disregarding what was stated there, examples such as "abhama dhamma" (O virtuous one, roam) and so forth are cited, then they belong solely to our school. But to refine oneself by means of improper tradition (*apaśruti*) without relying on this method is the conduct of the ignoble. As the historians say: "Even by concealing [the truth] out of contempt, one who listens falls into hell."
For Bhāmaha has indeed cited: "In caves or on the roads, we do not eat food as long as learned Brahmins do not eat.
The meaning is that [the types of poetry] are manifold.
In the *Vṛtti*, it was merely stated that [suggestion] is included within *dhvani*;
he explains how this leads to the undesirable consequence that it would not be an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) by saying "in itself" (*ātmani*) and "of such a kind" (*yādṛśa*).

The meaning is: "that in which the suggested sense has become subordinate. He states the reason for its not being included [in the previous categories] with the words beginning with "na" (not), etc. [He explains] "samasta" (entire), etc.
The meaning is "qualities and so forth.
"Like other ornaments" means "like bracelets and the like, which are well-known in the world."
The meaning of "athetyādi" and so forth is as follows: if it is argued that this ornament called *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is both pervasive and the primary subject (*aṅgin*),
then [the response is] "tarhi" (in that case).
The construction is as follows: because of the mention of "miserliness" (mātsarya), it is expressed by means of a periphrasis (*paryāyokta*) that "this very system of ours is being adopted.
The phrase "even this much" means "even the predominance of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)."
"Thus he shows" means that he demonstrates the meaning stated by the passage beginning with "not again," and so forth.
"There too" [means as follows].
The meaning is: "even in Bhāmaha’s example.
He anticipates another position and refutes it with the words "yadi tu" (if, however), etc. [He says:
"but merely by not relying on this method, through [the fault of] hearing incorrectly," etc.

The meaning is: by means of a mere semblance of hearing, without grasping the meaning of the scriptures from the mouth of the guru himself after first approaching the guru according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding the phrase "with contempt," the ellipsis is "toward the knowledge and toward the guru."
"Without covering," that is, having concealed oneself;
"he goes," meaning he reaches it.
To the question "What is that example cited by Bhāmaha?", he says: "By Bhāmaha."
Regarding the phrase "in the houses":
