it is well known that when learned Brahmins do not eat food in our houses, whether at home or on the road, that food lacks primacy; likewise, it is well known that a suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) follows the expressed meaning (vācya).
Even in the case of the figure of speech *saṅkara* (commixture), when one figure of speech adopts the shadow of another figure of speech, [the latter is subordinate].
Indeed, this *Locana* [states] that the words of the Blessed Vāsudeva prohibit the giving of the *rasa* by way of a synonym;
for he himself says: "And that is for the purpose of ceasing the giving of the *rasa*.
Furthermore, there is no aesthetic charm (*cārutva*) in this suggested prohibition of the giving of the *rasa* by virtue of which its predominance might be suspected.

Rather, that very act of not eating—which is strengthened by the implication [of the Brahmins' meal] and which occurs in the absence of feeding the Brahmins—becomes *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) in the manner described, and thus embellishes the primary subject, the purpose of the meal.
For it is not intended here that "his meal shall be free of poison"; rather, the point is that according to the ancients, *paryāyokta* is indeed an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
This refers to the cases of *apahnuti* (concealment) and *dīpaka* (illumination).
This has already been determined previously. For this very reason, he says "well-known" (prasiddham);
the meaning is that it is recognized, established, and authoritative.

Previously, it was stated that this [object] cannot even be a candidate for the designation of "simile" (*upamā*) and so forth; thus, by way of this shadow-like illustration, it was spoken as an example. Nevertheless, in order to complete the sequence of the enumeration and to fit it into the framework of the treatise, it is stated once more: "Because there is no predominance of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*), it is not *dhvani*. This is because, through another perspective, the same single entity might be suspected of being *dhvani* precisely by virtue of its being a suggested meaning within a simile.

As for what the author of the *Vivaraṇa* has investigated at great length through an elaborate array of examples—claiming that there is no connection of the simile (*upamā*) with everything [in the verse]—that is useless, worthless, and easily refuted.
The syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Intoxication produces joy; that [joy] produces the bodiless god [of love], which shatters pride; we enjoy that which is dear to the young."
"Speech" means [speech] directed toward the King of Cedi;
this is the ellipsis. "By way of synonyms" means:
"By means of understanding through another mode" means by way of comprehension through a different manner.
"It prohibits the giving of [poisoned] food" means it makes known the cessation of the giving of poison.

The meaning is that the intention of the Blessed One—namely, "May this food prepared with poison by the resolve of the King of Cedi not become poisonous for me," or "May my meal be free from poison"—becomes suggested (*vyaṅgya*) to those who possess a sensitive heart (*sahṛdaya*).
It is connected [in the original text] as: "there is no beauty."
The sense is that beauty belongs to the expressed meaning alone.
"Tadvyaṅgyā" means "that which has the aforementioned suggested meaning."
"That very thing is the expressed; that very thing" means "in the manner described," which is to say, by being characterized as the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) whose nature is comprehension.
"Relating to the context" means for the purpose of eating;
that is to say, the meaning is that one eats food remaining after study (*adhīti-bhukta-śiṣṭa*) which is established by the context.
He states that it is not primary because the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is not intended, saying: "For this [suggested meaning]... and so forth.
This refers to Vāsudeva.
It was not intended for the King of Cedi, nor was it meant to inform him.
He concludes with the word "iti" (thus).
He explains the term *prasiddhapada* (well-known word) in three ways, beginning with "pratīta" (well-understood).

Anticipating the objection that there is redundancy because this is merely the first mention of what was already stated previously in the context of "the negation of the speaker" (*tīpakāpahnuti*) and so forth, he says "pūrvam" and so on, adding "itthamayā chāyayā" (in this manner, by way of this aspect), thereby stating that although the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the same, there is no redundancy due to the difference in the modes (*prakāra*).
The meaning is "in this manner.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "It has been stated once again that it is not *dhvani* because there is an absence of predominance of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) element.
Regarding the word "entity" (*vastu*):
The meaning is that even though the simile is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), its nature is that of a subordinate matter (*vastu*).
By demonstrating the connection with the simile, he states that [the objection] is easily refuted, beginning with "intoxication" (*mada*) and so forth.
Intoxication (*mada*) is the joy produced from indulging in a particular object.
"Delight" refers to attachment to sense objects;
"pride" is the inflation of the mind,
and its "shattering" is a qualification of the bodiless one (Anaṅga).
He beheld his eyes, which bore the longing for union with his beloved and the unbearable grief of his mind.
It is so; for here too, even though [the elements] are produced in successive order, the relationship of standard of comparison (upamāna) and object of comparison (upameya) is easily established.
Indeed, there is no lack of the relationship of standard and object of comparison among things that occur sequentially.
For instance: Daśaratha was like Rāma; Daśaratha’s son, Raghu, was likewise like Daśaratha;
and the lineage of Dilīpa was like Aja. How wonderful is this fame of Rāma!
Thus, it does not fail to exist.
Therefore, what is this alarm that sequentiality, simultaneity, or contextual relevance obstructs the simile? Enough of following the example of milking a she-ass!
[This applies] even in the case of the *saṅkara* (commixture) ornament.
When there is the mention of two contradictory ornaments, when their simultaneous occurrence is impossible,
and when there is no logical reason or fault for choosing one over the other, that is *saṅkara* (commixture).
Thus, there is one type [of *samudāyopamā*] based on its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

As in my own work: "This woman, whose face is like the moon, whose eyes are like dark lotuses, and whose row of teeth is like white jasmine—possessing a charming form produced from the sky, water, and land—was created by the Creator."

In this case, regarding the phrase "it.i" (thus), there is a *saṅkara* (commixture) because both the metaphor (*rūpaka*)—that the moon is her face—and the simile (*upamā*)—that her face is like that [moon]—are simultaneously suggested; yet, since both cannot coexist, and since there is no evidence to favor the rejection or acceptance of either one, the determination remains solely between the suggested and the expressed meanings. Therefore, how can there be any possibility of *dhvani*?
As for the second type—the coexistence of verbal and semantic ornaments in a single instance—even there, what doubt can there be regarding the suggested meaning?
For example: "O Smara, you delight your beloved like Smara himself through embracing him.
[This is called] *bālapriyā uttarā*.
The meaning is: "even though each subsequent [member] is produced by each preceding one.
By this, its sequential nature is stated.
[Regarding the term] "upamāna" (the standard of comparison).
The meaning is that because they produce a modification of the mind (*manovikāra*), it is possible to conceive of their similarity.
He demonstrates the relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) among these successive [states] with the words "like Rāma.
In this case, the similarity should be understood as consisting in the possession of specific excellences (*guṇaviśeṣavatva*).
"It is not that it does not exist" means that it certainly exists.
He concludes with a derisive remark, beginning with "Therefore," and so forth.
"Commixture (saṅkara) is fourfold—due to the distinctions such as commixture by doubt (sandeha-saṅkara) and so forth.
He demonstrates their definitions according to the opinion of Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa with the words "viruddha...
[etc.]: when there is an "ullekha," that is, an "ullāsa" (manifestation), of two contradictory ornaments.
"Simultaneously" means at the same time. "The impossibility of their occurrence" means the impossibility of those two functioning together.
When one of the two is apprehended, the apprehension occurs through the exclusion of the other;
this is the principle (*nyāya*). Manifestation (*bhāna*) is the means of proof (*sādhaka*), while a defect (*doṣa*) is the sublater (*bādhaka*).
[The example is] "the moon" (*śaśī*).
The three qualifiers beginning with "śaśivadane" (O moon-faced one) are, respectively, the grounds for the [consequences] beginning with "in the sky.
"Eka" means: upon the rejection or the acceptance of one of the two positions.
The word *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
Regarding the phrase beginning with *vyaṅgya*:

because there is no certainty as to what is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and what is expressed (*vācya*), even the possibility that it is a *dhvani*—based on the predominance of the suggested meaning—is present right here [in this verse]. In this very [verse], there is both a *yamaka* (paronomasia) and a simile (*upamā*).

The third type: where multiple poetic figures (arthālaṅkāra) reside in a single part of a sentence, since two of them are equal [in prominence], which one is the suggested (vyaṅgya)? For example: "When the sun has set, because its rising and falling are equal, the weary day enters the cave of darkness as if to find a dwelling."

Thus it is. For here, the description of the noble son (*kulaputra*) as being eager to undertake the vows appropriate for the calamity of his master is shown to be a *rūpaka* (metaphor) that functions through a partial transformation (*ekadeśavivartin*).
Furthermore, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is expressed by the word "iva" (as if).
Thus, these two types have been described:
"The ornaments of word and meaning reside together in a single sentence;
and 'conjunction' (saṅgara) is also designated as such because it enters into a single component of a sentence."
And so it is. But the fourth type is that in which there exists a relationship of the assisted and the assister (*anugrāhya-anugrāhaka-bhāva*) among the figures of speech (*alaṅkāras*).
For example: "The tremulous glance of the large-eyed woman was indistinguishable from a blue lotus in a strong breeze."
Was it taken from the female deer by her, or was it taken from her by the female deer?
In this case, although the comparison between the gazing [of the heroine] and the gazing of a female deer is suggested (*vyaṅgya*),
it is nonetheless subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) because it serves as a supportive factor that brings about the emergence of the poetic figure of doubt (*sandehālaṅkāra*).
For the resolution of the doubt occurs precisely through that which is supported.
As it has been said: "Where figures of speech exist by means of mutual assistance and do not attain their own existence independently, that too is *saṅkara* (commixture)."
The meaning is "dear to children.

Having shown *saṅkara* (commixture) in the form of occurring within a single sentence, he now shows *saṅkara* in the form of the coexistence of parts of a single sentence, beginning with the words "where... (*yatra*).
"Because of similarity" means because of the similarity in being the object of expression (*vācyatva*). "The master," etc.

When the master has met with calamity, the act concerning the day—which describes the noble son who is eager and intent upon taking the appropriate vow—is expressed through the metaphorical representation "the cave of darkness. This is because the sun possesses the status of a master; therefore, its departure constitutes a calamity, its dwelling in the cave constitutes the taking of a vow, and the act of entering it constitutes the exertion for that purpose. Thus, the phrase "the cave of darkness" functions as a verbal metaphor (*śābdarūpaka*).
That which is understood is "bhāva" (the state of being).
He states the consensus regarding the two distinctions already mentioned with the words "tad idam" and so forth.
By this verse, the definition of the two stated distinctions is demonstrated.

In accordance with the *Vṛtti* text, he provides an example of *saṅkara* (commingling) where the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) stand in a relationship of the assisted and the assister: "pravātā...
and "tayā...".
The meaning of "tayā" is "by Śrī Pārvatī."
[Objection: But even if it is an auxiliary (*anugrāhaka*), why does it become subordinate (*guṇībhāva*)? To this he says: "by being that which is to be assisted" (*anugrāhyatvena*).
The word "of the doubt" (*sandehasya*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. "The final resolution" (*paryavasāna*)—[is what follows].
The phrase "of the suggestive simile" (*anugrāhikāyāvyaṅgyopamāyāḥ*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
In that case, because the suggested meaning is not intended as predominant, it does not fall within the domain of *dhvani*.
However, when there is the possibility of two ornaments coexisting, the expressed and the suggested are equal in their predominance.

Alternatively, if the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) resides there by being subordinate to the expressed meaning (vācya), then that is the *locana*; thus he says, "When [there is] an ornament," and so forth.
In this way, the status of *dhvani* is refuted even in the fourth variety.
As for the two middle varieties, it has already been stated that there is not even the possibility of a suggested meaning.

Regarding the first type, however, he raises the doubt that there might be some possibility [of its occurrence] in examples such as "O moon-faced one" (*aśaśivadanā*) and so forth, and then refutes it with the words "by two figures of speech" (*alaṅkāradvaya*).
He says "equal" (*samam*);
the sense is that both [figures] are being suspended in doubt.

Now, what should be done in a case where the suggested meaning alone shines forth as the primary element? For example: "Indeed, the wicked have no love for virtues; they seek only fame. It is said that the moonstone melts when the beloved's face, like the moon, is seen. In this instance, the excellence of the beloved’s face is not directly expressed; rather, it is suggested through the description of the moonstone melting at its sight. Thus, how can this be considered a case of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggestion is subordinated)? This objection is answered by the following verse: "The excellence of the face is not directly expressed, but is suggested by the description of the moonstone melting. Therefore, because the suggested meaning is predominant, this is indeed a case of *dhvani* (suggestive poetry). This is because the excellence of the face is not directly stated, but is suggested by the description of the moonstone melting. Consequently, since the suggested meaning is predominant, this is indeed a case of *dhvani*. Furthermore, in the verse "The moonstone melts when the beloved's face, like the moon, is seen," the excellence of the face is not directly expressed; rather, it is suggested by the description of the moonstone melting. In this regard, one might raise an objection with the words "Now, [if it be argued]... (atheti), based on the intention that here the *arthāntaranyāsa* appears as the expressed meaning (*vācya*), whereas the *vyatireka* and *apahnuti* appear as suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) and are thus predominant.
To that, the reply is given: "Then that too... (*tadā so 'pi*).
Regarding this fourth variety, the *Bālapriyā* commentary introduces the text of the *Vṛtti* with the intent of demonstrating the absence of suggestion (*dhvani*), stating: "He says that...
[and] "Because of being oscillating.
This means: because it is being doubted due to its status as either the expressed meaning (*vācya*) or the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
"Is it not so," and so forth;
"wherein" means in that kind of figure of speech known as *saṅkara* (commixture).
Alas! There is no affection for virtue in the wicked who rely solely on worldly fame;
indeed, the moonstone weeps at the sight of the moon, but not when the face of its beloved is beheld.
Such is the shadow [of the meaning].

"Attachment to virtues" (guṇānurāga) means a lack of affection for the virtues of certain people even when they are being praised by others. He states the reason for this as follows: "Because of their renown," and so forth.
The meaning is: "of those who lack an investigation into the reality of things.
He supports the general statement with a specific example, beginning with "it is said" (*kila*), etc.: "It is said that the moonstone (*śaśimaṇi*) exudes [fluid] when the moon is seen."
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is: "When the beloved’s face is seen, [the moon] does not exude [moisture].
The intended meaning is: if the moon-gem possessed an affection for the beloved, then why would it not flow upon seeing her face?
This refers to the method of *vyatireka* (negative concomitance).
The meaning is that this is *apahnuti* (concealment), because it reveals the sense that "the moon is indeed the face of the beloved.
Regarding the phrase "by way of being suggested" (*vyaṅgyatvena*) and so forth: the meaning is that it appears as something suggested and as the primary element.
It has been stated in the commentary that the very mention of "confusion" (saṅkara) serves to dispel the notion of [the figure] being *dhvani*;
yet, while that [figure] may indeed be within the scope of *dhvani*,
it cannot be said that it is *dhvani* itself.
This follows the logic already indicated under the figure *paryāyokta*.

Furthermore, even regarding the figure *saṅkara* (commixture), the mention of "commixture" in certain cases is merely a conventional designation; this is not actually *saṅkara*, but rather the second variety of *dhvani*, named *alaṅkāradhvani*.
Whatever has been examined regarding *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) should be followed here as well.

Now, he states the general method for dispelling the possibility of a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) among all the varieties of *saṅkara* (commixture), beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). The connection is: "even in some cases of the figure of speech *saṅkara*."
The meaning is that it is differentiated from all distinctions.
For "intermingling" (*saṅkīrṇatā*) means a state of mixture or a state of being blended;
in that case, how could there be primacy for one [element], as in the case of milk and water?
The praise of another subject that has departed from the immediate context is Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant); it is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
The description of something irrelevant (aprastuta) that implies the relevant (prastuta)—this is the meaning.
And that implication (ākṣepa) is threefold: by way of the relation between the general and the particular, by way of the relation between cause and effect, and by way of similarity (sārūpya).

In that regard, he makes the formal proposition—that in the first two types, there is equal prominence of both the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*)—with the passage beginning with "the irrelevant" and ending with "prominence. In that context, even when there is a relationship of general and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-bhāva*), there are two possible ways: the irrelevant general is expressed by words, while the relevant particular is understood; this is one type.
For example: "Alas, the cruelty of saṃsāra! Alas, the wickedness of calamities!
Alas, the endless courses of Fate, who is crooked by nature!"

For here, the predominance of fate—which is everywhere of a general nature—is described as an *aprastuta* (irrelevant) element; yet, when something specific has perished in the context of the actual subject matter, it culminates in that particular instance.
Since even there the specific part is pervaded by the general, the general expressed meaning (*vācya-sāmānya*) possesses predominance just like the suggested particular (*vyaṅgya-viśeṣa*).
Indeed, there is no contradiction in the simultaneous predominance of both the general and the particular.
But when a non-contextual particular implies a contextual universal, then the second [type of *saṅkara*] occurs. To explain how this is so, he says: "It is *saṅkīrṇatā* (intermingling).
The gloss of the term "being mixed" (*miśratvam*) is "the state of becoming one" (*lolībhāvaḥ*), which means absolute fusion.
"Because of the context" refers to this [definition] belonging to Bhāmaha;
"context" means being the subject under discussion.
He explains the essential meaning as: "the description of that which is not the subject under discussion."
"Description" (varṇana) refers to the statement of the meaning of the words of praise;
"there are two ways" means there are two modes.
"Sa" means that which consists in the cognition of a particular from a universal.
"Daivaprādhānyam" means the predominance of destiny.
And there is also the reading "daivasvātantryam" (divine sovereignty).
"In all cases it is of a general nature" means that it is present throughout [the categories], such as the cruelty of transmigratory existence and so forth.
The meaning is that everything exists in dependence upon that [pleasure]. "In some case" means in the form of a beloved woman, a son, or the like.
Here he demonstrates the equal primacy of the suggested (vyaṅgya) and the expressed (vācya) with the words "tatrāpi" and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the particularity of the suggested may have primacy, how could that belong to the expressed, which is a generality? To this he replies: "of the particular aspect" (viśeṣāṃśasya).
Regarding the term "predominance" (*prādhānya*):
it refutes the possibility of [the presence of] *dhvani*.

For even in the case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), when [the connection between] the expressed subject and the unstated [subject] arises either from the relation of general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) or from the relation of cause and effect (*nimittanimittibhāva*), [the unstated subject remains subordinate].
When there is a connection with the suggested [meaning] which is the subject at hand, then the expressed and the suggested possess equal prominence.

In that case, when the unmentioned general [meaning], being expressed, is connected with the contextual particular [meaning] which is suggested, then— even though the particular is what is cognized— because the general is invariably concomitant with that particular, the general also possesses prominence.
Even when the particular is dependent upon the universal, if the universal is predominant, then because all particulars are included within the universal, the particular also possesses predominance.
*Locana* explains that "mode" (*prakāra*) is as follows:
"That fool, who thought the drop on the lotus leaf from his mouth was a pearl, listen to something even more [ridiculous] than this."

When it is being slowly taken up, having dissolved through the light action of the fingertips, he flies up from there and cries out "Alas!"—yet day after day, he does not sleep because of his inner grief.

In this case, the possibility of greatness in an inappropriate place is introduced as a general theme (*sāmānya*), whereas the intended subject is the possibility of a jewel in a drop of water, which is a particular form (*viśeṣa*).
It has been stated that there is no contradiction even when both the general and the particular are simultaneously predominant.
Thus, one type, though possessing two divisions, has been examined by the section beginning with "yadā tāvat" and ending with "viśeṣasyāpi prādhānyam.

Applying this same logic to the relationship between the cause (nimitta) and the effect (naimittika), [the author] indicates that it too possesses two modes; the sense is that the predominance of the universal is invariably concomitant with the predominance of the particular.
"For it is not contradictory" means that, as in the case of "weave a cloth that is not red," there is the prescription of two or three [attributes]; this is the sense.
"This" refers to...
"From the beginning" means from the start;
that is to say, produced first of all.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "Listen to this which is about to be said.
The phrase "it was mistaken for a pearl" means that, in comparison with what is about to be described, that [mistake] of the dull-witted person is quite insignificant;
the sense is that because the delusion of it being a pearl is possible due to its similarity [to one], the delusion of a water droplet being a pearl might occur.
"Listen":
listen also to something other than this which was previously mentioned.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "The finger," etc.
The word "he is dull-witted" (jaḍa) is also to be supplied here;
the meaning is that he is a dull-witted person who has the delusion that the pearl-jewel has been produced [from the finger].
Regarding the word "tatra":
it means "in that drop of water.
However, in the reading "kutroḍḍīya" (having flown up where?), it should be understood that the word "tasmin" (in that) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
When it is being slowly and gently grasped with the thought that it is a pearl,
by the light action and slight movement of the tip of the finger, it remains stuck to the very finger; such being the case,
[the verse says] "it flies up."
The word "this" (*ayam*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
The meaning is that, because he has not seen it, thinking "this pearl of mine has flown up into the sky and departed," he does not sleep due to inner grief.
And this same principle applies to the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*).

But when, by the force of mere similarity alone, the *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) indicates the relationship between the non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) and the contextual (*prakṛta*), [the author] shows this in the *Locana* with the words "by means of the cause" (*nimitta*).
Sometimes the non-contextual cause, being expressed, implies the contextual effect;
as for example: "Those who feel joy at a rise in fortune and do not abandon one in times of calamity..."
They are one's kinsmen and friends; the rest of the world is intent on its own self-interest.

Here, the unmentioned state of being a friend or kinsman is described as the cause (nimitta) in order to manifest his own relevant quality of having trustworthy speech, which is prompted by his devotion to the virtuous.

In this case, although the effect (naimittika) is perceived, it is the perception of the cause itself that becomes predominant as the animating principle; thus, there is a predominance of both the suggested (vyaṅgya) and the suggester (vyañjaka).
However, sometimes the unmentioned effect, being described, manifests the relevant cause.
As on the bridge—
[I remember] heaven without the *apārijāta* tree,
the chest of the Lord of Madhu devoid of the Kaustubha gem, and the mass of Śiva’s matted hair without the moon.

In this passage, Jāmbavān describes the recollection of Hari’s chest— which is devoid of the Kaustubha jewel and the Lakṣmī— as an "incidental" (aprastuta) motif, in order to manifest the "relevant" (prastuta) qualities of serving elders, longevity, and skill in conduct as the causes for his being appointed as minister.
In that context, although the cause is perceived, the effect remains the expressed (vācya) meaning.
On the contrary, because it is sustained by that very cause, it makes itself prominent; thus, the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya) are indeed equally primary.

In that regard, there are two modes: sometimes the aesthetic charm (camatkāra) arises from the expressed which is not the subject at hand (aprastuta), while the suggested aspect depends entirely upon it.

As it was said by our teacher Bhaṭṭendurāja: "O Vetāla, you who took the lives of him by whom your own life was surrendered to you, by whom you were raised up with strength, upon whose shoulder you long remained, and even to whom you offered worship—you who perform the act of taking his life with a mere smile, O brother, sport in the foremost rank among those who return favors."
Regarding the phrase "here, in an improper place": the word "of the dull-witted" (*jaḍānām*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. As for "those who": [the reference is to those who hold such views].
The other has a conduct contrary to what was described above.
The sign is the mark of being one whose speech is trustworthy;
[this occurs] through attachment to virtuous persons.
The meaning is: "highly esteemed by virtuous people.
The meaning of "naimittika" is: "one whose words are trustworthy."
"It is simply the perception of the signs.

The meaning is that, indeed, without the speaker's being perceived as having such qualities as being a kinsman and so forth, his status as one whose words are trustworthy would not enter the path of cognition.
"Saggam" (to heaven).

I remember the heaven before the churning was complete, devoid of the *pārijāta* tree; the chest of Madhumathana, lacking the splendor of the Kaustubha gem; and the mass of Shiva’s matted locks, which had not yet attained its full beauty.
Thus ends the section on "shadow" (chāyā).
The triad beginning with "vṛddha" (old) serves as a qualification for the term "prastuta" (the subject at hand).
[The phrase] "he makes [her] raise her neck" (uddhurakandharīkaroti) [is used].
The meaning is that it makes [something] primary.
"Looking toward its face" (tanmukhaprekṣam) implies, therefore,
that it is not primary.
Regarding the term "vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*): although here, by virtue of similarity of form, some other relevant subject is implied through the mention of the eye, nevertheless,
it is precisely the irrelevant account of the Vetāla that produces the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
For this matter is not impossible—unlike the case of a censure directed at an insentient object—and it is not unpleasing; thus, the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is not the primary element here.

However, if the relevant subject (*prastuta*), being suggested by the description of an irrelevant qualifier (*aprastuta-viśeṣaṇa*) such as "insentient" which is otherwise utterly improbable, produces aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), then this is *vastu-dhvani* (suggestion of a fact).
As in my own verse: "O multitude of emotions! Having forcibly invaded the hearts of people and making them dance with various gestures, you sport about while concealing your own heart."

Therefore, I think that ill-taught man calls you dull-witted because he considers himself sensitive; his own dullness, I believe, is a subject for praise only because it allows for the possibility of your being his equal.

According to the principle that "a certain great person, though free from passion, appears as if possessed by passion," even one whose expansion of darkness has been dispelled by the light of profound discernment may conceal himself amidst the world and cause the world to clamor; yet, while accepting his own non-appearance [as real] before that very world, when he is treated with contempt by that world as "this man is a fool," it is then that his supramundane conduct is truly brought to light. (Bālapriyā)
The readings are "tvam utpādita" and "saparyām pura".
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of similarity":
the meaning is by the force of a resemblance consisting in being an agent of harm toward one who has assisted through the sustaining of life and so forth.
"Of that which is under discussion alone": the word "of the expressed" (*vācyasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Here he states the reason, beginning with "for not," and so forth.
"And not unpleasing" means that it is indeed pleasing.
"If," and so forth.
The construction is: "being impelled by that which is insentient and so forth.
The words beginning with "atyanta" are qualifiers of the term "insentient and so forth" (acetanādi).
That [impulsion] is by means of that in which there are qualifiers of its object—that is, of the irrelevant subject matter—which are absolutely impossible.
"This is *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact)," meaning that this is not the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
[The word] "bhāva" means...

"O multitude of entities (*bhāvavrāta*), you—the collection (*vraja*) of things such as the moon, gardens, and so forth—play in such a manner; this is the connection [of the words]. Therefore, for that reason of playing in this way..."
On account of his conceit that he possesses a refined sensibility— the pride that "I am a man of taste"— that ill-instructed and ill-behaved person calls you dull-witted.

However, the dullness of this person who speaks thus—the fact that he is called "dull-witted"—is due to the possibility of his being equal to you, that is, because of the prospect of his attaining equality with you.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "I consider this to be a ground for his praise."
The word "yena" (by which) is connected with "pracchādayan" (concealing), and so forth.
As it has been said: "To one who knows reality, this world is like a fool, a madman, or a ghost;
and even though he knows reality, he appears to the world like a fool, a madman, or a ghost."
"Gāḍha" means:
he whose expansion of darkness—the mass of the gloom of delusion—is dispelled by that very light which is intense discernment (*viveka*). "Making eloquent" (*vācālayan*)—means:
The meaning is that he utters many words pregnant with self-contempt.
Within himself— that is, in his own person—
he perceives an absence of brilliance (apratibhāsa), which has been superimposed upon him by people.

Now, if it is a relation (*sambandha*), even then, since that which is expressed—being similar [to the subject] but irrelevant—is not intended as the primary focus, it falls within the domain of *dhvani* itself; for it is by way of being suggested (*vyaṅgyatayā*) that it is manifested as the primary element. Indeed, the world treats such states of affairs as the arrival of the moon in a garden with contempt, thinking, "This [moonrise] is dull. *Locana*: It is manifested primarily as something suggested. For the world disregards such things as the arrival of the moon in a garden, thinking, "This is dull."

On the contrary, he causes the mind of one person to be tormented by the anxiety of longing, while making another subject to the power of great joy; thus, by means of causes for transformation, he forcibly makes the world dance according to his will.
Yet, no one knows what this man is like within his heart;

on the contrary, because he is exceedingly profound, highly clever, perfectly free from pride, and exceptionally adept at play, he is—precisely for that reason, and rather on account of the very grounds for suspecting his cleverness—regarded by the world as a fool.
And for the very same reason that the self is conceived as being insentient (*jāḍya*), the connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*) is likewise conceived; therefore,
if it is said of this world, "You are insentient," then since such a multitude of entities is well-known to be unrefined,
that statement is, on the contrary, a praise.
It is implied that this world is more wretched than even the insentient;
thus he says: "But when...
and "Otherwise..."

Otherwise, however, the sense is that while there may be other distinct figures of speech (alaṅkāra) or specific varieties of figures, the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) can never possess primacy. Regarding the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the mention of *samāsokti* within the copulative compound (*dvandva*), it is intended to include the entire class of figures beginning with *vyājastuti*, which are capable of being permeated by a suggested meaning.
*Bālapriyā* explains the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) with the passage ending: "He is dull-witted... up to "...is praise."
The grammatical connection is: "Thus it was disregarded.
By whom? By the world as the agent. And what [was disregarded]? That which consists of the garden and other such objects.
The word "pratyuta" means not only that he is not dull-witted, but rather that his nature is even clever.
"Of another" means of one who has met with his beloved.
"Having forcibly assailed" is explained as: by those who cause transformations according to their will.
"By means of the causes of transformations," such as longing, joy, and so forth, "through their manifestations.
This is the explanation of the phrase "having concealed his own heart"—namely, "and not," and so on.
This is the detailed exposition of the word "on the contrary"—namely, "most profound," and so on.
The word "he" (saḥ) is also connected here [to the previous statement].
He explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "If he," and so forth.
"He" refers to the multitude of entities characterized by the aforementioned qualities.
The word "jaḍa" (insentient) is to be construed with the word "sambhāvita" (conceived). The explanation of the word "tataḥ" (from that) is "for that very reason.
This means: from the nature of the play described in the manner previously stated.
The qualification of the word "kāraṇāt" (from the cause) is "on the contrary, through cleverness," and so forth.
The explanation of "sahṛdaya" (connoisseur), and so forth, is "the self," and so forth.
"That" refers to this.
The meaning is "then.
The connection is: "that is the praise of this world.
The sense is: "what indeed is that praise?"
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "At that time," etc.;
"at that time" means at the moment of making such a statement;
"the dullness of one who is thus," etc.
This is the meaning: for the statement that a person is insentient depends upon the established fact that an insentient thing is sentient.

This being so, since the person would likewise possess the same status (yogakṣema) [as the insentient object], it would follow that the person is also potentially sentient; thus, the statement "you are insentient toward the person" would result in nothing but a literal eulogy.
In this way, having explained the non-contextual expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*), he demonstrates the ultimate meaning: "even from the insentient."
"He says that" means: he states that which was previously mentioned regarding the nature of sound (*dhvanitva*) when it is predominant in what is perceived through similarity.
He shows that the particle *eva* (only/just) is displaced in its position by saying "otherwise indeed."
The purpose of stating the meaning of the word "tu" (but) is that, otherwise, this would indeed be a different figure of speech altogether.
Thus, the summary here is as follows: [Locana] begins to provide a general response to all these points with the words "tadayamatra.
The intention is: how much more could be written for every single word?

In this regard, an example of *vyājastuti* (feigned praise) is as follows: "What is the use of inquiries concerning the affairs of others' houses? However, being by nature talkative and possessing the disposition of a Southerner, I am unable to remain silent. Alas! Your beloved fame wanders like a madwoman from house to house, through the marketplaces, the squares, and the drinking saloons."
In this instance, the suggested meaning consists of praise, and by means of it, the expressed meaning itself is embellished.

As for that which was cited by someone: "O Lord, the Earth was your grandmother; immediately after her, she became your mother; now she is your wife, girt with the ocean as her girdle, for the perpetuation of the lineage;
and when a full hundred years have passed, she shall again become your faultless daughter-in-law—is this not indeed fitting in the family of kings who are masters of all political science?"
Thus, this appears vulgar to us, as it serves as a cause for recalling something utterly indecorous;
and what praise has been offered by this?
For how much is it to say, "You are a king by hereditary succession"?
Such instances of "disguised praise" (vyājastuti), being censured in the assemblies of the wise, should indeed be disregarded.
When a change [in state] occurs without obstruction by a cause,
that emotional state (bhāva) indicates both the intended meaning and its obstruction.
Thus [it is said].
Here too, when the expressed meaning (vācya) is predominant, there is the figure of speech called Bhāva (Emotion).

This is because a specific modification of mental state (cittavṛttiviśeṣa), whose connection with a physical change such as vocal activity is unobstructed and constant, is present. [The commentary] says "again" (punar) in the sense of "furthermore. *Bālapriyā*.
He explains [the phrase] "being a subordinate part of another figure" because there might otherwise be a misunderstanding; [he says] "it is a specific type of figure.
This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*).

In a context where there is a description of something irrelevant (*aprastuta*), when the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) consists in the power of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) produced by that expressed irrelevant object (*vācya*), [it is a specific figure].
However, when that [indicated] element is the subject at hand (*prastuta*), then the figure of speech there is indeed *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description).

But where the subject matter (*vastu*) indicated is predominant, the intention of the author of the treatise is that there is only *vastudhvani* (Suggestion of a Fact) and no figure of speech. This is the meaning. [The term] "consisting of praise" (*stutyātmaka*)...
The meaning is that this is a glorification of the quality of being "one whose verses are excellent" (uttamaśloka), in that your fame pervades the entire universe.
Regarding the word "āsīt":
*snuṣā* means the wife of one's son.
Regarding the term "extremely indecent":

the memory of indecency had already begun to sprout when the grandmother was addressed as "mother"; however, by describing her as a "wife" and a "daughter-in-law," that memory is manifested all the more clearly—this is the intention behind saying "extremely indecent.
Having stated the fault in the expressed meaning (*vācya*), he now states it regarding the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) with the words "And what... and so forth.
"How much is this?"—the meaning is that no specific excellence over other kings is perceived.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with *vyājastuti*," he states the *bhāva* alaṃkāra as taught by Rudraṭa, which was previously mentioned by the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*), using the verse beginning with "yasya... (of whom...).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: that whose modification is unimpeded, and by which cause it arises, makes known both that intention (*abhiprāya*) and its obstruction; this is "existence" (*bhāva*).
With the intention that there is also a twofold division here, he says "atrāpi" and so forth.
He explains the defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) with "yasya" and so forth.
The specific mental state such as passion (*anurāga*) arises from its relation [to an object].

The explanation of the term "unobstructed" (*apratibandha*) is "determined" (*niyata*). This refers to that in which the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is subordinate, following only the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
In that case, figures of speech such as *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) are clearly expressed as verbal ornaments (*vācyālaṅkāra*).
Where the suggested meaning exists merely as a flash of intuition, or even when it follows upon the expressed meaning, there is no *dhvani*; or where its predominance is not perceived.

The *bhāvālaṅkāra* (the figure of speech consisting of an emotion) is that object—characterized by being available for enjoyment at will and so forth—which, by means of a particular cause, makes known the intention (*abhiprāya*) of the speaker, which consists of a specific modification of the mind. For example:

"Since I am alone, a young woman, and likewise the master of this house has gone abroad, whom can you ask here for lodging? This poor mother-in-law of mine is indeed blind and deaf, O foolish traveler! In this instance, the fact that she is alone, a young woman, and that her husband is away serves as the cause for making known her intention, which is the desire to enjoy him at will; thus, it constitutes the *bhāvālaṅkāra*.
In this context, since the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) serves as an embellisher (upaskāraka) within each individual word-meaning, the expressed meaning (vācya) is primary.
However, it has been established that when the suggested meaning is predominant, there is no poetic figure (alaṅkāra) at all; therefore, enough with further elaboration.
"Yatra" refers to the poem (kāvya).

Regarding the term "ornaments" (alaṅkṛti): it is precisely because they are ornaments that they serve to embellish the expressed meaning (vācya). Regarding the phrase "mere intuition" (pratibhāmātra):
"Where there is the comprehension of an obscured meaning in a simile or the like"—
this refers to "the following of the expressed meaning" (*vācyārthānugama*).
The sense is that there is a following along with the expressed meaning in such a way that it possesses equal prominence, as in the case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
"It is not perceived" means: by which reason—namely, by that which is to be established by the sentence—it is not clearly understood; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In the reading "yena pratibaddhena," however, the meaning of "pratibaddhena" is exactly as stated [before].

"That is the cause" means that the *anubhāva*—such as an action or the like—of a particular mental state (*cittavṛtti*) is the indicator (*gamaka*) of that particular mental state by way of being the suggested cause (*vyaṅgyahetu*). That is the meaning of "that is the cause."
With the intention of providing an example that will be stated later, he shows its cause with the words "as desired," etc.
The meaning is that the sense intended by the heroine and others is: "I am to be enjoyed by you as you wish; there is no obstacle whatsoever.
[The word] "alone" means:
*Tathā* means "in this manner" (as a conjunction).
*Tat* means "that," which is to say: that [time] when I was of such a kind and had gone to the householder's [residence].
"Is there indeed not your mother-in-law? Ask her," [the speaker] says here—"this one," and so forth.

Regarding "the suggested meaning" (*vyaṅgya*) here: the meaning is that through words such as "alone" (*ekākinī*), there is the suggestion of her own lack of any other lover who might enjoy her company, and so on.
By this statement, the fact that one’s own self is offered as an object of enjoyment according to [the recipient’s] desire is illuminated.
Now, one might object: "In this case, the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is merely the act of giving. Therefore, he states in general terms: "When the suggested meaning is predominant," and so forth.
Furthermore, the example beginning with "it conveys an obstruction to that" should be understood from the work of Rudraṭa.
The three verses beginning with "vyaṅgyasya" are the *parikara* (concluding) verses.
Regarding the word "yatra" in the phrase "yatrāprādhānyam," he explains it as "in poetry.
The reason for its lack of predominance is its following after the mere expressed meaning (*vācya*).

In this context, the "cause" is the quality of embellishing the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*), and this has been indicated by the term "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*); thus he says: "Precisely because of its being an ornament.
He explains the phrase "the suggested [meaning] is merely a flash of intuition" (*pratibhāmātra*) along with an example, beginning with the words "where," and so forth.
"Obscure" (*mliṣṭā*) means indistinct.
"Cognition of the meaning" (*arthapratītiḥ*) refers to the cognition of the suggested sense (*vyaṅgyapratītiḥ*).

He explains [the passage] with the words "by the expressed" (*vācyena*) and so forth, in order to avoid the redundancy that would arise from the phrase "following only the expressed" (*vācyamātrānuyāyin*).

That alone should be considered the domain of Dhvani, free from any admixture [of other figures], where the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) resides while the word and its primary meaning remain subordinate to it.
Therefore, there is no inclusion of *dhvani* elsewhere. For this reason as well, there is no inclusion: because *dhvani* is declared to be the primary essence (*aṅgin*) of a specific type of poetry.
Furthermore, its constituent parts—the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), the qualities (*guṇa*), and the styles (*vṛtti*)—will be explained [later].
Nor is it well known that the whole (*avayavin*) is merely the same as its separate parts (*avayava*).
[Thus,] the predominance [of the whole] does not shine forth.
Nevertheless, even if one attempts to force an interpretation, it does not penetrate the heart,
as in the case of the various commentaries composed by others on the verse beginning with "deva prasīda nijatāsu."

Therefore, the designation "suggestion" (dhvani) does not apply in four cases: even when the suggested meaning is present, if it is subordinate; if there is indistinct perception; if it is equal in prominence to the expressed meaning; and if its prominence is unclear. Where, then, does it apply? He says: "only when intent upon that. The meaning is that it is abandoned [in these cases] due to the possibility of the ornament entering into a state of commingling (saṅkara).
The claim that it is by means of the *saṅkārālaṅkāra* (the ornament of confusion) is incorrect;
for if it were intended as an indication of other ornaments, it would be overly complex (*kliṣṭa*).
"And for this reason" [is said].

The meaning is that there is no identity between the *alaṅkāras* and *dhvani* not only because they rely respectively on the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācya-vācaka*) and the relationship of the manifested and the manifester (*vyaṅgya-vyañjaka*), which are mutually contradictory, but also because of the contradiction between the nature of the subordinate and the nature of the principal, like a master and his servant; the word "part" (*avayava*) means each one individually.
He says this: "as something separate.

Now, one might object: "If it is not thus as something separate, then let it be so while falling within the midst of the aggregate"; anticipating this doubt, he says: "But if there is non-separateness..."

Even then, the explanation of the phrase "not dear to the ignorant" (na sa bālapriyā) is that it does not shine forth clearly; thus, it is "forcedly constructed. And that [construction] is an "addition" during the stage of critical examination through the investigation of reasoning.
"It does not enter" means that it dissolves in the absence of an investigation through reasoning; this is the intended meaning.
He states an example of this, beginning with "For instance" (*yathā*) and so forth.
Regarding the word "O Lord" (*deva*):
it refers to the previously cited verse beginning with "I entreat you, therefore be gracious" (*prārthaye tāvat prasīda*).
The explanation of the phrase "not sound" (na dhvaniḥ) is "there is no conventional usage of the term 'sound'.
Regarding the phrase "even though it exists," the word "of sound" (dhvaneḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The explanation of what was stated as "in four ways" is: "when the suggested meaning is subordinate," and so forth.
The commentary on the term "commingling" (saṅkara) is: "the entry of one ornament into another," and so forth;
the meaning is that this refers to the aforementioned [definition] due to the possibility of the entry of figures such as *samāsokti*.
He refutes the literal meaning [of the opponent's position] with the words "by means of the ornament of saṅkara" and so forth.
Regarding the word "itaḥ" in the commentary, he explains it by considering its meaning to be "for the reason that will be stated hereafter," beginning with the words "not only...
[and continuing with] "not identity."
The meaning is "the absence of identity.
Regarding the phrase "aṅgi" and so forth,
the meaning is "of the states of being the principal (aṅgin) and the subordinate (aṅga)."

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since no whole (avayavin) distinct from its parts (avayava) is perceived, and since the whole is nothing other than the parts themselves, the negation of such a whole is untenable. Anticipating this, [the author] refutes it by showing that the intended meaning of the singular number in the word "part" (avayava) is what is meant; he says:
"each one," and he states:
"he says that," because the term "separately existing" (pṛthagbhūta) has precisely the same meaning as what was already stated.
Now, regarding the term "separate" (*pṛthagbhūta*):
the word "part" (*avayava*) is to be understood as the ellipsis; likewise for the "whole" (*avayavin*).
Falling within the aggregate and having its own nature established by the aggregate—let it be so; let there be a whole (*avayavin*).
In the commentary, [it says] "the state of being subordinate to that."
The meaning is that it is manifested by the whole (avayavin).
However, in the case of non-separation, its status as a part of that [whole] exists; but it is not identical to it in essence.
Even where reality (tattva) resides, because the scope of *dhvani* is vast, it does not consist of that [reality] alone.
The phrase "stated by the wise" (*sūribhiḥ kathita*) indicates that this is an utterance originating from the learned;
it is not asserted as something that has proceeded in an arbitrary manner.
For in the first place, the grammarians are indeed the wise, because all branches of knowledge are rooted in grammar;
the "eye" is simply the collective whole.
Because other constituent elements are also present therein,
and while that [element] exists even when perceived among those constituents,
it does not possess the nature of an ornament.
Precisely because it is subordinate;
whereas that which takes the form of an ornament (alaṅkāra) is not *dhvani* due to its lack of predominance. Thus he says: "But it is not the very essence [of *dhvani*]."

Anticipating the objection that "surely you have merely conferred the status of primacy upon some particular figure of speech (alaṅkāra) and called it 'dhvani' and its 'soul'," he says: "or even where...

Indeed, we have not designated this as being any one specific figure such as *samāsokti* and the like, because it exists even when distinct from them, and because it has been demonstrated to exist even in the total absence of the essential nature of figures such as *samāsokti*, as in the examples "attā ettha" and "kassa vā ṇa."

Thus he says: "Not merely being restricted to that. Regarding the term *vidvadupajñā*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning that speech whose first commencement (*upajñā*) was by learned persons (*vidvadbhyaḥ*).

Therefore, by the rule "upajñopakramaṃ," the neuter gender is applied based on the *tatpuruṣa* compound; "of that" means "of the member. "The state of being that" (*tatvam*) means "the state of being the whole" (*avayavitvam*).
He states the [intended] meaning in the eyes—namely, "even then," and so forth.
"Even then" means even at the time of falling into a state of intoxication from wine;
"he" refers to that constituent part which possesses the form of the whole.
It is only one, neither a collection nor a composite whole consisting of a collection. He states the reason for this: "because it exists even in others," meaning "because of its presence therein."
The meaning is: "because it exists in the aggregate.
As for the passage beginning with "nanu" (but surely), the word "kaścit" (someone) refers to... [text continues].
The meaning is "one of the varieties such as *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation).

In the commentary, the phrase beginning with "where also" (*yatrāpi*) refers to cases such as *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) and so forth; specifically, in the case of *paryāyokta*, as in the verse beginning "Wander, O righteous man" (*bhrama dhārmika*).
And in the *saṅkara* ornament [beginning with] "there is no attachment to qualities," etc.,
the word "reality" (*tattva*) means "the state of being a whole" (*avayavitva*).
This means preeminence. Regarding the phrase "being established in that," the meaning is being established in that which possesses those parts (the whole).
This means that it culminates in poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
Regarding the statement that because *dhvani* has such a vast scope, it does not culminate solely in that [ornament], Locana explains this with the words "For not... and so forth.
The term "in *samāsokti*" is used by way of accepting the opponent's view that *dhvani* is included within *samāsokti*.
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), figures such as *paryāyokta* are included.
This is the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*),
and it exists both as *dhvani* and as the very essence (*ātmatva*) of poetry.

"Even in its state of being devoid of that"—meaning even when it lacks contact with figures of speech such as *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) and so forth—"of that" refers to the aforementioned *dhvani*.
This is a further explanation of what was already stated: "such as *samāsokti*."
The phrase "ityādi" means "in such passages as";
it is to be connected with the term "because it has been shown."
In order to establish the correctness of the usage "vidvadupajña," he says "vidvadbhyaḥ" and so forth.
And they (the learned) employ the term "dhvani" for those phonemes that are being heard.

Likewise, by other wise men who follow that doctrine and perceive the true meaning of poetry, the *Locana*—which [otherwise] would leave no room [for this usage]—is shown to be consistent with the mixture of the signified and the signifier.
Regarding the phrase "while they are being heard":

according to the [grammatical] analysis, it is said that the final sounds produced by the series [of sounds] reaching the cavity of the ear are what are heard; thus, the sounds born of sound are those being heard.
It is established, at least, that these possess the nature of the resonance of a bell.
And these are designated by the term *dhvani*.
As the venerable Bhartṛhari has said: "That which is produced by the organs through conjunction and disjunction is the *sphoṭa*; the sounds born from that sound are called *dhvanis* by others."
Thus, even the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), which is characterized by the nature of a resonance corresponding to the ringing of a bell and so forth, is designated as *dhvani*.

Likewise, those phonemes (*varṇa*) being heard— which are denoted by the word "sound" (*nāda*) and serve to manifest the *sphoṭa* grasped by the final cognition— are also spoken of by the term *dhvani*.

As that very Blessed One has said: "In such a way, by means of conditions that are inexpressible yet conducive to apprehension... [The *Bālapriyā* commentary: Now, intending to establish—on the basis of common scholarly consensus—that all four (the suggested meaning, the word, its denoted meaning, and the suggester) are denotable by the term *dhvani*, [the author] first [proceeds], for the sake of establishing that the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is denotable by the term *dhvani*, in accordance with [the following verse]:
He explains [the verse] with the words "In the ear," and so forth.
"The ear-cavity" refers to the space delimited by the region of the ear that is similar to a cavity. "By means of a continuum" [is the meaning].
The meaning is "by way of the succession of waves. Regarding the phrase "in the system": it means "in the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others."
"Sounds born from sounds"—
the meaning is that they are the final ones.
"Of these" refers to those [sounds].
The meaning is: "of the final sounds among those sounds produced from sound. Regarding the word "ghaṇṭā" (bell):
the intention is that it is similar because it is produced by a preceding sound.
Regarding the word "yaḥ" (which): [it refers to the bell].
This verse is intended to demonstrate the distinction between the *sphoṭa* and the sound (*dhvani*) from the perspective of their production.

"By means of conjunction and disjunction" (*saṃyogaviyogābhyām*) refers to that which is the conjunction and disjunction of the articulatory organs (*karaṇa*) with the [respective] places of articulation (*sthāna*).
The instrumental case in "by the organs" (*karaṇaiḥ*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
The meaning is "by means of the tongue-tip and so forth.
This is clear in the *Prātiśākhya*.
"That *sphoṭa*" means that the sound which first arises is called *sphoṭa*.
"Sounds born from sounds": the meaning is "those being heard.
"By others" means...
The meaning is "by those who maintain the theory of production.

As stated by the author of the Vṛtti: "In the view that [sounds] are non-eternal, that sound which is first produced by these [articulations], preceded by the contact, the [conventional] place of articulation, and the separation [of the organs], is called *sphoṭa*," and so forth.
The phrase "the bell, etc. refers to this.

The resonance of a bell or similar object is "anuraṇana" (reverberation); the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is said to be "standing in its place" or "equal to it," which is the reason for designating the *vyaṅgya* by the term *dhvani*.

Now, one might object: "In this way, only a specific type of *vyaṅgya* would be designated as *dhvani*, but not rasa and so forth, because they lack the nature of reverberation. To this, he says: "anuraṇana... (the word "reverberation" is used).
The sense is that this is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, he establishes that both the expressive word (*vācaka*) and the expressed meaning (*vācya*) are to be treated as *dhvani*— beginning with the words "In this way," and so forth.
The phrase "designated by the term *nāda*" means they are designated by the term *nāda* by the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).

The meaning is: they are the manifestors of that *sphoṭa* which is to be grasped—thoroughly apprehended in its clearly manifested form—by that cognition of the final phoneme which is assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme.
"Those" refers to [the phonemes].
The meaning is that these are the phonemes (*varṇa*).
"By means of conditions" (*pratyayaiḥ*) means by those which are indefinable— that is, impossible to explain as "this is such-and-such."
By means of those factors conducive to apprehension— namely, those favorable for the apprehension of the manifest form of the sphoṭa—
the essential nature of the word is determined once it has been revealed by the sounds.
Thus, here both the word and its meaning, which are the manifestors, are also designated by the term "dhvani. Furthermore,
even though the phonemes (varṇas) exist with only that much duration, [they are not perceived].
As it has been said: "If the intellect does not grasp even a sound uttered with the slightest effort, or if it does not clearly perceive the phoneme in its entirety,"

Thus, while those very [phonemes] are being heard, that which is distinct from the speaker’s well-known activity of articulation and consists of the various differences in tempo such as rapid or slow, is called *dhvani*.
As he himself said: "But after the manifestation of the word, the modifications [of sound] pertain to the differences in tempo."
The sounds (dhvani) bring about the manifestation, yet the essence of the sphoṭa is not differentiated by them.
Thus, we have stated that *dhvani* is a function distinct from the well-known functions of words— namely, denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and intention (*tātparya*).
In this way, *dhvani* consists of all four [functions].

And through connection with that [dhvani], the entire poetic work (*kāvya*)—by means of the intervening cognitions (*pratyaya*) produced regarding the object of sound (*śabda*) as manifested by *dhvani*, namely the indistinct cognitions whose object is the *sphoṭa*—its essential nature (*svarūpa*), that is, the nature of the *sphoṭa*, is determined and clearly known.

As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "For many cognitions, which serve as means and possess an indefinable form, arise when the word is being manifested by *dhvanis*; they are conducive to the apprehension of the manifested form and lead to the grasping of the word's own nature. (*vyaktarūpagrahamānuguṇā hyanupākhyeyākārā bahava upāyabhūtāḥ pratyayā dhvanibhiḥ prakāśyamāne śabde utpadyamānāśśabdasvarūpāvagrahe*)
"they become causes.
By "by them" is meant that they are designated by the word *dhvani* because it is used [as a synonym] for manifestors (*vyañjaka*).
Therefore, in order to establish that the operation of manifestation (*vyañjana*) is also subject to the linguistic usage of the term "resonance" (*dhvani*), he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
Regarding the phrase "in those of such a limited dimension":
the meaning is "in those characterized by such a dimension as this [sound] is perceived by the sense of hearing."
The word "api" (also/even) is used in the sense of conjunction;
its connection is with the phrase "while [the letters] are being heard.

The meaning is: while the phonemes remain in their own nature as possessing specific dimensions, and while they have thus reached the status of objects of the auditory faculty in their very same undivided form.
The connection of this [passage], which contains verses of corroboration, is with the section beginning with "the speaker who is other than... and so forth.
Regarding the term *alpīyasā*:
it refers to a sound uttered even with very slight effort.
The intellect does not grasp [the phoneme] as something divided;
or rather, it grasps the entire phoneme clearly.
The point is that partial grasping and non-grasping are impossible for a phoneme because it is partless (*niravayava*).
By this, what was stated as "only so many being heard" has been justified.
"He" means one whose activity is of such a kind.
Regarding the phrase "of the word" (*śabdasya*):
this verse is explained in the *Mañjūṣā* as follows—the ellipsis being that "after the manifestation of the word, which is the *sphoṭa*, modified sounds (*vaikṛtā dhvanayaḥ*) arise.
These [sounds], however, exist in a difference of mode (*vṛttibhede*), that is, in the difference of modes such as fast (*druta*) and so forth.
They converge there and serve as the causes;
however, the meaning is that the *sphoṭa* is not differentiated by them.
Furthermore, their "modified" nature (*vaikṛtatva*) arises from their being produced by factors such as indolence.
In the reading "vṛttibhedam," the meaning of "samupohanta" is "producing.
"Catuṣkam" means the tetrad beginning with the suggested sense (vyaṅgya).
"Sound" (ghvani) is that which is conventionally designated by the term "sound.
Furthermore, "entire poetry" refers to poetry as a composite consisting of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), the expressed meaning (vācya), and the operations of the expressive words (vācaka).
"By that" [refers to this].
That which is designated as "poetry" (*kāvya*)—being essentially sound—is called "suggestion" (*dhvani*) because of its similarity in the quality of being suggestive.

Now, the elucidation of such *dhvani*, which possesses a vast scope through the synthesis of the types and sub-types to be described hereafter, cannot be achieved by the *Locana* through the mere exposition of a few well-known poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*). Therefore, [the author] says:
*dhvaniḥ*.

Therefore, the designation of both distinction and non-distinction is not improper; [the term] "vācyavācakasaṃmiśra" means "mixed with the denoted and the denoter. This is a *madhyamapadalopa* (middle-term-omitted) compound, meaning "mixed together with the denoted and the denoter. Just as in the expression "cow, man, and beast," a conjunction is understood here even without the word "ca" (and).
Therefore, the suggested meaning (*dhvani*) is also called *dhvani*, as is the expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*),
because both possess the quality of being suggestive (*vyañjaka*) by virtue of "resounding" (*dhvanati*).
Furthermore, the suggested meaning is also called *dhvani* because it is "blended together" through the intermingling of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*).
Because it is "suggested" (dhvanyate);
"sound" (śabda) is the act of sounding, that is, the operation of sound, and this is not of the nature of denotation (abhidhā) and the like.
Furthermore, that which has become one's very self is also *dhvani*;
and that meaning which is designated as "poetry" (*kāvya*) is also *dhvani*.
Because it consists of the fourfold forest of the types already mentioned, he states the common reason for this very purpose: "due to the equality of being manifestors.
The meaning is that the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor is common—that is, it exists in a general form across all positions.

Furthermore, as for what was stated, "Because verbal conceptualizations are infinite," and so forth, he refutes that with the words "and not of such a kind. The forthcoming classification is as follows: there are two primary forms.

Its divisions are as follows: *arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is transferred to another) and *atyantatiraskṛtavācya* (where the expressed meaning is completely set aside) belong to the type where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*);

while *asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence) and *saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning has a perceptible sequence) belong to the type where the expressed meaning is intended but subordinate (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).
Therein also are internal subdivisions.
"Of that which has a great scope" means: of that which pervades all objects of definition.

"By the very fact of [the poem] attaining the status of *dhvani* through being composed of that collection which is denoted by the word *dhvani*"—this is the meaning. (From the *Bālapriyā* commentary).

The phrase beginning with "vyatireka" (distinction) means that in passages such as "dhvani is the soul of poetry," there is a designation of difference— namely, that dhvani is a specific variety of poetry— whereas in passages such as "that [poetry] is dhvani," there is a designation of non-difference.

"Not not appropriate" means that it is indeed appropriate. This refers to what was stated regarding the five elements, beginning with the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), being subject to the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*).
He explains the passage beginning with "vācyatvādi" (the state of being denotable, etc. in accordance with that [preceding context]—namely, "vācyavācaka," and so forth.
"Thus, it is the middle one" means that the sense is that it is both denotable and mixed; such is the intended meaning.
"Even without [the word]" means that the meaning is that the essence of sound (*śabdātmā*) is what is designated as "poetry" (*kāvyam*).
He states the result of the aforementioned explanation with the words beginning "by that," etc.
"Because it resounds" means "because it manifests"; this is the sense. The intention is that the suffix [in the word] *dhvani* is used in the active sense (*kartari*).
He states that the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is intended by means of a combined word, saying "it is mixed," and so forth.
"Vibhāvya" (manifesting) means by way of a conjunction or connection with both the determinants (*vibhāva*) and the consequents (*anubhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "because it is suggested" (dhvanyate),
the intention is that the suffix is used in the passive sense (karmaṇi).
He explains the word "consisting of sound" (śabdātman) with the words "the act of sounding" (śabdanam), and so forth.
"Dhvani" means "resounding" (dhvananam). In this sense, the suffix is applied in the abstract sense (*bhāve*), such that "dhvani" signifies the act of resounding; this is the intended meaning.
"For this very reason" [is said].

Since it is intended that the fivefold nature of meaning for devotees constitutes "suggestiveness" (*dhvanitva*) in this treatise, the meaning is that this is because of the statement of a common reason.

With the intention that the term "suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatva*)—in order to establish the commonality of the reason—refers to the relationship between the suggested and the suggester (*vyaṅgya-vyañjaka-bhāva*), he explains it with the words "the suggested," etc. (*vyaṅgya*...).
Since they are equal, it is entirely appropriate for those whose minds have been transformed by that [realization] to feel such fervor;
nor should they in any way manifest a state of mind defiled by envy.
Thus, the proponents of the non-existence of *dhvani* have been refuted.
"There is such a thing as *dhvani*.

And it is both that whose expressed meaning is unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*) and that whose expressed meaning is intended but subordinate (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*)," says the *Locana*. By using the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*), he indicates that [the definition] is not over-extensive;
by the word "only" (*mātra*), he indicates the absence of being the primary element (*aṅgitva*).

In that regard, it refers to those whose minds are cultivated (*bhāvita*) and directed (*praṇihita*) toward the essential nature of resonance (*dhvani*), or whose minds are cultivated—that is, permeated—by that form which produces aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*); for this very reason, their minds are the cause of transformations such as the closing of the eyes. [The term] "those who maintain the doctrine of non-existence" (*abhāvavādinaḥ*) refers to the following.
The meaning is that they are also divided into three intermediate types. He states the result of refuting them with the words "it exists" (*asti*).

With the intention that when an example is presented, any suspicion of figurative usage (*bhāktatva*) becomes easy to raise and easy to refute, he provides an opportunity for the presentation of examples.

Without first resolving the issues regarding its figurative nature (*bhāktatva*) and its non-definability (*alakṣaṇīyatva*), which ought to have been addressed, the author of the *Vṛtti* himself proceeds to define its divisions in accordance with the upcoming restatement of the *Uddyota*: "And that [is]...

(*sa ca*). Even though the meaning of the word *dhvani* is fivefold—[considering] by what, where, from what, whose, and for what—one can easily establish the appropriate grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by resorting to the sense of the *bahuvrīhi* compound.

In the case of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning [is subordinate], the term "expressed" (*vācya*) refers to its own nature; thus, the suggested meaning is called "one whose expressed meaning is not intended" (*avivakṣitavācya*) because its own nature is not intended—that is, it has been made non-primary.

This applies similarly to that where the expressed meaning is intended but not primary (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*). The general form of the relationship between the suggested and the suggester is common—that is, it is the same—such is the construction.

He states the purpose of the inclusion of the words "only" (*mātra*) and "specific" (*viśeṣa*) in the phrase "merely in that which is not well-known as a specific figure of speech" (*tadaprasiddhālaṅkāraviśeṣamātre*), with the words "by the inclusion of the word 'specific' (*viśeṣa-grahaṇena*)," and so forth.
The word "of the figure of speech" (*alaṅkārasya*) is to be supplied [as the object].
With the intention that the word *mātra* signifies a mere trace (*leśa*), he says: "the absence of being the primary element" (*aṅgitvābhāvam*).
The word "āha" (he says) is to be supplied [from the previous context].
He states it in another way: "tene vā" (or by that).
That is, by that sound as the agent.

One might object: "Is it not improper for the author of the *Vṛtti* to demonstrate the varieties of *dhvani* with the words 'And that' (*sa ca*) and so forth, without first resolving the position regarding its figurative nature (*bhāktatva*) which follows in the sequence? To this he replies: "When the examples are presented," and so on.

The meaning is: once the examples of *dhvani*—such as that where the expressed meaning is unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*)—have been shown, the doubt that "since indication (*lakṣaṇā*) emerges therein, *dhvani* is merely figurative" (*bhaktireva dhvaniḥ*) is easily raised;

however, because the distinctions between their respective forms and so forth, which establish their mutual difference, are clear, the resolution of that doubt is likewise easy. This is the intended sense.
"According to the restatement in the forthcoming *Uddyota*":

the meaning is that [the author] himself stands in the place of the author of the *kārikās*, for otherwise, the restatement in the second *Uddyota*—namely, "whether it be *anuktavācya* or *vivakṣitavācya*"—would be untenable.

Now, one might ask: among the five meanings of the word *dhvani*, with which meaning in mind is this grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed as "*dhvani* is *avivakṣitavācya*," and so forth? To this, he says: "Even in five ways," and so on.
In five ways, [it exists] in the nature of the signifier and so forth.

Among these, "signifier" refers to the word when, according to the position that the referent is sound (*dhvani*), it is not intended to be expressed; "by which word" refers to that by which the signified is expressed; "in which" refers to that particular word.
The term *yataḥ* means "from which word";

*yasmai* means "for the sake of which," i.e., as its purpose; and *yasya* means "of which," i.e., as its relation. It should be understood that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound [meaning] "that by which [these things are so designated]."

In this same way, it should be understood that even when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), the suggester (*vyañjaka*), and the poem (*kāvya*) function as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of a compound, the same applies.
Regarding the position that the word *dhvani* signifies the expressed meaning (*vācya*), he states the distinction: "in the expressed meaning" (*vācye 'rthe*).
[He then says] "its own self" (*svātma*).
It is said that [the subject] is twofold in general.
An example of the first is as follows: "Three kinds of men gather the gold-flowered earth:
the brave, the learned, and he who knows how to serve."

Or, in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound, [the term] *locana* may mean "that which is unintended (*avivakṣita*) and yet expressed (*vācya*)" or "that which is intended for another purpose (*vivakṣitānyapara*) and yet expressed (*vācya*). In that context, the literal meaning sometimes becomes unintended due to reasons such as its logical impossibility.
Since it is intended as "arising at some time," it brings about a cognition extending up to the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) through the power of its own inherent excellence;
for this very reason, the meaning (artha) here is the primary suggester (vyañjaka).
In the previous case, it was the word [that was the object].
But is it not a contradiction to say both "intention" (*vivakṣā*) and "being directed toward something else"?
