Rather, the meaning is that it is the "seed" because it is brought under the sway of *sahṛdayatva* (connoisseurship), which is synonymous with "resonance in the heart" (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*).
There is also a reading: "the seed is the life.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because," and so forth.
"In that" means:
when there is a sublation of the primary meaning.
Even though the capacity to denote its own referent is equal [in both cases], the word "smoke" comes to rest in its own primary referent.

In the expression "there is a bath in the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the fact that the primary meaning of the word "Gaṅgā" is sublated is precisely the reason [for its secondary usage]; the meaning is that this very sublation of the primary meaning is the seed of *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication).
If one were to argue, "In that case, here too there would be both sublation of the primary meaning and *lakṣaṇā*," he says "not so" (*na ca*).
He raises an objection regarding the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) with the words "But if this were so," and so forth.

The cognition of *rati* (love) and other such emotions, which arises immediately after the cognition of the *vibhāva* (excitants) and other factors, is exactly like the recollection of fire and so forth produced by the cognition of smoke and so forth; therefore, it is not produced by the operation (*vyāpāra*) of words, let alone being produced by *vyañjanā* (suggestion). This is the meaning. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The cognition of *rati* and so forth under dispute is not verbal (*śābdī*), because it is produced by a cognition of an object produced by words, just like the recollection of fire and so forth produced by a cognition of an object generated by the word 'smoke'."

What is it that you seek to prove here: that the cognition of mental states such as another's *rati* (erotic passion) is not produced by the operation of the word, or rather, that the cognition of *rasa* is so?
In the first case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

With the intention that, in the second case, the absence of an illustrative example constitutes a defect because the perception of rasa differs from the perception of other [objects], he asks with a touch of irony, beginning with "this" (*idam*), etc. He explains the question with "why," etc.
Regarding the word "here" (*atra*): [the following applies].
The meaning is "in poetry.
As for the phrase "and not":
the meaning is that such an error must not be committed.
To the question "Why?", he says: "For thus," and so forth.

This means that if the apprehension of worldly mental states and their fluctuations is accepted as being the very essence of rasa (rasatva), then the word "merely" (mātra) implies the remainder of the sentence: "the apprehension of rasa."
"What is 'rasanā'? The meaning is this: the linguistic usage of the word *rasa* is based on the quality of being relished (*rasanīyatā*).
And there is no such relishability in a cognition consisting of inference, because it is not observed in inferences of fire and so forth.
To the question, "What then is the perception of rasa?", he says: "But that which... and so forth.
By the term "extraordinary" (*alaukika*), the savoring of worldly pleasure is excluded. Showing the reason for its being extraordinary, he states its cause: "In poetry... and so forth.
"It is not that" means it is not the taste of the essence [of direct perception].
The connection is with the phrase "by way of the similarity between recollection and inference," which serves to exclude [the possibility of it being a form of perception].
"By the worldly" means that which exists in the world. "Effect" refers to smoke and so forth, which are the effects of fire and so forth.
The sidelong glances and so forth are [the effects] of mental states such as passion;
fire and so forth are the causes.
That inference of a cause from its effect, such as passion and so forth, [is the third type].
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is included.
By the phrase "one whose heart is refined" (*saṃskṛtahṛdaya*), it is shown that the refinement of the perceiver (*pratipattuḥ*) is also useful for the apprehension of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
[The term] "the excitants and so forth" (*vibhāvādikam*)...
The meaning is "women and so forth. The phrase "while experiencing" implies "from poetry or drama," as is the ellipsis.
"By way of neutrality" means by way of belonging to another.
The phrase "does not apprehend" is also to be connected with the term "the excitants and so forth."
If one asks, "How then does that pleasure [arise]? he says, "But rather... and so forth. Regarding the word "hṛdaye" (in the heart):

it means by virtue of being the very life-force of a relish (*carvaṇā*) suited for becoming identified with that [object], without having recourse to the path of inference, memory, and so on, through the budding of the savoring of rasa that is about to become full.
Furthermore, this savoring (carvaṇā) did not previously arise from any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such that it could now be a memory;
nor has it arisen at present from any other means of valid cognition whatsoever.

Because perception and the other means of knowledge do not operate regarding that which is non-worldly (*alaukika*), for this very reason the technical usage of *vibhāva* and so forth applies only to what is non-worldly.
As it has been said: "The term *vibhāva* is for the sake of specific cognition; in the world, only a cause (*kāraṇa*) is designated, not a *vibhāva*."
The *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) is likewise indeed extraordinary;
for it is said that "it is called *anubhāva* because it causes [the spectator] to experience (*anubhāvayati*) the representation (*abhinaya*) produced by speech, body, and spirit.
For this "experiencing" is nothing other than becoming one with (*tanmayībhavana*) those mental states.
In this context, however, "world" (loka) refers only to the effect (kārya) and not to the consequent emotion (anubhāva).

For this very reason, with the intention that the mental state belonging to another is not perceived, the term "stable emotion" (sthāyin) was not included in the aphorism: "The production of rasa results from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory emotions (vyabhicārin).
On the contrary, its inclusion would have been like a thorn [in the argument].
The transformation of the stable emotions (sthāyins) into aesthetic flavor (rasas) is said to occur through propriety (aucitya);

that is, by the force of "consonance with the heart" (hṛdayasaṃvāda)— which is "assent" (sammati)— meaning by being brought under the sway of that "sensitivity of the connoisseur" (sahṛdayatva), which is a synonym for it.

"Fullness" (pūrṇī) means by way of the sprouting cause of that tasting of flavor which is about to become full—the tasting of the *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree) that will bear fruit as proficiency in the means for attaining the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*).
"By inference" (*anumāna*)... [text continues].
The meaning is: "without depending upon" such means as inferential knowledge, memory, and so forth, beginning with the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

"Consisting of that" (*tanmayī*) means: it is appropriate for those who possess aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*) to undergo a state of identification (*tanmayībhavana*) with the various mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*); and the "enjoyment" (*carvaṇā*) which is suitable for that [identification]—referring by implication to the *vibhāvas* and so on—is because they constitute its life-force, that is, because they are instrumental to it.
The meaning is "by way of commonality.
The phrase "one apprehends the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth" is to be supplied.
It is clearly stated elsewhere that the savoring of rasa occurs precisely when the excitants and the rest are perceived as common [to all].
He refutes [the view] that [rasa] consists of memory and so forth with the words "And not," etc.

"For this very reason" means that because the apprehension of rasa is extraordinary (alaukika), the technical designations such as "determinant" (vibhāva) and so forth applied to its causes are also extraordinary.
Regarding the phrase "as he said":
the word "the Sage" (muni) is to be supplied.
"Vibhāva" means for the purpose of cognition.
The *vibhāva*— such as a beloved woman, a garden, and so forth— is that by which the permanent (*sthāyin*) and transitory (*vyabhicārin*) emotions are specifically cultivated and known.
The meaning is that the specific cognition of the mental state does not arise from the *anubhāvas* alone, because an *anubhāva* such as tears can possibly be produced by many different causes.
"World," and so forth.
The meaning is that in the world, regarding the causes of mental fluctuations, the conventional usage is simply "object" (*kāraṇa*) and not "dissolution" (*vibhāva*).
"That which this... [refers to this].
The grammatical connection is: "this is abhinaya" (acting).
Regarding the term "anubhāvayati" (makes one experience), the ellipsis is "the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva) and the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva)."
The phrase "it is called *anubhāva*" implies that it is stated immediately thereafter;

furthermore, it is stated in the *Rasagaṅgādhara* and other works that the various mental states (*cittavṛtti*) residing in the hearts of the sensitive spectators (*sāmājika*) are designated as *vibhāvas* and so forth by means of their being manifested (*vibhāvanā*) and so on.
Here, the author states—"that mental state"—to show that this experience is distinct from ordinary worldly experience.
The term "experience" (*anubhavana*) here does not mean merely the comprehension of another's mental state;

rather, it refers to the audience’s becoming one with those mental states—which consist of the permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) and so forth—by means of the cultivation of those respective mental states.
The meaning is that experience consists precisely in the awakening of one's own corresponding mental state through the contemplation of those [foreign] mental states.
He states the authoritative proof for the meaning already explained, beginning with "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
The meaning is: "for this very reason," because experience is of the nature just described and is not merely an inference of another's mental state; therefore, for that very cause.
[The phrase] "not another's" and so forth follows.
However, the meaning is that one's own mental state alone is experienced by the members of the audience.
Regarding the phrase "not performed":

in order to satisfy the expectation of "by whom," the commentary on the Sūtra states: "Because of the arising of a beautiful relish (carvaṇa) through the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the mental states appropriate to the transitory emotions (bhāva) and the consequent physical expressions (anubhāva)."

Furthermore, because in the state of knowing the mental fluctuations of others—which is useful for achieving resonance with the heart—one perceives the underlying permanent emotions (sthāyibhāva) such as love through signs like horripilation in a garden;

and because the transitory emotion (vyabhicārin), although being itself a mental fluctuation, is experienced only while remaining subordinate to the primary mental fluctuation, it is therefore counted among the excitants (vibhāva) and ensuants (anubhāva).
For this very reason, this alone constitutes the fulfillment of the state of being relished.

Because it takes the form of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*) through the subordination of worldly mental states— such as joy arising from causes like the reunion with kinsmen occurring in the course of a literary composition— it is here merely a manifestation (*abhivyañjana*),
not a cognition (*jñāpana*).
Nor is it a production,
like the operation of a cause.

The meaning is as follows: although it would have been necessary to include the term "sthāyin" (the permanent emotion) in the genitive case [as in *bālapriya-sthāyinaḥ*], that was not done because the cognition of the permanent emotion (*sthāyipratīti*) arises through the mention of the "anubhāva" (consequent emotion) alone.
He says "tat" and so forth to show that if the term "sthāyin" were included here, it would result in a contradiction.
That is the means for grasping the stable emotion (*sthāyin*).
Regarding the word "thorn" (*śalya*):
the meaning is that since aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) consists in the comprehension of another's mental state, it would produce an undesirable result by causing the realization of such a meaning.

[Objection: But if this is so, how can the statements of the authors of the Sūtras and others found here and there—that "the rasa is the permanent emotion" (sthāyī)—be consistent? To this he says: "But of the permanent [emotions]" (sthāyinas tu). This means: "but of the permanent emotions residing in the respective heroes and so forth. He clarifies this very propriety with the word "that" (tat).

The meaning is that when the excitants (*vibhāvas*) and ensuants (*anubhāvas*) belonging to that [permanent emotion] residing in another person give rise to a beautiful aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*) through the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the corresponding mental state within the soul of the sensitive spectator (*sahṛdaya*).

And it has been stated in the commentary on the *Kāvyānuśāsana*: "Appropriateness (*aucitya*), moreover, consists in the fact that those things well-known as causes and so forth, by virtue of being present in that permanent emotion, now serve as the basis for the status of excitants and so forth due to their utility for aesthetic relish. Furthermore, he states that there is another ground for designating the permanent emotion as "rasa" (aesthetic flavor): "in the heart," etc.

For the savoring of rasa is preceded by a resonance in the heart (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*), and the cause of this resonance is the thorough knowledge of the mental dispositions of the world, since such resonance does not arise for one devoid of that knowledge.

In that state, there occurs the comprehension of the stable emotion (*sthāyin*)— such as love (*rati*) and the like— through causes such as the presence of beautiful women and through effects such as horripilation, which have been repeatedly ascertained to be pervaded by their respective causes.
The meaning is "therefore.

Now, one might object: since there is no difference in their being mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*), the transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*)—just like the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*)—should not be included in the Sūtra. To this he says: "But the transitory... The meaning is that the transitory emotion is mentioned among them because, with respect to the permanent mental modification, it functions as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) and consists primarily of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
In connection with this, he explains the production of rasa as stated in the Sūtra, beginning with "ata eva" (for this very reason).
"This alone is the production of the state of being relished"—
this refers to the production mentioned in the Sūtra.
The meaning is that it is simply the perfection of the state of being relished (*rasyamānatā*).

As it is stated in the *Abhinavabhāratī*: "How then is 'perfection' [mentioned] in the Sūtra? This does not refer to the rasa itself, but rather to the aesthetic experience (*rasānubhūti*) which has that [rasa] as its object. If, through the perfection of that [experience], there is the perfection of the rasa whose life is entirely dependent upon it, then there is no fault whatsoever here."
To explain what this "being tasted" (rasyamānatā) actually is, he states its nature with the words beginning with "yat" (that which...).
Regarding the term "prabandha":

it refers to worldly mental states such as joy and so forth that arise from causes like the reunion with kinsmen when they proceed in a continuous sequence (*prabandhena*). By the subordination (*nyagbhāvena*), that is, by the suppression or exclusion of those [worldly states], [the aesthetic flavor is produced]. This is the meaning.
He states the essential nature of *carvaṇā* (relishing) with the words "ataśca" and so forth.
"Ataḥ" means because it is extraordinary (*alaukika*) due to its distinction from ordinary mental fluctuations (*laukikacittavṛtti*).
Here, *carvaṇā* refers to the relishing that has rasa as its object.
He shows what is excluded by the particle *eva* with the words "but not," and so forth.

Just as the function (*vyāpāra*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the sense organs, is making known (*jñapana*), or just as the function of [materials] such as a staff or a curved stick is production (*utpādana*), so too [is it for] the eye. Now, if this is neither a making known nor a production, [what then?]
What, then, is this?
This aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is not something supernatural.
Is it not the case that the excitants (*vibhāva*), and so forth, are here merely indicative causes (*jñāpaka-hetu*)?
Or is it a producer?
It is neither a communicator nor a producer;
rather, it is conducive to aesthetic relish (*carvaṇa*).
But has this not been seen elsewhere? Precisely because it has not been seen, it is said to be *alaukika* (extraordinary).
[Objection: In that case, rasa would be without a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Let it be so; what follows from that?
Since joy and proficiency are established through the very savoring (*carvaṇā*) of that [poetry], what else remains to be seen?
[Objection: But this is without a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). [Reply: No.
Because it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and because the specific nature of cognition itself consists in the act of relishing; enough with further elaboration.
And for this reason, this aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is transcendent (*alaukika*).

Since even *lalita* (elegant) and *paruṣa* (harsh) alliteration possesses suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) with respect to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), despite its lack of utility for the direct expression of the literal meaning,
how could there even be a suspicion of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) therein?
Indeed, the relish (*carvaṇā*) of that [flavor] is seen to occur solely through the intense pressing of the words that constitute poetry.
For that very poetry does not have the function of making known (*jñāpana*) or producing (*utpādana*) the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth; this is the meaning.
He raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*), etc.
By what was stated previously, this savoring of rasa (*rasacarvaṇā*) is not of the nature of cognition (*jñapti*).
Nor does it follow that it has the nature of accomplishment;
rather, the meaning is: "then what is its essential nature?
This refers to [the following].
The meaning is that it consists of the form of the savoring of rasa.
He states the answer with the words "But this," and so forth.
The point is that the incapacity [of rasa] for cognition or production is an ornament of rasa, because it is extraordinary (alaukika).

One might object: "If there is an absence of either being a causal factor (*kārakatva*) or being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*), then the employment of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth for the sake of the cognition of rasa would be useless;
yet if they do exist, rasa would not possess its transcendent nature. This objection is raised with the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely).
For in the worldly realm, there is a rule that a cause must be either a causal factor or an indicator.

With the intention that the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth are not useless because they serve the purpose of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*) even in their absence [in the actual world], he offers a rebuttal with the words "not indicative" (*na jñāpaka*), etc.
Against this, an objection is raised with "But surely" (*nanu*). He provides the resolution with "Because" (*yataḥ*).
He raises a further objection with "But surely" (nanu).
"In this way" (evam) means:
provided that rasa is supramundane (alaukika).
"The taste would be non-authoritative (apramāṇa)," meaning that if it were non-authoritative, it could not serve as a means for understanding how to attain the auspicious and avoid the inauspicious.
To the objection that even if it falls into the state of being non-authoritative, it might still perform its function, he says: "Let it be."
Regarding the phrase "joy and proficiency":
it means joy and proficiency;
or else, proficiency preceded by joy—the meaning is "for the sake of the accomplishment of that."
Now, one might object that if rasa is thus non-empirical (*alaukika*), there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it; hence the objection begins with "nanu. He answers: "No.

To the further doubt—"But since rasa is admitted to consist of a specific kind of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*), how can its establishment through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) even be possible?"—he says: "Of a particular kind of knowledge (*jñānaviśeṣasya*)."
As it has been stated in the *Abhinavabhāratī*: “Tasting (*rasanā*) is indeed of the nature of cognition,
but it is distinct from other forms of cognition, because its means— the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth— are unlike those found in the mundane world.”
He further establishes the extraordinary nature (*alaukikatva*) of rasa with the words "And therefore," and so forth.

For if rasa were cognizable solely through expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*), its worldly nature might somehow be suspected, as in the case of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*). However, even by means of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like—which are devoid of expressiveness—it is indeed a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyatva*). Moreover, no object suggested by alliteration has ever been observed in the world; thus, for this reason also, the extraordinary nature of rasa is established. This is the meaning.
Having thus established the transcendental nature (*alaukikatva*) of rasa, he says "What... and so forth, reconnecting with the subject at hand.
Therein, the meaning is that rasa is suggested even by alliteration (*anuprāsa*).
"What is indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?"— the meaning is that since even denotation (*abhidhā*) itself is absent, there is no possibility at all for indication, which follows upon it.

He provides experience as the proof for the fact that the very nature of the word, independent of the operation of denotation, manifests aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), beginning with the words "consisting of poetry" (*kāvyātmaka*).

The world of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya-loka*) is that which consists of poetry, distinguished by its resonance (*anuprāsa*) and so forth, while reading the *Locana* and experiencing it through relish (*carvaṇā*), rather than [merely] the poem itself;

for in that regard, according to the maxim "even those things which are taken up are to be abandoned," there is no further utility once the cognition has been produced. Thus, here even the word possesses the function of suggestion (*dhvanana-vyāpāra*).
For this very reason, there is the state of having no perceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama*).
As for what was said by someone that there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), that is due to ignorance.

For a treatise, once uttered, while establishing its meaning through the force of convention (*samaya*), how could it convey two meanings simultaneously, given that it is impossible for multiple contradictory conventions to be remembered at once?
Or, if they were not contradictory, there would simply be a single sentence-meaning. Furthermore, even sequentially, it is impossible for it to function with an intervening pause.
Even when the sentence is uttered again, it remains the same, because the context, convention, and so forth remain as they were.
If a word were to convey a different meaning by setting aside the meaning obtained through context and convention, that would result from its "squeezing," that is, its repetition.
The savoring of that [savor] is *rasacarvaṇā*.
He explains what was stated with the words "it is seen":
the meaning is that the very same poem which has been read and savored is again and again read and savored.
"But not," [it is said].
This refers to the word "kāvya" (poetry) when it has acquired its conventional meaning—
that is, in the context of the aesthetic relish (*rasacarvaṇā*) therein.
It is indeed non-utility, and not [the absence] of it;
the meaning is that utility certainly exists.
The principle beginning with "upetya" (having granted) is intended to demonstrate the reasoning for why something already established through cognition would otherwise be useless.
“Those things which are to be abandoned even by means of [certain] methods are declared to be methods;
for the restriction of methods does not necessarily remain fixed.”
The meaning is "by way of logic.
The intention is that this logic does not apply here.
He states the conclusion with the words beginning with "iti" and so forth.

He states that the previously mentioned quality of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)—namely, its lack of perceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama*)—is also an indicator for the point already explained, by saying "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
"For this very reason" means precisely because the nature of the word itself functions as a suggester (*vyañjaka*) without depending on the denotation of a meaning.
The underlying sense is that if the suggestiveness of a word were dependent solely upon the mediation of the cognition of a meaning, then a sequence would necessarily be perceived.
"There would be a split in the sentence" (vākyabhedaḥ syāt).
The sense is that this is because a poem conveys two meanings: the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya).
He provides justification for what was stated as "through ignorance of that" with the words beginning "the treatise" (śāstram), and so forth.

A treatise (*śāstra*) is a sentence distinct from poetry (*kāvya*). Regarding the term "convention" (*samaya*): it means by the power of the convention—that is, the linguistic agreement (*saṅketa*)—between specific words and their respective meanings; that is to say, by way of the assistance provided by the apprehension of those respective conventions.
"Establishing the meaning" contains the reason;
"simultaneously" means at one time; "contradictory" [is the predicate].

They are "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because they have contradictory objects as their domain; or rather, the meaning is that it is impossible—due to the impossibility of recollecting two conventions for two contradictory objects at the same time.
The sense is that when a particular object is present through context and so forth, it obstructs the recollection of the convention for the other object.
Two meanings constitute a contradiction;
how could it cause one to understand, that is, how could it bring about cognition?
[This would be impossible] unless there were non-contradiction.

The meaning is: "when there is a mutual relationship by virtue of being directly connected to a single action. The phrase "of two objects" (*arthadvayasya*) is to be supplied by transposition (*vipariṇāmena*).
An example of this is: “The white [horse] runs. (*śveto dhāvati*)
It should be understood that [the phrase] begins with "May Mādhava protect me at all times," and so forth.
Regarding the word *tāvān*:
it means "as much as is perceived."

The meaning is that there would be a single sentence-meaning, for no distinction is admitted within a sentence-meaning. Regarding the phrase "in succession," the ellipsis is: "How could a treatise convey two meanings [simultaneously]?"

In this regard, he states another reason: "having ceased" (*viramya*). The meaning is: because there is a connection with that operation of the word which occurs after having ceased [from its previous function], therefore [it is so].
"Sa eva" means that which is the meaning of the sentence as it has been understood;
the word "eva" (only/exactly) is used for emphasis.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "because of [the ambiguity of] the context of the ritual convention (*samaya*) and so forth.

The *Locana* explains: since there is an absence of restriction, it follows that regarding the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*," one might ask what proof there is that its meaning is not "one should eat dog-meat.
In that case as well, there would be no definitive limit, leading to a state of lack of confidence; thus, the splitting of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) is a defect.

In this case, however, since it is the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth themselves that, being presented, are oriented toward becoming the object of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*), there is no need for conventions and the like.
Nor is this comparable to the realization derived from a technical treatise, such as the thought, "I am enjoined here, I shall perform [the action]," or "I have accomplished my purpose."

In that case [of ordinary perception], because it is directed toward a future task, it is worldly; but here, due to the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, it arises as something whose essence exists only at that moment—like a wonderful flower—and is not connected to preceding or succeeding times. Thus, this aesthetic relish of rasa (*rasāsvāda*) is entirely different from both worldly enjoyment and the experience of yogis.

For this very reason, even in verses such as "O mountain-dweller" (*śikhariṇi*), if the reading were *samayādiḥ*, the meaning would be: "He by whom the matter was previously understood. This is the sense of the word *saḥ*.
In the phrase "convention and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes context and other such factors.
He states the reason for this: "of context and so forth.
This means "of context, convention, and the like."
Now, [the author] says "prakaraṇotthādi" etc., in response to the objection that there should be no dependence on convention (*samaya*) and so forth;
the word "of the treatise" (*śāstrasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Regarding the phrase "niyamābhāva iti": [it means] "because of the absence of a restrictive rule."
The meaning is that there would be no restriction regarding the comprehension of the meaning; by means of that absence of restriction, what is the valid cognition? What is the means of knowledge?

The phrase "it follows [this consequence]" means that if one accepts that a sentence conveys its meaning without depending on the conventional usage of specific words, the context, and so forth, then a sentence such as "agnihotram" (the fire-sacrifice) would result in being a prescription for eating dog meat.
Regarding the phrase "even there": [it refers to the same point].
The meaning is "even in another sense.
*Iyattā* means "establishment" (*vyavasthā*). There is also a reading *niyatatā*.
The word *iti* indicates the reason.
"Lack of confidence" (*anāśvāsatā*) means the state of not being informative due to the meaning being uncertain.
He concludes with the words "Thus, in this way," and so forth.

Ordinary worldly and Vedic sentences, distinct from poetic compositions, convey only a single meaning—whether simultaneously or sequentially—when assisted by convention (*samaya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth; therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the cognition of multiple meanings. If one were to admit that a sentence conveys meaning without depending on convention, context, and the like, it would lack authority because it would be non-cognitive (*abodhaka*) due to having an indeterminate meaning; thus, syntactical split is considered a defect.
The essential meaning:
he states the distinction regarding poetry with the words "But here," and so forth,
[concluding] with "only the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so on."
By the word "only" (eva), there is an exclusion of that which is suggested by taste (*rasa*) and so forth.
"Being communicated" (*pratipādyamāna*) means being made known by a poetic sentence assisted by convention, context, and so on.
"Carvaṇā" means the relishing of rasa and so forth. "Samaya," etc., [refers to the following].
The phrase "towards rasa and so forth" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

In poetry, convention, context, and other such factors are useful only for the comprehension of the meanings of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth; and following the comprehension of the excitants and so forth, there occurs the cognition of the specific suggested *rasa* and so forth, determined solely by those very excitants as the restrictive factors.

Therefore, the sense is that even if there is no dependence on convention (*samaya*) and so forth with respect to that [cognition], there is no fault of having an indeterminate object. He states "And not" (*na ca*) and so forth as a digression:
"In this action, I am enjoined during the state of cognition."
The cognition that "I shall do it" arises from the scripture at the time of performance, while the cognition that "I have accomplished my purpose" arises after that;
however, the cognition produced by poetry is not equal to that. This is the meaning.
To the question "Why?", he says: "In that regard," and so forth.
"In that regard" means in the cognition produced by the treatise. "The subsequent," etc.

The meaning is: with a focus on that which is to be done at a later time; however, in this case, regarding poetry (*kāvyam*), it is like a "wonderful flower" (*adbhutapuṣpa*), comparable to a flower produced by means such as sorcery (*indrajāla*).
"Arisen" means produced.
"Relish" (*rasapratīti*) is the savoring of the aesthetic flavor (*vibhāvādi*) and so forth.
That alone is [the rasa], which has its essence (*sāra*) precisely in that present time.
He states what is excluded by the word "only" (eva): "but not... [he says].
Now, one might object that the knowledge of a yogi is indeed different from worldly cognition; to this he replies: "the yogi... [and so on].
"Precisely for this reason... [he says].
Since that [metaphorical function] might serve as an indicator for some particular variety of suggestion (*dhvani*) consisting in the relish of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*),
it is indeed this *bhakti* (metaphorical function) which, among the various types to be described hereafter, serves as an indicator for one or another specific type;

for, even without depending on the sequence beginning with the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*), sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) perceive the speaker’s intention— consisting of flattery and affection— through the *locana* (the eye of poetic insight).

For this very reason, the author of the *Granthakāra* stated that there is an absence of *bhakti* (poetic function) in *dhvani* where the intended meaning is other than the literal (*anyaparavācya*), speaking in general terms.
We, however, have said this in order to convince the stubborn opponent: "Let there be *lakṣaṇā* (indication) here;
but what can you do, even if enraged, against that which is of imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama*)?"

But if it is not objected that in cases such as "asuvarṇapuṣpām" (the golden-flowered one), where the expressed meaning is unintended, the rest on the suggested meaning occurs even without depending on the causal complex of indication—namely, the sublation of the primary meaning and so forth—then enough with this prolixity;
he concludes: "Therefore, [it is] bhakti. // 18 //
Now, it may be argued: let it be that "sound" (*dhvani*) and "suggestion" (*bhakti*) are not one and the same form;
and let it be that "suggestion" is not the definition of sound.
However, it will serve as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Where there is *dhvani*, there is also *bhakti*; thus, *dhvani* is characterized by *bhakti*. However, this is not the case everywhere.
And what is established for the opponent by this much, or what is lost for us?
To this, he says: "Of someone," and so forth.
Now, devotion has indeed been described by the Citsukhas;

and by way of that illustration, [the author] speaks of *dhvani* as well. "Experiencing" means: from that very source, they experience such extraordinary excellence (*saubhāgya*) which is not shared by others. *Bālapriyā*: [The meaning is as stated]. "Experiencing" means: from that very source, they experience such extraordinary excellence (*saubhāgya*) which is not shared by others. *Bālapriyā*: [The meaning is as stated]. The meaning is that they know.
This is the intended sense of why it was explained in that manner at the outset.
Here, the author provides corroboration through his own words, beginning with "for this very reason," and so forth.
If it is asked, "In that case, why have you yourself explained [the text] by accepting the definition? he says: "By us, however...
and "the stubborn fool.
The meaning is: "one who is seized by the speech of the materialists (nāstika)."
The connection is with the words "thus it has been said.
Now, one might ask: "Tell me, whose anger is it? To this he says: "If, however... [referring to] "the resting upon the suggested meaning."
The sense is that even regarding a desired object, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) does not possess the power [to apply]. // 18 //

Now, in order to refute the position that [the word] is a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), he raises that doubt by first restating what has already occurred, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*) and ending with "suggestion is indicated by the word" (*bhaktyopalakṣito dhvaniḥ*).
To the question "How will it be an indicator?", he replies with "Where... (*yatra*) and so forth.
Just as a crow and the like are not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a house and such, [so too is the word].
Nor is it a definition;
rather, the meaning is that devotion, like the mere possibility [of a thing], serves as a cause for the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
He introduces the verse as a response to this with the words "Not yet," and so forth.
"Tāvat" signifies agreement;
"etad" means it is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The meaning is that it is universally accepted that a thing cannot be a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) in every case. And by the phrase "by this much":
the meaning is "merely by the fact that devotion is an indicator."
"Truṭitam" means broken or severed.
He introduces the passage beginning with "If [it were so]," etc., with the words "Now, [is it not so? and so forth. [The question is:
"What is the use of that definition?"

The meaning is that the formulation of a definition of *dhvani* is fruitless, because the result of a definition—which is the cognition of *dhvani* through its differentiation from other things—has already been accomplished by the very function of suggestion (*bhakti*), which serves as its indicator.
He explains the intended sense of the passage beginning with "that [is] denotation" (*tad-abhidhā*) and so forth, which constitutes the resolution, starting with "abhidhāna... and so forth. [He says:
"the relation between the denoter and the denoted."
The phrase "along with poetry" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And therefore...
[it] might be possible in the case of the denotative function (*abhidhāvṛtti*).

Furthermore, if it is asserted that *dhvani* is indicated solely through the function of secondary metaphorical indication (*guṇavṛtti*), then by means of the function of primary denotation (*abhidhā*), the entire class of other poetic figures would likewise be indicated; consequently, the composition of individual definitions for each figure would result in futility. Moreover, once the definition has been established by others, our own position is already proven. (Dhvanyāloka 1.19a)
And if its definition were formulated by others, for us there would simply be the establishment of our own position. (19)
Or even if the definition of *dhvani* has already been formulated by others, our position is already established;
for "that *dhvani* exists" is not our thesis (*pakṣa*).
Since that [existence] is already established, we have achieved our desired objective without effort. Thus ends the discussion.

Even those who have declared that the essence of *dhvani* is indeed inexpressible and to be experienced only by the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) are not thorough examiners of the matter; for they will perceive and come to know its entire variety of divisions. Anticipating the objection, "What is the use of a definition for that? he says: "If, however... (*yadi ca*).
For the relationship between the signifier and the signified is pervasive across all classes of poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
Consequently, once the function of denotation (*abhidhā*) has been established by the Grammarians and Mīmāṃsakas, what further role would remain for the authors of poetic ornaments?

Likewise, when logicians declare that "an effect arises through the power of its cause," what new contribution could there be for agents or knowers such as God? Thus, everything would become purposeless.
Thus he says: "the consequence of the futility of formulating a definition.

With the intention of asking, "Even if there were no discovery of what was previously unknown, and we have merely correctly determined what was already known, what fault would there be? he says: "Furthermore," and so forth.
"Much less," etc.;
the ellipsis is "from our effort.
Thus, [he refutes] the threefold doctrine of non-existence.
By one who rejects [the view] that devotion is included within [the other categories], its uncharacterizability (*alakṣaṇīyatva*) among those very [categories] has already been rejected.

For this very reason, no root verse (*mūlakārikā*) is heard that directly aims at its rejection. However, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*), for the sake of completing the bed of objects of knowledge (*prameyaśayyāpūraṇāya*), explicitly [rejects it] regarding the operation of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāre*). This is [the position of] Bālapriyā.
"Of the authors of treatises on ornamentation" means "of the authors of works on poetics. [The question] "What is their function now? refers to this.

and since that [refutation] is not possible if *dhvani* were indefinable, the position that it is indefinable is also refuted as being inseparable from the refutation of those alternatives.

Regarding the phrase "the bed of the object of cognition" (*prameyaśayyā*): it refers to a specific arrangement or configuration of the object of cognition. For, according to the principles already stated and those yet to be stated, even if the general and particular characteristics of *dhvani* have been established, if its ineffability were [admitted], then that [ineffability] would necessarily follow for all things whatsoever.

If, however, by this hyperbolic statement regarding sound (*dhvani*), [the author] intends that [poetry] surpasses other types of poetry through those [qualities], he refutes that position by restating it with the words "Those who also... and so forth.
By the method already stated, the general definition—"wherein the meaning or the word..."—has been established.
But by the method to be stated later, the specific definitions will follow, beginning with "transferred into another meaning" (*arthāntare saṅkramitam*) and so on.
In that regard, in the first chapter (uddyota), the author of the verses (kārikākāra) established only the general definition of *dhvani*.

In the second chapter, while providing a subordinate classification and the specific definitions, the author of the verses stated by way of restatement the fundamental division as "of two kinds," namely "of all."
The meaning is: "of both worldly and scriptural [works].

Without the eye, does light shine even by moonlight?

Thus ends the first chapter in the *Dhvani-saṅketa*, titled *Sahṛdayāloka-locana*, illuminated by the illustrious and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Abhinavagupta.
